en: Preface to the *Xianju bian* (Collection of Works on Leisurely Dwelling), composed by Wu Zunlu, *Xuande Lang*, Acting Vice Director of the Court of Judicial Review (*Dali si cheng*), and Supervisor of the Qingzhou Liquor Administration in Hangzhou.

The five colors manifest in harmony; thus, the fiery dragon, the *fu* and *fu* patterns, illuminate their forms. The eight musical instruments sing in alternation; thus, the *ying*, *jing*, *huo*, and *wu* melodies resound.
The martial leads its harmony, and speech is embellished by the literary; it is just like this. Why is this so? When the will has a direction, words arise from it;
words cannot be treated with contempt, and thus they take form through literature. However, as cultural trends declined and decayed, people became negligent and failed to reflect;

consequently, the literary style exceeded the substance, and the principle did not overcome the rhetoric. Thus, some incurred the ridicule of being like a decorative sash or handkerchief, while others gave rise to the frivolities of Zheng.

In the case of Wei’s expositions, which employ analogies and draw connections between categories, there are still instances where he errs; yet when it comes to probing the hidden and fathoming the profound, what could possibly serve as a standard for comparison?

To be substantial without being crude, refined without being flowery, to expound the True Doctrine, open the doors and windows of the Sage, propagate the Name and Teaching, and provide a model for those who come after—this is precisely what is seen in the writings of the Venerable Master Yuan. [End of Excerpt]
In human terms, his surname was Xu, his given name Zhìyuán, and his courtesy name Wúwài; he styled himself Zhōngyōngzǐ (The Master of the Mean) and was a native of Qiántáng.
At the age of eight, he received full ordination at Lóngxīng Monastery in his home prefecture. At twenty-one, he transmitted the Three Contemplations of Tiantai from the Dharma Master Yuánqīng.
His spiritual countenance was clear and serene, the resonance of his Way was concentrated and pure, and his virtue permeated both the hidden and the manifest realms of learning.

Whether opening scrolls to roam the eyes within or without, one must trace the waves back to their source; in composing writings and crafting phrases, one invariably exhorts toward the good and punishes evil.
There is no conduct to be heard that is not worthy of selection, nor any book viewed that is not from the Sages.

One cultivates benevolence through self-mastery, never failing for even a single meal’s duration, and cherishes the study of the Way without neglecting a single moment of time. Looking up to the High Mountains, one warms oneself like [the sun] upon them.

Jade possessed an innate nature that delighted in goodness, a quality he had received from his celestial endowment; in his prime, he was able to compose literature not through the instruction of a teacher.

He especially favored stillness and silence, devoting himself exclusively to a life of reclusion. He cast aside worldly excursions and shut out human affairs, dwelling contentedly in a chamber of only ten feet square.
Reclining upon a low stool, he would leisurely peruse a single scroll of a book; immersed in deep contemplation, he was so absorbed that he was unaware of the distinction between self and others.
As for its distinction: wherever the wind of the Way blew, scholars returned as if to their own homes; scrolls and volumes filled the gates, and monks and nuns crowded the corridors.
Upon briefly hearing his discourse on the succession of teachers, doubts were instantly dispelled; by perfecting the ritual of receiving the texts, all became vessels of the Dharma.

Like the ringing of a bell, the response was virtuous, like an echo in a valley; they forgot their fatigue. This, moreover, was a supreme condition for benefiting sentient beings, and the ultimate human capacity for instruction.

If one were to examine his devotion to the Precious Vehicle (*ratnayāna*) and his mastery of the secret scriptures, he elucidated the bequeathed intent of the "single sound" and expanded upon the true meaning of the "four hooves.
He raised the sun of wisdom to radiate light and brought forth the Great Matter (*mahā-vastu*). He unfurled the clouds of compassion to spread moisture, sheltering and nourishing all quarters;

he bestowed enduring benefits, filling libraries with volumes of texts. His studies extended beyond these to encompass the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, as well as the Confucian and Mohist traditions. To such an extent...

In his scholarly compositions, he followed many established models; his poetic verses moved the spirit and floated with refined elegance. He never gave a moment’s thought to minor writings or short notes;
even his casual remarks and spontaneous expressions possessed a marvelous charm. Having suffered from chronic illness since early in life, the Master often remained exhausted;

lying upon his couch, he seldom applied himself to the refinement of his pen. When disciples presented him with a writing tablet, he would frequently dictate orally, resulting in a disordered arrangement of phrases and clauses.

Synthesizing literary forms and prosodic laws, they resound with a spontaneous perfection that requires no further editing or refinement. For one who analyzes principles, when the intention is profound, the principle excels;
for one who proclaims principles, when the principle is lofty, the expression triumphs.

Thus, by prioritizing the root over the branches and selecting the substantial while discarding the ornamental, the "Great Soup" remains unseasoned yet its flavor endures, and the "Great Jade Tablet" remains uncarved yet its natural quality is revealed. How could this compare to...?
To compare the final echoes of a dog’s barking with the elaborate carvings of intricate patterns—how could they possibly be judged for their merit?

Beginning from the Bingwu year of the Jingde era and ending in the Xinyou year of the Tianxi era, I have collected his writings, totaling sixty fascicles, titled the *Xianju bian* (Collection of Leisurely Dwelling).

As he applied his ceaselessly active thoughts to produce this work, I, who am but a humble connoisseur, joyfully anticipate that those capable of appreciating true melody will surely listen with discernment.

Those whose hearing surpasses this, I request, shall wait for future generations. As for the sutras, śāstras, commentaries, sub-commentaries, topical outlines, and annotations, as well as various works on external studies that have been compiled into independent collections, totaling one hundred and seventy fascicles, these shall all circulate separately and are not included in this present collection.
Preface to the *Zhongyongzi* (The Master of the Mean), by the monk Zhìyuán of Qiāntáng, styled Wúwài. Aside from lecturing on Buddhist scriptures, he was fond of reading... [the rest of the text].

In the writings of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Yangzi, and Mencius, there are frequent instances where they studied the archaic script (*guwen*) to honor their Way, and also delighted in composing pentasyllabic and heptasyllabic verse to express their inner nature and temperament.
Whatever they obtained, they would immediately cast the drafts into a worn-out bag;
they never transcribed a single clean copy, as children quickly used them for the cost of grease and candles. Thus, much of their work has been lost.
This summer, while recuperating from illness at the foot of Mount Gu, I had my junior disciples transcribe what remained of my writings.
Should I later acquire further insights, I intend to compile them accordingly as well. This is not for the sake of seeking renown in this age, but rather simply to follow my own inclinations.

Two Poems Written at Gushan Expressing My Feelings in My Study During Late Autumn, Sent to Master Shou-neng Presented to the Poetic Monk Bao-xian Presented to Zhao Pu I dwell alone on this solitary mountain, My heart weary from the world’s toil. The autumn evening deepens its chill; The moonlight shines upon my window. The myriad phenomena are empty and still, Yet the mind remains restless and unsettled. I long for a companion in the Way, To share these thoughts with me. The year is fading, the days grow short; The wind blows cold through the pines. The lamp flickers in the night’s quiet, Its light illuminating the room. I sit alone, reflecting on the past, My spirit wandering through the void. I send these words to my friend, Hoping he will understand my heart. The autumn sky is vast and clear, The mountain peaks are steep and high. The clouds drift slowly across the valley, The water flows silently by. I gaze out at the distant horizon, My thoughts reaching toward the heavens. I wish to find a fellow traveler, One who shares my love for the Way. The world is filled with turmoil and strife, The path of truth is obscured by dust. I seek a sage to guide me, One who can dispel my doubts. May we meet again in the future, To discuss the mysteries of the Dharma. The autumn wind is sharp and biting, The mountain air is cool and crisp. I write these verses in my study, To express my innermost feelings. May they reach my dear friend, And bring him peace and joy. The autumn moon is bright and full, The mountain streams flow clear and pure. I sit in silence, contemplating the Way, My mind free from all attachments. I send these words to the monk Bao-xian, Hoping he will appreciate my intent. Spontaneous Verses on the Night-Blooming Tree; Written While Ill, Inspired by the Visit of the Venerable Tiyuan, Who Brought Me the Commentary on the *Ruiying Jing* and the Annotated *Yinfu Jing*, Sent to the Venerable Tiyuan; Self-Deprecation upon Rising from Sickness; Four Spontaneous Quatrains (with Preface). [Preface] The night-blooming tree (*nyehé shù*) is a species of the *shānzhū* (Michelia) family. Its flowers open at dusk and close at dawn. It is said that when the Buddha entered nirvana, he manifested as this tree. I have long admired its fragrance and beauty, yet I had never seen it in person. This spring, while convalescing from illness, I happened to see one growing in the garden of the Venerable Tiyuan. It was in full bloom, and its fragrance permeated the air. I felt deeply moved and composed these four quatrains.

Furthermore, the Venerable Tiyuan has recently presented me with the *Ruiying Jing Shu* (Commentary on the Sutra of Auspicious Responses) and his own annotations on the *Yinfu Jing* (Scripture of the Hidden Talisman), both of which are profound and subtle works. I am deeply grateful for this gift. Thus, I have appended these verses to express my appreciation and to record the occasion of our meeting. **Quatrains:** 1. **On the Night-Blooming Tree:** The night-blooming tree stands tall in the courtyard, Its fragrance fills the air, pure and sweet. When the moon rises, its petals unfold; At dawn’s first light, they fold away. I have long heard of its wondrous scent, But never before beheld it in person. Today, by chance, I encounter it here, And feel a deep sense of wonder and joy. 2. **To the Venerable Tiyuan:** You have brought me the *Ruiying Jing Shu*, A work of profound and subtle meaning. Also, the annotated *Yinfu Jing*, Its words concise, its principles vast. Your dedication to the Dharma is truly rare; I am deeply moved by your kindness. May you long enjoy good health, To continue propagating the True Teaching. 3. **Self-Deprecation upon Rising from Sickness:** Lying ill for many days, I have been idle; My body and mind were weary and dull. Now that I have risen from my bed, I look back and feel ashamed of myself.

My former vigor is now but a memory; My old ambitions have all faded away. Yet, though I am but a humble monk, I still wish to seek the Way of the Buddhas. 4. **Spontaneous Verse:** The world is filled with suffering and turmoil; Only the Dharma can bring true peace. I pray that you, O Venerable One, Will always remain steadfast in your practice. May we meet again in the future, To discuss the mysteries of the scriptures. For now, I bid you farewell, With these few lines of verse. [End of Preface and Quatrains]

Now, the principle of awakening is perfectly clear and profound, utterly devoid of subject and object; it is truly refined and tranquil, so how could there be delusion or enlightenment? Yet, subsequently, like a bubble...
Born from the great ocean of clouds, one dots the vast expanse of the early morning; gazing into a mirror, one fears having lost one's head and flees in terror;

with cataracts in the eyes, flowers appear, and one stands waiting for them to bear fruit. Alas! Once the deluded mind of a single thought moves, the illusory scenes of the nine realms suddenly manifest.
Birth and death are like a loom, entering and exiting as cause and effect interweave to rise and perish; thus, one falls of one’s own accord into the mire.
How deeply pitiable are these myriad creatures! How can one fully express the magnitude of this? Our Great Holy Honored One dwells in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and is able to establish the Great Purpose.
By the power of his benevolence and compassion, he perceives such matters as these;

thus, though formless, he manifests forms like a dragon soaring in the sky of the Dharma, and though unspeakable, he speaks until his words fill the entire Dharma-realm. Thus, through the eight phases of manifestation, he achieves Buddhahood.

In ancient times, when the Lord Śākyamuni ruled over India, he manifested formlessness through forms and spoke wordlessness through words, thereby restoring the nature of all sentient beings;
from this, Buddhism arose. The high or low nature of its teachings corresponds to the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties;
thus, there are both the sudden and the gradual approaches, which subsequently merge into one, which is called "opening and revealing" for the sake of the common folk.
When the multitudes lead their transformation and restore their nature, treading upon the Great Way and abiding in the Secret Treasury, how can they be fully described?
Reaching the Later Han dynasty, the Way was transmitted to the East; the sovereign of the time looked up to its divine origin, and the common people were molded by its teachings.
Thus, it stood as one of the three alongside the teachings of Zhongni (Confucius) and Boyang (Laozi). To examine the teachings of Zhongni, he extolled the Tang [dynasty].
The Way of the Three Kings of Yu honored benevolence and esteemed righteousness, thereby restoring the state to that of a true King and aspiring toward the status of a Sovereign (Di).

The teachings of Boyang extolled the simple and unadorned Way of the Three Augusts (Huang), advocating the abandonment of sagehood and the casting away of wisdom, thereby restoring the state to that of an August One and aspiring toward the era of knotted cords.
Yet, even these two approaches, when discussing the nature of life and destiny, have not reached the ultimate limit.
If one speaks of retribution within the context of Mind-Only, one has not yet reached the three periods of time;
nevertheless, for governing the world and securing the state, it cannot be dispensed with for even a single day. How magnificent!
Its status as a teaching within the realm is clear. As for the instructions of the Śākya [Buddha], they point to the entirety of the void-like worlds.
That my own mind is not merely saying that the Great Ultimate gives birth to the two polarities and that the Mysterious Female is the root of Heaven and Earth;

it is also examining how good and evil are meted out through retribution, which is entirely my own karma, rather than merely saying that the Supreme Lord is impartial and the heavenly net is vast and wide.
In this way, one can see the presence of Confucianism and Daoism within it; though it is all-encompassing and complete, it reaches even further.
Regarding those who rescue their spirits and investigate the ultimate principles, I have merely indicated the general direction;
as for fully elucidating their subtlety, this resides in the teachings of the Śākya clan. Furthermore, it is already clear that these are a teaching from beyond the realm.
Within the realm, one governs the body, which is called the "outer teaching"; beyond the realm, one governs the mind, which is called the "inner teaching."
In the past, Ruan Xiaoxu correctly held that the distinction between the "internal" and "external" was not unfounded.
Therefore, those of our generation who claim that the three teachings are identical have nearly missed the mark; yet those who claim they are vastly different have likewise not grasped the truth.
Why is this? Because there are varying depths in the restoration of human nature and varying distances in the scope of what is discussed, one cannot help but find them to be distinct.
As for the transformation toward goodness and the distancing from evil, the overcoming of cruelty and the abandonment of killing—these cannot but be shared [by all].

The Sutra in Forty-two Sections is likely a collection of essential sayings from among the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings, compiled by sages and worthies of that land after our Buddha’s parinirvana, intended to instruct the world with urgency;
it consists of forty-two sections in total, which were gathered and recorded as such.
Regarding this sutra: in the distant past, when Dharmaratna and Kumārajīva arrived from the land of Brahmā, they first transmitted its true transformation to the people of China;
yet, as some had not yet placed deep faith in it, they translated these texts to enlighten them, thereby establishing the source of the broad dissemination of the teachings.
As for me, Yuan, I have long been inwardly devoted to the Ultimate Way. I have often lamented that although this sutra was the very first to be transmitted here, [it has remained obscure].
Since this work is ancient and lacks explanatory commentaries, later generations have had no means of hearing its meaning; is this not nearly a forgetting of one's roots?

I have therefore composed these annotations to expound its essential purport, hoping thereby to propagate the true spirit of our Buddha and assist in the benevolent transformation of our sovereign, so that the common people may ascend to the realm of longevity and tread the path of awakening.
Preface to the *Sūtra on the Universal Entry into the Inconceivable Dharma-Gate*:

In the past, our Heaven-Between-Heavens (the Buddha), like a dragon soaring or a tiger transforming, emerged preeminent among all things. He reverently remained silent while contemplating the Way, yet he realized clearly that there was nothing to be attained.

Thereafter, he looked down and observed the various species of beings: their nature is one with his own, yet their emotions differ from his. For this reason, they flow through the cycle of birth and death.
Yet they forget to return to their source, clinging to false illusions and refusing to let them go; thus, within that which is nameless and signless, they create names and signs to speak of it.
If one could simply restore their original nature, what would these names and signs amount to?
It is like grasping an empty fist to deceive and entice a child; once the child’s wailing has ceased, one opens the fist and extends the hand—what then remains?

Is it not the case that these twelve divisions of the scriptures and eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma are merely the sages grasping empty fists to deceive and entice the infantile among deluded followers?
Thus, while the Way has no distinction of superior or inferior, its expressions may be difficult or easy.
If the expressions are simple and the meanings are clear, it will enable people like you to follow the words, find the gate, and enter.
Those who wait for the day’s end may find therein the *Sūtra on the Universal Entry into the Inconceivable Dharma Gate*.
Examining the samādhi gates listed in this sūtra, there are actually twenty-eight; yet if one were to extend this by analogy, they would exceed all measure and calculation.
How magnificent! The realm of the Tathāgata cannot be reached by walking step by step; it is the most profound dharma.
Is it not stated in this very text that patience is attained without waiting for something to be grasped? This sutra is the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa*.

Preface to the Commentary on the Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra:
Now, the true nature is fundamentally quiescent; how could a single dharma exist therein? When the deluded mind stirs in secret, the myriad objects of perception arise.

Thus, suffering and pleasure fluctuate as one clings firmly to acceptance and rejection; the distinction between the ordinary and the sagely becomes heavy with the weight of what is abandoned and what is pursued, as they seek only escape from the world.

Conversely, this leads to falling into ruin; thus, some are submerged in the realm of ordinary beings, some sink into the Lesser Vehicle, and some are stalled in partiality—how can the nine realms be fully described?
The Great Sage surveyed them from above and took pity on them, intending to point toward that deluded mind so as to restore it to its true nature.
Thereupon, he expounded the teaching of universal emptiness and non-abiding, ruthlessly slaughtering the various delusions and causing the great capacity for awakening to flourish.
It is through this that the two vehicles attain a mind of unimpeded ease, and it is here that Bodhisattvas realize their unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

Is there anyone who rectifies the heterodox, preserves sincerity, enlightens all beings, and accomplishes great tasks who does not proceed by this path? Is the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* not of this same category?
Moreover, when the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) poses the inquiry below and Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) offers the response above, the phrasing is meticulous and the underlying intent profound.
When the sun of simple wisdom rises, the great night dawns; when the sword of insight is brandished, the web of delusion is rent asunder.

The merit of the Tathāgata’s correct contemplation and benefit for beings is now manifest, while the wisdom that does not retreat from the realm of evil conduct is further revealed. Alas, that this Dharma gate has not been transmitted to this degenerate age!
Though I, though unworthy, have received the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*), I am a follower of the One-Nature school of Nāgārjuna and the lineage of Zhiyi.

Having attained a shallow understanding of the profound essence and a rough grasp of the refined meaning of the Three Contemplations, I have relied upon this preeminent school to comment on this profound scripture.

As for the title of this sutra, it is named after its person and its dharma; its substance is that both the phenomenal and the noumenal are like illusions, and that both sentient beings and Buddhas are identical to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Its principle is the contemplative observation through which all discrimination is extinguished. Its function is the removal of attachments, wherein there is nothing to be removed. It is great.

When the vehicle is taken as the teaching, the Great [Vehicle] loses its great characteristics; by relying on emptiness, one perceives only awakening, like entering the sea and seeing only a single expanse of level water.
Who would say that the three periods of time—past, present, and future—come and go? How could one speak of the high and low of the ten realms?
To equate bodhi with non-action and to blend all Buddhas with sentient beings; to have no seeking for nirvana and yet realize nirvana swiftly; to [be free from] birth and death...
By relinquishing [attachments], one distances oneself from the cycle of birth and death; this is like finding a pearl where there was no phantom, rather than grasping at pebbles in a spring pond.
It is ordinary enough to be transformative, yet sublime enough to serve as a ladder.

Thus, through the *Ekakṣaṇa-samādhi*, cultivation is revealed as non-cultivation, and the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*) is manifested as non-attainment yet attainment. In this way, conventional designations are not destroyed, nor is annihilationism asserted.

Preface to the Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā:

Now, the Ultimate Way is nameless; yet without names, there would be no means to expound that Way. True Emptiness is beyond speech; yet without speech, there would be no means to recognize that Emptiness.

Thus, names are applied to the nameless and speech is employed for the unspeakable. Since the capacities of sentient beings are divided into the categories of sharp and dull, [the teachings have been established accordingly].
Therefore, the teachings possess the distinction of being detailed or concise; this is like variously binding snares and traps—the intent is the same: to obtain the fish and the hare.

Yuan has read this commentary three times; he has probed its profound principles, deeply investigated its practices, and exhausted his thoughts upon its teachings.
Thus, he was able to perceive that its phrasing is concise yet elegant, its principles subtle yet far-reaching, and its practices solely focused on awakening the mind.

The teachings consist solely of the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] sūtras, which exhaustively reveal the principle of transcending the reception of worldly rewards and fully elucidate the origins of the Sage Lord’s parinirvāṇa.

The great meaning of this single scripture is as clear as pointing at one's own palm; such is the essence of this commentary. Can it not be called the pivotal key to awakening and the path for entering the Way?

Among scholars, those who have appeared from generation to generation have not been lacking; yet, those who have studied and lectured upon this sutra are few, and those who have composed commentaries to extol it are unheard of.
Consequently, its profound phrasing and abstruse meanings are nearly on the verge of falling into oblivion—a matter for great lamentation.

Thus, I, Yuan, disregarding my own ignorance and dullness, have ventured to undertake the task of editing and refining the text. Where the sutra contains passages that were not clearly divided, and where the commentary lacks explanation, I have provided them.
The meanings have all been distinguished and categorized; by extending these principles, I ensure that the exposition of the meaning remains unobstructed.
Therefore, I have titled my work the *Yanyi Chao* (Commentary on the Explication). While it is certainly unable to fully manifest the ultimate truth, I hope it may serve to enlighten the ignorant.
Should there be anything I do not know, I await future sages; may those who see and practice with me understand my intent. At this time, the third year of the Huangsong...

Now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, upon which gateway should practitioners rely for cultivation and realization in order to attain the goal of Bodhi? He replied: "Although the sutras are indeed..."
Although the gateways of the various teachings differ, they are all for those of sharp faculties who attained awakening during the Buddha’s lifetime.
Since his parinirvāṇa, the intention of the Sage has had a single point of return: one must rely upon the verbal teachings to contemplate and practice them, so as to be able to reach Bodhi.

Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* serves as the vanguard for the final entrustment and the precursor to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; it is for this reason that it employs Ānanda to initiate the request for instruction.
After the practice-gates were established, the Tathāgata commanded the twenty-five sages to each discourse on what they had realized, and he had Mañjuśrī evaluate their merits and shortcomings;
yet he ranked Avalokiteśvara as the foremost.

Is this not because Avalokiteśvara awakened to the Way through the faculty of hearing, taking the object of sound as his basis for the teaching, and through reflection and cultivation reached the state of non-arising? Therefore it is said: "From hearing and reflection..."

When practicing to enter samādhi, one should know that all the gateways of practice taught in the various sūtras are entirely contained within the gateway of Avalokiteśvara, for they all rely upon the teachings.
Therefore, when reaching nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata repeatedly and earnestly exhorted and instructed that nirvāṇa can be attained by relying on four dharmas.
What are these four dharmas? First, drawing near to virtuous friends; second...
"Listening to the True Dharma, reflecting on its meaning three times, and practicing according to the teachings—this is it. Someone said:

One should seek this meaning for oneself to understand how the Gate of Avalokiteśvara universally encompasses all.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions share a single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. This is because it takes in all the ten directions to their ultimate limit.

It was there that the Great Master Jingxi took the doctrinal meanings of the *Mysterious Teachings* and integrated them into the contemplative mind of the *Stop-and-Contemplate* (*Zhiguan*) practice, so that practitioners at the stage of names might recognize that the characteristics of phenomena have a point of return and attain mastery in cultivation.

Zhiyi attained awakening through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Zhiyi first attained awakening through the *Lotus Sutra*), and thus he expanded the school of Nāgamitra and expounded the scriptures of Vulture Peak; therein, the school was divided into three distinct branches.

The wings of the teachings and practices unfold and mutually reflect one another to form a grand design. What is called the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) explains the titles [of the sutras] only to discuss the intent of transformation;

the *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) comments on the scriptures merely to analyze the literal meaning of the words. It is only upon reaching the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) that the methods of practice are discussed.

Thus, the teaching resides in the *Xuanyu* (Profound Text), while the practice resides in the *Zhiguan*. The intention is to let understanding and practice support each other to perfect one's own mind; for this reason:

The three divisions (sanbu) require one another; it is impossible for even one to be lacking. Yet, in this final age, while those who can speak [of the teachings] are numerous, those who realize the principle (ri) are especially rare.

Therefore, within the practice gate (gyōmon), he diligently points them out. Thus, when the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) concludes its explanation of the ten wonders (jūmyō) of the Trace Gate, it then defines "opening" (kai) in terms of realizing the principle.
Consequently, the essentials for realizing the principle must lie in the Ten Vehicles (jūjō); thus says the Great Master Jingxi.

Fearing that later generations might obscure the essential meaning, the Master further established ten gates within the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) to conclude the Ten Wondrousnesses (*shimiao*), so that they would all converge upon the inconceivable realm of the three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment (*yinian sanqian*) within *zhi-guan* (calm abiding and insight).
Only then is it revealed that the teaching was not established in vain, for there is a sequential path to awakening the principle.

Thus he said: "Therefore, I have extracted the Ten Wondrousnesses as the fundamental framework of the contemplative method," and further: "When both [the principle and the practice] are clearly manifest, this is the practice of the *Lotus Sūtra*."
Zhi Cheng further stated: "Therefore, I have restated these ten gates so that contemplative practice may be understood. Thus, one knows that all is subsumed within the mind and its objects;
by pointing out the gates of contemplation, one ensures that the methods of practice are not forgotten even in moments of haste or distress. This is the essential intent behind Jingxi’s composition.

What our school discusses is that the deluded mind of a single kṣaṇa is itself the principle of the Three Truths, fully endowed with the three thousand phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants."

This point was only indicated at the very beginning of the section on the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, yet it has never been explicitly pointed out in other texts.
This is because *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are teachings concerning the ultimate practice of one’s own mind; therefore, they both take the Three Thousand Worlds as their guiding compass.
Thus we know that there are no phenomena within the three realms, but these are created solely by the mind. Just as a painter creates the five aggregates, form arises from the mind.

My hope is that these may be shown to my descendants; how could I dare present them to those of profound learning? At this time, [I am] thirty years of age.
In the second month of spring in that ninth year, at the ordination hall of Chongfu Temple in Qiantang, he compiled the *Diannianji* (Chronicle of Imperial Reigns).
Regarding the person known as Luzhangzi, his clan, surname, and given name remain unknown; he once composed one scroll of the *Diannianji*.
From the opening of heaven and earth down to our Song dynasty, this work briefly records the names and titles of all one hundred kings throughout the succession of abdication and succession,
the orthodox lineages of the five phases in their mutual generation, the locations of capitals, the designations of regnal years,
and even those who were usurpers, pretenders, or regional hegemonists; thus, the traces of ten thousand ages need not await a broad perusal of the various histories.

Everything is clearly visible as if one were looking at the palm of one's hand. Furthermore, regarding the titles of emperors, those of the legitimate line are recorded in vermilion, while those who usurped or were false are recorded in black;
this serves to distinguish the crooked from the straight and to manifest praise and censure.
Is this not intended to provide a warning for posterity, so that they may know their respective ranks in heaven and be deterred from seeking to usurp them?
Is this not a concern? It is surely intended to rectify the great essentials of human relations, rather than merely recording dates and eras.
Having read his writings and understood his underlying intent, I have therefore composed this preface.
Postscript to Wang Pi Rixiu’s *Fayan* (Words of the Law):
The *Fayan* as a book is vast and all-encompassing; the Way of the Two Emperors, the Three Kings, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius is entirely contained herein.
Is it not the model for a hundred kings? Is it not the divining stalk and the tortoise shell for ten thousand generations? Since the time of Mencius...

Among those who have upheld the Holy Way with such vigor, none has equaled Master Ziyun (Yang Xiong). Now, as for the sages and those who followed them—whether in speech or in conduct—is it not difficult to remain entirely free of flaw?
For this reason, although Yang Xiong was a man of virtue, he made flattering remarks regarding Wang Mang. As stated in the "Chapter on Filial Piety":
"Since the time of the Duke of Zhou, there has been no one as illustrious as the Duke of Han; in terms of diligent toil, he surpassed even the Ministers Ai and Heng. Li [Shao]... [text fragment].
Taking the *Guǐ* as a standard, consider the "Beautification of Qin" and the "Beautification of the New" written before Wang Mang’s assumption of regency.

In these texts, it is said that the "Great New One" received the mandate from the Supreme Deity; could this have been the case before his assumption of regency? Liu Zongyuan remarked that the conduct of the Duke of Heng must not be emulated, for if one encounters such circumstances, the result will be the opposite.
Furthermore, when Mencius praised the Master as being far superior to Yao and Shun, he was likewise implicitly criticizing Zhongzi.
If it were not so, how could one say that the fault lay with the Duke of Ai? Is this not a reversal of the truth?

Thus we know that Yangzi praised Wang Mang by comparing his virtue to that of the Duke of Zhou; therefore, it is clear that saying he "exceeded the Duke of Ai" was not intended as a satirical inversion.
Perhaps Yangzi’s words were a subtle expression of expediency (*quan*). Alas! What path did Ziyun study? He studied another path; I do not understand his "subtlety."

This is indeed unrefined, even if one claims it is truly studying the Way of Zhongni. As for the Master’s humility, I have never heard of it being like the sycophancy of "Ultimate Filial Piety" or "Beautifying the New.

I consider those words of flattery directed at Wang Mang to be precisely what they are. The explanations of the former scholars all serve to gloss over Yang Xiong’s literary excesses while concealing his faults;
their intention was to magnify Yang Xiong’s Way, yet in doing so, they actually diminished it—this is to be ignorant of [the truth].
"What is the Way of Master Ziyun? Even though the worthy man or gentleman cannot entirely avoid faults, if they have a fault, they must recognize it themselves;
having recognized it, they must reproach themselves. How could this be the same as the petty person whose faults they invariably conceal and who cannot reproach themselves?
Zhao Dun said, "The saying 'one brings sorrow upon oneself' surely refers to me. Wu of Wei said, "My transgressions were small."
"Abandon this great wrath; you must not emulate it! Alas, Master Yun’s virtue surpasses that of Zhao Dun and Wei Wu by far.

How could he wish to gloss over his own faults? It was to ensure that in ten thousand generations, when unworthy types encounter his descendants and covet the sacred regalia, they would not fail to rectify themselves, but instead would surely resort to sycophancy to serve them.
If they succeed, they will say: 'I knew [it would come to this].'"

When the mandate of Heaven moves on and one’s efforts truly fail to succeed, to say, "I am merely following the humility of Zhang Ziyun," while practicing a thousand deceptions and ten thousand frauds to change one's countenance for the sake of gaining favor—is this not due to the lingering evils of the "Reforming Appearances to Welcome the New" (Ge-mian-qu-rong)? Therefore it is said:
"One intends to magnify the Way of Ziyun, yet instead diminishes it. I maintain that if Ziyun were alive today and heard my discussion, he would surely [agree].
To be able to endure evil for the sake of the state is a principle further elucidated by Liu Zhongtu of recent times;
yet his words do not transcend the fault of glossing over errors. How could this be anything other than a failure to comprehend the Way of Yang Xiong?
Only Pi Rixiu of the Li Tang dynasty considered these words to be incorrect, and thus composed a postscript to clarify them. I approve of his view and have therefore expanded upon it here. Alas!

If only Master Ziyun had deeply contemplated that the Way’s practice involves the loss of one's life and that birth and death are subject to the mandate of Heaven—so that in his speech he would have no fault comparable to the flattery of Lord Ai-heng, and in his conduct he would have no fear of the disaster involving the throwing of himself from the pavilion—would this not have been utterly perfect?
Yet it was not that Master Ziyun did not know; rather, it was the difficulty of facing such a critical situation. Thus it was with the Master of old.

When he saw Duke Ling of Wei inquire about military formations, he replied with discourse on ritual vessels; when he heard that the Minister of War of Song intended to harm him, he said, "Heaven has bestowed its virtue upon me.
These were the words and deeds of the Sage Master. Master Ziyun studied the Way of the Master, yet there was something he had not fully attained.

Was this what was meant by the aforementioned distinction between the Sage and those who come after him—concerning their words or their deeds? It is indeed difficult to find anyone free from flaw. This is correct.

"If one comes [to this realization], then the words and deeds of the Sage Master are sufficient. To plan for kingship and fail to achieve it, yet still find that the resulting condition reaches the level of hegemony—consider this.
*Xianju bian* (Collection on Leisurely Dwelling), Volume XII; *Xianju bian*, Volume XIII.
Preface to the Boundary Inscription for Maṇi Monastery at Gushan, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Song.
On the fifth day of the fourth month in the summer of the ninth year of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú era, the year being Bǐchén (5987), I first chose this place to establish my residence.
The Head of the Monastery intends to instruct future learners with the doctrine of the Three Contemplations of Tiantai. To examine its origins:

although Śākyamuni’s establishment of the teachings diverges in its gradual and sudden approaches and varies in its Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna proclamations, when it comes to bestowing the precepts to regulate body and speech and designating concentration and wisdom to eliminate mental delusions—thereby leading those who follow the shallow to investigate the profound and enabling those who are ordinary to ascend to the state of sagehood—the underlying principle is one and the same. I...

I, though lacking in talent, have long devoted myself to this practice; how much more so now that I have not yet ascended the steps of sagehood and my own body and speech are not yet pure—how could the matters of the precepts and discipline be abandoned for even a single day?
Alas! To lack them would make one a mere beast, while to differ from them would make one a wild fox;
since I study the Way of the Sage with the aim of self-correction, how could I dare to despise or discard it? In this world, there are those who claim to be "enlightened," yet...
To observe [the precepts] and yet oppose the Vinaya—is this not delusion? This monastery was established long ago, yet its grounds remain in their natural state.
My friend, Master Zewu, walks the Way with an upright person and is able to take the Vinaya as his own responsibility; moreover, he understands my aspirations.
Consequently, he came to my residence with nine of his disciples, assembled the community for a shared meal, and regulated the proceedings according to the Vinaya.

The ritual procedures for boundary-determination (*sīmā-bandha*) were finalized; thereafter, the distribution of food, the protection of robes, the summer retreat (*varṣā*), and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) each found their proper place.

Subsequently, by externally regulating conduct through the Vinaya and internally cultivating wisdom and insight, the True Dharma was made to endure for a long time—what path could there be that does not proceed from this?
As for the right and wrong of boundaries, the types of objects used as markers, and the signs displayed in prominent locations, these were established to inform those who come after.
Preface to the Boundary Marker for Huating Xingsheng Monastery:
In ancient times, sage emperors and enlightened kings realized that the vastness of the nine provinces and the breadth of the four seas could not be governed by one person alone;
therefore, they divided the land and established feudal lords. There were five ranks of noble titles and five zones of territory, and they disseminated the five teachings to instruct the people.
The various people were assigned lands to produce tribute to serve the royal house; rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments all issued from the Son of Heaven.

The people of the five domains were all the subjects of the Son of Heaven, and the calendar and systems of governance were entirely received from the Son of Heaven. Those who opposed this were merely individuals who violated the fundamental order and disturbed the established norms. Is it not likewise so when the Dharma King establishes his transformation? Thus it is said: [The text continues: "The various people were assigned lands to produce tribute to serve the royal house; rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments all issued from the Son of Heaven. The people of the five domains were all the subjects of the Son of Heaven, and the calendar and systems of governance were entirely received from the Son of Heaven.
Those who opposed this were merely individuals who violated the fundamental order and disturbed the established norms. Is it not likewise so when the Dharma King establishes his transformation?"
The realm of Jambudvīpa is vast; when upholding the Dharma, it is difficult for the entire Saṃgha to assemble.

Therefore, it is permitted to establish boundaries according to specific locations so that the Dharma may be accomplished without the fault of causing weariness and damage to the Path through constant travel. The rules of discipline and ritual protocols all originate from the Tathāgata;
the monks of the two divisions are all the subjects and sons of the Tathāgata. Regarding matters of the precepts and discipline, how could they not be received from the Buddha?

If one were to abandon [this teaching] and fail to practice it, would that not be the work of heavenly demons or external paths? Thus, my teaching is for those who violate the statutes and disrupt the constant order.
The original name of Xingsheng Monastery in Huating was Changshou Luohan; during the present dynasty, its plaque was changed twice.
Initially, the bestowed name offended the taboo of the Imperial Ancestor, so it was again changed to its current name. In the second year of the Qianguo era of the Han dynasty...

In the year Jǐyǒu (1729), a local resident of the district, Zhāng Sìzǐ Rén, donated his own residence to establish a vihāra, performing Buddhist rites to repay the boundless kindness [of his parents].

From that time on, it has flourished as a Buddhist temple for sixty-seven years. However, because it was originally a site for the natural dwelling of monks, no formal monastic regulations had been applied.
A presiding śramaṇa said, "I am a śramaṇa of the Chan school," and another śramaṇa said, "I am a śramaṇa of the Vinaya school."
I sighed in admiration for a long time and then commanded several individuals versed in the Vinaya to establish the boundaries here;
thus, all systems and regulations were received from the Buddha—is this not magnificent? Alas!

In the world today, those who practice the Buddha-dharma, from the imperial capital downward, consider the regions of Wu and Yue to be the most flourishing; within the lands of Wu and Yue, they consider Huating to be the greatest.
In even this town, where a Buddhist temple was established less than a hundred years ago, there is no formal demarcation of the boundary (sīmā);

how much more so, then, in other regions? If the great boundary is not demarcated, then the rituals of receiving precepts, preaching, and the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā) cannot truly be performed.
Observing this, one knows that as the distance from the Sage increases, the decline of the Dharma is indeed like this. Now, these two superior men...
One who can take up the affairs of this institution—tasks discarded in these末代 (mòdài) times—and raise them up for practice;

one who can rejoin the great guiding cord that has been severed and set up the great banner that has already toppled, enabling those of inferior capacity to aspire toward such heights—the benefit of protecting the Dharma by such a person is surely immeasurable!
The monks of this monastery, Zhìyún and Zǐhuá, are truly my own disciples; they have come by boat to Qiántáng to request my words.
For my sake, he composed this preface and inscribed it upon the plaque.
Ninghaijun Zhenjue Jixiang wrote this preface for me.
Residing in a hut on Mount Gushan, I have been confined within its gates to nurse my illness; ashamed to announce myself to the world, I have not associated with the people of the age.
The Elder Master Mingji sent a letter to me, saying: "The monastery where I reside is named Zhengjue (True Awakening).
In the past, when the Qian family ruled the territory and the Buddhist cause flourished in Yangzhou, a subordinate official named Dong Xun erected it on a street;
this was in the first year of the Taiping Xingguo era. Its former name was Fengqing, which His Majesty the Emperor has now changed to its current title."

The corridors and halls were not incomplete, and the annual sacrifices were not neglected; yet, because the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) had not been established, the Dharma regulations could not be implemented and the Vinaya precepts could not be cultivated.
Those who understand this feel shame, and I too feel shame. The Great Vinaya Master, Venerable Zeyu, was my friend;
having once stayed with me overnight, I told him the circumstances. Zeyu said, "It may be done," and subsequently joined me along with his disciples.

On another day, he came to my residence and, in accordance with the *Vinaya*, established the boundary markers; once the demarcation was set and the rules for the precinct were completed, he posted a notice for those who would come after.
Since you, sir, delight in hearing of the path of goodness, I hope you will provide an introduction to explain the reasons behind this, so that it may be handed down to eternity.
I therefore granted his request, saying: "Now, when humans are born they are still and tranquil—this is their heavenly nature. It is only when moved by external objects that they stir."

Regarding the desires of human nature: when external objects seduce from without without limit, and internal desires stir within without restraint, one is unable to turn back upon oneself and the principles of Heaven (Tianli) are extinguished.
Therefore, the Awakened King established the precepts and rules to provide humanity with restraint;
if coarse violence does not arise, then the principles of Heaven are easily restored. Thus, in order to dwell in a palace and carry out these precepts, one must necessarily...

The commencement of the boundary-formation (*sīmā-bandha*): through the formation of the boundary, one delineates the cardinal directions and intermediate points and establishes the characteristics of the various classes of objects;
the boundaries thus arise, and the mental consciousnesses of the assembly are thereby focused.

Once these standard regulations (*dharmaparyāya*) and the *karmavācanā* rituals can be performed, and once these regulations are in practice, coarse violence is thereby stilled and the heavens are restored through this principle; only then does one come to know the Buddha.

That the Sage’s Dharma is great and the Sangha is exalted does not arise apart from the establishment of *sīmā*; were it not for these established regulations (*yīzhāng*), they could not be implemented.
If these regulations are not implemented, then coarseness and violence cannot be quelled, and the natural order of Heaven (*tiānlǐ*) cannot be restored.
Furthermore, how could one otherwise know the greatness of the Buddha’s Sage-Dharma or the loftiness of the Sangha? Alas! How can those who establish *vihāras* afford to neglect this?

If establishing boundaries through ritual demarcation (*sīmā-bandha*) is considered a matter of urgency, then what the wicked call "benevolent shrines" and "Buddhist temples" must refer to the practice and the regulations of the Buddha;

it does not refer to mere grandeur or magnificence. Alas! With upper beams and lower rafters, cast metal and molded clay, sumptuous kitchens and sweet meals, and the clanging of bells and beating of drums—if one does not put into practice the monastic rules and regulations, can such places truly be called Buddhist temples?

This is not permissible. Even if one dwells in an earthen hut with walls of woven thorns and weeds, where food is often exhausted, and builds a stupa from gathered sand or paints the likeness of the Honored One with fingernails—if one truly practices the rules of discipline and ritual protocols, it may be called a Buddhist temple.

Whether such a place is a temple or not can be known by observing whether these protocols are put into practice or not. Alas! Since the Buddha’s extinction long ago, the True Dharma has been lost; yet, there are those who...
When he was promoted and employed, the people of his generation were either greatly incensed or burst into loud laughter;
thus, those of middling or inferior capacity feared such laughter and anger that, even though they knew [the truth], they could not put it into practice.

When the elders gathered as teachers and śramaṇas who possessed the Way, they sought companions courageous in the Dharma; having found such a person, the Vinaya Master Wugu was able to bring it to completion.

How magnificent is this! By uniting Chan and Vinaya to establish the texts for the *sīmā* (boundary) system, he ensures that those who come after may dwell therein, thereby stilling their coarseness and violence, returning to their own personhood, and restoring the principles of Heaven. How can the greatness of such benefit be fully described?
I admire his establishment of these institutions in an age when they had fallen into ruin and his practice of the Way during a time when it was difficult to follow.
If I had no one to petition, I would have spoken of this myself; how much more so now that there is a request?
I hope that future readers who read my preface will understand that I am not afraid of either great anger or great laughter.
Record of the Re-establishment of the Great Boundary at Agate Courtyard:
On the twenty-ninth day of the third month of spring in the ninth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era of the Song dynasty, the "Disciple of the Middle Way" purchased a mountain to nurture his illness.
He obtained the slope of the setting sun on Mount Gu, which is called Agate; there was a Buddhist hall upon that slope, which he likewise [renamed].

Ma-nao (Agate) took the matter to the elders and consulted the official registers; he then learned that it was founded by the Prince Wusu during the second year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, the *qīnglóng* year of Dīnghài.
For generations it had been a monastic residence for a long time, yet although the buildings and corridors were complete, the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) had not been demarcated.
He therefore urgently requested his friend, the Vinaya master Míng-lǜ, saying, "I have chosen the Master Wú."
Master Wugu approved this. Four months later, on the third day of the fourth month, he assembled the monks and, upholding the Dharma, established the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the community.
Subsequently, as those who came to study became numerous and the halls and chambers were cramped, the disciple Hao Cai led the Xìn clan to expand the buildings;
thus, the newly constructed structures once again occupied their natural sites. Master Wugu further [entrusted] five of his disciples...
People untie the old and tie the new, expanding their outward manifestations.

From this point on, pavilions, terraces, halls, and galleries, as well as springs, rocks, flowers, and bamboo, shall all be included within the scope of ritual practice (*zuo-fa*). Thus, it is not merely a matter of practicing meditation, expounding the Way, and cultivating one’s innate nature;
furthermore, matters of receiving teachings and indulging in ease shall all be carried out accordingly, and there shall be no [restriction].
To transgress the regulations established by the Buddha—this was on the twenty-first day of the fourth month in the third year of the Tianxi era. Alas!
Those who are disciples of the Buddha must surely follow the Buddha’s regulations; if they do not follow these regulations, I maintain that they are not disciples of the Buddha.
Oh, how long it has been since the Sage passed away! The Great Dharma has become diluted, and those who study Buddhism have divided their sectarian domains, resulting in such differences.
If one is fond of cinnabar, it is surely because they lack that which serves as a constant reminder of the precepts; if one craves the sweet, it is because they loathe its pungency.
Those who regard the wisdom of principle as mere fanciful talk choose and reject according to their own emotions, thereby deviating from the Right Path.

If one wishes to enter the gate of liberation and ascend to the realm of eternal bliss, how can this be achieved? How could such a person know that the nature of ordinary beings and sages is equal, and that all are born [into this same reality]?

The reason why the Buddha’s teaching unifies all yet ordinary people cannot restore themselves to that state is that they are deluded by their physical forms, which inevitably leads them to be caged within birth and death.
Therefore, the transgressions of the body are not rectified without the Vinaya;

the confusion and distraction of the mind are not integrated without Samādhi and Prajñā. When these are restrained and harmonized, with the internal and external supporting one another, one may still fear that the Way—
If one does not understand that the nature of things cannot be restored, how much less can one who is biased toward a single perspective and treats others as mutually exclusive?

Therefore, although I have specialized in instructing people in the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), I still dare not forget the training in the precepts and the Vinaya. It is finished! Who will be the one to dwell here after me?
Will it be a practitioner of dhyāna-contemplation? A builder of merit? Or a reciter of the scriptures? Let them read my [record].

Only after reading these writings did I come to know that the regulations of the Dharma King ought to be followed in common; knowing they are to be followed in common, I realized that we all return to the same Way.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of that year, following a rain, I recorded this matter at Diecui Pavilion.
The Record of the Boundary-Delimitation at Fajiyuan:

In my study of Buddhism, I have also read the books of Zhongni (Confucius). I understand that the essence of ritual and music lies in bringing peace to superiors, governing the people, and transforming customs.
Yet, ritual tends toward depletion while music tends toward excess; through the constraints of ritual, people grow weary.

Music is harmonious and brings joy to people; therefore, it is said that "Ritual (Li) diminishes and then advances, taking advancement as its ornament," while Music is full and then returns, taking return as its ornament.
This is just like the Buddha’s instruction of humanity: there is Chan-wisdom (dhyāna-prajñā) and there are Precepts (śīla).
Thus, when Chan-wisdom is cultivated, the distinction between self and others vanishes; when the Precepts are practiced, likes and dislikes are discerned. Therefore, Chan-wisdom is empty...
Those who are well-versed in worldly affairs take pleasure in what they advance, while those who observe the precepts grow weary of their own practice.

Is it not a mark of worthiness to find joy in what others find wearisome and to persevere in what others find tedious? The Faji Monastery is situated in the northwestern corner of Qiantang Prefecture;
bordering the lake and backed by the city wall, it is as remote as a place beyond the mundane world. Formerly, when the Qian family held hegemony...
During the Wu-Yue period, a subordinate official named Master Weng, who served as the Prefectural Governor of Quzhou, established it for the Great Elder, Master Qingxiang;
this was in the [blank] year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Imperial Court.
After the Elder passed away, his disciple Master Qizheng succeeded him. They beat the drums together at meals and, clad in woolen robes, discussed the Way, which they truly called Chan.
Because of this, the matter of establishing the *sīmā* (boundary) had remained neglected for a long time and was not yet implemented.
Master Zheng feared that failing to follow the teachings of our Buddha would lead to the reproach of being unworthy of one’s robes. He once said to his disciples:

"I have heard it stated in the Vinaya Piṭaka that on 'natural ground' (*svabhāva-bhūmi*) or 'ground of great dharma' (*mahādharma-bhūmi*), those who are weak cannot withstand me; I wish to request [the establishment of the boundary] there."
The Vinaya-master established the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for them, following the Buddha’s regulations and silencing their private criticisms. "How do you all feel about this? he asked.

The assembly bowed their heads in unison and, having thus reached a consensus, they requested the Vinaya-master, saying: "We shall choose a suitable location, prepare the seating, assemble the Sangha, and perform the ritual to establish it.
Alas! The practice of the Vinaya standards has long been neglected; it is only now that the Master knows how to promote it.
"Is it not also worthy to compose a literary record? The Venerable Xubai has repeatedly visited my gate to discuss matters of governance, hoping that I might provide an account.
Therefore, I have recorded this for him. *Xianju bian*, Volume 13.

I lament that the establishment of the water-strainer (parisrāvaṇa) has been neglected for a long time.

Having once followed the *Nèifǎ zhuàn* (Account of the Inner Dharma) by Yìjìng to fashion one myself, I was troubled that I could not put it into practice. Consequently, I composed a eulogy for it, hoping that the Vinaya Master Dōushuài would truly dare to adopt its use.

The Benevolent One established his teachings with compassion as their foundation; thus he prescribed the water-strainer so that insects might not be harmed. Filtering and pouring, one drinks and uses [the water] without causing injury.
When benevolence resides in the heart, it is never forgotten even in moments of haste. If one still takes pity on these minute creatures, how could one neglect those that are large?

If such is the case for the lowly among different species, how much more so for those of the same kind who are our superiors—how could one ever act contrary to this? Since the Sage has long since departed, the water-strainer...
The Way declined and its regulations were dismantled, vanishing like dust in the wind. Alas! Yijing took compassion as his nature; his system was profoundly brilliant.

He led others to protect their lives, and I, a later student, look up to this former sage with reverence. Having fashioned [the rules] but not yet put them into practice, my heart is filled with shame. To preserve the spirit of the sheep so as to recognize the ritual is to ensure that the great principles do not deviate.

Now that the ritual objects are complete and the gate of compassion is opened, my friend— *Note: This passage appears to be a preface or colophon by a later scholar reflecting on the legacy of the Tang dynasty monk Yijing (635–713 CE), who is renowned for his translations and his work on monastic discipline, particularly regarding the protection of life through vegetarianism.*
Tushita, foremost in upholding the Vinaya, has completed this water-strainer for daily use. When one desires benevolence, benevolence arrives; who could say it has been lost?
This is the resolve regarding the water-strainer.
The Śākya established his teachings to bestow bounty widely and save the various capacities of beings through compassion and reverent benevolence.

Because he was mindful that water contains minute insects, he ordained that his disciples who engaged in drinking or using water must filter it with a fine cloth bag and then re-submerge it in a spring so that they might survive.
Alas! Were it not for one whose benevolence is great and whose universal salvation is ultimate, how could this be?
Who is capable of paying heed to such extremely subtle matters? Since the Sage departed, the institutional systems have long since declined and are nearly ruined;
people merely offer empty words without observing the reality of these facts. Even the monks of today do not recognize their scale or appearance, let alone receive them and practice them daily.
I have long been grieved by this, and thus I have followed the exposition of Yijing.
Its tailoring is said to be simple and essential (Yijing’s *Nèifǎ zhuan* states: "Take four feet of fine silk; grasp the edges and pull them taut to bring the two ends together;

stitch them so they adhere; attach straps to the two corners and place hooks on both sides; insert a horizontal rod between them to spread it out to a span of one chi and six cun; tie both ends to pillars; and place a basin beneath).

Once completed, hang it in the thatched hall to complete the requisite number of religious articles (the Buddhist religious articles consist of six items: the three robes, the alms bowl, the water filter, and the sitting mat). As for taking it up and using it..."
"I have not yet been able to do so. Someone said, "Once it has been crafted, you must use it. To craft it and not use it is no different from not crafting it at all;
is this not practicing deception? I responded with a grave expression, saying, "You do not understand me. That I do not use it is, in fact, its greatest use in the world. Why is this?
Now, as for the teachings of Zhongni (Confucius), there is nothing he loved more than life and nothing he detested more than..."
In these degenerate times, those who cannot preserve the Way and lose the rites— those who hunt with fire when the insects have not yet hibernated,
who encircle marshes in spring, who ambush herds, and who take the young fawns and eggs— these are called those who are violent toward the things of Heaven.
Furthermore, there are elder brothers who are unkind to their younger brothers, fathers who are unkind to their sons, and teachers [who are likewise].

If one is not compassionate toward their resources, and a ruler is not compassionate toward the people—if upon seeing the construction of a water-strainer one were to say, "The followers of Śākya are compassionate and forgiving even toward the most minute beings in the water, let alone insects, let alone birds and beasts, let alone fawns and eggs;
how much more so toward younger brothers, sons, resources, and the people! How could I not [practice compassion]?"—[then one would truly understand].
"Having received the Way of Zhongni, I take cherishing life, benevolence, forbearance, and compassion as my core concern.

If I were unable to cherish life, practice benevolence, forbearance, and compassion, I would not only be a transgressor against Zhongni, but would truly be a source of shame to the followers of Śākyamuni.
Ritual and measure are cultivated thereby, and the breeze of benevolence is spread thereby; thus it is said: 'My non-employment is, in fact, a great employment.'"
In this world, there may be those who later feel resentment toward me for not using [the filter] when purifying water; yet even their resentment arises from my refusal to use it.
Therefore, although my manufacture of the water-strainer is a mere pretense, it nonetheless benefits both the Confucian and Buddhist traditions.
Thus, some may withdraw in shame.
Record of the Birth of the Buddha (with Preface) In the rites of the Confucians, one must offer sacrifices before eating; when a gentleman has business, he does not forget his roots.

It is said that the birth of the Śākya [Buddha] was intended to provide food for sentient beings, serving as a sacrifice to the spirits of the wilderness and to Hārītī. This is the application of the śramaṇa’s mind.

To take pity on those of different species is not to forget the fundamental benevolence; to take pity on those of different species is compassion (*maitrī*). These two arise from the same source yet have different names.
Now, observing that among later students few fathom this origin, the practice of "being born" has consequently become discordant:

when being scrupulously clean at the house of a donor (*dānapati*), they may mix in discarded items; when staying in the communal hall, their trays and vessels become filthy and disordered. Therefore, I have depicted their appearance.

I record these deeds to show them to future generations; furthermore, when sacrificing to a deity, one treats it as if the deity were present, for enjoyment depends on sincerity—this is true even in Confucianism, let alone for those who follow the Buddhist precepts.
Now, those dwelling together in the community should collect [offerings] in clean vessels and place them before this image.
After a long while, they should offer them to the birds, beasts, fish, and shellfish. The lay donor’s family should take the raw rice from the monastic meal once it has been finished.

One should prepare a single vessel of offerings for that image and then distribute them; however, the Vinaya also permits sending food for offering at the two meal times (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* also states:
"Furthermore, at the end of the procession, place a platter of food to offer to Hārītī"). If one were to offer beforehand, the monks would not need to each contribute individually;
yet I fear this might be inappropriate at that time. It is now proper for each person to contribute their portion first, and then gather them together to make the offering.
Once individuals apply their minds separately, they will all reflect upon the Buddha’s regulations;
it is hoped that those of superior capacity will diligently practice them, for it is said that "the sacrifice of the worthy shall surely receive its blessing."

The fifteenth fascicle of the Southern Edition of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: While the Buddha was traveling through the village of Kalandaka, there was a malevolent spirit (yakṣa) who took his name from that place;
he devoured meat and killed living beings, and moreover, he ate one person from that village every day.

The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, but the fool would not accept the teaching. The Buddha then manifested himself as a powerful spirit who shook the demon’s palace, causing the spirit to emerge from it.

When he encountered the Buddha’s transformation-body, he fell prostrate to the ground in a swoon. The Buddha stroked his body with a hand of compassion, whereupon he immediately rose and sat up, exclaiming:
"How wonderful! Today I have regained my life and body. Great King, may you pardon my transgressions!
The Buddha manifested his true form and further preached the Dharma for him, causing that spirit to receive the precept against killing. On that day, in the wilderness...
In the village there was an elder who was due to die next; once the spirit had obtained him, it immediately offered him to the Buddha.
The Buddha established a name for him, calling him "The Elder Hand. The spirit addressed the Buddha, saying: "I and my retinue rely solely on flesh and blood to sustain our lives.
Now that he has received the precepts, what shall we have to subsist upon? The Buddha replied: "From this day forward, you shall command the śrāvakas [to provide for you]."
"Disciples, wherever there is the practice of the Buddha-dharma, you must all cause food and drink to be given to you.
For this reason, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus: from this day forward, you should always provide food to those wilderness spirits (kṛtya).
If there is a dwelling place where one cannot give [this], know that such persons are not my disciples."
The *Jiguizhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Have Returned from the Netherworld), fascicle one, states:

When a donor first prepares the offerings for the noble Sangha and subsequently serves food to the monastic assembly, he further places a single dish of food at the end of the serving line to offer to the mother Hārītī.
This mother, in her previous life, made a vow due to certain circumstances to devour all the children of Rājagṛha; she subsequently took rebirth [as such].
The yakṣa gave birth to five hundred sons who daily devoured the men and women of the royal city. The Buddha then hid his youngest son, named Priya (Beloved), and the mother went searching for him.
The Buddha said to her, "If you still cherish even one out of your five hundred sons, how much more so should you cherish others, even just one or two?
The Buddha then transformed her, leading her to receive the five precepts. She then invited the Buddha, saying, "My five..."
"What do you eat now? the Buddha asked. He replied, "The monasteries where the bhikṣus reside provide sacrificial food every day for you to satisfy your hunger.

In the various monasteries of the West, they invariably paint the image of a mother holding a child on her lap at the entrance halls or beside the kitchen; there may be five or three children to represent her likeness."
One day, [the monk] presented a lavish array of offerings before her; she was none other than the mother of the host of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Possessing immense power and influence, those who suffered from illness or lacked offspring would offer prayers to her, and all their wishes were fulfilled.

The details are explained at length in the Vinaya. In China, she was previously known as the "Famous Ghost Mother" (Guizi Mu). (Now, upon close examination, the Buddhist temples of this region all depict two deities on their gate walls, with a woman behind them; this is likely her surviving image. Since both [the father and mother] receive sacrifices, they are depicted together.)

Some have established images of lay devotees (gṛhapati); these are those whose hands are long. On the western wall is the form of Āṭavaka, and on the eastern wall is the one manifested by the Buddha; it is now clarified that for the ritual offerings, only the image of Āṭavaka is depicted.
