Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
This is a record of a review lecture by a disciple of Master Wugu of Qiantang on the Vinaya.
I have been recuperating from illness at Gushan for two years, keeping myself apart from the world. My gate stands idle and my secluded paths are overgrown with moss and deep weeds;
the tracks of carriages and horses have never been there. I often find solace in this solitude, remaining content and free from distress.

I take pleasure in hearing of others' virtues as if they were my own; yet, regretting that I cannot personally chant their praises before the world’s gentlemen, I have frequently recorded them on tablets and scrolls to bequeath them to future generations.
On the sixteenth day of the second month of spring in the first year of the Tianxi era, the Vinaya Master named Ruzhe (lit.
"Selecting the Wutong")—a friend of mine—came seeking me out by boat, finding shelter beneath the lush foliage.
He sighed with the pure wind in the forest for a long time, and then said to me: "I understand the Way of the Śākya school.
Without the study of the precepts (*śīla*), there is no means to restrain one's outward appearance or to curb one's violence.
Once one's deportment is refined and coarseness does not arise, then meditative stillness and wisdom can be brought forth, and the realm of the sages and worthies can be ascended."
Therefore, the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni) established it as the foremost teaching, and the Nanshan lineage inherited its profound transmission.

Now that the Dharma has declined and people have become so full of deviance that they take self-indulgence to be the path to enlightenment and regard the precepts as superfluous, the teachings are on the verge of extinction—remaining but a single thread.
Is this not something to be deeply feared? It is for this reason that I diligently lecture and transmit them; it is not... [for any other].
These are merely empty words, yet they do have the intent to revitalize and put them into practice. Those who study under me are numerous;
among them, there are those who look toward the path with trepidation, and there are those who abandon their efforts midway. Those who are truly able to shoulder the burden are but one in ten.
I have long wished to broaden this Way, and thus I have secretly devised a plan to encourage and advance them. Among those who come to study, there are some capable of expounding it.
Those who have thoroughly mastered the Vinaya commentaries shall have their names recorded in the lecture hall: once a year and once a month. For each lecture they attend, a name is recorded;

for a second lecture, it is recorded again; and for repeated lectures, it is recorded repeatedly. This is so that those who do not lecture may know to exercise caution, and those who attend one lecture or more may know to be encouraged.
When there is both caution and encouragement, those who stand at the threshold in awe will surely become disciplined.
"One who halts midway while holding the reins must apply the whip to reach their destination before they can proclaim their arrival to the four quarters.
If one acts in accordance with their words, the Way of the Precepts (śīla) will return to its source without being far removed; it is nothing other than my Way, for we are of one accord.
How could I dare to deliberate with you on this? It is without distinction. I responded with trepidation, saying, "I have heard of the Precepts..."
The Way of the Vinaya is spread across the palm leaves; when its rightful person is found, the Way flourishes, and when that person is lost, the Way declines.
Is it truly thus that my friend applies his mind? I venture to congratulate the house of precepts and discipline for having found such a person.
What need is there to fear the loss of the Way? I delight in his excellent words and his many skillful exhortations, and have therefore set pen to paper to record them.
Epitaph. Epitaph for the Stupa of the Great Song High Monk Acharya Ciguang.
The life and deeds of the Acharya are recorded in the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha). He passed away during the Yongxi era at the age of seventy-five, with fifty years of ordination seniority.
"Wu" is the courtesy name for my late teacher; "Xiujin" is his style name; Lu is his clan name; Gusu is the place where he grew up;
the Three Contemplations of Tiantai are the Dharma-gate he studied; Zhiyin is the master from whom he inherited the lineage;

Qiantang Ciguang Monastery is the place where he transmitted the Way; and "noble, upright, frugal, and simple" describes the conduct he maintained. My teacher’s name was Yuanqing. He received... [the Dharma].
Ah, thirty-one years after his passing, a dharma-descendant named Zhiyuan recovered his remains from another’s dwelling.
He sold his own clothing and hired laborers to carve a stone and construct a stupa, interring them on the Marrow Slope of Mount Gushan.
Three years later, fearing that future generations might not know of this, he inscribed a record upon the cliff to the left of the stupa to mark it. At that time...
Recorded on the third day after the full moon, the *yǐsī* day, in the tenth month of winter in the second year of the Tiānxī era.

Regarding those of ancient worth who possessed virtue and good deeds worthy of praise, their descendants invariably inscribed them upon metal and stone to ensure their fame was clearly established. Thus it is with this record of the meritorious conduct of the late Dharma Master Śāriputra of Fàntiàn Temple.
Alas! In later generations, there was a preceptor named Bhadra (Fan Tian), whose virtue among the followers of Śākya was praiseworthy.

Four years after his passing, a disciple named Congzheng, fearing that the master’s illustrious legacy might perish, went to the foot of Mount Gu and repeatedly sought out the Recluse (Qianfu) to request the compilation of his teachings;
it has now been half a year since he made this plea. I commend him.
His disciple Zhong then composed this account for him: The *ācārya*’s name was Qingzhao, his courtesy name was Ziwen, and he was surnamed Hu;

he was a native of Qiantang. In his youth, he grew weary of worldly life and withdrew into the gates of emptiness. He served his master at Kaihua Monastery, and at the age of thirteen, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) at Kaiyuan Temple in Kuaiji.
Having cultivated roots of goodness from past lives, his conduct remained untarnished and pure throughout his years. When he reached the age of twenty...
Eleventh, while once reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I felt ashamed that my mouth chanted its words while my mind remained obscure regarding their meaning.
Suddenly, the aspiration to study arose in me, and I heard that the teachings of Tiantai unify all natures and preside over all schools.
At that time, there was a Great Dharma Master named Yuanqing who transmitted this Way at Fengxian Temple in the same prefecture.
He then served him by facing north for seventeen years, attending to his every need with diligent devotion. His reputation grew lofty and his achievements were preeminent among his peers;
after his master passed away, the *ācārya* succeeded him. In expounding the Way and instructing others, he possessed the spirit of both a father and a teacher, and thus many juniors flocked to him.
Before long, he moved his residence to Mount Shibi, where he lived in serene contentment amidst the forest.
Regarding the map of its final state: to the south of the city of Yue lies Fan Tian Temple.

Within the temple is the Upper Chamber (*shangfang*), which was the place where the former Chan Master Yan cultivated his true nature. It leans against green cliffs in the rear and overlooks the clear river below;

though it is situated close to the mundane world, it stands transcendentally beyond worldly affairs. The abbot of the temple, the Śramaṇa named Yuming, delighted in the Sudden Teaching and admired it.
Gao Yi subsequently established an upper hall as a lecture courtyard and earnestly invited [the Master] to reside there in order to transmit the teachings to future students.
When he declined, he was not permitted to do so; thus, he proceeded via Shibi to take up residence at Fantian Temple. This was in the fourth month of the first year of the Jingde era.

Once the true wind had spread and those far and near had followed his transformation, and the conditions for his transformative work were exhausted, his karmic retribution also came to an end. Thereafter, he encountered...
The Venerable Miliu entered parinirvāṇa at his residence on the twenty-sixth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Tianxi era.

He was fifty-five years of age and forty-one years since his ordination (*bhikṣu-saṃvatsara*). His disciples, mourning him with filial devotion, interred his entire remains according to ritual protocol to the right of the Chongjiao Monastery on Mount Daci.
While serving as the Magistrate of Qiantang, Zhang Gong Junfang, the Secretariat Vice-Director, held him in high esteem.

The Master commissioned artisans to carve stone into a stupa to commemorate this. The *Dharma Flower Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) and the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Contemplation), as well as various other sūtras and śāstras, were expounded by the Ācārya more than one hundred times in total.
Among his disciples who transmitted his teachings, there were ninety-seven individuals, beginning with Xiànrùn.
Formerly, while the Ācārya resided at Fàntián Monastery, he once dreamed of a strange person who said to him: "Dwell here for ten..."
Three years have passed until now, and the proof has been realized at the end. Alas! Even if it were merely a coincidence in a dream, would it not perhaps inspire faith?
The Ācārya’s nature is grave and steady; he does not prize ostentation. Beyond his lecturing and recitation, he dwells uprightly in a quiet chamber, remaining composed and at ease.

He did not cultivate connections for the sake of reputation, yet his fame has been transmitted to posterity. He possessed no wealth or food to gather a multitude, yet his disciples numbered nearly a thousand.
Not deceiving or boasting in order to startle the world, yet the world may still turn toward his benevolence. The gentleman says:

to sever these three maladies and attain these three benefits—would this not be difficult to achieve in this degenerate age? Though one might wish not to praise him, how could those who possess true knowledge neglect him?

I have held the brush of a local historian amidst the rivers and lakes; whenever there was even a slight act of goodness or a minor instance of evil, I often recorded it upon tablets and scrolls to exhort and warn.
Is not the conduct and practice of Preceptor Chengkuang truly extraordinary? Having responded to the request of his disciples, he has also lent this account as an instruction for them.
Recorded on the fifth day of the fifth month of the summer in the fourth year of the Tianxi era, the year of Gengshen.
The Record of the Servant’s Spring:
The Servant’s Spring is located at the northwest corner of the Buddha Hall of Maṇi Monastery on the ruins of Gushan in Qiantang County.
It is several feet deep and not more than ten *xun* wide. Its color is pure white and its taste is sweet; one may draw from it without exhaustion, and though it is stirred, it remains undisturbed.
Yicheng offered me a drink; there was no ill omen of the empty pitcher. As the water soaked the fields, I was moved to lament the loss of my irrigation mechanism. How extraordinary!
On the twenty-second day of the ninth month of autumn in the ninth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, a guest presented me with several stalks of "strange bamboo.
I ordered my servants to plant them; as soon as the servants applied their spades and dug the earth to a depth of one cun, this spring gushed forth.
At that time, from summer until autumn, it did not rain; the grasses and trees mostly withered and died, and all springs were exhausted.
Yet this spring alone was seen to perform the merit of moistening things and aiding humanity—this was because it did not alter its constant nature.
It is just as when a gentleman, amidst the extremities of poverty, distress, and decline, does not change his Way, often refining his speech and establishing himself in integrity.
Truly, that which secretly benefits all things moves me with wonder; thus, I dredged and excavated it to form a pond.
Since it was obtained through the agency of a servant, I named it "Pufu Spring" (The Servant’s Spring). Some remarked, "The title 'Pufu' is not elegant; it should be changed.
I replied, "In this world, there are those who obtained [water] because of a predatory beast and consequently named it 'Tiger-Run,' and those who had it transformed by means of a seductive woman."
Consequently, Shugu was titled "The Maid of Wushi. Is a male not more noble than a seductive female spirit?

Is a human being not far superior to a predatory beast? If one does not object to the titles "Tiger-Pawed" or "Maid of Shu," yet alone despises the designation "Servant," then one must value alien species while degrading one's own kind, and prefer the strange and the fantastic while loathing the pure and the upright.
"I have no desire to take it; moreover, this spring was actually obtained by my servant. To abandon it and fail to acknowledge him would be to forget its origin.
To forget the origin and turn one's back on righteousness is something my heart cannot bear.
Although the title 'servant' is vulgar and lowly, and everyone loathes it, I can never change that designation. Someone said, "That is so, my son."
The intent behind this [work] is beyond my knowledge; perhaps it was written later by someone else.

*In Praise of the Three Laughs*, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Sòng Dynasty (with preface).

Formerly, Master Huiyuan lived in seclusion on Mount Lú; he would see guests off only as far as the Tiger Brook as his boundary. Although the Emperor of Jìn possessed the majesty of ten thousand chariots...
Even the formidable authority of Huan Xuan, which could intimidate the sovereign, could not humble him;

yet when he escorted the Daoist Lu Xiujing and the Confucian Tao Yuanming, he surpassed them. Once they were awakened, they walked hand-in-hand, pacing back and forth, looking at one another with broad smiles.
One might sigh: "Is it not that when the Way reaches its ultimate, worldly affairs are forgotten? To this day, people continue to depict their forms.
Rong [Zhi] called it the "Three Laughs Diagram," regarding it merely as a source of amusement; how could he have known the intent behind the Three Sages' application of their minds?
Therefore, I have composed this eulogy to clarify it:
The traditions of Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism— Their essential principles are fundamentally harmonious. To cling to one's own position is to remain obstructed.
Forgetting the trap is the way to attain freedom; there is a bond of mutual understanding that requires no words.
It is thus with the Three Dukes: though their robes differ, their hearts are one. Seeing the Great, they forget the small;
crossing the stream, they leave no trace. Looking at one another and smiling, they find joy within.

In the Night Lecture Pavilion, I describe how one must follow the Way with sincerity and practice it by relying upon its proper locus. If one acts in reliance upon such a place, then Śākyamuni’s Vulture Peak and Confucius’s Zhurui and Si Rivers are not merely physical sites;
it is by relying on these places that their Way was practiced. Thus, I have established this small pavilion here at Mount Gu.
On the ridges of Nampō, with tall bamboos facing a placid lake, birds offer no vulgar sounds and the clouds possess an air of leisure;

secluded from the world of men, it is truly a place for sublime excursions. Yet, that which is named "Night Lectures" is intended to extend the doctrine of Mind-Only and broaden the Way of our Buddha in order to instruct the realm of ghosts.
One might ask: "Can the realm of ghosts be instructed? I reply: "They can."
This is the instruction. Now, those who are manifest and corporeal are the "human," while those who are obscure and hidden are the "ghosts.

Whether in the realm of the obscure or the manifest, all possess a mind. Since they possess a mind, they can be transformed; since they can be transformed, the principle of Buddhahood is not far off. Alas!
Among those who are manifest and corporeal, there are many who, upon hearing the True Path, resist it with obstinacy and refuse to accept it. How could this be?

As for the reach of instruction, how can one know that what is obscure and hidden is truly beyond the scope of teaching? Furthermore, our Buddha’s teachings have already reached the realm of ghosts and spirits;

though I am unworthy, I have the honor of studying the Way of the Buddha, and thus I venture to look up to him as my model. Therefore, the establishment of this Night Lecture Hall surely has its profound purpose. As for the moon being perfectly full in the high, empty sky—ten thousand... [text ends]... (Note:

The source text appears to be a fragmentary prose passage concerning Buddhist pedagogy and the authority of the Buddha's teachings on the supernatural. The final phrase "高空月正萬" likely refers to the moon shining clearly in the vast sky, serving as a metaphor for the clarity and universality of the Dharma.)
The whistling of the pipes is utterly still; strange trees stand rigidly upright as the peaks seem to hasten toward one another.

At such a time, are the flowers in the sky merely the objective realm? Is the echo in the valley merely sound? Since there is no speaking in speaking, and no hearing in hearing, one knows not whether the object is oneself or oneself is the object.
Though all phenomena (*dharma*) are vividly manifest, not a single dharma can be grasped. Alas! Such is the reality of the fundamental principle.
Is it not also due to the assistance of this pavilion? Were I not situated within this pavilion, how could I have been able to observe in such a manner?
How could those who dwell in seclusion and obscurity have heard of this? Therefore, the establishment of this pavilion does not merely serve for ascending to heights and gazing afar;
rather, it is what is meant by "the Way proceeds by depending on its locus. Thus, I have named this pavilion the "Night Lecture Pavilion."
The benefits to me are truly manifold; thus, the name "Night Lectures" encompasses all these excellences.

If, at times, one forgets worldly concerns and sits in silence to cultivate the "vast and courageous qi," it is called the "Cultivating Simplicity Pavilion. If one gathers friends through literature, it is called the "Literary Assembly Pavilion.
If one views the flora and trees in spring, it is called the "Brocade Pavilion. If one seeks coolness during the scorching summer, it is called...
When the autumn moon shines serenely upon the Xunfeng Pavilion, it is called the Moon-Viewing Pavilion; when sunny mountains stand in opposition, it is called the Layered-Green Pavilion;
when gazing at lingering snow, it is called the Jade-Peak Pavilion; and when basking in the warm sun, it is called the Embracing-Noise Pavilion.
As I reflected on these, I discovered seven or eight such distinct names. If my friend Zhu could further enhance its utility, then it would truly possess a magnificent name.
Special titles should be established anew so that future generations may know that although there are many names, they all originate from a single pavilion.
This is just as the nature of the mind is one; when it encounters various categories, it transforms and thus gives rise to all manner of phenomena (*dharma*).
When all manner of phenomena arise, all manner of names are established. How could the nature of the mind be different? Phenomena are also the mind, and the mind is also a name. Why?
Is it for the sake of the physical form? It is absent yet luminous; birth and Buddhahood share a single thread, and self and others follow one principle.
Through this, the principle of the Buddha can be perceived. Is such benefit not indeed contained within this pavilion?

Should there be one who attains our Buddhist teaching and ascends this pavilion to discern its name, they will understand my intent. The pavilion is one zhang in height, and its width is increased accordingly.
It measures four chi in height and consists of four bays; it is neither stained with red nor whitened with lime, remaining natural and plain.
To behold such a structure is like looking back upon the age of dwelling in caves or nest-like huts. I fear that this may already be an excess of luxury.

In the first month of spring in the second year of the Tianxi era of the Great Song, in the year Wuma, several students of the Gate School (Menxue) contributed forty thousand coins of gold to construct it for me. It was named Haocai.
This person has personally overseen the project and, now that the construction work has been completed, bows twice with his head to the ground to request a record of its origins;
thus, I have composed this account. Recorded at Gushan.
Three or four *li* to the west of Qiantang County lies Mount Gu; it is both low and narrow, yet unlike the other mountains, it does not connect with them.
Standing solitary amidst the lake, it appears as though it does not seek to align itself with the others, possessing an air of self-sufficiency.
For this reason, the eyes of many gaze upon it, and the wise delight in its excursions. Those who cherish the extraordinary often come to dwell there, some intending to spend their final years.

According to its maps, there were five Buddhist monasteries and one hermitage situated there. Among the sages and men of distinction who frequented it since ancient times, their number was no less than that of today.
As for those such as Bai Juyi, Yuan Micro, Zhang You, and Xu Hun, they either composed inscriptions upon its monuments or wrote poems about its temples;
thus, this mountain has become the preeminent scenic landmark of Qiantang and is renowned throughout the world.
It is well known that although lofty peaks and overlapping ridges encircle the lake one after another, they seem to feel ashamed in comparison to this mountain.

Alas! Just as a mountain may be low and narrow yet refuse to align itself with the multitude of peaks, so too there are scholars who, though dwelling in a subordinate position, do not flatter those in power nor rely upon influential connections;
even if they harbor benevolence and uphold righteousness, they stand out above their peers.
Those of similar disposition will surely treat him with contempt and insult; thus his name cannot become manifest and his Way will not be put into practice. Alas!

Mountains are maligned because they are solitary, and scholars are detested because they are solitary. O mountains! O scholars! How vast is the distance between what people like and what they dislike!
It would be appropriate for Xun Qian to apply his love for mountains to his love for scholars.

Regarding the recording of dreams, one might ask: "Can dreams be recorded? Indeed, dreams can be recorded. King Gaozong dreamed of obtaining Yue; Confucius dreamed of placing his tablet between the two pillars;

the Jin state dreamed of the two *shu* spirits; the Qin state dreamed of the *Juntian* music; and Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly—all of these are recorded in the Classics, the Histories, and the various philosophical treatises.
Dreams are clear and manifest; for this reason, from the *Xiànyǐ* (The Manifestation of Dreams) down through the historical records and annals of successive dynasties, it is the same.

How could dreams not be recorded? If one asks, "Do dreams possess good fortune or misfortune? I reply: dreams themselves have no good fortune or misfortune; good fortune and misfortune arise from man.
When a gentleman has a dream of good fortune, he does not rely upon it to neglect his virtue; when he has a dream of misfortune, he is able to reform his faults to cultivate himself.

Because of cultivation, the gentleman ultimately receives its blessings; whereas as for the auspicious dreams of the petty person, they rely upon them to indulge their passions, and as for their inauspicious dreams, they pass them by without correction.
Thus, the petty person ultimately receives his calamities. Therefore it is said: "Dreams have no inherent good or ill fortune; good and ill fortune arise from the person.
I have heard your instructions regarding the Confucian records of dreams; may I now ask about the Buddhist tradition?
"Does this record of dreams have a basis in reality? He replied: "The dream of the golden drum and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the dream of the king—how could these not be records of dreams?
[The questioner asked: "If one clarifies them through principle, are dreams not empty? He replied: "If they are clarified through principle, how could they be merely the dreams of a single night?
A hundred years are also a great dream. While the good and evil of a hundred years can be recorded, how could the good and evil of a single night [not be so]?"
Is it not recordable? Alas! To record a hundred years of empty goodness to deceive future generations—I would rather record one night’s actual dream.

Therefore, I record this dream. In the eighth month of autumn in my thirteenth year, while lying in a secular dwelling, I dreamed one night that our Buddha was observing the summer retreat in the palace of the Dragon King, and that I had obtained the honor of attending upon him. As for what he said:
As for the Dragon Palace, its halls and pavilions are not lofty or prominent like the dwellings of worldly people, but are merely vast and spacious.
The brackets and beams are simple and plain, lacking the ornate carvings of mountain scenery; the balconies and windows are open and airy, without the adornment of red or vermilion lacquer.

The Buddha’s appearance is full and long, of a dark purple complexion, and he wears a dark blue-black *kāṣāya* robe; there is only one elderly *śramaṇa* present. [This is] distinct [from other accounts].

When the meal was finished, he preached the Dharma; I only saw his mouth moving, but in the end heard nothing at all. When the summer retreat ended, he emerged from the sea, and members of the royal family escorted him to the shore.
I followed him into the vast wilderness, unable to distinguish any direction, as the landscape stretched out boundlessly before my eyes.

After traveling for some time, there appeared a being resembling the gods and ghosts depicted in worldly paintings; it prostrated itself before me, the Buddha, and offered me many layers of fine garments.

I requested instruction on the Way and the Dharma; the Buddha then used an elephant as a metaphor for me. Shortly thereafter, he brought an elephant to offer to the Buddha and mounted it to depart, and I followed him.
After entering the Pine Gate for several li, we saw a forked path in the distance.
About one li further, there was a small Buddhist temple with its gates and eaves painted vermilion and its walls plastered white. Two men in magnificent robes stood to the left of the gate.
The above describes the manner of welcoming: the Buddha dismounted from his elephant and handed the reins and bridle to me; I accepted them and tied them to a tree.
The Buddha nodded his head and smiled as if to say, "I know your intention. Suddenly, I awoke from the dream. Upon reaching my father, I related this to him.
My father sighed deeply and said, "Because you were frequently ill when you were an infant, I [had you]..."
"I have sent you forth from the household life so that you, my friend, might take Confucian studies as your foundation and seek official emolument at the Imperial Court to bring glory to our clan.
Is your dream not rather a sign that you will long become a disciple of the Śākya and transmit the Way? Do not speak of this dream to others;
it is auspicious. Yet, I harbor a secret doubt: if the Buddha appeared in the dream, it was likely in the form of a golden radiance, yet [the dream] turned out otherwise."
Did he have the same monastic appearance? Eight years later, I studied the Three Contemplations (*sān guān*) of the Tiantai school under Master Fǎngxiān (whose name was Yuánjì).
An advanced fellow student of his explained the Four Teachings (*sì jiào*) to me and said, "In the Tripitaka Teaching, the Buddha appears in the likeness of a *bhikṣu*.
My heart was filled with wonder and joy for a long time; I thought to myself, "Could the one I dreamed of previously have been Śākyamuni? It is certainly so."

It was a matter of doubt. Ten years later, he regretted that the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*—the ultimate scripture—and the subtle words of Zhizhe Dazhang’an had not been transmitted to the world for over two hundred years.
At that time, while suffering from illness at Suixin Temple, he was investigating the meaning of the scriptures.

Upon reaching the fifteenth fascicle, which describes the Tathāgata’s descent into the wilderness to subdue the spirits and demons, he realized that this was the omen of his former dream. He said: "As for me..."
Is there not a karmic affinity for this *Nirvāṇa*? Seven years after I began composing this work at Chongfu Temple, I again dreamed of two śramaṇas lingering at my gate.
Gazing at them from afar, I recognized them silently within my mind, thinking to myself, "These must be Avalokiteśvara and Nāgārjuna.
I hurried out to welcome them; Avalokiteśvara entered through the door on the right, while Nāgārjuna entered through the door on the left.

I followed behind him with my shoulder slightly turned toward him, and after walking several paces, I suddenly thought to myself: "To go forward and bow is the proper etiquette. I then hurried forward;
having completed the prostration, I addressed him, saying: "Avalokiteśvara compassionately covers the entire Dharma-realm, and Nāgārjuna is truly the patriarchal master of our school.

I only pray that your wisdom may increase in clarity and that the roots of my transgressions may be purified. Having spoken these words, I bowed again. Avalokiteśvara bestowed his instruction for a long time.
However, he could not recall [the details] clearly; Nāgārjuna merely said, "You saw an ancient person (whose name was Mengjue) casting a sword.

Desiring only to benefit and not to cause harm, Mengjue then composed the *Nirvāṇa Sandhinirmocana-tri-guṇa-ji-gui* in twenty fascicles, the *Fayuan jiyao* in two fascicles, the *Ke* in eleven fascicles, the *Baifei chao* in one fascicle, and the *Fenjing tu*.

One fascicle of the Commentary and one fascicle of the Hymn by the Master were completed; before three years had passed, he ceased his writing. He then resumed public lectures and the transmission of the teachings. Alas!
Was this not the protective mindfulness of the Buddha, the Benevolent One? Was it not the secret empowerment of the Two Sages?
Otherwise, how could someone as noisy and inferior as I have been able to carry on this sacred literature?
A friend asked me, saying:
"You have exerted your body and mind and endured the toil of reflection regarding the teachings of Tiantai, diligently striving to uphold and propagate them;
yet, as for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, you have neither heard it transmitted from a teacher nor composed a record of its lectures."
The disciples and later students raised these doubts, saying, "Is it not said, 'Have you practiced them? We do not know how this can be.
[The Master] replied, "Alas! Is there such a doubt? Indeed, there is such a doubt, but I have an explanation.

In ancient times, when the sage Duke of Zhou assumed the regency, he established the rites and created the music, issuing commands throughout the world that were brilliant and majestic, reaching their peak during the House of Zhou."

The royal bonds grew weak and the cords of propriety were severed; rites and music fell into ruin, and proclamations went unheeded. Although Confucius possessed sage virtue, he lacked a sage position.
Thus, he edited the *Shi* and *Shu*, standardized the rites and music, assisted in the Way of the *Yi*, and abridged the records of Lu to compose the *Chunqiu*.

By this means, he replaced [the functions of] reward and punishment, causing rebellious ministers and treacherous sons to stand in awe. Zhongni had no other purpose than to continue the Way of the Duke of Zhou.

After the death of Confucius, the subtle words were lost and heterodox movements arose; it was then that Mencius appeared, expounding the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius to distance himself from Yang Zhu and Mo Di.
When the Han dynasty arose, the rulers were a mixture of hegemon and king, and Wang Mang usurped the throne through treachery;

it was then that Yang Xiong appeared, composing the *Taixuan* and the *Fayan* to expound the Way of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, and Mencius in order to remedy these evils. From the Han and Wei down to the Jin, Emperor Hui lacked the Way.

During the chaos and turmoil of the Central Plains, when systems of reward and punishment had ceased to function, Wang Tong was born in the Sui dynasty. He cultivated the Six Classics to serve as a substitute for reward and punishment;
beginning with the reign of Emperor Hui of Jin, he continued the work on the *Zhongyong* and the *Xuanxue*, thereby expounding the Way of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Mencius, and Xunzi.

When the Tang dynasty gained the empire, after Fang Xuanling and Wei Zheng had passed away, Wang Ji, Yang Jiong, Lu Zhi, and Luo Binwang produced writings of licentious extravagance that subverted and threw the orthodox tradition into disorder.

After the Way [of Confucius] had declined, Han Yu and Liu Zongxuan arose; they revered antiquity and returned to simplicity in order to expound the Way of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Mencius, Yang Xiong, and Wang Tong.
Viewed from this perspective, those of different eras acted as masters to one another. Though the ages differ, the individuals differ, and their expressions differ, the Way remains the same.
It was never heard that the Duke of Zhou personally transmitted it to Confucius, nor that Confucius personally transmitted it to Mencius. This is the case within our own Buddhist tradition as well.
The Master was likewise so. It is not heard that Mañjuśrī’s school of the Single Nature (ekaprakṛti) was transmitted face-to-face to Nāgārjuna;
nor is it heard that Nāgārjuna’s doctrine of the Three Contemplations (trivipaśyanā) was transmitted face-to-face to Huiwen.

Yet the world universally says that Nāgārjuna was the teacher of Mañjuśrī and that Huiwen was the teacher of Nāgārjuna. The Way of Nāgārjuna and Huiwen reached its culmination at Mount Nanyue and Tiantai.
Zhang Da-zhi drew forth and extended [the teachings], and later Zhanran established the school, composing his *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary*.

Although it had reached nearly two hundred years [of transmission], it was only after Jingxi [Zhiyi] refined and finalized it that it attained ultimate perfection. As for the subtle purport I personally realized while searching through the *Nirvāṇa* commentaries, it was my teacher Jingxi who revealed it to me.
Who would say there is no lineage of oral transmission? If one considers the direct face-to-face instruction...

If one were to say that the transmission of the Way can occur through personal instruction, then Xun Qing transmitted it to Li Si by face-to-face teaching, yet he served as Chancellor to the First Emperor of Qin;

or that it was transmitted to Yuan Song by face-to-face teaching, yet he flattered Emperor Wu of Zhou. To destroy the teachings of Śākya and ruin the Buddha—how could such acts constitute the transmission of the Way through personal instruction?
I consider the attainment of the intent of the ancients and the practice of the Way of the ancients to be true transmission.
In transmitting [the teachings], one does not fixate on the person's appearance nor their voice; that one does not know the reason for its beauty is what constitutes true transmission.
*Xianju bian*, Volume 16; *Xianju bian*, Volume 17.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
An Essay for Ancestors.
In the ninth year of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú era, the cyclical year being Bǐchén, the month beginning on Jǐhài, and the day falling on Línrénshēn.
On this day of the Gengyin year, I, [Name], a dharma-grandson, reverently offer this memorial of tea and medicine, kneeling before the spirit of the Grand Master, Acharya Ciguang.
Among the ancient biographies of eminent monks, it is said: "If one’s true practice remains hidden, one is lofty yet unnamed;
if one possesses little virtue yet adapts to the times, one is famous yet not lofty. That which is famous but not lofty is not worthy of record; that which is lofty..."

If names were not established, then [virtue] would not be fully realized; I have now recorded the words of the worthy and enlightened of past and present, for all consider them words of wisdom that shall not be erased for a hundred generations.
Alas! My ancestor’s insight was upright and lucid, and his practice of the Way was pure and correct. He did not flatter those in office nor associate with the vulgar of the age.
He did not employ eccentricities to cultivate a reputation, nor did he use profit to advance others. He cast aside the frivolous and the false, remaining resolute and self-contained.

Because he attained [realization] while remaining unknown to the world and his followers were truly few, the reason his magnificent achievements and lofty conduct are disseminated through the *Biographies of Monks of the Great Song* is that they were selected for their sublimity rather than their fame.
In the past, Nāgārjuna transmitted the Way of Mañjuśrī, expounding it through his words; thus, the school of the Single Nature flourished in India. Zhiyi transmitted Nāgārjuna’s [teachings].
This study was extended and developed; thus, the meaning of the "Three Contemplations" flourished in Zhendan (China). After Zhiyi passed away, Zhang’an succeeded him, followed by Zhiwei.
Zuoxi expounded and interpreted it, while Jingxi recorded and transmitted it, causing the Way to grow ever greater.
Consequently, those in later generations who entered through its gate have been few. Only our Patriarch [Zhanran] possessed a spirit that transcended the common crowd.
He manifested his talent through the clarity of his independent judgment and instructed those who came to study him so that they would surely reach the profound ultimate;

thus, those who were obstructed by the literal text or held divergent views were thereby silenced, and the teachings of Tiantai were thereby made magnificent. How could the subtle benefits he provided in secret be measured?

Furthermore, among those in the world who study Buddhism, some prioritize principle and disparage phenomena, while others prioritize phenomena and disparage principle, their outward forms and dress...
Although we are the same, what we rely upon is vastly different. My ancestors constrained themselves with the precepts and illuminated themselves with rational contemplation;
they engaged with phenomena without being mired in them, and examined principles without becoming dissipated by them. Thus, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* describes my ancestors, saying:
"At every *poṣadha*, they would secretly sprinkle [water] without ceasing," and further, "Whether one was worthy or unworthy, they invariably demonstrated the One Vehicle’s perfection."
This is what is meant by "the mental covering. Were it not for one who illuminates the Buddha’s intent and penetrates the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), who could possibly reach such a state?
At his passing, a divine light emerged from the well and celestial music resounded through the night; Zhan’an (Zhiyi) experienced a prophetic dream, and a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber.
Such were the signs of his spiritual efficacy and resonance. This was because he transmitted the Dharma with profound sincerity and benefited all beings with supreme compassion.
"How could he have come this far? My ancestor passed away at Ciguang Monastery in the third year of the Yongxi era.
After his cremation, his disciples moved to other prefectures, and his sacred relics were lodged in a private residence for over twenty years.
There, two śramaṇas named Guangjun and Baolong visited and recovered them, keeping them at Jingzhu Monastery for nearly another decade."
I, [Name], am truly base and unworthy; yet I reflect that in the past I received the Dharma from Fengxian, and Fengxian transmitted the Way to Ciguang.
Thus, I regard Ciguang as my patriarch and myself as his descendant.

Consequently, I gathered his sacred remains and interred them on the Jasper Slope of Mount Gu, constructing a stupa of piled stones to mark the site. It is neither carved nor adorned, manifesting his frugality.
It is neither circular nor square, for fear of presuming equality with the Sage. Its square exterior expresses the nature of square-extensiveness;

its circular base expresses the principle of perfect roundness. It is engraved with the eight virtues of Nirvana to manifest its function, and inscribed with the four lines of the Snowy Mountains to manifest its essence.
Thus, may those who behold it access the principle through the phenomenon and aspire to its spirit.
If we receive this transformation, will the teaching of our ancestors not remain undegenerated? Alas! It has been thirty-two years since our ancestors passed away;
is it because this degenerate age disregards the worthy and opposes righteousness that things have come to this?

Or is it that the spirits of our ancestors, having a karmic affinity with me, were waiting for me to perform their burial? This cannot be known. As the *Li* (Rituals) says: "As for one's ancestors..."
To praise one who lacks virtue is to deceive; to know of one’s goodness yet remain ignorant of it is a lack of clarity; to know of it yet fail to transmit it is a lack of benevolence.
These three things are what the gentleman finds shameful. Now that this tomb has been completed, I venture to present these meager offerings.
Having come to know his virtue and goodness, I have praised and transmitted them; truly, there is no shame in this. I humbly pray that he will graciously accept this.
A Text for Sacrificing to the Spirit of Mount Gu:
In the year of Bingchen, the ninth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era; in the month established by Wuxu, on the day Renyin, at the hour of Jisi;
I, the śramaṇa [Name], respectfully present this offering of tea and *chuan* leaves to sacrifice to the Spirit of Mount Gu.
The spirit contemplates and divinely receives the mandate of Heaven to preside over these mountains and forests, bestowing blessings upon the good and bringing calamity upon the licentious;

it harms those who are excessive and blesses those who are humble—this is the virtue of the spirit. To be accepted by it requires sincerity; to be fragrant before it requires illustrious virtue—this is the response of the spirit.

If there are virtuous people in each generation who cultivate themselves with humility, will the spirit not bless them? Or if they strive for sincerity and hope to attain illustrious virtue, will the spirit not accept their offerings?
If one does not receive blessings and offerings, how can the virtue of the deity be manifested and its response made evident?
There was a high monk of the Holy Song dynasty named Ajari Ciguang, whose conduct while alive was exemplary and whose reputation after death remains enduring;
he was truly a man of the Way among the disciples of Śākyamuni. He possessed what the Confucians call the "good person" and what they call "practicing humility. From—
From the time of his donation until now, thirty-two years have passed; his sacred remains have fallen among the common people without having been interred.
This poor monk laments that the worthy man has lost his proper place and grieves that this degenerate age lacks righteousness.
Therefore, I have spontaneously built a foundation of piled bricks upon the ridge of this mountain and carved a stone stupa to enshrine them, following the rites of the Buddha. Thus, let the stupa...
A mountain gains a point of reliance, and because of the stupa, its value increases; how could this be compared to burying the bones of an ordinary person—a ghost of one who lacks wisdom?
If this stupa remains peaceful and secure, then for a hundred generations those who behold it will know that a high monk dwelt here.
Hearing of his character, there will surely be those who desire to emulate him. Thus, the benefit to the Teaching is indeed great; such is the spirit.
Does not the virtue of this merit—of goodness and humility—become thereby even more manifest? This poor monk possesses no illustrious virtue, yet he does possess sincere sincerity.
Now that I have business at this mountain, may I dare to offer tea and *chuan* leaves as a sacrifice to the deities?
May you descend to receive them and graciously enjoy this offering.
Furthermore, the Inscription for Sacrificing to the Spirit of Mount Gu:

In the first year of the Tianxi era, the year being Ding-si, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month—the day of Gui-chou, following the new moon on the day of Gui-chou—the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan respectfully presents this offering of tea and *chuan* leaves to the spirit of the God of Mount Gu. This poor monk...
Reading the books of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, I heard of Cheng Zigao, a high official of Qi, who said to Qing Yi:
"I have heard that while alive one should be beneficial to others, and after death one should not harm others. Even if I were of no benefit to others while alive, could I, after death, harm them?
When I die, I shall choose a plot of land where no crops are grown for burial; this is for fear of obstructing others."
This is merely to till the soil; how much more so for our Buddha, who takes true stillness as his wind and pure frugality as his instruction?

Since the three realms are like an illusion and all conditions are empty, those who follow this teaching ought not to practice elaborate burials. This poor monk has achieved little in his study of the Way, yet my heart prizes what is upright and simple.
I fear that after my passing, there may be those who do not know me and who, mingling with the vulgar world, would preoccupy themselves with ostentation and luxury.

To honor his polished burial mound while inflicting injury upon wealth and people, he has instead excavated a cave on a secluded and useless ridge of this mountain to bury ceramic vessels, preparing a place for the concealment of his remains in the future.

He entrusts his final affairs to his disciples: within these mountain forests, spirits have their presiding masters; let him therefore offer sacrifices with tea and *chuan* leaves, prostrating himself in reverence.
May you graciously accept this offering.
[Text for the removal of the clay effigy:

The people have long been fond of excessive sacrifices; therefore, Confucius said, "Excessive sacrifices bring no blessing," and further stated that they are not the spirits [to whom offerings should be made].
Such sacrifices are but flattery. If the people of antiquity had truly been free from this corruption, how could the Sage Master Confucius have issued such a warning?
The customs of today are tens of thousands of times worse than those of antiquity;
in every village lane and household, they erect earthen figurines called "Land Deities" or "Five-Passing Gods," and Buddhist temples do the same. I purchased a mountain and obtained Ma'erguopo.
The site was named after agate, and the temple was likewise named after it. Beneath the eastern corridor of the temple lay these three earthen figurines;

I therefore ordered two of them removed and retained only the one designated as the "Local Deity" (Tùdì). I changed its name to "Protector of the Monastery" (Hùgālánshén) and composed this essay to inform him:
"I have heard that in the rites of sacrifice established by the sage-kings, those who bestowed laws upon the people were enshrined with sacrifices."
Those who died in the diligent performance of their duties were sacrificed to; those who stabilized the state through their labors were sacrificed to;

those who could ward off great calamities were sacrificed to; and those who could resist great afflictions were sacrificed to. As for the sun, moon, stars, and planets, they are what the people look up to with reverence;
the mountains, forests, rivers, valleys, and hills, they are from which the people obtain wealth and resources. None outside these categories are included in the sacrificial canon. Alas!
In your land, it is unheard of for earthen figurines to receive offerings; it is unheard of for them to be diligent in affairs;
and it is unheard of for them to provide stability to the state or to ward off calamities and misfortunes.

Since they do not even rank among those worthy of veneration, and furthermore possess no wealth or resources to benefit others, how could you disrupt the rites of propriety and usurp the sacrifices of the ignorant masses? In the past, during the Li Tang [Tang Dynasty]...
The Duke of Liang abolished one thousand seven hundred licentious sacrifices in the Jianghuai region, retaining only four temples:
those of Great Yu at Kuaiji, Zi Qu at Qiantang, Taibo at Gusu, and Ji Zha at Bilin.
I know that the Duke of Liang truly followed this Way in his conduct. Furthermore, the name "Five Lords" (Wutong) originates from our Buddhist tradition, referring to the heavens...

The divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the supernormal power of bodily mastery—these five are possessed by those who have attained the celestial or rishi states.
Because their afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been eliminated, they lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) penetrations.

For the common folk to surreptitiously appropriate these names to designate such spectral apparitions and malevolent demons—is this not an error? Thus, since the names lack reality, they furthermore do not belong to the class of beings entitled to the sacrificial canon.
In that case, how could your earthen figurines possibly hope for such good fortune here? Furthermore, I have heard that the King establishes seven sacrifices for the common people:
those to the Lord of Fate (Sì-mìng), Zhōng-lòu, the National Gate (Guó-mén), the National Roads (Guó-háng), Tàiyàn, the Door (Hù), and the Hearth (Zào).
The King himself establishes these seven sacrifices, while the feudal lords establish five sacrifices for their states: those to the Lord of Fate and Zhōng-lòu.
It is said that at the national gates, on the national roads, and for the public *li* spirits, the feudal lords establish five sacrifices;

the great officers establish three sacrifices, namely for the clan *li* spirits, the gates, and the roads; the lower officials of the rank of *shi* establish two sacrifices, namely for the gates and the roads;
and the common officers and commoners establish one sacrifice, either for the household door or for the hearth. Now, you earthen figurines are not those for whom such sacrifices are intended.

If that is so, does the doctrine of the "land" not resemble the ritual of the Central Chamber? I reply: the Central Chamber presides over the hall and the domestic quarters, and thus it may bear some resemblance;
yet even that does not extend to the sacrifices of the common people. Now, for the people to sacrifice to their own land is contrary to the rites.
Furthermore, I have heard that the instructions of women do not pass beyond the inner gates; they do not roam the courtyards during the day, and when they walk at night, they do so with torches.
"Then for a statue of a woman to sit alongside a deity and oversee affairs—is this not 'the hen governing the dawn'?
This is an extreme injury to education and harm to righteousness, unfit to serve as a model. Judging from this, it is clear that a statue of a woman should likewise not be retained.
I am a follower of Śākyamuni; our Buddha has established a precept that regarding the grounds of a *ārāma* (monastery), [one must not allow such things]..."
He established a shrine for it and offered daily sacrifices, calling it the "Protector of the Monastery" (Huguālánshén).

If this is so, would it not be appropriate to change the name of the local deity to "Protector of the Monastery"? Alas! I study Buddhism to cultivate my mind and study Confucianism to govern my person;
how could I dare to follow what is contrary to propriety or employ erroneous names? If the spirit has any numinous power, it must surely understand me.
After the images had been removed for over a month, a disciple came to see me and said, "Although I was charged with destroying them, I privately feared they might bring about calamity.
Now that more than a month has passed and no harm has occurred, your wisdom is indeed clear.
May I venture to suggest removing the statues of those who protect the monastery (gārala-pālaka) so as to provide more space for the monks' quarters? I replied, "That will not do. I..."
As for discarding those two [practices], it is to eliminate what is contrary to propriety and involves assuming false names;
as for retaining this one [practice], it is to follow the Buddha’s regulations in order to repay his grace. Even if those two were to cause ten thousand harms, I would still discard them;
even if this one could never cause harm, I would firmly retain it. Furthermore, I am dwelling here in peaceful harmony with you all.
I find rest here, I discourse on the Way here, and I establish my person here; thus, the earth’s kindness toward me is not small.
Therefore, I have retained this space of ten *fangzhang* to daily honor its sacrifices as a way to repay that virtue. How could this be called "fearing calamity and seeking fortune"?
If even the Buddha were without established rites, I would still feel it appropriate to offer him sacrifice, let alone when such rites do exist. How could I, because of his [non-existence],...?
"Can one bring calamity upon it and yet deceive it? How could one bear to seize away even a space of ten square feet?
It would suffice merely to repair and maintain it. Alas! Is it only in serving the spirits that this is so? It is the same in serving human beings. Let my young disciple take note of this.
The disciple withdrew and carried out the repairs; thereafter, his offerings of food and incense were increasingly reverent day by day.
A Self-Commemorative Inscription for Master Zhongyong (Composed on the seventeenth day of the second month; he passed away on the nineteenth).
In the year [blank], the month [blank], I respectfully offer this libation of clouds, mountains, wind, and moon before the spirit of Master Zhongyong.
O Spirit, you take the primordial permanence of the Dharma-realm as your foundation and the wondrous nature of the precious orb as your essence; therein, movement and stillness do not exist.
In the primordial state, how could there be any traces of coming or going?

Yet, when the seven apertures were bored and Chaos died, when the six sense-faculties were divided and the spiritual essence dispersed, it caused you to perceive your own mind as distinct from external objects.
You cling to the duality of life and death; thus you are tossed about beyond cessation, shrouded in darkness beyond clarity.

Zhao, I have once wished to cause you to return to the state of Chaos (the term "Chaos" originates from the *Zhuangzi*, but while I employ the words, I do not employ the intent; the words are near while the principle is far, and they cannot be made uniform).
To return to clarity and brilliance within the non-illusory Dharma, one must provisionally formulate illusory teachings.
Yet, if even the non-illusory does not exist, how could illusory dharmas possibly exist? You, Zhongyongzi, have also subtly grasped this essential meaning. Since you have received it...
Since those born of illusion must inevitably undergo illusory death, I entrust myself to this illusory body and suffer this illusory illness;
thus, I dictate these illusory words so that my illusory disciple may take up the illusory brush to compose this illusory text as a pre-emptive offering for you, the illusory Zhongyongzi.
Furthermore, I wish to cause infinite beings to know that all phenomena are like illusions. If it is thus, then the Illusory Samādhi is present.
Alas! Even samādhi is like an illusion. May you enjoy [this offering].
*Xianju bian*, Volume 17;
