*Discourse on the Residual Effects of Good and Evil*, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
The *Yì* says: "In families that accumulate goodness, there will surely be a surplus of blessings; in families that accumulate evil, there will surely be a surplus of calamity. (Old Text)
It is said that good and evil extend to one's descendants; hence the terms "residual calamity" and "residual blessing. Yet the world universally doubts this.
Now, Gou Gao accumulated evil yet had the residual blessings of Shun and Yu, while Yao and Shun accumulated goodness yet had the residual calamities of Zhu and Jun.
How can such sacred words lack corroboration? To use uncorroborated words as instruction for people is to mislead them.
To turn away from evil and double one's goodness—could this possibly not be the intention of the Sage?

Thus, Niu Sengru composed the "Treatise on the Exhaustion of Good and Evil," asserting that accumulated goodness brings blessings to the person and accumulated non-goodness brings calamity to the person, with neither leaving a remainder.
While the principle is admirable, how can it contradict the scriptures of the Sage? The Sage speaks of a "remainder," whereas Sengru speaks of "no remainder."
Is this not a reversal? When I examine the words and the intent of the Sage, they are like gazing at the blue sky and beholding the bright sun—how could they not be clear?

Yet, because the muddled expositions of former scholars have clouded and obscured them, those among the monastic and secular elites who possess talent often fail to see the Sage’s intent and remain deluded by his words.
I shall therefore summarize and set them forth: as for the matter of lingering retribution...
The doctrine of "remaining blessings" (yùqìng) pertains to oneself rather than to one's descendants. Why is this so?

Furthermore, when a scholar practices benevolence and righteousness and fulfills loyalty and filial piety, this is what is called "accumulating goodness. How could such a person merely enjoy fortune for a single lifetime?

In truth, it is to leave behind a virtuous reputation for a hundred generations. To leave behind a virtuous reputation for a hundred generations—is this not precisely "remaining blessing"? As for those who are rebellious and perverse...
Those who are cruel and murderous are said to accumulate evil; how could they merely bring calamity upon themselves in a single morning?
They also leave behind a shameful name for a hundred generations. Is leaving behind a shameful name for a hundred generations not a lingering consequence?
Furthermore, as for the greatest accumulation of goodness, was it not that of Yao and Shun? To this day, people attribute the goodness of the entire world to them, yet the goodness of Yao and Shun—
It may not necessarily reach such an extreme; therefore it is said: "To bestow bounty widely and relieve the masses—even Yao and Shun found this difficult.
Now, that all the world's goodness is attributed [to them] is proof of their remaining blessings. As for the accumulation of great evil, was it not Jie and Zhou?
Yet even to this day, while the world's evils are attributed to them, the extent of Jie and Zhou's actual wickedness may not have been as such.
Since this is the ultimate [of evil], it is said that the wickedness of Zhou was not as extreme as this.
Now, to attribute all the evils of the world to him is the evidence of his lingering calamity. Alas! The purport of the sages' words is subtle yet manifest.
Because former scholars have erroneously transmitted them, those who seek to cast aside the old interpretations have drifted away and forgotten their way back.

Although I, Ru, know that good and evil cannot be extended to one's descendants, I have failed to examine the errors of those who speak thus and have remained wavering regarding the words of the Sage;
therefore, I discuss this to block such deceptive arguments, lest others should think otherwise, awaiting only the gentleman.
The Duke of Zhou’s Punishment of Bo Qin:

The *Liji* (Book of Rites), *Zengzi Wen*, states: "When the Duke of Zhou acted as regent and governed from the throne, he applied the laws for the heir apparent to Bo Qin, desiring that King Cheng understand the之道 (dao) of father and son, ruler and subject, and elder and younger.
When King Cheng committed a transgression, [the Duke of Zhou] would then administer a flogging."
Regarding why Bo Qin was used to demonstrate to King Cheng the way of a crown prince, Zheng Kangcheng said:
"If one strikes Bo Qin because of King Cheng’s transgression, it will be sufficient to move and instruct him. I, however, maintain that there was no such matter of the Duke of Zhou striking Bo Qin;
it is likely that those who transmitted the account were excessive, and the Han Confucians subsequently recorded it falsely. This was not the teaching of the Sage Master, Zhongni.

Regarding what has been recorded here, Kong Cheng (Dong Zhongshu) followed suit and added arbitrary annotations; he was not among the seventy disciples who received the Sage’s teachings directly from his presence.
Allow me to attempt a discussion of this: Duke Zhou was a Great Sage. In governing his own household, he possessed the way to govern a state;
thus, he was able to serve as a model for the four seas and provide instruction for ten thousand generations. Punishments must be based on guilt, and rewards must be based on merit.
To not fear the powerful and to not insult the widowed or the orphaned—this is the concern of a sage. If he acts thus toward the people, how much more so toward his own children?
Therefore, when the sage’s intention is sincere, his mind becomes correct; when his mind is correct, his person is cultivated; when his person is cultivated, his family is harmonized;
when his family is harmonized, the state is well-governed; and when the state is well-governed, the world is at peace.
Furthermore, Bo Qin was the very personification of the legacy; if he were to receive lashes for no fault, it would mean that the Duke of Zhou was striking himself.
If King Cheng committed ten transgressions in a day, Bo Qin would receive ten lashes; if he committed a hundred, Bo Qin would receive a hundred.
Alas! That Bo Qin should receive lashes for no fault—how extreme is this madness and excess, beyond all appeal!
The Duke of Zhou knew that Bo Qin was innocent, yet he struck him; how extreme was his deception of his own heart!
Now, Gao Yao’s cruelty toward Shun was not as severe as this. Why is this so? It is because Gao Yao truly did not recognize Shun’s worthiness and sagehood;
he merely mistreated him out of the natural aversion of his feelings. The Duke of Zhou, however, knew that Bo Qin was innocent, and furthermore—this is not [the case with Gao Yao].

To claim that the wickedness of one's feelings is merely a matter of striking King Wu with a stick to intimidate him because he had committed a transgression would be far more cruel than [the treatment of] Gu Sou;
how could this possibly be the intention of a sage?
On the Discourse of Life and Death Being Without Good or Evil:

To Master Zhongyongzi. When he lay ill upon his bed, his hands and feet were about to become rigid and his spirit was on the verge of departing, yet he remained serene and free from distress, strengthening himself through the Way.
When a guest came to inquire after his illness, he rose from his seat to avoid the couch.
They shook hands and spoke, saying: "Of all that is great in what one loves, is there none greater than life? Of all that is great in what one hates, is there none greater than death?
Observing you, it seems you have no particular love for life, nor do you seem to have any particular hatred for death.
I am perplexed and venture to ask about the Middle Way. He sighed deeply and said: "Great indeed is your question! Stay, and I shall tell you. How rustic you are!"
The people of the world only know to loathe death, yet do not know to loathe life—is this not a cause for great lament?
What is the reason? Now, branches must have roots, and currents must have sources. Alas! Is it not the case that life is the root and source of death?
Since there is life, how can there be no death? Life is the beginning of man; death is the end of things.
Since there are people who possess a beginning and an end, there is consequently birth and death. Thus, the Nirvāṇa-sūtra says: "The sisters Virtue and Darkness follow one another;
a wise master accepts neither. This means that by not accepting birth, one is free from death.
Furthermore, spring must be followed by winter, and day must be followed by night. If one loves spring and hates winter, or loves the day and [hates the night]...
Is it not truly foolish to distinguish between "evil nights"? Birth and death are just like spring and winter, or day and night;
what is there to prefer or loathe? Thus Zhuang Zhou said: "Take non-being as the head, take life as the spine, and take death as the hips.
Therefore, one knows that existence and non-existence, life and death, are but a single entity. How could one preserve the spine while discarding the hips? This is my view.
Because of this contemplation, I have no preference for life and no aversion to death. Furthermore, I am now forty-seven years old;
compared to Yanzi, who did not say that his life was granted by Heaven, even if I were to reach the age of ninety-eight, I would still be but a premature child compared to those like Rong and Peng.
High and low define one another, and long and short lean against each other—this is the nature of all things.
How could there be such a thing as knowing when to stop? I lack the virtue of Yan Hui, yet my longevity exceeds his;
how could I dare harbor a sense of insufficiency? However, these are all doctrines concerning the realm within; they are not the principles of my realm beyond.
Were I to speak of them, I fear that those of middling capacity would be caught at the brink of life and death, while those of inferior capacity would laugh at them in derision.
The guest said, "I wish to hear your discourse on that which lies beyond the realm, so as to dispel my ignorance and parsimony.

I replied: "The principle of Heaven is quiescent, possessing no trace whatsoever of arising or ceasing. It is through the movement of deluded sentiments that the marks of coming and going are perceived.
It is like using clear eyes to gaze upon a bright, cloudless sky; there is only a single, pure void, entirely free from blemish or obscuration. Should one stare with fixed eyes..."

If one exerts oneself in viewing [phenomena], delusory flowers arise in confusion. Since these flowers have arising, they also have ceasing. The ignorant person, without cause, delights in the arising of flowers and loathes their ceasing;
yet they do not realize that flowers are fundamentally non-existent from the start. Their attachment to likes and dislikes is merely a futile exertion. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"All this arises from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature, and instead employing various delusions."
"Because these perceptions are not real, there is cyclic existence. Furthermore, it is said: "Since there is not even birth, what can one call cessation? And again:
"Birth, cessation, going, and coming are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. This is precisely what is meant by this.
For this reason, when I observe it thus, I feel no joy in birth and no fear in death. The guest said: "How beautiful are these words! They are indeed most appropriate."
"To return to the singular, essential meaning, there is no duality; I shall receive your words and practice them accordingly.
Yet, between your two explanations, whom am I to follow? I replied: "The Buddhas always rely upon the Two Truths when preaching the Dharma; how could I dare to contravene this?

My former explanation was the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and my latter explanation was the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). I have sought the answer by means of both the conventional and the ultimate."
I observed that in life there is nothing truly worth rejoicing over, and in death there is nothing truly worth loathing.

Furthermore, these two views have often contended within my breast, yet the ultimate truth has prevailed. I thought to myself: "Whichever of these two views I attain will be sufficient to govern my mind.
Although Mencius said, "Fish are what I love, and bear's paws are also what I love," [the latter must be chosen].
Furthermore, these two cannot both be abandoned; one must choose between the fish of conventional truth and the bear’s paw of ultimate truth.
Would it not be a matter of great beauty if you could truly renounce the fish of conventional truth to eat the bear’s paw of ultimate truth? You must strive for this!
The guest was suddenly startled and looked up, saying, "I have never heard of such a thing. How could I dare not contemplate it day and night so that I may reach this Way? Thereupon—
He prostrated twice beneath the bed, followed along the wall and departed. (On the fifth day of the first month in the first year of the Qiánxìng era, my son Zhōngyōng fell ill and did not recover;
I then dictated this text orally and commanded my disciple Yúnqīng to record it.)

The *Fushan Huoyin Lun* (Treatise on Blessings for the Good and Calamities for the Lecherous) states: Regarding the saying that blessings attend the good and calamities attend the lecherous, some argue that when verified by actual events, there are many instances where performing good brings calamity and committing evil results in fortune.
Is it because ghosts and spirits lack spiritual efficacy? Or is it because the *Geyan* (Apophthegms) are close to being false?
Therefore, this treatise analyzes these matters to demonstrate them to those who are ignorant: what the world calls "fortune" refers to wealth, nobility, high status, peace and health, and long life;
what it calls "calamity" refers to poverty, lowliness, obscurity, execution, and an early death.
If one loathes that wicked people enjoy wealth and nobility while virtuous people dwell in poverty and lowliness, then one will repeatedly turn back and harbor doubts.
To insist that ghosts and spirits lack spiritual efficacy is a statement bordering on slander; such is the sentiment of the common man.
Is what the gentleman calls "calamity" and "blessing" any different? For one who practices benevolence, there is the manifest fame of great harmony that descends for ten billion years;
even children and women know to value and cherish it—how could this not be blessing?
How could it be that being poor, lowly, and obscure, or suffering execution and an early death in a single lifetime constitutes a calamity?
Bo Yi and Shu Qi were indeed poor and lowly, yet they were called "the virtuous men Bo Yi and Shu Qi. Bi Gan was indeed executed, yet it was said that "the Shang had three men of benevolence.

Yan Hui was indeed short-lived, yet it was said that "Hui for three months did not depart from benevolence. By this, one knows that it is not merely the circumstances of poverty, obscurity, execution, or premature death that define a person's worth.
If, in future generations, people hear one's name and love one as they do their own parents, this is what is called blessed goodness.

Conversely, for those who are unkind, there are manifest names of extreme evil that descend for billions of years; even children and women know to despise and loathe them—how could this not be calamity?
How could it be merely a matter of wealth, status, honor, well-being, prosperity, and longevity in this single lifetime?

Fuyang Shang received the state of Qi; he was truly wealthy, noble, and exalted, yet he was called "the solitary man Shou" (Du Fu Shou), and it was further said that he "boasted of virtue though he possessed none.

His peace, security, longevity, and old age were beyond measure, yet all were deemed unkind and unprincipled, causing those who heard his name in later generations to despise him as they would a beast. This is what is meant by "calamity for the licentious. Alas!
Is it not better that one’s illustrious name endure for billions of years, causing people to revere one accordingly, rather than a single lifetime of wealth and honor?
Is it not better that one’s evil name endure for billions of years, causing people to despise one accordingly, rather than a single lifetime of poverty and low status?
Therefore, what the world calls fortune and misfortune consists of things small and immediate; what the gentleman calls fortune and misfortune consists of things lasting and profound.

"One who attains the great attains it through the distant. As the *Shi* says, "The joyful and benevolent gentleman seeks fortune without crookedness," which I take to mean seeking the great through the distant.
Someone asked: "When Jizi set forth the five blessings, do you have nothing to take from that? I replied:

"Who would say that one who possesses wealth and longevity through benevolence and righteousness does not attain them? But as for one who possesses wealth through a lack of benevolence—how could that be considered a blessing?"
"As for nobility, I have no interest in it; what Confucius called 'wealth and honor obtained through unrighteousness' is, to me, like floating clouds.
Mencius said: "To occupy a high position through a lack of benevolence is to spread one's ugliness above the multitude.
Moreover, among the Five Blessings of Jizi, the fifth is 'delighting in virtue. Since what one delights in is virtue, yet one obtains wealth [through its opposite], how can this be right?"
To live long, be healthy and peaceful, and complete one’s natural lifespan—is this not truly magnificent? Mencius said, "Cultivate the rank of Heaven, and the rank of men will follow.
Therefore, I take no interest in those who attain wealth, honor, health, and a full life by mere luck without possessing virtue.
Thus, what I previously called the "greatness" or "smallness," and the "distance" or "nearness" of blessings, is contained within the Five Constants (the Five Virtues). Alas, Grand Chancellor Wu!
Bi Yi received bribes from the world and was wealthy and noble in his time; yet people to this day despise him, surely calling him a slanderer and a villain.
Wu Yuan offered loyal counsel and met death in his time;
yet people to this day honor him, surely calling him a loyal and worthy man, such that he is enshrined in the sacrificial codes, never ceasing to partake of blood offerings.
The evidence for blessings upon the virtuous and calamities upon the lewd is as clear as day—how very clear it is!
If one practices goodness and enjoys wealth and honor, while another commits evil and suffers poverty and low status, why even bother to debate it? It is self-evident.
*The Collected Works of Reclusive Dwelling*, Volumes 18 and 19.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
The Biography of Zhongyongzi (Part One).
Zhongyongzi’s given name was Zhiyuan; "Wuwai" was his courtesy name. Having studied the teachings of the Western Sage, his surname followed that of his teacher.
He once polished his speech and conduct in an effort to approximate the Mean, fearing that even in moments of haste or distress he might suddenly lapse.

He forgot his original name and instead styled himself Zhongyong (The Mean), so his friends followed suit in addressing him as such. Someone asked, "As for the meaning of 'The Mean,' it originated from the Confucian school;
you, a follower of the Buddha, are merely plundering and appropriating it—how can you claim it?

He replied, "Confucianism and Buddhism differ in their terminology but are unified in their principles. There is none among them that does not transform the people, leading them to cultivate goodness and distance themselves from evil."

Confucianism is the teaching that adorns the body; therefore, it is called the "External Canon" (waidian). Buddhism is the teaching that cultivates the mind; therefore, it is called the "Internal Canon" (neidian).
Since there are only body and mind, the distinction between internal and external is established. How could the simple folk of the world transcend body and mind?
Were it not for these two teachings, by what means could they be transformed? Alas! Confucianism and Buddhism—how are they different? Or rather, how are they one?

They act as a mutual front and rear; thus, in the lands of the barbarians where the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius is not practiced, it is likewise unheard of that they practice the Way of the Śākya.

Because people are limited by the boundaries of this realm and find the records of the world’s registers unrecorded and human sentiments unfathomable, they gravely slander our teaching, claiming it may be abandoned. There are those in the world who are hindered by...
The followers of Śākyamuni have long magnified their own teachings and often treat Confucianism with derision;
yet how could they know that without the teaching of Zhongni, the state would have no means to be governed, the family no means to be at peace, and the person no means to be secure?
If the state is not governed, the family is not at peace, and the person is not secure, by what means could the Way of the Śākya be practiced? Therefore, I cultivate my person through Confucianism.
To govern the mind, one must study Buddhism with earnest devotion, wearing it upon one's breast and never daring to be lax or negligent, for even then one fears not reaching the Way;
how much more so if one abandons it? Alas! To love Confucianism while hating Buddhism, or to prize Buddhism while disparaging Confucianism—how could such a person hope to approximate the Middle Way?
Someone rose from his seat and said, "As for the Confucians' clarification of the Middle Way, I have heard it in the 'Zhongyong' chapter."
Shi said, "I have not yet heard of the 'Exposition of the Mean' (*Zhongyong*). You should briefly explain it to me. The Master said, "Sit, and I shall tell you.
What Shi calls the 'Mean' (*zhong*) is what Nāgārjuna refers to as the meaning of the 'Middle Way' (*madhyamā-pratipad*). He asked, 'What is its meaning?
[The Master] replied, 'As for all phenomena (*dharmas*), they are transformations of the single mind. Since the mind has no fixed form, how could phenomena exist? "

The more it is lost, the more it exists; this is because its nature is inherently complete. The more it is preserved, the more it vanishes; this is because its substance is not something that can be grasped as an entity.
It is neither lost nor preserved; herein the meaning of the Middle Way is manifest. These three aspects cannot be divided if one analyzes them, yet they cannot be conflated if one synthesizes them.

They pervade the ten directions without being expansive, and span the three periods of time without being profound. They are utterly浑浑 (mysterious and profound) and 灝灝 (vast and boundless)—such is the state of all sentient beings.

Those who are deluded are those who fail to realize this; the Buddhas are those who have awakened to this. Alas! How could the myriad words spoken by the Sage (Śākyamuni) ever surpass this essential meaning?
Since the Sage departed, the subtle words have been lost, and those who study them cling to the branches while abandoning the root, or draw from the stream while forgetting the source.
Consequently, some are swept away into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while others are stuck in existence (*bhava*). Those swept away into emptiness claim that all things have utterly vanished.
When there is nothing attained and all is tranquil, when there is not even a trace of distinction—who can be called ordinary and who can be called sage?

Yet when they fall into error, they become confused about cause and effect, muddled regarding good and evil, and abandon the precepts and moral principles. Those who are stuck in existence stubbornly cling to it and manifest their attachment to the dharmas of existence.
How could the ordinary person then be the sage? How could the self then be the other? Such is the nature of their failure.

To rigidly fixate on self and others so they cannot be shifted, to miredly resent enemies and kin so they cannot be reconciled, to be bound by proximate teachings while losing sight of distant principles—this is called "floating in emptiness" or "adhering to existence.
Which of these is superior? It is said that floating in emptiness is an excess, while adhering to existence is a deficiency.
Is it then better to be empty? No; excess is like deficiency. Only the Middle Way is superior. May I venture to ask about this Middle Way?
The Way says: When it is said that something exists, it vanishes into non-existence; who then can say it exists?
When it is said that something does not exist, it manifests with distinct forms; who then can say it does not exist? Thus, there is the attainment of not departing from non-existence:

resentment and kinship are equalized, things and self are harmonized, the immediate teachings are made universal, and the ultimate principle is reached. There is also the attainment of not departing from existence: [the above distinctions are realized].
Therein causality is clarified, good and evil are distinguished, the precepts and regulations are applied, and ritual propriety and righteousness are cultivated.
How great indeed is the Middle Way! Is it not the name for that which wondrously encompasses all phenomena? Is it not what is called the intrinsic nature?

If one truly realizes this, then even emptiness and non-existence will have no attachment within the center; how could there be any attachment at all? Alas! Is the great malady of the world anything other than grasping?
"Confucians and Buddhists slander one another, and those who hold to existence and non-existence condemn each other;
therefore, I have styled myself 'Zhongyong' (The Mean) to rectify myself and avoid blame. Someone said, "Excellent! Excellent! May you thus attain success. He bowed twice and departed.
The Biography of Zhongchun, the Son of the Mean.

When Zhongchun was born, his speech was such that he immediately understood filial piety and fraternal duty; his parents regarded him as somewhat extraordinary and did not let him mingle with ordinary children.
He once used water moistened with plant juices to draw characters on stones to practice writing, and he gathered flowers to arrange them.
He considered it a mere pretense to lecture and instruct others, speaking only of filial piety toward parents and harmony among brothers.
Yet he possessed a fervent ambition that transcended the mundane; his parents could not oppose him, so he renounced the world to become a Buddhist follower.

At the age of eight, he received full ordination at Longxing Temple in Qiantang—which is now Dazhong Xiangfu Temple. By fifteen, he had a subtle understanding of the *Sāo* and *Yā* poems and took a liking to them.

He composed twenty-one *lüshi* (regulated poems) in the Tang style. Having received the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius from his master, he took their Way as his model and composed literary works to instruct the world.
Once, while suffering from illness, he engaged in self-reproach, saying: "You, son of a Buddhist, have already shaved your hair and disfigured your physical form;

yet you do not practice the teachings of Śākyamuni, but instead yearn for Confucian learning. To forget your roots and turn your back on righteousness—how could this truly be called following the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius?"
This is the essential purport [of our teachings]. You should for now study Buddhism, and later study Confucianism as a supplement; you must consider this carefully.

At that time, Dharma Master Shiyuan was transmitting the method of the Three Contemplations (sanguan) of the Great Master Zhiyi at Fengxian Temple. I carried my books on a pole and went there to join him, remaining among the ranks of the youth for three years.
When the Master passed away, I subsequently left the community to live in seclusion; sometimes my clothing was worn out, and sometimes my provisions were exhausted.
Exhausting my efforts through illness, I have diligently studied the sutras and śāstras, exploring their meanings and gaining realization within my own mind;
yet I do not prize ostentation. When others called me foolish and taciturn, I heard them say: "In the study of the Way, it is valued that one reaches the source and stills the mind.
If one flaunts one's abilities and boasts of one's understanding, desiring others to purchase it, I am not such a person."

Like a traveling merchant or a seated peddler, he once lamented that since the passing of Master Jingxi, many of the subtle words and profound principles of the Tiantai school had fallen into ruin and remained unrecovered;
furthermore, though there were those who practiced, those whose explanations deviated from the Way and contravened righteousness were likewise numerous.
Thereupon, he devoted himself to the task of editing and correction, harboring a firm resolve to provide support for the tradition, ultimately producing some one million characters.
When I spoke of broadening the Way, someone said to me: "Since Jingxi has passed away, does the understanding not reside in you?
Is your reputation and conduct merely comparable to Jingxi’s, or are they as far apart as the Yellow River and the Han? I replied: "As for understanding, it is not yet there;
but as for reputation and conduct, it is so, it is so. When people criticized my writings, my disciples informed me, and I [responded].
He said, "Wen Zhongzi once remarked: 'If the wise criticize me, I shall offer refined words in apology; but if the foolish criticize me, what shall I do?
Furthermore, I intend to uphold the Way of the Sages to provide a subtle and moistening influence upon people.
If my words are correct, there will surely be those like me in future generations who will cherish them; if they are incorrect, they will be extinguished like ashes before long."

"Alas! Does my Way merely consist in contending for victory with those who bark like dogs? When those reckless fellows once slandered me from behind, they subsequently turned their faces toward me and came to visit;
I received them with the utmost courtesy. When people asked me the reason for this, I replied: 'The guest represents Heaven and the host represents Earth.
To fail to receive a guest with courtesy is to violate Heaven. To violate Heaven brings misfortune; moreover, it would be to return their own slanders upon me.'"
"Is the fruit real, or is it empty? If it is real, I shall change it; that person is merely instructing me and is thus my teacher—what cause for anger is there?
If it is empty, I can laugh at it as a source of joy—what reason for resentment?
Furthermore, words of disparagement or praise are like echoes in a valley."
The Biography of Zhongyongzi, Part II:
Zhongyongzi was thirteen years old when he dreamed of following the Buddha into the sea. When summer ended, he set out on his journey;

they traveled together into a vast wilderness where there were creatures resembling the ghosts and spirits depicted in worldly paintings. The Buddha bestowed instruction upon him for a long time. At the age of thirty, he sought nirvana.
In the *Jingguo* (Scripture on the Fruits of Karma), there is an account of subduing the spirits and demons of the wilderness;

furthermore, it records that when two śramaṇas were composing a record of their dreams, they said that Nāgārjuna and Avalokiteśvara had conversed with them for a long time, and I therefore wrote a piece titled "Record of Dreams.

Some have said to me: "Dreams are but the wandering of the soul occurring by chance; how can they be real? Why use them to write? They are merely human aberrations. To this, I replied: [The text continues: "The Buddha said... (the remainder of the passage follows).
Alas! All phenomena are empty and one; all are like dreams. A hundred-year life is a great dream, and a single night is a small dream.
If a great dream can be recorded, why should a small dream not be recordable? If one knows that a small dream is illusory, why not realize that a great dream is likewise illusory?
My recording of this dream has a specific purpose; those who would blame me for it— [The text ends here.]
"Is this recording a dream? Only one who truly knows me would record such a dream. In my instruction of later students, though they frequently disobey me, I continue to instruct them.
Should any among them depart, I have not a single word to detain them, saying: 'To welcome those who come without rejecting them, and not to pursue those who leave—this is the Way of antiquity.
Yet, when provoked by certain events, I am unable to maintain forbearance; only after a moment do I feel regret."
He did not like to compare appearances, nor did he like to inquire about one’s destiny, nor did he like to select auspicious days.

Thereupon, he composed the "Treatise on Blessings for the Good and Calamities for the Wicked" and the "Discourse on Selecting Days" to correct the customs of his time. He never entered the gates of those who held official rank, saying:
"Dantai Maiming never went to Yan’s chamber except for public business; how much less should I, a man outside the conventional world, seek to know [the opinions of] those in office?"
"To hold office is merely the business of a scholar; I have already donned the dyed robes [of a monk], so how could I dare to disrupt the vocations of the four classes of people?
It is not that I am arrogant, but I have long been afflicted by illness and have styled myself a 'sick man,' even composing a 'Biography of the Sick Man.

Though I am emaciated, wasted, and lean, I do not tire of expounding the Way to instruct others, from the scriptures of the Tripitaka down to the teachings of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Xunzi, Mencius, and Yang Xiong."

The books of Wang Tong were often read by him while walking and embraced while sitting; he composed the "Seven Admonitions" (*Qizhen*) and had them engraved upon stones at his seat to admonish himself.
Residing on the southern slope of Mount Gu, with thatched huts and bamboo beds, he lived in serene contentment, saying, "Between luxury and frugality, I would rather choose the latter;
this is where I devote my efforts. He once said to his disciples, "After my death..."
Do not perform an elaborate burial to wrong me; do not select a special site to build a stupa to misrepresent me;

do not petition those in authority for an inscription to falsely praise me. You should simply bury two joined earthenware vessels and set up a stone marker before them, recording only the year, month, name, and title.
I have heard that when a person performs good deeds, if one does not yet praise them, it is like leaving a disease untreated.
Not yet recovered from his illness, when he saw the unrighteousness of others, he failed to offer them counsel, as if his own ailment were still not healed.
When a guest spoke words that were unreasonable, he remained silent and gave no reply. At the age of forty-one, he wrote the *Lun* (Discourse), which states:
"The virtue of the Middle Way has been rare among men for a long time; it is truly difficult to find one who can call themselves a follower of the Middle Way and actually practice it."
The world may be deceitful, yet I take their deceit as my own.

*Exhortation to Study*, Part I (with Preface).
The nature of ordinary people knows that they ought to apply themselves to learning, yet some fall away from it; thus, this "Exhortation to Study" was written.
Alas! Learning must not be neglected for even a moment, and the Way must not be departed from for even a moment. Since the Way is clarified through learning, can learning be neglected?
Since the realm of the sages and worthies is reached through the Way, can the Way be departed from? Thus, if the learning of ordinary people is not negligent, they may reach the level of the worthy;
if the learning of the worthy is not negligent, they may reach the level of the sage. (As was the case with) Ran Qiu.
In this study, one can reach the level of Yan Yuan but fall short of embodying the full form [of the Way] only because the heart-mind becomes weary;
thus it is said: "It is not that I do not delight in your Way, but my strength is insufficient. The Master said: "The worry for those who lack strength is that they will abandon the Way midway;
now you have merely drawn a line [to limit yourself]. Yan Yuan’s study could have reached the level of the Master, yet he did not equal the Sage Teacher.
He died young; had he not died, how could we know that he was not the equal of Zhongni? It was because his learning was never indolent.
Therefore it is said: "The son of the Yan family loved learning; unfortunately, he died young. Now, however, he is gone. Someone asked:
"Does a sage learn? He replied: "What words are these! What words are these! Between the common people and the worthy, there is still a difference..."

If one knows how to learn, how could even a sage be indolent in his studies? For Heaven, though characterized by hardness, is able to learn flexibility from Earth, and thus does not violate the four seasons;
Earth, though characterized by softness, is able to learn hardness from Heaven, and thus is able to produce metal and stone.
Yang, in its process of generation, likewise learns severity and destruction from Yin, and thus the withered grasses die. Yin... [is likewise able to learn growth from Yang].

In the midst of this austere and destructive [season], there is also the study of generating through Yang; thus, shepherd’s purse and wheat sprout. Now, is this Heaven? Is it Earth? Is it Yang? Is it Yin?
They study one another without ceasing, and thereby all things are perfected. If Heaven did not study flexibility, it would have no means to cover;
if Earth did not study firmness, it would have no means to support; if Yang did not study Yin, it would have no means... [to function].
"To open the yin without learning from the yang provides no means to close it. The Sage has nothing else [but this]; he simply acts according to heaven and earth, yin and yang.
These four matters are what one learns without indolence. Where would the Sage find indolence? Someone rose from their seat and said, "I am humble and ignorant;
I am fortunate that you have dispelled my delusions. I wish to hear about the Sage’s learning of the *Zhongyong*. Master Zhongzi said, "Sit down again. I shall speak."
I tell you, does your book not say: "Only the madman who can maintain mindfulness becomes a sage; only the sage who fails to maintain mindfulness becomes mad"?
Therefore, even in moments of haste or distress, a sage never ceases to mind and study the Right Way.
The Master was a Great Sage, towering above his peers and transcending his kind; since the birth of mankind, there has been no one like the Master.
That he entered the Grand Ancestral Temple and questioned about every matter was learning from the temple attendants;

that when three people walked together, he would choose the good among them and follow it was learning from his fellow travelers; and that upon entering the Zhou state, he questioned Laozi about the rites was learning from the Archivist.
Was it that the sagehood of Zhongni was not equal to that of the temple attendants, the fellow travelers, or the Archivist?
It is because the Sage feared that if one did not contemplate the Right Path yet still studied it, one would end up becoming狂 (mad). Therefore he said:
"If you possess the loyalty and good faith of Qiu, though you may not possess his love for learning, you will be like him. Someone asked: "The Sage is born with knowledge;
why must he study? [The Master replied: "To know and then study is the way of the Sage; to study and then know is the way of the ordinary person. Although...
Among sages and ordinary people alike, there are none who do not rely upon learning. Confucius said, "A gentleman cannot fail to learn.
Zi Lu said, "The bamboo of the Southern Mountains is straight even without being bent; when cut and used as an arrow, it penetrates even rhinoceros hide.
By this account, what need is there for learning? Confucius said, "If one feathers the shaft and sharpens the point, its penetration will be [great]."
"Is this not indeed profound? Subsequently, Zilu bowed twice and said, "I reverently accept your instruction. Alas!

Is it not the case that the learning of the sages involves fletching the arrow with feathers, sharpening the point, and whetting the blade so that it penetrates deeply? Could those who are born with knowledge simply remain haughty and refuse to learn?
Exert yourself in study!
Even sages and worthies must apply themselves to learning; how could anyone below the level of sages and worthies become accomplished without it?
Learning is like food, drink, and clothing: whether one is a sage, a worthy, or a commoner—though these three differ—[they all require them].
When one is hungry and seeks food, thirsty and seeks drink, or cold and seeks clothing, there is no difference [in their nature]; how then can learning be any different?

Only birds, beasts, earth, and wood need not learn. Alas! There are foolish men who indulge in food and drink without weariness and pursue profit through reckless borrowing without ceasing, yet when it comes to learning, they may study in the morning and become indolent by evening. How is this possible? It is because they possess the spirit of spring.

There are those who become indolent during the winter while studying; yet, if one were as insatiable for learning as they are for food and drink, or as reckless in pursuit of wealth and profit, what concern would they have about not becoming widely learned? Would they not become gentlemen? One might ask: "In this world, there are those who are utterly foolish, unable to distinguish between beans and wheat, and ignorant of the changes of cold and heat; can such people be made to study? Can they be taught? [The answer is: No. They cannot. However, those who possess the capacity for discernment and the desire for knowledge—how could they fail to achieve it? How could they fail to become gentlemen? It is only when one lacks the capacity and lacks the desire that one fails to succeed. Therefore, the Master said: "If you are capable and desire it, you will surely attain it. This is why the ancient sages established schools and appointed teachers. It is because they knew that if one possesses the capacity but lacks the desire, or possesses the desire but lacks the capacity, both will fail to achieve anything. Thus, the Way of the Sages is vast and profound, yet its principles are simple and clear. To summarize: if one has the capacity and applies oneself with diligence, one will surely attain the Way. If one lacks the capacity or lacks diligence, one will surely fail. This is the constant principle of Heaven and Earth and the unchanging law of all things. Therefore, the wise person strives to cultivate their own nature and diligently pursues learning, never ceasing until they have attained the ultimate goal. This is what is meant by "the Way of the Sages is not difficult; it is simply that people do not practice it. If one practices it, the Way is easy; if one does not practice it, the Way is difficult. This is the reason why the ancients valued education so highly. To neglect learning is to neglect one's own nature; to neglect one's own nature is to neglect the Way; and to neglect the Way is to neglect Heaven. Therefore, the wise person values learning above all else. This is the true meaning of the Master’s words. To study and yet become indolent is indeed a great pity. But if one is truly devoted to learning, what obstacle could prevent them from becoming widely learned? What obstacle could prevent them from becoming a gentleman? It is only the lack of capacity or the lack of desire that renders one incapable of success. Therefore, let us all strive to cultivate our natures and pursue learning with unwavering resolve. It is said that extreme folly arises from a lack of instruction and a lack of learning. If a teacher were to instruct them without weariness, those whose minds do not grow indolent could surely ascend to the realm of the sages;
what worry would they have about failing to distinguish between beans and wheat?

Furthermore, the fool knows when he is thirsty to drink, knows when he is hungry to eat, and knows when he is cold to put on clothes. Once he understands these three things, he is no different [from others].
Plants and trees differ greatly; how could they not be capable of learning? Yet they cannot be taught.
Is the most foolish of men unable to record a single word daily? If one accumulates days into months, one will have recorded thirty words.

If one accumulates months into years, one will have recorded three hundred and sixty words. If one continues this for several years without slackening, one will approach the state of being broadly learned.
Have you not heard it said again? If one takes up even a single small good deed and practices it, accumulating day by day until a month has passed, one will possess thirty good deeds in the body.
Accumulating month by month until a year has passed, one will possess three hundred and sixty good deeds in the body.

One who accumulates them for several years without slackening—is such a person not close to being a gentleman? As for those who remain fools or petty men without ever changing—[how can they be compared?]

Because he did not study, the Master of the Middle Way sighed deeply and said: "I have often seen those who are ashamed that their wisdom does not reach [the mark] or their talent is not quick, and thus cease their studies;
yet I have never seen one who is ashamed that their consumption of food and drink is not as much as others, and thus cease eating and drinking.
To cease eating and drinking is to bring about the end of one's life—why must one feel shame for not consuming as much? Thus he ceased his studies.
If one were questioned [on this], it would be the same as being like birds, beasts, earth, or wood; why then must one feel ashamed that one’s talent and wisdom do not equal those of others?

If one feels shame simply because one’s talent and wisdom are inferior, then by extension, one should also feel shame for not being able to eat and drink as well as others, and thus one should abandon eating and drinking.
Viewed in this light, is this not a great error? I am also extremely dull-witted, yet whenever I reflect upon my own talent and...
That my wisdom does not reach that of others is far indeed; yet, knowing that food and drink cannot be ceased, I have not dared to be negligent in my studies.
At the age of forty-four, though I am ill and exhausted, my hands have never let go of a scroll.
This is because I fear being equal to mere earth, wood, birds, or beasts; it is not that I dare seek to reach the realm of the sages, nor do I seek—

Even when I heard of those who had attained renown and wandered through courtyards or strolled across open fields to temporarily nourish my sight and exercise my mind, I never dared to neglect my studies.
Thus, when climbing mountains, I thought to learn their loftiness; when facing water, I thought to learn its clarity;
when sitting upon rocks, I thought to learn their hardness; and when gazing at pines, I thought to learn their integrity.
Facing the moon, one reflects upon learning from its brilliance; when the myriad phenomena stand in array, each possessing its own excellence, I shall take them all as teachers and learn from them.
Though the myriad phenomena are silent, they can still be learned from; even among a person’s myriad evils, there must be at least one good quality.
If one takes that single good quality as a teacher and learns from it, who would say this is not so? The Master of the *Zhongyong* said: "In the world there are..."
There are things that one seeks but may not obtain; there are things in the world that one seeks and will certainly obtain.
That which is sought but may not be obtained is *li* (profit); that which is sought and will certainly be obtained is the *Dao*.
Regarding profit, even if a petty person seeks it ten thousand times and fails ten thousand times, they seek it with ever-greater vigor; regarding the *Dao*, the gentleman seeks it...
That one must obtain it yet looks toward the path with timidity, thinking to oneself that one's strength is insufficient—this is merely the fault of a petty person seeking profit.
Confucius said, "Is benevolence far away? If I desire benevolence, then benevolence arrives. This means that if one seeks it, it is certain to be obtained.

A Letter of Judgment on the Case of Luo Yan, dated the Twenty-first Day of the Tenth Month.
A Śramaṇa, Shi [Name], respectfully bathes himself in pure water and addresses this letter to Your Honor, Official [Name]:
The Dharma of the Buddha is not of antiquity; it first appeared during the Eastern Han dynasty. As for its essential nature:
As for the application of purity and stillness, benevolence and forbearance arise therefrom;

thus, while the three teachings have flowed in nineteen streams, the two teachings [Buddhism and Daoism] have provided benefit to those above and below, remedying the deficiencies of Confucianism and Daoism—this is indeed ultimate. I shall now summarize and set it forth:

when the fires of Qin consumed the Six Classics and the Han dynasty arose with its mixed hegemonies, the people became callous and customs degenerated, strife and plunder were rampant, and ritual propriety and yielding had gradually diminished. Thus, Zhong... [text continues]

The benevolence and righteousness of the Ni (Confucian) school and the Way and Virtue of Boyang (Laozi) have nearly ceased to exist; it is only by relying on the teachings of our Buddhists that they are preserved.

Having established the conduct of people through the retribution of the three periods of existence, they further clarify the principle of the single mind’s emptiness and stillness to exhaust its ultimate truth.
When the people hear these doctrines of retribution, even those who are greedy, base, stingy, or parsimonious may find themselves inspired to change for the better.
This is to provide for those in urgent need. Among the people, there are those who have heard the teachings of emptiness and stillness;

even men who pride themselves on their utility and vigor may, by these means, come close to maintaining the state of the female and preserving weakness. If one can provide comprehensive relief, the Way of universal salvation will prevail. If one maintains the state of the female and preserves weakness, the wind of simplicity and purity will flourish.
When universal salvation prevails, the principles of ritual and yielding become manifest; when the wind of simplicity flourishes, punishments and penalties are laid aside.
If one benefits the people through this, then the Way of Zhongni (Confucius) and Boyang (Laozi) will not be far from being restored.
Therefore it is said: "To benefit those above and below, and to remedy the deficiencies of Confucianism and Daoism. Yet, when successive rulers favored these teachings, they lost their true intent;

those in monastic robes served them, but were not the right people. When the intent is lost, regulations and restraints cannot be maintained; when the right people are absent, there is only silence and detachment.

They do not maintain [simplicity], but instead take pride in ornate and magnificent architecture; they do not value modesty, but instead flaunt themselves with light clothing, corpulence, and satiety.
To hold that "much" is noble would cause many to ruin the Way; to claim that "strangeness" is beautiful would delude many who hear it.
As these practices are passed down from one to another, they gradually become established customs, thereby causing the winds of purity, stillness, benevolence, and forbearance—
Was it not for this reason that they were utterly exhausted? From this point on, the calumny of "silkworm-eating" and "parasitic consumption" arose.
This was merely the fault of those who favored and practiced [the teachings], not the fault of the teaching itself;

yet rulers and subjects of past ages failed to examine the origins of these matters, and seeing only the unworthiness of its followers, they transferred their anger toward the virtuous men and the teachers of the doctrine.
There are those who frequently violate the monastic discipline of the Buddha and yet seek to execute the teachings of Śākyamuni;

how is this any different from blaming Yao for the faults of Danzhu, or finding fault with Shun because of Shangjun? It is like taking medicine and, when the dosage is improper, casting the blame upon Shen Nong;
or setting fire to something and, when it results in a conflagration, resenting Sui Ren. How tragic! I, [Name], am unworthy, having studied the Way of the Buddha.
It has been many years since I have roughly grasped its essential points and developed a sincere desire to support it;

I do not dare to treat this as my private concern, but rather wish to make it public for all posterity in order to remedy its defects. Therefore, I have deeply contemplated long-term consequences lest my plan fail.
I have observed that among the scriptures of the Śākya school, there is a sūtra titled "The Forty-two Chapters," which was translated during the Han dynasty.

A Letter to Dharma Master Xuan of Jiahe:
Now, those who propagate the teachings bear the noble trust of the Dharma King and act as the emissaries of the Tathāgata;

they must take the destruction of heterodoxy and the manifestation of orthodoxy, the stirring up of the turbid and the exalting of the clear, as their divining stalks for later students and their eyes and ears for all living beings—this is their own duty.
If one is incapable of fulfilling this responsibility and remains silent, merely guarding oneself, then one is a mere corpse drawing a salary and filling a vacancy within the Buddhist gate;
even if one lectures and teaches, what purpose would that serve? Some may say that such contentious debate is of no benefit to one’s own practice (*svacaryā*); I, however, say this is not so.
For it is only by means of the trap (*jāla*) that one obtains the fish, and only by embodying the teaching (*śāsana*) that one practices the path. Without the names and teachings...
As for correct practice, why must one not engage in contention? Therefore, the gentleman has nothing with which to contend.

If it must be something, let it be archery. For those who do not yet understand the right or wrong of verbal instruction but are instead anxious to achieve realization through cultivation—it is like seeing a bowstring and immediately seeking out a roasted owl;
such is an overly premature calculation. How can this compare to fathoming the depths and investigating the subtle mechanisms, acting solely for oneself?
If people were to act in accordance with what they say, would not the benefit be vast? Therefore, when Zhongni governed, he insisted that names must be rectified;
and in the final testament of Nirvāṇa, the urgent priority was to correct errors. Regarding the Dharma Master Mingli of the Four Knowledges, he was among the most eminent of the predecessors;
he once established the term "evolving according to conditions" for the distinct principle of Tiantai, while swallowing up the meaning of the *Awakening of Faith* like a whale.
There was a man named Jiqi from Yongjia, one of the most outstanding figures among the younger generation, who claimed that [Master] Li’s discourse was merely a flowery explanation.
Consequently, these two theories were presented side by side like arrows and stones, and none of the eminent masters in Hangzhou offered a critique.
The fledgling students were greatly perplexed; how much more so for this debate, which concerns the realm of the Buddha—save only for the Dharma Master.

I have exhausted the principles and fully realized the nature through the Way of Tiantai, and transmitted the meaning of the *Awakening of Faith*, making the subtle manifest and elucidating the profound.

It is my hope that by examining its merits and shortcomings with a mind intent on the Dharma, and wielding my brush like a sweeping canopy across the heavens, I may settle right from wrong so that those with infinite potential may recognize the path of the true and real;
this is my aspiration. If it is thus, how could I be deemed unworthy of the Dharma?

The King’s gracious entrustment is indeed like a mandate from the Tathāgata. I respectfully present this letter, composed of the writings of the two masters, to inquire after your well-being as the golden wind blows high.
Written on the full moon day of the eighth month of autumn.

The Life of Dharma Master Bei of Ciguang Monastery in Qiantang Dharma Master Bei’s name was Wenbei, his courtesy name was Zhaoben, and his secular surname was Zheng; he was a native of Hougan County in Fuzhou. From childhood, he served as a disciple at Taiping Monastery.

His nature was exceptionally perceptive, surpassing that of ordinary children; he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Bodhicitta-uttara-tantra* (Yuánjué jīng).

He refined himself in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra*, the *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and other scriptures without exception. In the third year of the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty, he received the *śīla* (precepts) at his home temple.

He maintained them with steadfast purity and rigorous self-examination, pursuing his studies with arduous resolve. He mastered both the sutras and the vinaya, possessing a refined literary style and being well-versed in the Five Classics and the various schools of philosophy (*zhuzi*).
During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Jianzhou in plain clothes, initially settling in Kuaiji.
From the Dharma Master Rou, he received the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* and studied it thoroughly through lecture and recitation.

After several years had passed, he again crossed the Yangtze River to visit Longxing Temple in Qiantang, where he sought out senior masters to investigate and discuss the great principles for the sake of further cultivation.

Consequently, regarding the branch of technical terminology (*nāma-saṃkhyā*), he reached the very depths of its essence; among the students who came from distant regions, there were none who did not follow him to seek his instruction.

Later, hearing that the study of the Three Contemplations (*sanzhuan*) of Tiantai could serve as a guide for dispelling all delusions and that it allows one to investigate the subtle workings of the mind-nature, he revered it with unwavering devotion.
Vowing to transmit and propagate this teaching, he encountered Master Zhiyin, who was propagating the Way at Ciguang Monastery;

he thus entered his gate in the first year of the Guangshun era of the Zhou dynasty. Thereafter, he wielded the blade of wisdom to harmonize the various schools and attacked the hardest points of ultimate principle with diligent perseverance.
He was as diligent and reverent as if treading on thin ice, never ceasing day or night;

his devotion to study was such that, by this time, he had thoroughly excavated the secret essentials of all the teachings of our school—including the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*—and fully penetrated their ultimate purport.
His wisdom and understanding were so brilliant that they were difficult to equal. At that time, there was a senior disciple named Master Wuen.
(He is included in the "Biographies of Exegesis" section of the *Great Song Biographies of Eminent Monks*. His lofty integrity was beyond compare, and his pure influence inspired all things.

Whenever he reviewed and recounted the mental contemplations with the Dharma Master, he grasped the essence and attained the meaning through spiritual intuition, needing no more than a single day. For this reason, they became friends who shared a mutual understanding of the Dharma;
he said to others, "Although Bei is but a junior, I can truly race alongside him on the path of exegesis; there is surely no difference between us in terms of seniority."
Since his teacher had passed away, he consequently faced north to serve him as his patron, for there is no fixed teacher in learning.

The Dharma Master’s temperament was profound and serene; all day long he appeared as if dull-witted. Yet when later students came to inquire about their doubts, or when his peers posed difficult questions to dispel ignorance and resolve confusion, his explanations reached both the substance and the phrasing.
Someone once asked him: "One who severs the seeds of the Buddha takes this precept as his ancestral standard; how can your insight and vision be such as this?"
"Why not instruct others in one particular field? He replied: "My master’s disciples are already numerous, and his teachings are quite extensive;
thus, the tradition of our ancestors has not fallen into ruin. I have withdrawn from the world to dwell in seclusion, following my own inclinations.

For over thirty years, I have sat in forgetfulness within this single room, refining my spirit through wondrous contemplation and continuing my reflections upon the Pure Land, remaining aloof from worldly distractions."
Because the multitude of streams each find their own distinct course, few at any time understand his interpretations and practices; only those who cherish the Way recognize them in silence.
An ancient said, "One of true practice hides their radiance; though eminent, they remain unnamed. Is this not so?
In the autumn of the second year of the Yongxi era, he contracted a slight illness. Suddenly, one day, leaning against a desk, he drew a circle and gazed upon it three times, looking at the sick man.

Whenever he was urged to practice self-cultivation, he would immediately stop; or when someone brought him food, he would ask about news from the Western Land [of Amitābha], and would respond by writing a verse that said:
"Alas! Those people of this floating world ask me for news of the West. That news has long been all-pervasive, yet the masses remain lost in their own delusions.
A single body of water manifests as hundreds of thousands of waves— Each wave and ripple is the seal of the Buddha. Every movement is truly Amitābha. I instruct you: always be diligent!"

On the eighteenth day of the tenth month, his illness gradually worsened. His attendant, Qingyao, weeping, pleaded with him, saying, "Master, you have practiced the path to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing for many years;
now that your allotted lifespan is drawing to a close, what auspicious signs are there?
He replied, "I previously drew a circle, which was the manifestation of the Pure Land I beheld. I intended to remain silent, but now it is because of your questioning."
Having finished speaking, he suddenly passed away with his feet crossed; thus was the evidence of his rebirth manifest. He lived to the age of sixty and had been a monk for forty-nine years.
During his lifetime, the Dharma Master immersed himself in the flavor of the Way and devoted himself to study, never letting concerns for food or clothing distract him.
Beyond his practice of dhyāna and meditation, he transcribed over ten thousand sheets of commentaries on the Northern and Southern schools of Chan, his literary style being most elegant.
Having attained considerable wealth, he produced several writings; his "Essay on the Separate Treatment of Remains" (Bie yihai wen) still exists.
When the Master of Universal Wisdom (Tonghui Dashi), Zanning, was compiling the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) in Hangzhou, he highly esteemed this work.

He also authored one scroll of "Verses on the Forty-eight Vows," one scroll of the "Diagram of the Nine Grades" (Jiupin tu), one scroll of the "Outline of the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations" (Shiliu guan jing ke), and two scrolls of the "Outline of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra" (Yuanjue jing ke).
*Chanyuan ke* (Outline of the Source of Chan), one fascicle; *Nianfo jiuku yu* (An Allegory on Saving Suffering through Buddha-Recitation), one article;

*Sixin tan yu* (An Allegory on the Four *Siddhāntas*), one article; *Sibusheng yu* (An Allegory on the Four Non-Arisings), one article; *Wenji* (Collected Prose), one fascicle; and *Shiji* (Collected Poetry), one fascicle.
Among the poems, the two pieces titled "Feeling Moved by Snow" and "Passing the Temple of Cao E" are most highly esteemed by poets. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongmin of Jiahe.

This is a true eulogy. I am not one capable of literary composition; however, as the grandson of the Dharma Master, I have been permitted to inquire into his past and record his life’s achievements directly for inclusion in the monastic history (*Sengshi*).

A Letter to Vice Minister Wu, Regarding the Preface to the *Xianju bian* (Collection of Leisurely Dwelling), Written on the Sixth Day of the Second Month.
By a certain Śramaṇa, respectfully having purified himself with water and incense, I address this letter to the Vice Minister (Your Honor).
It has been over a year since I last attended literary assemblies; yet, admiring your lofty character and thirsting for your noble discourse, I have not forgotten you for a single day. I, [Name].
Recently, as my chronic illness suddenly flared up, I have been prostrate upon my pillow in a quiet chamber.
On the first day of this month, an attendant suddenly announced that Master Li, the District Magistrate of Qiandao, had sent a messenger with a letter.

Upon opening it, I quickly glanced at it and found it was a preface written by the Vice Director of the Imperial Household for my own humble collection of writings titled *The Collection of Leisurely Dwelling* (*Xianju bian*). I was suddenly startled awake by this and leaned forward [from my bed].
Bending over it to read as I unrolled and refolded it, I immersed myself in its study with such deep contemplation that I wondered if the paper had transformed and the ink had faded;
how could it have stopped at merely being "re-read three times"? Its phrasing is brilliantly clear and its meaning is profoundly deep.

The gains and losses of antiquity and the present, and the strengths and weaknesses of literary composition—all are contained herein. Furthermore, regarding my own work, it has elicited the praise of Confucius’s "embroidered robe" (a mark of highest honor).
Cai Yong’s sigh regarding the quality of silk is perhaps an exaggeration; I privately suspect it may be so.
Whether my reckless words are truly false or truly true, you, Vice-Director, have invested them with your own deep feelings and refined them with your grace.
Since you, Vice-Director, are a man of leisurely silence and dignified elegance whose speech serves as a model for the world, you do not speak lightly—how could this be granted in vain?
These words are indeed true! They are but the wild and crude compositions of a sickly recluse from beneath the forest trees—a mountain song and a field chant.
How much more so for you, Vice Minister, who bears the great reputation of a master of literature and stands as a preeminent figure among the scholars of the academies.

Though you may now be constrained like a silkworm in the office of taxation and customs, you shall soon be elevated to the position of a court spokesperson. You are destined to compose the classics and the edicts to embellish the imperial enterprise and establish its legacy.
"I vow to compose this life's work to bring forth the majesty of the royal governance; how could I possibly use such extraordinary literature to grace the collection of a mere rustic?
Thus, I have hesitated in my heart for a long time, yet suddenly I have made a solitary decision. Why is this?

Furthermore, the great gentleman employs his mind solely in accordance with the Way; he does not differentiate between stillness and agitation, nor does he obstruct himself with outward forms or dress."
The fruit of the Way is the same; my literary fruit is precisely this. Therefore, you must surely manifest it for me and proclaim it far and wide.
If this is so, then the Vice Minister is truly one who understands my music. Indeed, music is not easily understood, and those who understand music are hard to find.
Since the Vice Minister already knows it and I have now attained it, even that ox pulling the salt-cart would still be able to [respond].

I am like Sun Yang’s horse; though I am emaciated, exhausted, and stumbling along, waiting for my end day by day, I can still distinguish cold from heat with my body, separate beans from wheat with my eyes, and discern right from wrong with my mind.
How could I not let out a cry for one who understands me? Now, I cry out for you, the Vice Minister; may you, the Vice Minister, listen to me.
From my youth, due to the influence of past habits, I have long cherished a fondness for the Empty Gate (the Buddhist path). At...
From the age of seven or eight, he cut his hair and discarded his robes to become a follower of the Buddha.
As he approached the age for capping, he took a great interest in the books of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius;

desiring to investigate the subtle and fathom the profound by studying under a master of the Way, he was constrained by his tonsure-master and unable to follow his aspirations. Consequently, he shut himself within his door and studied alone in quietude.
Being without friends, he often obtained the books of the Five Classics and read them for himself;

although he could not fully recognize every character nor fully distinguish every phrase and punctuation mark, he was fond of seeking the ultimate intent of the sages and masters and synthesizing their teachings.

This was like Jiu Fang Yin’s appraisal of horses, which disregarded the colors of black and yellow to discuss their divine spirit and swiftness—far superior to those who merely... [the text trails off].
Those who merely chant with clamor and those who seek out phrases and extract lines have already become as far apart as Hu and Yue.

Only by reading the *Yi* does one come to know that it is rooted in the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*), which unfolds the Two Polarities (*liangyi*), and within which the natures of the Five Constants (*wuchang*) are enshrined.

Thus it is said: "The Way established for Heaven is called Yin and Yang; the Way established for Earth is called Softness and Hardness; the Way established for Humanity is called Benevolence (*ren*)."
For this reason, King Wen of Zhou set forth the four virtues to expound upon their meaning, and the Sage Master [Confucius] paired them with the Five Constants to support them;
he then placed Qian and Kun at the beginning. From this, one knows that the Five Constants are the source of the transformational influence of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius.
Upon reading the books, one realizes that the primitive simplicity from the time of the Three Sovereigns downward was not a practice to be perpetuated for a hundred generations.
The Way of these [ancient kings] cannot be fully explained by mere words; therefore, the Sage Master established the Way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings as a model for later generations.
He honored the ritual of yielding and shunned the use of weapons, which is why he placed the Two Canons at the beginning.

Although Tang and Wu possessed the virtue of remedying the corruptions of their times, this was not the fundamental intent of Zhongni. Thus the saying goes: "The Martial [music] reached the height of beauty, yet it did not reach the height of perfection."
By reading the *Shi*, one comes to know that only after Heaven and Earth exist do husband and wife come to be;

only after husband and wife exist do father and son come to be; and only after father and son exist do ruler and minister come to be. Thus, the husband and wife constitute the root of the two polarities (*er yi*) and the head of the three cardinal relations (*san gang*).
This is why the *Guanju* is placed at the beginning. By reading the *Chunqiu*, one comes to know that the House of Zhou declined and the barbarians rose.
When the people became treacherous within the Middle Kingdom and King Ping moved the capital to the east, his edicts and commands were no longer effective;
ritual, music, and the power of military expedition no longer issued from the Son of Heaven, but rather from the feudal lords.

Therefore, Zhongni (Confucius) compiled the records of the state of Lu to compose the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals), using praise and censure to evaluate the feudal lords and penalizing the high officials to rectify the Way of the King. Thus, it is said: "Ritual, music, and military expeditions..."
"From the point when the feudal lords emerged from their subordination, it has been ten generations since they began to rarely fail to lose [their states].
Moreover, from Duke Yin of Lu to Duke Zhao, it was ten generations before the government was lost and he died at Qianhou; this is the very proof.

Therefore, the *Chunqiu* begins with the reign of King Ping and Duke Yin of Lu. Although the blind speculations of former scholars claim that it begins with the 'Worthy Kings,' this is merely the talk of later students."
To transmit it in such a manner—how could this not contradict the words of the Sage Master in the *Analects*? Only the *Ritual Classics* (*Lijing*) were recorded by disciples;
they were intermingled by various Han scholars and rearranged by later worthies.

As for the reason why [the current order] appears at the beginning of the work, it all arises from human sentiment and is certainly not the Sage’s intent. Once one has understood this within one's own heart...

He was courageous in his pursuit of learning and said, "Although I lack the instruction of a teacher and the mutual refinement of a friend, I shall take the Five Classics as my standard to elucidate the Sage’s intent;
in establishing my teachings and composing my words, I believe I shall be worthy.
Thereupon, he set to work with his brush and inkstone, never ceasing day or night, intending to clasp Mencius by the sleeve with his left hand and pat Yang Xiong on the shoulder with his right.

Wandering among the Confucian officials, he proclaimed and chanted the civil teachings; with his golden lips and wooden tongue, he delivered the great instructions to this declining age, causing the Way of the Three Kings and Two Emperors of Heaven not to be far from restoration.
Before long, however, his body was afflicted by a debilitating illness, which suddenly obstructed his progress in learning.
Feeling despondent and unhappy, his noble ambitions grew faint. One day, reflecting upon himself, he said: "You are a disciple of Śākyamuni; are you not like a flower blooming in the void?"
Is this world but floating clouds? Are wealth and honor but echoes in a valley? Are speech and words but flashes of lightning?

And what of this physical life—how can it be so entangled by illness and the loss of one’s resolve? From this point on, I shall devote myself exclusively to seeking the Buddhist scriptures and reflecting inwardly upon the nature of the mind.

I shall cast aside all worldly affairs and unify them within the single mind; therefore, regarding the path of literary composition mentioned previously, I shall no longer strive to fulfill that ambition.
As for his later works, although they were fundamentally based on Confucianism, he expounded upon Buddhist teachings with a vigor twice as great;
he frequently drew upon Laozi and Zhuangzi to support his arguments. Alas, how could people not know this?
Thus, in my writing, I have been unable to remain pure. [This refers to] Gongsun Long’s "Discourse on the Non-Existence of the House" and Sima Qian’s many... [omitted].
"This love is something I have brought upon myself. If in future generations there should arise a sage like Zhongni, will he not condemn me?
Thinking thus, I was unwilling to leave behind even a single fragment of writing, desiring only to evade the censure of posterity.
However, while convalescing on Mount Gu and living in seclusion among the woods, friends came from afar and repeatedly urged me to compile and record [these thoughts]. Thus, [I have complied].
He answered with his former resolve, saying: "What harm is there? We are each merely expressing our own aspirations.
As for the Three Teachings, their roots are the same while their branches differ; in instructing the people and governing the world, do they not together form a complementary whole?
What you have recorded should properly be included in this collection to be bequeathed to posterity. Thereupon, he complied with his request. Thus it was.
Whatever I subsequently obtained, I have recorded therein; poems, prose, and eulogies appear interspersed, and it is titled the *Xianju bian* (Collection of Leisurely Dwelling).
This is akin to the *Congshu* (Collected Books) of Lu Wang; my intention is merely to keep it within the family threshold to bequeath to my descendants.
How could I dare hope that it might by chance meet with a connoisseur who would bring it to light? Now, having beheld what the Vice Minister [has written]...
To compose a preface for this gift would surely be most unfortunate.

I shall therefore entrust my junior disciples to compile his writings so that each may follow its own category, placing his magnificent compositions at the forefront to be handed down to future generations.

This will allow scholars and commentators to see them without confusion, to realize that the Three Teachings converge in a single goal, and to avoid words of disparagement. May he thus bring me to completion!
As for the Prefectural Vice-Governor: indeed, there have been many worthy men of former generations who composed prefaces for monks.
Yet, such as the Preface by Hanlin Academician Wu (Rong) for Chan-yue and that by Vice-Prefect Bao for Master Zhou, they merely pointed toward the realm of song and poetry;

how could they clarify the principles of civil culture? As for their rhetoric and logic, when compared to magnificent prose, those [earlier works] would surely turn pale with shame. However, as for...

thus, I have hastily set down these disordered words to recount the aspirations of my life, so as to express my gratitude for the kindness of one who appreciates my voice.
