A Letter of Thanks for the Visit of the Provincial Governor and Imperial Secretary Wang.
The third day of the second month. The Śramaṇa [Name] respectfully purifies himself with water and incense, grinds his brush, washes his inkstone, and writes this letter to present to [Your Honor].
I, [Name], an official attendant of the Prefectural Governor and a lowly member of the Gate of Emptiness, have disfigured my appearance and maintained my integrity to master myself;
I have restrained my anger and stilled my desires to clarify my thoughts. Although I may find some utility in the Way, I am in fact of no use to the world;
thus, I have long been able to hide away beneath the crags and rocks, keeping no contact with the secular world.
Furthermore, afflicted by a chronic illness of melancholy, emaciated and exhausted, I sit leaning on a small table and walk supported by a staff;

my body frequently becomes like withered wood, yet my mind remains conscious. Even so, I am still able to rejoice in the simple transformation of one man and wear the benevolent governance of two heavens;
as I study Buddhist scriptures and bathe in the source of spiritual cultivation, I often forget the suffering within my own body. If...
Thus, there was the "advantageous appearance" of the noble gentleman; yet when one listens intently to his pure discourse, it already lies beyond the reach of ordinary thought.
Why is this? Since one cannot even enter the gate of those who hold office, how can one have the advantage of appearing before the noble gentleman?

And since one cannot have the advantage of appearing before the noble gentleman, how could one possibly listen intently to his pure discourse? Last autumn, in the ninth month, suddenly there appeared—
When a messenger arrived at my humble thatched hut to deliver your instructions, bidding me to join you on the same boat to sip tea and discuss the Way, I was then confined to my bed by illness;
I was both startled and overjoyed—a joy beyond compare. How could you have known my name, and why did you summon me?
Although I was unable at that time to hasten to your presence and attend your seat, I am nonetheless deeply grateful for your favor.
My mind has long been unaware of its own direction. As the ailments of this spring have intensified, I have remained bedridden in a state of daze.
Suddenly, I heard those attending to my illness say that you, sir, had halted your golden carriage before me, while the various officials delayed their jade steps behind.
A short while later, you indeed condescended to visit my humble dwelling, stooping down toward my sickbed; from the grace of your inquiry, I suddenly beheld you.

The gentleman listened intently to these pure words; what was previously considered beyond the reach of thought has now been obtained all at once—how could such an encounter occur even within the thatched huts or mountain caves? It is most fortunate, most fortunate!

On the second day of the second month, you again moved by your profound compassion and benevolence to provide me with *ziguishen* (purple cassia powder) for my consumption, for which my heart is filled with precious gratitude.
This exceeds even what was mentioned before. I humbly reflect that in the past, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a Dharma Master named Jiyou, a monk of great spiritual attainment.

Whenever the Prime Minister Wang Dao visited him, he would loosen his belt and lie down; however, when the Minister of the Secretariat Bian Hu arrived, he would compose his countenance and sit upright.

When asked the reason for this, he replied: "Prime Minister Wang regards people through the Way of the Wind (the influence of character), whereas Minister Bian regards them through the Way of the Rites."
It is simply because you examine all things through the lens of ritual propriety that it appears so.

Furthermore, you who hold the mastery of Gao Kui within yourself yet humble yourself to accept the duties of Gong Huang—your dignified grace is such that even the "double-pupiled" ruler would take note of you, and your refined style is such that the whole world looks up to you;
thus, you are far superior to Wang Dao. As for me, I am but a sick man dwelling beneath the forest trees; therefore, being no man of the Way, I am unable to offer you consolation.
Why is it that those who are weak and ill are not reproached for their lack of ritual decorum?

Is it not because you, my honored attendants, harbor a benevolence toward the blind as if you must assist them, and a compassion for those suffering from heat as if you must fan them; is your heart of pity and sympathy so profound as this?

Or is it perhaps that the Great Gentleman, through diligent humility in his dealings with subordinates, has made this the great instrument for establishing his own character and bringing peace to the people? I, [Name], [am thus moved].
At first, my heart was moved with emotion; next, it was filled with joy—not for my own sake, but because I have met a true知己 (a soulmate);
nor is it to praise your ability to harbor benevolence. Rather, it is to celebrate that our Sovereign has obtained a worthy minister and the common people have obtained a capable governor.
Why is this so? It is because you must surely extend this benevolent love and tireless humility—
When the mind reaches a thousand *li*, the people within those thousand *li* will be clothed in the harmony of springtime and will feel joy in their vocations.
Thereupon, the administration is perfected; like the *Gantang* tree, he takes up the pivot of power to govern the state and discuss the Way.

He presents what is acceptable and replaces what is improper, spreading his benevolent love and laborious humility—originally directed toward himself—to the four seas. Thus, the people of the four seas are further transformed.
In the harmony of the "Spring of Yang," all find joy in their respective vocations.

If one proceeds in this manner, to lead a ruler to the heights of Yao and Shun and to restore the era of Fuxi and Nongzi is as easy as turning over one's palm. By inferring from this, one can perceive the intent behind your efforts:
how could you be merely a sick man among the forest trees? Although I have been tossing and turning upon my mat, my nature remains dull and simple.
Since Zhi’s mind possesses cognition, he is already distinct from wood or stone; thus, supporting his frail body and leaning upon his desk, he dictated these words orally.

He requested that his disciples take up their pens to record them as a written document. Whether this be appropriate or not, whether it be forgiven or punished, it rests solely upon the command of your honor.
I have respectfully dispatched a student to carry this letter to be presented before your official standard; I humbly hope for your esteemed consideration.

In the leisure time between official duties at the Taiwan Provincial Broadcasting Station, I humbly request that you deign to cast a glance upon this. This person, [Name], cannot bear to express the depth of his gratitude and trepidation.
Sincerely yours, [Name], prostrating twice.
Record of the Juehua Pure Land Repentance Court in Deqing County, Huzhou.
A subordinate county of Wuxing Commandery is Deqing County; within it is a villa called Xintang Villa, where there is a benevolent shrine known as Juehua.
It is truly a place where the people of heaven seek blessings and a dwelling for Buddhist monks to settle in truth.
Previously, the temple monk Zhilong guided the lay believer Sun Xiue to solicit the masses to create three sacred images, which were called the [Three] No-... (the text is incomplete).
The Amitāyus [statue] was called Guanshiyin and Dashizhi.

Subsequently, the Sun brothers—Renyan, Rensheng, and Liyan—constructed a hall of over thirty bays to house their images. They further invited the monk Zhilong, a man of integrity and discipline, to preside over them.
Thus, the incense and lamps were maintained daily, and the ritual services grew increasingly solemn.
The followers of the Buddha have a place of refuge, which they have designated as the "Pure Land Repentance Hall.
A guest arrived from Xi溪 (Xixi) and informed me of this matter, urgently requesting that I compose a record for it; I therefore relate it as follows:
Confucius said, "I have not yet seen one who, upon seeing their own faults, can inwardly reproach themselves. Alas! To be able to reproach oneself—this is truly rare.
To reform one's faults and hope to become a virtuous person or a gentleman—how difficult this is! Otherwise, why would the Sage Teacher express such profound lamentation and exhortation?
Furthermore, when our Buddhists encourage repentance, it is truly because those who deeply self-reproach are those whose reform of faults is greatest.
Why is this so? It is because the Buddha of Benevolence expounded the single vehicle of quiescent extinction.

The principle establishes the matters of retribution across the three periods of time, so that those who comprehend this principle may turn back their delusions, and those who merely believe in the phenomena may transform toward goodness.

Since the common masses are unable to diminish their transgressions, one thereby causes them to observe their own minds and recognize that no form of action is without its corresponding guilt—is this not what is called "profound self-reproach"? Facing these images and...
Is it not the greatest form of repentance to vow never again to create new [evil], and then to point toward the Pure Land as the supreme assembly,
regarding this Sahā world as merely a transient inn? If even one person can practice this Way to instruct every household,
guide every village, extend it to the state, and reach infinity, I know that the people of the world will immerse themselves in the Way and bathe in its virtue.

If one can merely find enough time in the day to harmonize the spirit with the true mark (*dharmatā*) and stride loftily toward the state of non-action, thereby reaching the ultimate realm of the Buddha—how could this be limited to the concerns of the virtuous man or the gentleman alone?
If this is so, then what need is there to worry that loyalty and filial piety will not be cultivated, or that ritual propriety and yielding will not be manifest?
Viewed from this perspective, is this not the teaching of Zhongni (Confucius) and the Benevolent One (the Buddha) in harmony?

If these teachings are held together as a unified whole to instruct the people, how great would the error be for those who forget the root and cling to the branches, looking upon one another with mutual suspicion?
Now, these several virtuous men have established this image and built this monastery, clearly intending to await future seekers so that they may repent;
therefore, I have set forth the way of repentance and composed this record for them.
To decline his request would be to greatly hinder the noble intentions of the assembly of śramaṇas and lay believers, and to deprive them of a vast opportunity for merit;

thus, it is appropriate to grant it. As for recording the expenditures on wealth and the grandiosity of its architectural splendor, I, being without talent, am plain in speech and lacking in literary skill, and am unable to compose such a work.
I must instead request that one who is capable undertake this task. This was written in the third year of the Tianxi era of the Great Song dynasty, the Jiwu year (1019 CE).
Recorded on the fourteenth day of the ninth month.

Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
In Reply to the Letter from the Lǒngxī Scholar:
Yesterday, you, a scholar of Lǒngxī, graciously sent me a letter; however, as my chronic illness has frequently flared up, I have not yet been able to reply. Recently, again...

He presented me with a selection of his writings as a gift; I read them all through, and found that their language and principles were upright and vigorous, while their spirit and resolve were stirring and uplifting.
They seemed intent on stripping away superficiality and returning to simplicity and rectitude. How grand are the words and how profound is the meaning!
If you do not consider me unworthy, I shall say that you know the Way of the ancients and possess the writings of the ancients; yet this too is merely the deluded hearing of a scholar.

This is my fault. However, while I have been dwelling in seclusion beneath the forest trees to nurse my illness and study the Buddhist scriptures, I have also harbored a considerable interest in these literary arts.
You, a scholar who knows me, have suddenly come to question me; for me to remain silent would be to fail as a person.
Now, I shall set forth one disordered discourse—listen, O scholar. For many have written treatises on literature, yet they all refute what is deemed monstrous.
In the pursuit of *wen* (refinement/culture), one should value its pure essence, so that it takes benevolence and righteousness as its foundation and takes the Way and its Virtue as its ultimate aim.

Otherwise, if one merely dwells on the phrasing of literary expression, it seems one has not fully grasped the Way of *wen*. I, being ignorant, venture to say that there are three aspects to the Way of *wen*:
first, the establishment of virtue; second, the establishment of merit; and third, the establishment of speech. Virtue is the root of *wen*; merit is the function of *wen*; and speech is...

What is the rhetoric of the literary? Virtue is that by which benevolence is nurtured and righteousness is maintained, through which propriety is made earnest and music is disseminated, so as to transform all things.
What is achievement? It is when benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and music suffer deficiency, one resorts to awe-inspiring punishments to prevent them;
thus it eliminates calamities and wards off misfortunes. What is speech? It is to recount these two [virtue and achievement] for the purpose of instruction.

If the world were to follow his words, then virtue and merit could be attained. Thus, taking rectitude as the fundamental basis for preservation and employing flexibility as the means of application—both the rejection and the exposition of these are merely literary expressions.
Therefore it is said: "Zhongni (Confucius) followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and took Wen and Wu as his model.
Were Yao and Shun not virtuous? Were Wen and Wu not meritorious? For this reason, I have often [discussed] benevolence and righteousness...
This means that because it constitutes "pattern" (*wen*), it can encompass all three. For how could these three exceed benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*)?
Someone might say: "To span heaven and weave the earth is what is called 'pattern'; this is the teaching of the sages. You claim that benevolence and righteousness do not bring disorder;

is this not the teaching of the sages? I reply: Benevolence and righteousness, as they exist in heaven, are called Yin and Yang; as they exist on earth, they are called softness and hardness. Without benevolence and righteousness, what else would there be?
Since the heavens are spanned by the Way, if there were not benevolence and righteousness, how could the earth be woven together?

Therefore, those born according to the nature of heaven and earth must have their hearts conform to the warp of virtue and righteousness, and their mouths must express words of instruction and rectitude.

In the application of these words, one aims to remedy the prevailing defects; every sentence serves as a whip, and every word acts as a warning. Yet, one still fears that there may be no [sufficient admonition].
To benefit the world, people instead compete with licentious phrases, flattering words, and restrictive prosodic rules;
they boastfully embellish their implements to please common sentiments—what benefit does this bring to edification? What benefit does it bring to edification?

Thus, only those who apply their minds to the public good and cultivate their inner nature can establish themselves in speech; if the mind is not impartial and the emotions are not... [cultivated], [they cannot].
Although their nature may be arduous and their phrasing perilous, there will inevitably be those who produce doctrines that contradict the Classics and oppose the Sages;

thus, following what the emotions dictate has never been seen to benefit the teachings. Someone might say: "The emotions stir within and take form in speech—how can it be wrong to follow the emotions?
I reply: There is indeed such a thing! However, one must regulate the emotions through the Mean (*zhong*); alas, this is the task for those who establish words.
There is nothing that does not arise from joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure moving within. If one rejoices without moderation, one’s speech becomes sycophantic;
if one is angry without moderation, one’s speech becomes censorious; if one is sorrowful without moderation, one’s speech becomes weak;

and if one is joyful without moderation, one’s speech becomes licentious. If joy does not lead to licentiousness, and sorrow does not lead to weakness... [anger does not lead to censoriousness, and joy...]
As for the sycophantic and evil, they shall be censured and punished; as for the good, they shall be praised and encouraged.

If one takes morality and virtue as the foundation and maintains them with pure sincerity, then these principles will be disseminated for a hundred generations and flow throughout the four quarters. Following the path of Mencius and Yan Hui, one will have no cause for shame regarding one's virtue. Thus it is said:
"When joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused, this is called the Central (zhōng); when they are aroused and all hit the mark of moderation..."
This is what is called "harmony and centrality," which is the great root of the world; harmony is the pervasive path of the world.
Therefore, I consider that approximating harmony and centrality to be the essential core of establishing one's words. If one possesses such virtue, can one’s achievements fail to follow?
It is through the practice of one’s words that this is attained. What do you, the scholar, think of this? I pray that you will give it due consideration.
Letter to My Disciples:
I have recently received your letter, in which you state that you have had the preface to the "Chart of the Dharma-realm" (Jiexiang) composed by me engraved upon stone to ensure its imperishability.
This is indeed appropriate. Although I am not gifted, I have recorded these matters in truth so that they may be transmitted to future generations. A guest has arrived from... [text continues]
As for the matter of Huating referring to me as "Wu Yun," he saw the characters for *jie-xiang* (界相) carved upon a stone and changed them to *jie-zi* (戒字).
Alas, how strange! Was it that the scribe was ignorant and made an error? Or was it that you lot, not knowing the reason, altered it recklessly?
If it were indeed the scribe’s mistake, it would still be your fault; for this preface was requested by you, and you were truly the ones responsible for it. It is just like...

When a tiger or a rhinoceros escapes from its cage, or when a tortoise-shell or jade is destroyed within its case, whose fault is it? Indeed, there are instances where characters are borrowed across the Classics, Histories, Philosophical Works, and Collections.

For example, "xiāoyáo" (逍遙) is written as "xiāoyáo" (消搖) in the *Liji*; "zǎomù" (早暮) is written as "zǎomò" (蚤莫); in the *Zuozhuan*, "burial of horse dung" is written with the character for "bow" (*húshǐ*);
and in the *Shiji*, "three times voiding dung" uses the same character. In the *Zhuangzi*, "fish-trap and rabbit-snare" (*quánzhì*) is written as "hoof-print" (*tí*); and in the *Shiji*...
In the *Wénxuǎn*, "quèluó" (雀羅) is written as "juéwén" (爵文), and "Wúyuè" (吳越) is written as "Yuè" (粵); these are all instances of phonetic loan characters (*jiàjiè*) or archaic orthography (*gǔzì*).

However, regarding the character for "boundary" (*jiāngjiè*), I have never heard it used as a loan for the character for "caution" (*jièshèn*). Moreover, how much more so in the case of the names "delimiting the boundary" (*jièjiè*) and "precepts" (*jièlǜ*), which originate from Buddhism?

Buddhism began in the Eastern Han dynasty, and its Vinaya-piṭaka was translated during the Later Qin; thus, the characters composed by later scholars for these terms are quite sufficient [to express their specific meanings].
Since Buddhism relies upon it, those who would borrow from it are few. Thus, the names "Kṣetrasīmā" and "Vinaya" are fundamentally derived from the Vinaya Piṭaka;
how could these two terms be altered at will? To engrave this upon stone is not intended to ensure immortality;
it serves only to spread infamy to future generations and invite derision from all quarters. Yet, those of discerning mind, upon reading it...
If one does not examine the reason for this, one must surely blame my own mind for its neglect and my studies for their paucity.
If, however, one does examine the reason, one must surely blame the errors of the scribe or the alterations made by later generations. Alas!
If everyone throughout the four seas in a hundred generations were to possess true discernment, they would certainly be able to blame my own mind for its neglect and my studies for their paucity.
What I fear is that after my passing, those who are still in their ignorance may regard me as merely an ancient, saying:
"This man was able to arrange the narrative; he must surely have had some learning. Once it is engraved upon stone, they will certainly consider it a model.

If they believe he possessed such learning and that his work is worthy of imitation, they will claim that the characters for the *kṣetraparigraha* (boundary-marking) should be written according to the orthography of the Vinaya scriptures.
If one happens to encounter those who see this as right, they slander it as wrong; those who hold this wrongness as supreme treat it as the truth.

Even if someone informs them of what is correct, they will surely resist and refuse to accept it, saying, "That was an ancient person; it is engraved upon stone—how could it be anything other than true?
From this, one teaches ten, ten teach a hundred, a hundred teach a thousand, until it reaches infinity.

"It spreads throughout the world as swiftly as the postal relay; how can this be? It is an inevitable principle that correct teachings are difficult to practice while false teachings are easy to follow.
If this is so, then I am one who confuses names and alters the fundamental, leaving future students as deaf and blind.
Is this not a source of great fear? Since I still know to feel such great fear, you must not misrepresent my writings to deceive future generations."
"How could you not feel even greater dread toward me? You ought to quickly erase and correct this so as not to bring shame upon me.
*Xianju bian*, Fascicle 24; *Xianju bian*, Fascicle 25.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān in the Song Dynasty.
Discerning the Name "Qiántáng" The names for Qiántáng as they appear in the *Shījì* and the *Hànshū* both lack the radical for earth (土). Yet, its origin remains unexamined. The *Shījì* states:
When the First Emperor traveled east and reached Qiandang, it was already known by that name during the Qin dynasty.

The *Geographical Monograph* of the *Book of Han* states that the western part of Kuaiji was situated in Qiandang. When Wang Mang usurped the throne and established the dynastic title "Great New," he altered names and changed designations;
consequently, he renamed Qiandang as Quanting. Since the commandery bordered the river, the local people suffered from this [flood]. Afterwards—
Hua Dexin, the Magistrate of the Council at the Han commandery, was a man of immense wealth who purchased land with his money to construct a sea embankment as a preemptive defense.

The local inhabitants relied upon his benevolence, and thus they inscribed a stele to record his merit. Consequently, the name was changed from "Wang Mang" (the false title of the usurper) back to "Qiandao," which was later written as "Qiantang.
The inclusion of the "earth" radical (*土*) in the character for "Tang" was likely intended to honor the merit of his initial construction. Therefore...

The character for "Qiántáng" is written either as a single radical or with the "earth" (土) radical; although these two forms are used interchangeably, I follow the ancient usage and prefer the single-character form.
Alas! Is it only the name "Qiántáng" that those of today do not model after antiquity?
In evaluating the inscriptions of Qiantang Commandery, a guest said to me:
"There are many surviving writings of Tang worthies from Qiantang Commandery; those whose rhetoric and reasoning are elegant and outstanding are threefold.
First is the 'Epitaph for Mount Xu' by Lu Yuanku; second is the 'Record of the Stone Classics' by Yuan Zhen; [third is the work by] Bai Juyi."
The "Record of the Cold Spring Pavilion" is next in merit; beyond these, there is nothing else to be taken from them.
I maintain that Bai Juyi’s "Record of the Stone Casket" does not fall behind these three works. For writing is the instrument for clarifying the Way, composed to rescue the age.
Had Bai Juyi been situated in the position of a high minister, he could have assisted the Son of Heaven with the Righteous Way and extended his benefits to all living beings. Thus it is seen.

The interests and harms of the four seas and nine provinces are all like those of West Lake; observing the sincerity and hypocrisy of the lords and governors of the states is like overseeing the officials of a county.
When rites and punishments accord with the mean, the people find no place for want, just as the waters of a lake are stored and released according to the seasons.
The compassionate heart and benevolent government are fully contained within this composition. Although Lu Yuanfu esteemed its phrasing, he merely recorded it in sequence.

The members [of the court] all follow the old explanations of former scholars and have not seen anything divergent; yet, this is a beneficial text that can serve as an instruction for honoring loyalty and rewarding filial piety.
However, these are merely the affairs of feudal lords, and the Way of the King does not adopt them. As for Yuan Zhen’s [writing on] Buddhism, he has indeed attained [a certain understanding].
Bai Juyi’s “Record of the Cold Spring Pavilion” is merely rhetoric that exaggerates the beauty of mountains and waters; it contains—

Regarding the use of literary expression, some say it is not so; I take [the truth] through the Way, as if taking it through words. The inscription on the stone casket is humble, and I am content to dwell beneath it.
Someone asks: "The Stone Casket and Cold Spring were both recorded by Bai Juyi; why is there such a difference between praise and censure? I reply:

Yangzi said, "As for Laozi’s discourse on the Way and its Power, I have taken from it only what is appropriate," yet he went on to "strike down benevolence and righteousness. [Thus, one's attitude toward the source does not necessarily dictate the tone of the resulting record.]
As for Guan Zhong’s abolition of ritual and music, I simply have no use for it; yet when he brought the feudal lords together and rectified the world, Confucius regarded him as benevolent.
However, regarding his construction of the *fandong* (a raised platform) and his blocking of the main gate, Confucius deemed him a man of small capacity.
Was Laozi and Guan Zhong so different? To love someone while knowing their faults, and for excellence not to conceal flaws—this is the way of the gentleman.
Regarding the *Epitaph for Marquis Cheng*, composed by Lu Shuwei:
the epitaph states that Marquis Cheng’s name was Zhoshe (昭說), his courtesy name was Dachuan (大川), and he was a native of Qingshan in Jiangdong.
Formerly, when the states of Wu and Yue were established as kingdoms, they received the imperial calendar from the Central Court; it was at this time that Dachuan rose from the commoners.
For generations, they have received the emoluments of Wu and occupied its noble ranks. Dachuang, who possessed innate talent from his youth, was endowed with a magnanimous character.

Whether it be military affairs, the rites of hospitality and celebration, sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples, or the duty of promoting the worthy and dismissing the unworthy—whenever one from the house of Dachuang emerged, though their wisdom was superior and their insight broad, and their office high and their rank weighty, when they came to oversee such duties, none could surpass them.

He was able to participate in deliberations; consequently, the people of Wu employed him, yet his rank and emoluments were not sufficient for his merit. His great reputation spread far and wide, filling the region south of the Yangtze River.
By nature, he was profound in benevolence and righteousness, and he bestowed his bounty extensively upon others, showering grace upon those below.

Even in eating and drinking, or in waking and sleeping, they could not forget him. Among the people of Wu and Yue, there were none who did not carry his literary works with them, study his learning, or engage in debate regarding his wisdom.

As for the scholars, those versed in the arts of yin and yang and the calculation of numbers, as well as those skilled in archery and charioteering— if they do not receive their due emoluments and are on the verge of perishing from hunger,
yet are permitted to enter and exit through the gates of the Great River (the royal domain) or are granted lands by the sovereign,

and they dwell in circular residences provided with abundant clothing, ornaments, carriages, and horses— then the supply of fine rice and grain, the expenditure on silks and fabrics, and the wealth of goods and treasures [are all provided for them].

Their utility is such that there is nothing it does not fill, from granaries and storehouses; furthermore, matters such as funerals, sacrifices, marriages, and weddings all proceed from the Great River.
Instances of this kind number in the hundreds. It is further said: "Moreover, those who are good men and gentlemen who delight in virtue and occupy the essential points are many;
thus even the sages and worthies find it difficult to manage them. Indeed, the Great River, because of its abundance of worthy men, is rendered weak by the clamor of the multitude.
He was killed by the people of Wu, and his bones were buried seven *li* south of the ancient city of Kuaiji beneath tall pines.
At that time, the people of the state were struck with awe by their national taboo;

fearing calamity and being obsessed with their own safety, they ensured that although he was a worthy man of the great river, the historical records could not record him, the bronze and stone inscriptions could not commemorate him, and the ancestral temple could not enshrine him for a hundred years.

Since his passing, no virtuous reputation has been heard of him. As I read his writings, I see that Shuwei laments that Lord Cheng’s retributions were not meted out, and he censures the people of Wu for promoting sycophants to harm the worthy.
I privately believe that Shuwei merely exposes the faults of Lord Cheng rather than recording his virtues. Why is this so?
He gathered scholars to purchase empty fame and bestowed favors abruptly to usurp the sovereign’s authority; such was his emptiness.
His reputation was sufficient to move the customs of the people, and his sudden displays of generosity were sufficient to win over the hearts of the populace;

he was one who harbored treacherous evil within, intending to plot usurpation and rebellion. As the *I Ching* says: "A minister murdering his sovereign, a son murdering his father—the way it comes about is gradual.
Had the people of Wu not discerned this early on, the altars of state would have become the possession of the Cheng clan. Mencius said: "Man..."
"One must first insult oneself before others insult one; a family must first destroy itself before others destroy it;

a state must first attack itself before others attack it. It was only fitting that Marquis Cheng lost the way of a minister and brought about his own destruction, and that the people of Wu subsequently killed him.
As for those who establish military merit and expand the frontiers, how could they compare to the Wei and Huo of the Han?
In reading the biography of General Huo, I see that the Grand Historian recorded:
Su Jian said to me, "I have often remarked that the Great General is most highly esteemed, and the worthy gentlemen of the world all praise him.

I wish for the General to observe how the famous generals of antiquity recruited and selected the virtuous; strive in this way! The Great General declined, saying, "Since the time of Wei Ji and Wu..."
The Emperor constantly gnashed his teeth against An Shi for harboring such numerous guests;

yet, it is the prerogative of a sovereign to personally attract scholars and officials, to recruit the worthy, and to dismiss the unworthy. Ministers merely uphold the law and attend to their duties—why should they recruit scholars?
General Biaoqi also followed this principle in his conduct as a commander. Even with the Han Emperor’s great power and prosperity, he still gnashed his teeth in resentment.
Even when Huan of Qi harbored doubts regarding the great achievements of Wei Qing and Huo Qubing, he did not dare to recruit and welcome virtuous scholars;

how much more so in the case of Wu and Yue during the Warring States period? Lord Cheng was but a subordinate official, yet he usurped the authority of his sovereign—how could the people of Wu fail to harbor suspicion?
The *Zuozhuan* records that Prince Shangchen suddenly began bestowing largesse upon the state and gathered many followers, exhausting his private wealth and even borrowing from the public treasury.

If the Minister had followed this course to the end, chaos would have been averted. Had the Marquis of Cheng observed the way of a loyal minister and son, and if there were truly worthy scholars, he would have recommended them to the Sovereign;
if they were truly unworthy, he would have dismissed them by the Sovereign’s command.

If he had thus allowed the Sovereign to receive all the credit for his governance, would there have been the calamity at Kuaiji? I have observed the writings of Shuwei and seen that the Marquis of Cheng...
The tracks of such lawlessness are as clear as pointing at one’s own palm; it is fortunate indeed that the historical records do not document his crimes.
Shuwei was a great Confucian scholar, yet he failed to censure Lord Cheng’s transgressions to serve as a warning for the future, instead regarding him as a worthy man—is this truly acceptable?
I harbor private doubts about this, and thus I record these words to await those who understand the Way of the Sages so that they may resolve my confusion.
Thus it was. [The author] distinguishes [the views of] Xun Qingzi:
Since the death of Zhongni (Confucius), heterodox schools arose in profusion and the Right Way was consumed by fire; the living people of the world, not turning to Yang [Zhu], then turned to Mo [Di].
Among those who returned to the teachings of Mozi, it was only Mencius and Xun Qing who authored books to clarify the Way of the Sages.
They traveled extensively to persuade the rulers of their time, with the intent to eliminate hegemonism and promote true kingship, and to drive out the corrupt to return to the pure.

Although their Way was not put into practice, their words remain as an empty legacy for the world, enabling those of a hundred generations hence to know how to reject the heterodox and honor the orthodox, and to revere benevolence and righteousness.

When ritual and music are practiced through actual conduct, the Way of the King can be restored; thus, those of the world who speak of great Confucian scholars invariably pair Xunzi and Mencius together in their praise.

Lu Ruyang, however, argued that because Li Si studied under Xun Qing and later became Chancellor of Qin, he used his influence to flatter the First Emperor, leading to the burning of books and the burying alive of the Confucian scholars, and consequently held Xunzi responsible for not knowing that Si was unkind.
Yet to transmit his Way while being ignorant of observation and hearing, he claimed that Xunzi was not virtuous and was no great Confucian scholar.

I say that Lu’s error lies in this: if one were to judge others as unvirtuous based on the lack of benevolence in this [Xunzi], then even though Yao, Shun, and the Duke of Zhou were all sages, you yourself would be as unworthy as Danzhu and Shangjun, and your younger brother would be like Guan Zhong.
As for the lack of benevolence in the Uncle of Cai, how can one say that because his younger brothers were unworthy and unkind, Yao, Shun, and the Ji clan were not sages?
If they were indeed sages, then how could one use the lack of benevolence in Li to blame Xun for his lack of virtue?
Someone may say: "The rulers of Tang and Yu knew their sons were unworthy and thus abdicated the throne to Shun and Yu; how can this be compared to [the case of Yao and Shun]?"
If one asks whether Xunzi failed to perceive that this was an act of benevolence and yet transmitted the Way, I reply: Is the abdication of a throne comparable to the transmission of the Way?
To transmit the Way is to provide instruction; to abdicate a throne is to hand over its regalia and authority.
Did Yu the Sage have no instruction for Zhu and Jun? One who knows another is unworthy and yet fails to instruct them—can such a person be called a sage?
"If Xunzi were in a position of authority and transmitted these [teachings], one might hold him accountable for being unvirtuous;
yet, is it not perhaps improper to hold him so accountable for his instruction? Confucius said, 'I would rather encourage their progress,' and Mencius said, 'If they come, do not reject them.
This is what is meant by the way of instruction. Someone asked: "What sort of man was Li Si? He received the teachings of Lü Ke."
"If they are instructed but remain unkind, is it because they are the lowest sort of fools? He replied, "They are indeed the lowest sort of fools.
Although they receive instruction, they regard benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music merely as tools for adorning their wickedness; they cannot put them into practice.

When they eventually gain power—as in the case of Qin, which burned the books and buried the Confucian scholars alive—what is there to wonder at? Confucius said, "Only those of the highest wisdom and the lowest folly do not change."
To shift the focus to the "lowest of the ignorant," even though it is said they hear of benevolence and righteousness, one cannot make them wise—is this not what Li Si was?
Master Luyang’s misrepresentation of Xunzi is already excessive; therefore, I shall clarify this.
"Delighting in Mountains and Waters" distinguishes between mountains and waters; the gentleman delights in them, and the petty person likewise delights in them—thus their delight is the same.
Yet the reason for their delight is different. As for the delight of the gentleman, it serves to restore one's true nature.

In human goodness, one strives to delight the emotions; the gentleman knows that human nature is fundamentally good, yet it is turbidified by the seven emotions and restored through the five constants.
The five constants are the means by which the emotions are regulated.

Observing this, the stillness of the mountain resembles benevolence (*ren*), and the movement of the water resembles wisdom (*zhi*); therefore, when one cherishes these qualities, the mind does not forget benevolence.
It is through knowledge that the mind does not forget benevolence (*ren*). When one possesses both benevolence and knowledge, every movement will necessarily accord with the Way (*Dao*).

Therefore it is said: "The benevolent person delights in mountains; the wise person delights in water. For the petty person, it is not so; they merely delight in the towering peaks to satisfy their eyes and the murmuring sounds to gratify their ears.
What benevolence is there? What wisdom is there? Yet when such a person acts, [it is contrary to the Way].
One will surely deviate from the Way; hence it is said: "The petty man lacks all sense of shame and restraint.

Now, the flying insects and the crawling creatures do not dislike the mountains, nor do the scaly and the shelled creatures dislike the waters; it is simply that they are unable to inwardly contemplate benevolence and wisdom.
Alas! There are those who shake their robes on high ridges and wash their feet in clear depths, yet whose hearts cannot restore themselves to their true nature.
Could it be that those who cannot follow the Way are merely fond of flying creatures, beasts, scales, and shells?
To argue that the First Emperor employed ghosts to labor for him—
claiming he used ghosts to move mountains— is neither recorded in the *Shiji* nor does it accord with human experience.
I also recognize that these erroneous doctrines are numerous; nevertheless, the rise of such errors must have its origins.

I suspect that the doctrine of "employing ghosts" was not originally the speech of men resentful of service or women left barren during that era, but rather that later generations transmitted it excessively, claiming it truly could employ ghosts. Why is this so?

It was because after Qin, through the strategies of *heng* (horizontal alliance) and *cong* (vertical alignment), swallowed the two Zhou states and brought about the destruction of the six kingdoms. Upon reaching [the Han],...

The First Emperor’s majesty shook the four seas, yet he could not master himself through ritual propriety nor maintain his position through benevolence; instead, his extravagant mind grew daily more fervent and his tyrannical governance increased day by day.

He became addicted to the use of arms and promoted magnificent palaces. He instituted severe punishments, deluded himself regarding immortals, took the Bai Yue tribes in the south, and built the Great Wall in the north—this was his addiction to weapons.
He constructed the Apang Palace and the Wangyi Pavilion—this was his promotion of magnificent palaces.
Those who slandered [the court] were executed by clan, and those who spoke in private groups were beheaded—such were the severe punishments.
Leading young boys and girls with cropped hair, he followed Xu Fu across the vast blue seas to seek Mount Penglai and gather divine elixirs, deluding himself with the idea of immortal transcendents.
At that time, the people could no longer sustain their lives; the simple, common folk looked upon one another in distress, saying, "May we, as brothers, somehow escape the clash of arms."
Those who have already died will likely not escape death from laboring on earthworks and timber projects;
those who might avoid such labor will likely not escape death by encountering the penal code. My brothers are already destined for death;
as for my children, how could they possibly avoid drowning in the great waves? They all said, "The First Emperor does not employ people, but rather..."
The "Spirits of the Laborers" (Yìguǐ) were already all suspicious that they would surely die;

therefore, when Chen Shè—a man of the common serf class—led a host of "crowd-assembled" followers to attack Qin, the whole world gathered like clouds and followed him like shadows, leading to the fall of the Second Emperor and his own death at the hands of others.
How could one know that this did not arise from the deliberations of the "Spirits of the Laborers"? Hence it is said: "I suspect the Spirits of the Laborers."
Is this not merely the rhetoric of men resentful of their lot and women lamenting their solitude? Alas!

When people today behold the precipices and anomalies of the mountains—those which have been naturally split asunder since the beginning of creation—they must claim that the First Emperor once tested his sword there.
When they encounter vast floods, they must claim that the First Emperor drove them forth to fill the ocean. Alas, the "Ancestral Dragon"!
The cruelty of that [reign] was not necessarily as extreme as this, yet the people, down to the present day, attribute all the world’s calamities and anomalies to it.
Perhaps it is because they have been led to speak thus that this guilt is cast upon Qin. Confucius said:
"For this reason, the gentleman hates to dwell in the lower reaches. Alas!
*The Collection from Secluded Dwelling*, Volumes 25 and 26.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
A Record of Errors in the *Jianming shu*:
Upon reading Qiu Guanting’s *Jianming shu*, I observed four errors therein, which I have therefore recorded. The first concerns the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, Year 4 of the Reign of Yin (Yin 4):
"Wei’s Zhouyu murdered his lord Wan," who was Duke Huan. Qiu states that "Wan" should instead be written as...

To mistake "Mao" (貌) for "Wan" (完) is an error. A name is used to summon its corresponding substance, yet in the end, one will avoid pronouncing it; therefore, once burial has taken place, a posthumous title (*shì*) is conferred.
If the Duke of Wei were named Wan, how could he be titled *Huán*? I say that Guangting is incorrect. According to the ritual, one does not avoid names that are merely similar in sound.

Commentators claim this is because such names are difficult to avoid; however, when the name of Shun or Yu was used, one did not avoid the word "wind" (*fēng*), as it shares the same phonetic component.
When the rain is called "rain," one does not avoid the character *qū* in the name of Kong Qiu; "Wan" and "Huan" are merely names that sound similar.

Thus we know that when the Marquis of Wei was named Wan, he did not avoid the character "Huan. What fault is there in this? The avoidance of names that sound similar is likely a restrictive convention developed in recent times.
At the beginning of the Yanhe era of the Tang dynasty, Jia Zeng’s father was named Zhong, yet Zeng was appointed [to office].
The Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren) who proposed the theory argued that since the pronunciations were identical but the characters distinct, there was no violation of ritual propriety (*li*).

Guangting countered that while the name was "Wan," it was impossible for him to receive the posthumous title "Huan" (the character for which shares the same pronunciation as "Wan"), and thus his claim that the *Spring and Autumn Annals* contained a scribal error was erroneous. Second, the *Shangshu*, "Wucheng" chapter, states:

"The vanguard turned their spears against one another, attacking those behind them as they fled north; blood flowed so thickly it floated the pestles. Kong Anguo explained this as "blood flowing so thickly it reached the mortars."
"‘Pillars’ (chǔ) is an exaggeration. Qiu says that the account of blood flowing so as to float pillars does not accord with human experience;
here, ‘pillars’ should be taken as an error for the character ‘shield’ (hàn). In the *Hanshu*, it says ‘blood flowed so as to float shields’ (lǚ), and ‘shields’ is indeed ‘shields.

They are commonly called ‘side-shields’ (bāngpái); this object is light in body and might thus float. I said: "An-guo’s statement that it is an exaggeration captures the essential meaning. Furthermore, [the text] records:"
To say that "the floodwaters overflowed to the heavens" implies that heaven itself might be submerged; this is merely an exaggeration, as Liu Xie termed it *kuashi* (hyperbole).
If one were to claim that a pestle could float because it was heavy, such a thing would not accord with human experience; yet to suggest that heaven could be submerged is an even greater error.
If that were so, what character in the phrase "overflowing to the heavens" (*taotian*) could possibly be mistaken? Mencius said: "With the most virtuous to attack the unvirtuous."
"And how could there be blood flowing enough to float pestles? Since Mencius was still relatively close in time to the Master, his records should not have been erroneous;

thus, he criticized ancient books for sometimes exaggerating events. Zhao Qi cited the *Shenggao* (Song High) from the *Shijing*, which says [the mountain] "reaches to the heavens," as an analogous case, yet he did not claim that the character "pestle" (*chu*) was a scribal error.
Third, in the *Lunyu*, the Master said: "If one does not have the eloquence of Zhuyue... and so forth.

"‘The beauty of the morning is difficult to escape in this present age’—Guangting says this refers to Confucius lamenting that what is esteemed in the degenerate age is merely eloquence and appearance.
If this were so, one could not say [the passage] possesses the beauty of the Song dynasty;
rather, the character 'you' (有) here must also be a transcription error for 'bu' (不). I said: "Zhongni was distressed by the times’ obsession with physical beauty."
It is then said: "I have not yet seen one who loves virtue as they love beauty. This is because at such times, the love for flattery is even more intense than the love for beauty;
hence it is said: "If one lacks the flattery of Zhoutuo while possessing the beauty of Zhaochao, it will be difficult to escape harm in this age.
This implies that if one possesses beauty but lacks flattery, one has not yet escaped harm; how much more so for one who lacks both, yet practices benevolence and righteousness? Thus...
The lack of righteousness in the state can be known from this. Guangting did not understand it and falsely claimed that the characters were erroneous. Kong Anguo’s commentary states:
"It means that one might expect to be as sycophantic as Zhu Tuo, yet instead one is as beautiful as Song Zhao;

it is difficult to avoid harm in the present age. I consider Kong’s explanation to be correct. Fourthly, the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) records that Song Yi said: "Now Qin is attacking..."

If Zhao wins the battle, its troops will be exhausted, and we shall take advantage of their debilitation. Qiu says that "taking advantage" (*cheng*) implies the duty of serving one's superior, which is logically inconsistent;
it should instead be the character for "to ride over" (*sheng*). This is because the meaning of "riding upon the victorious to pursue the defeated," or "the strong riding upon the weak," is the same.
I say that the character "take advantage" (*cheng*) is correct, for since they are exhausted first, we take advantage of them from behind; this is precisely what is meant.
The character "chéng" (承) is used here because its meaning of "receiving from above and offering to below" is identical to that of the preceding passage; thus, the character "chéng" is employed.

To "mòng" (乘) means to ride upon one's own victory, whereas "rígéng" (剛乘) refers to the superior riding upon the subordinate. How could this be the same as the latter meaning of "receiving what was previously worn out by another"?
Alas! The great scholar Guāngtíng may have erred in his judgment of right and wrong; should not later scholars be cautious?
Li Xizhi’s "Reply to Liang Carushu on the Evaluation of the Merits and Demerits of Literary Composition" contains many points that accord with reason;
however, there are indeed instances where the phrasing and composition lack refinement. As for the *Zhongshuo* of the Wang family, it is commonly transmitted as being by the Duke of Tai (Laozi).

The *Jiajiao* (Family Instructions) is indeed by him. I maintain that Zhongyan’s writings possess such purity of diction and sincerity of principle that they do not fall beneath the *Fayan* (Discourses on the Dharma).
Yet, as for the popular transmission of the *Jiajiao*, even a child of three feet could laugh at its vulgar and uncouth language;

compared to the *Zhongshuo* (Discourse on the Center), it is as far apart as heaven and earth. And yet, Li Ao contended with them in the realm of literary composition, failing to recognize his own lack of skill.
Is it not that those who travel this path have perhaps too dim a faculty of discernment?

I once read Xi Zhi’s letter in response to Huangfu Shi, in which he laments that the *Jiu Tang Shu* is so vulgar and shallow that it fails to exalt the sublime virtues of Gaozu, Taizong, and the successive sagacious emperors;

he thus declares his desire to revise and edit the national history to produce a work of enduring authority, adopting the spirit of Confucius in bestowing praise or censure to capture the Heavenly... [intention].
I shall take the discernment of right and wrong as my foundation; what the factions deem right, I do not necessarily deem right, and what the factions deem wrong, I do not necessarily deem wrong.

Should my writings be completed and transmitted, those who are wealthy and noble yet lack merit and virtue will not necessarily have their fame proclaimed to posterity, whereas those who are poor and lowly but possess moral integrity... [will be so proclaimed].
That which is complete is not necessarily not resplendent for eternity;

I find this argument most inspiring and have always regretted that Heaven did not grant Xi Zhi a long life so that he might cultivate his studies to fulfill his aspirations and complete his work, thereby sparing figures such as Sima Qian and Ban Gu the shame of their predecessors.
Yet, upon observing that the *Zhongshuo* and the *Jiajiao* share identical phrasing, I began to suspect that Xi Zhi had merely engaged in superficial editing.
The national histories, in their condemnation of evil and praise of good, are not without error. Alas!
To place Yu Zhongshuo and Yu Jiajiao in the same category, or to transmit Laozi alongside Han Fei—how can such evaluations of the Li Tang era be so profoundly misplaced?
Having obscured the merits of past sages and misled later scholars, I have therefore composed this essay.

It is said that even the flaws in white jade can be polished through practice; as Lu Shiheng remarked, "Though something may issue forth from a skillful mind, it may still incur the derision of those with clumsy eyes. How true this is!
While reading the *Zhongshuo*, Wenzzi first presented ten memorials to Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty; when they were not heeded, he returned to live in seclusion between the He and Fen rivers.

There he tilled the soil for food and raised silkworms for clothing, living with serene contentment. Subsequently, he lamented the decline of Confucian culture and sighed over the loss of the Way of the King.

When the [tradition] had fallen into ruin, he continued the Six Classics by composing the *Zhongshuo* (Discourses on the Mean) to instruct his wise and virtuous disciples—some one thousand in number—on the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Zhou, and Confucius.

When the Tang dynasty arose, those who assisted Emperor Taizong in achieving great tranquility and nearly attained the Way of the King were all disciples of Zhongyan. Thus we know that Heaven intended to destroy the Sui...
Chang Tang presented his strategies to Emperor Wen, but the Emperor could not employ them; instead, he bound him with official stipends, causing him to withdraw into seclusion.
There, he instructed Xuanling, Ruohui, Zheng Jing, and others, who later became the virtuous ministers of the Tang.
Thus we know that the Way practiced by Taizong was the Way of Wenzhongzi. Alas! The Way of Zhongyan was truly magnificent—yet how much of it remains in the *Zhongshuo*? (Ten)
The work was compiled by his disciples, including Xue Shou, who recorded his deeds and words after his passing; it is largely modeled upon the *Analects*.
Most scholars of the Tang dynasty claimed that it plagiarized the *Analects*, and thus Zhongyan’s Way and the phrasing of the *Zhongshuo* were largely ignored and not praised.
Only Lu Gui-meng, Pi Ri-xiu, and Sun He slightly extolled its merits.

It was not yet possible to ward off their insults and illuminate his profound mysteries. However, when the Grand Master Sun Han of our Sagely Court composed the "Discriminating Essay on Zhongzi," it may truly be said that he warded off those insults and illuminated the profound mysteries.
Consequently, those who indulge in reckless polemics were unable to block the path;
from this point forward, later students have felt shame for not reading Zhongyan’s books and shame for not knowing Zhongyan’s Way, thereby enabling [the tradition] to endure for a hundred...
That the world has universally attached itself to the Way of King Tong is due to the power of Master Han;

I venture to measure that the various worthies such as Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan all failed to praise Wen Zhongzi—was it because they envied his virtue and wished to exalt their own Way, or was it because they truly did not know his Way and thus criticized him?
If they were merely envious and obscured by bias, then these worthies themselves cannot escape being [mere followers of] Wang Tong.
As for Yang Zhu and Mo Di, did they not know that in later generations there would be one like Mencius to thoroughly refute them?
If they truly did not understand their way and yet criticized it, then Han Gong was far more virtuous than the scholars of the Tang;
yet even Han Gong still censured Xue Shou and others for having shallow talent and weak pens, being unable to record good deeds as they truly were and instead arbitrarily adding embellishments.
If one were to equate the punctuation and phrasing of this work with that of the *Analects* and model its account of Zhongni’s life after his own, I venture to say such an approach is incorrect.
Even if Zhongyan’s life had coincidentally shared certain traits with those of Zhongni, how could this have allowed Bi Shou to conceal them and fail to describe them?
When matters happen to coincide, how could Han Gong know they were spurious? How could one distinguish [the authentic] from the different simply because it does not match Zhongni?
Those who employ deceptive speech may all claim their own doctrines are as real as the sentences in the *Analects*.
If readers take those texts as models to clarify the Way, what harm is there? When the Duke of Wei asked about military formations, Confucius answered with matters of ritual vessels;
when King Liang of Wei asked about benefiting the state, Mencius replied with benevolence and righteousness. Thus, [the substance of the teaching remains the same despite the different contexts].
Huan Tui wished to harm Confucius, yet Confucius declared, "Heaven has bestowed virtue upon me; what can Huan Tui do to me?
When Zang Cang slandered Mencius to Duke Ling of Lu, Mencius said, "That I have not met with favor from the Lord of Lu is the work of Heaven;
how could the son of the Zang clan cause me not to meet with favor? These instances are all consistent in both wording and meaning with the *Analects*. Alas!
To call Zhongshu's statement "not permissible" may be criticized as being unfair to Mencius; yet if it were not so, then Bi Shou’s recorded words would likewise be without fault.
As I read his text, I fear that later generations might still be confused, and thus I have spoken this to clarify it.

Regarding the "Inscription on the Humble Dwelling" (*Lòushì míng*), popular tradition attributes it to Liu Yuxi; this is erroneous. It was likely composed by some vulgar and frivolous person who, driven by reckless vanity, plagiarized Liu Yuxi’s great reputation to deceive the ignorant and ensure its circulation. As for the composition of such an inscription: [The text continues with the argument that true inscriptions record the virtues of the deceased or the achievements of the site, whereas this work merely extols the virtues of the dwelling itself.]...

Thus, the author of this piece is not Liu Yuxi. Furthermore, the style and content of the "Humble Dwelling Inscription" differ significantly from the authentic works of Liu Yuxi found in the *Quan Tang Shī*. Its diction is coarse and its sentiments are shallow, lacking the refined elegance and profound insight characteristic of Liu’s genuine writings. Therefore, one should regard this as a spurious work rather than a masterpiece of the Great Tang.

Not extolling the virtues of one's ancestors serves as a warning against transgressions by pointing to specific matters; anything that falls outside these two categories cannot be called an inscription (*ming*).

Extolling the virtues of one's ancestors is exemplified by the inscription on the Tripod of Song (*Songding ming*); pointing to matters to warn against transgressions is exemplified by the inscription on the Golden Man in the Ancestral Temple of Zhou (*Zhoumiao jinren ming*).
Popular tradition attributes the "Inscription on the Humble Dwelling" (*Loushi ming*) to this latter category, yet it neither extols the virtues of one's ancestors nor... [retreats].

It is not the case that one merely points to specific matters to warn against transgressions; rather, those who are extravagant, boastful, and self-aggrandizing compare themselves to immortals and dragons.

Furthermore, they claim, "Only my virtue is fragrant. Yet, consider Yanzi’s wish to "not boast of his own goodness," the fact that the Sage Teacher did not dare call himself benevolent, or how Yu bestowed honors upon great scholars while knowing in his heart the path of the sages—how could there be such words of madness and perversity?
Lu Ji said: "An inscription should be broad yet concise, and warm."
This inscription is neither profound nor concise in its meaning, nor is its language elegant or refined; how could it possibly be the work of Liu Yuxi?

Those who are ignorant might go so far as to carve it upon jade tablets and hang it on their walls, fearing that later students and the unenlightened would admire Liu’s name, memorizing it by mouth and heart to serve as a model—would this not be a grave error? Therefore, I have composed this text to clear Liu Yuxi’s name.
I feel ashamed that I must rescue the errors of those who came after me; yet if they have consciousness after death, Yu Xi will surely feel my kindness.
*Xianju bian*, Volume 26.
*Collection of Writings from Secluded Dwelling*, Volume 27,
composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
The Dog that Responded to the Meaning (with Preface)
Eighteen *li* by water travel to the northwest of Qiandang County, there is a village called Yidian (The Grateful Dog). Formerly, a man kept a dog that was very well-trained.
Once, while traveling, he fell asleep intoxicated among the grasses as a wild fire approached from all sides, on the verge of burning him.

The dog was able to quickly reach the riverbank, soak its body in water, and drench the grass; thus, the master escaped disaster. When the man woke up, the dog’s strength was exhausted and it had perished.
Moved by its righteousness, I buried it there; the people of the district called the place "Dog Burial.
Later, the Regional Inspector changed the name from "Dog Burial" to "Burial of the Righteous Dog. While traveling by boat past that site, I composed this essay to commemorate it.
Vast and boundless are the moving creatures, yet among them, man alone is noble. The Way established for man is said to consist of benevolence and righteousness.
If these two are not practiced, one is of the same kind as the beasts. Yet even beasts can practice these; how then do they differ from man? How admirable is this dog!
It performed a meritorious deed in this place, saving its master from being burned by using its intelligence to soak the grass with water.
Though his body may perish, his name shall not fall;
alas, when a person possesses the heart of a beast, they are treated as kin because of their form; yet when a beast possesses the heart of a human, it is cast aside because of its form.
This is a matter of the heart—how can form distinguish it? A person with the form of a dog who performs good deeds here [is thus distinguished].
A dog in human form, harboring evil without ceasing; alas for this wicked man, why does he not die quickly?
The Prefect bestowed a name upon him; there is a purpose in this teaching, and I shall now critique Xie’s sandals.
To the west of Qiantang County lies a lake called West Lake; within the lake is a mountain called Gushan; to the west of the mountain is a slope called Manao.
This sick man has resided upon this slope for two years and constructed a pavilion atop it. From the north of the lecture hall, one follows a winding bamboo path that ascends steeply;
from there, one gazes level across the lofty mountains and looks down upon the vast expanse of water, beholding the seasonal splendors of spring and the moods of autumn.
Spread out before my eyes, the rain may have ceased by day and the clouds rolled up at dusk; the mountain ridges vie for their verdant hues and the flowers and trees compete in their splendor.
It is as if thick indigo and powdered pigment were splashed upon a screen, or like fine brocade reflecting through lapis lazuli.

Thus, during my leisure from lecturing, I lean against the railing and gaze afar, remaining thus until the end of the day, unaware of any other concerns. Alas! Is it that the external environment deludes me, or am I deluded by the environment?
Whenever the rain ceases and the mountain waters flow down, the secluded paths become marshy and the mountain rocks rugged and obstructive to travel.
Thereupon, I recalled how Xie Kexi, who gave himself over to the pleasures of springs and rocks, would climb mountains and ascend ridges wearing wooden clogs;
he would remove the front teeth when going up and remove the rear teeth when coming down. As an infirm man, I have adopted this design for my own ascent.
Descending from a height, one relies on the treads; when in danger, one can find safety; when treading upon the perilous, one makes it level. I have examined the reason for this:
it is because the *sun* (sandals) reduces what is in excess and supplements what is deficient. When climbing a mountain, the front rises while the back lowers;
by removing the front teeth [of the treads], one reduces what is in excess; by retaining the rear teeth, one supplements what is deficient. This is why climbing a mountain is made secure by them.
Furthermore, when walking down a mountain with level-soled sandals, one raises the back and bends the front;

by removing the rear teeth, one diminishes what is excessive, and by retaining the front teeth, one compensates for what is deficient. Thus, walking down a mountain with level-soled sandals is a means to achieve stability and ease.

Therefore, being able to find stability amidst danger and traversing perilous terrain with composure is due to nothing other than this principle of diminishing the surplus and compensating for the deficiency. Alas!
If one maintains this Way to walk through the family, the state, and the world, what cause for concern would there be regarding collapse or peril?
That which leads to collapse and peril arises simply from reducing what is sufficient to serve what is superfluous.
This is like failing to follow the design of Duke Xie’s sandals while wearing the shoes of an ordinary man; when ascending a ridge or climbing a height, one will inevitably stumble and fall.
This is a matter of great concern. I have examined the intentions behind Lingyun’s use of these objects; he entrusted them to this practice to correct the world and leave behind a warning.
How could it have been merely about sandals and clogs? Six hundred years have passed since the death of the Duke Kangle. How can one inquire further? Alas!

The practice of using the posthumous title *zi* (style name) for those who succeed to the rank of *shi* (official), such as calling him "Gongming," is according to the Confucian rites. Upon examining the teachings of the ancient emperors of India, one sees that they used the designation "son" to encompass both father and mother;
from this, it is known that avoiding one's given name was not their standard of propriety. Furthermore, among those sages and worthies...

To speak of the *zhì* (courtesy name) while omitting the *míng* (given name), or to speak of the *míng* while omitting the *zhì*, is because the *míng* and the *zhì* arise from the same source yet have different designations;
it is not a distinction between a fixed essence and the manifestation of virtue.

Furthermore, since the shaven head differs from the *zhāngfǔ* cap and the square robe differs from the *féngyè* scholar’s gown, why must one establish a *zhì* to imitate the Confucians? Nevertheless, even if one traces back to the origin...

Since there are those who follow the Way and possess its meaning even without formal instruction, those among the ancient śramaṇas of the Central Kingdom who were pure, simple, steadfast, and resolute—standing out as eminent figures—had both their names and reputations established together. My friend Jiqi was a native of Yongjia;

his appearance was dignified and his spirit clear, his aspirations were lofty and his speech upright. Previously, he studied the Dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* at Fengxian Temple and associated with...
My fellow disciple studied the Great Meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* at Shibi and followed the same path as I;

thus, having observed his conduct intimately and known his virtue, I was able to examine his name and its substance, and conferred upon him this style-name. The writing says: "To reach the ultimate and abide in sincerity and faith, so as to manifest clearly throughout the world.
The *Analects* of Confucius states: "He who reaches the ultimate in practice and abides in the Way of sincerity and faith will have his influence made manifest."

The *Yà* (Elegant Sayings) states: "In the world, 'yǎ' (elegant) means 'zhōng' (central); 'qí' (even/equal) also means 'zhōng'. Examining these two texts, it is clear that 'qí' is taught as meaning 'zhōng'.
Thus we know that my friend has established his name by continuing the Way of Great Centrality; how could this have been in vain?
Indeed, as for the Way of Great Centrality, none but a Sage can reach its ultimate realization, and none but a Junzi can hope to practice it. This is recorded in the *Shū* (Book of Documents).
It is said: "Establish the use of the Great Ultimate. The saying goes: "The virtue of the Middle Way—how supreme it is!

Furthermore, the ancient enlightened kings ascended to the heavens above and descended to the central lands below; they manifested proof of the Middle in their lives and discoursed on the Middle in their teachings. Alas!
If the Buddhists' esteem for the Middle is thus, and the Confucians' esteem for the Middle is likewise so, then how great indeed is the significance of the meaning of the "Middle"! My friend.
To aspire to the True Teaching while extensively mastering the Confucian arts, and to hope for the Mean as one’s guiding principle—is this not indeed appropriate?

Let one’s understanding hope for the Mean so as to be free from the stagnation of emptiness or existence; let one’s conduct hope for the Mean so as to be free from the error of partiality or depravity;

let one’s affairs hope for the Mean so as to be free from the fault of recklessness or narrow-mindedness; and let one’s speech hope for the Mean so as to be free from the defect of calumny or flattery. When these four are complete, cultivate them within—
As for the person, the realm of true purity is not far away; as for transforming others, the teaching of the Sage proceeds without being commanded.
In this way, more than half of the meaning is already grasped by merely pronouncing his name; the significance of "Manifesting Virtue" (Zhangde) is seen herein.

Regarding the selection of days, the practitioners of the Yin-Yang school maintain that the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of a day is presided over by benevolent or malevolent deities; these deities assist Heaven in governing the world.
Therefore, one who violates an inauspicious day will inevitably encounter calamity, while one who selects an auspicious day will surely be granted blessings.
The people have been deluded for a long time; whenever they undertake any change or action, they invariably select an auspicious day, hoping thereby to avoid calamity and attain fortune.

I do not believe this. For good and bad fortune, disaster and blessing, depend upon the person and not upon the day. The Book says: "Only the Supreme Lord is not constant; to those who do good, He sends down a hundred blessings;
to those who do not do good, He sends down a hundred calamities. If there truly were such a thing as a deity, [it would be so].
One who assists Heaven in governing must be able to punish crimes and reward merit. If one performs good deeds on an inauspicious day, how could they hasten their own calamity?
If one commits evil on an auspicious day, how could they receive its blessing? To perform good and hasten calamity is for punishment to be disproportionate to the crime;
to commit evil and receive a blessing is for reward to be disproportionate to the merit. Thus, rewards would go to those without merit.
If the innocent are punished, then the spirits will surely toy with the authority of Heaven;

those who arbitrarily exercise power and bestow blessings have certainly had their lands reduced and their ranks stripped long ago, for how could the Supreme Deity, in all His wisdom, still hold the handles of reward and punishment for such as these?

Amidst this ignorant and debased custom, people abandon loyalty and filial piety without practicing them, and neglect ritual and righteousness without cultivating them, yet they compete to choose auspicious days.
How is one who wishes to evade calamity while sycophantically seeking blessings any different from one who hates being drunk yet forces himself to drink wine?
The *Wangzhi* states: "Those who rely on ghosts and spirits, seasons and days, divination and casting lots to mislead the masses shall be executed.

The commentator says that in the present age, the observance of mourning, funerals, building roofs, marriages, and the use of divination manuals cause the people to turn their backs on ritual and violate the regulations.
How great is the harm caused by this! Alas, I have heard that for a family that accumulates goodness, there will surely be an abundance of blessings;
I have never heard that one brings forth fortune by choosing an auspicious day. For a family that accumulates evil, there will surely be an abundance of calamity;

I have never heard that one incurs disaster by choosing an inauspicious day. Therefore it is said: "Good fortune and misfortune, blessing and calamity, depend upon the person and not upon the day. Thus, I—
In undertaking any matter, one must necessarily choose the Way and act according to it; choose the rites and follow them; choose friends and associate with them;

choose a neighborhood and dwell therein; and choose a teacher and serve them. Diligently refining one’s reputation and sharpening one’s integrity, one ensures that there is no loss of the "heavenly rank," yet the selection of auspicious days is not among these concerns.

In the Preface and Biographies, regarding those sons of the Śākya who possessed expansive talent and insight: they were those whose inner being was permeated by the Three Studies and whose outward gaze encompassed the Five Sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

The Three Studies refer to morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). The Five Sciences refer to grammar, medicine, logic, craftsmanship, and the causes [of phenomena]. "Science" (*vidyā*) means clear understanding.

This is what is called refined discernment. To depict the physical form while transmitting the spirit is the ultimate pinnacle of artistic skill. Now, in depicting the physical form, one prizes resemblance;
once resemblance is achieved, it is essential to capture the vital essence (*jing-shuang*) within the brushstrokes and ink, for only then can the spirit be transmitted.
Because this is no different from the subject’s actual being, the world calls it "true likeness" (*xiashen*). How could this possibly be compared to the splashing of ink?

If one were to depict mountains and waters with reckless eccentricity, or represent ghosts and spirits by following mere impulses and personal whims without any standard of measure, this would surely be the wild extravagance of technical skill.
Therefore it is said that "rendering the appearance and transmitting the spirit" is the ultimate perfection of technical mastery. The Venerable Jiu was a native of Qiantang;
in addition to his formal religious practice, he became renowned throughout the regions of Wu and Yue for his ability to transmit the spirit, being esteemed as a high monk.
The great scholar Xi Shangren recorded his likeness; though still water reflects an image and a bright mirror reproduces a form, they do not compare to this.
Alas! That the refinement of art can reach such a state leads me to realize: is it not likewise so for those who study the Way of our Master Confucius?
Confucius attained the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the Duke of Zhou—a Way that is brilliantly manifest.

Nevertheless, just as humans possess physical forms, among the thousand years or so following the passing of Zhongni (Confucius), those who were able to succeed him in his Way were only Meng Ke, Xun Qing, Yang Yong, Wang Zhongyan, Han Yu, and Liu Zongyuan; they may truly be called those who captured his likeness and transmitted his spirit.

As for Shen Buhai, Shang Yang, Zhuang Zhou, Liezi, Zhu Xi, and Zizi— Please note that the provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion supplied. If you require a continuation or have further text to provide, please let me know.

Nowadays, scholars speak of "splashing ink to depict mountains and waters" or "letting loose strange forms to portray spirits and ghosts," asserting that one should follow one's own feelings and act according to whim;
how could such talk be modeled upon the standards of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius? Alas! To capture both the form and the spirit is the highest level of portraiture;
to capture the form but not the spirit is the next best; and to fail to capture the form while merely attempting to produce a human likeness is inferior.

Furthermore, what is there to be said of those who, in depicting human countenances, instead produce the forms of beasts? Li Si studied the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius under the gate of Xun Qing;

yet, having served as Chancellor to the "Ancestral Dragon" (the First Emperor), he burned the Six Classics and buried the Confucian scholars alive, employing severe penal laws to oppress the common people.
He left the world in a state of agitation until the Qin dynasty was finally extinguished. Is this not exactly like [depicting a man as a beast]?
The human form is depicted as that of a beast; because the superior person’s artistry was exquisite and his brushwork marvelous, this account is recorded.
It shall also serve as a warning for those who study the Way.
*Xianju bian*, Volume 27.
Collected Works of Secluded Dwelling, Volume 28.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Sòng Dynasty.
Refutation of the "Discourse on the Succession of Yǔ."
Zhong the Retired Scholar’s "Discourse on the Successor to Yu" is essentially intended to refute the followers of Śākyamuni.
