He maintains that while Yao faced the flood and Yu governed it, if there were a successor to Yu’s diligence in later generations, his achievements would have been distinct; yet this was not the case. He then proceeds to present Confucius as one who could succeed to Yu’s legacy, followed by Mencius, Yang Xiong, and Wang Tong.
He concludes that in these declining ages, the social order has no guiding principle, and those above have lost their hold over those below.
He presumed upon the Buddhist pagodas to instruct the ignorant with strange and deceptive delusions, seeking to influence the standard canons of the successive sages;
he defiled and destroyed the very foundation of the teaching and brought ruin to both family and state. Since the invention of writing, who has been more harmful than this?

For several generations, those capable of clarifying the truth and expelling such evils—those able to succeed the legacy of Yu—were none other than Han Yu. You, O Master, say that you [the Emperor] followed Han Yu in his exclusion [of Buddhism].
To disparage the Buddhists while claiming that those who can succeed to the achievements of Yu are utterly unlike them is an extreme error.

When the floodwaters overflowed and the common people were shrouded in darkness and torpor, Yu rode upon four types of vehicles, following the mountains and hacking at trees; he diverted the nine rivers toward the four seas, and the myriad people were finally able to eat grain.
As the saying goes, "He kept his palaces and residences humble yet exerted all his strength in the ditches and canals"—as for Yu, I have no fault to find with him.
Nevertheless, as for his merit in rescuing the people, the people truly received his bounty. Furthermore, if the teaching of the Buddha were indeed as harmful as a great flood,
yet Han Yu merely used empty words to reject it— without ever being heard to suppress that teaching or sever its lineage— it was because at the time of Han [Yu],
Buddhism was flourishing more than ever and the Buddhist followers were increasingly numerous, such that even the Son of Heaven held it in reverence.
If there were no leisure for such matters, then among the high officials, ministers, and great officers, those who are esteemed would be exceedingly numerous;

yet when Han Yu remonstrated against the Buddha’s relics and offended the Sovereign, he was banished to the remote wilderness—how could this possibly stem the source or block the flow to alleviate the urgent distress of the people?

If you consider the establishment of empty words to be the way of a successor to Yu, then even the Sage Great Yu himself would have been nothing more than a person of empty discourse regarding the names of Yi and Ji in the "Yugong" (Tribute of Yu).
In their words, there is no substance regarding the actual management of the waters. Alas!

Master Zheng, in venerating the Sage through his writings, has exerted great effort to exalt the Way of Han Yu, yet this has caused the ancient scriptures to all become false doctrines and the achievements of the Great Yu to exist only in word without merit.
Is it not tragic that he suppresses the virtue of the Sage and distorts the sublime maxims to such an extreme? Furthermore, [his arguments] are superficial...

How could the teachings of the [Buddhist] diagrams be at odds with those of the Confucians? The principle of retribution for good and evil is the profound expression of "blessing the virtuous and bringing calamity upon the licentious";

compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity represent the ultimate of "extensive charity and the salvation of the multitude. The methods of subduing and gathering are one with ritual and punishment, and the five precepts return to the same source as the five constant virtues.
As for returning from delusion to the truth, it is like the "Return" hexagram, where thunder emerges from beneath the earth.
"This is seeing the heart of Heaven and Earth. Liu Zhitou said: "Since the emergence of living beings, they have been fond of fighting, seizing, and mutually killing one another;
they have lost their true nature, becoming perverse, chaotic, and licentious, unable to return to their origin. Confucius held fast with his remaining words because he did not occupy a high position.
Yet, as Yang Zhu, Mo Di, Huang-Lao, and others increasingly mixed their doctrines, these teachings split apart, and our Buddhist discourse [arose]."
Later, [the teaching] emerged to push back the turbidity and return to the source; what we now call "being quiescent while alive"—ah, was it not because Zihou’s vision was so profound?
Judging by this, the fact that Han [Yu] slandered Buddhism while Liu [Zongyuan] believed in it is merely a difference in the likes and dislikes of their respective dispositions.
How could Han’s censure and refutation be equated with continuing the legacy of Yu? Furthermore, regarding the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma:

Nothing was more flourishing than during the Sui dynasty, yet Wang Tong was unable to speak exhaustively to refute it; this was to fail to support what was toppling and to fail to aid what was in peril.
How much less could he have clarified its Way? Thus, the *Zhongshuo* says: "The state of Liang fell into peril despite the cultivation of fasting and purification;
this was not the fault of Śākyamuni. The *I Ching* says: "If it is not the right person, the Way will not manifest itself."
Someone asked the Buddha, saying: "The Sage is indeed a sage. Furthermore, you, Sir, have already ranked Wang Tong as the successor to Yu.

Since Wang Tong lived during the Sui dynasty and witnessed the flourishing of Buddhism yet did not reject it—this being because he lacked the merit of governing the waters and had to wait for Han [Xin] to bring order—he may thus be considered the successor to Gung.
Yet, is it not perhaps improper to rank Wang Tong as the successor to Yu? Furthermore, if one were to do so...

As for those who claim that Han’s empty words can succeed to the legacy of Yu, figures such as Cui Hao, Wei Yuansong, and Zhang Bin—who all deluded their sovereigns into the extermination of the Buddha—truly possess merits exceeding even those of Yu.

If their achievements are considered successors to Yu, then Han’s empty words are merely the accomplice to the crimes of Cui and Wei; moreover, they are directly guilty of the "execution by drowning" (ji) themselves.

If those who suppressed and rejected Buddhism were merely continuing the legacy of Yu, then why did the sage emperors and enlightened kings who propagated the Buddhist teachings not all suffer from the calamities of the great flood?
The three sagacious sovereigns of our Imperial House have all honored this teaching:
the Great Ancestor summoned monks to the Western Regions, while the Second Ancestor restored the fallen rites by establishing translation bureaus to transcribe Sanskrit texts and broaden its path.
The Imperial Preface to the Sacred Teachings was composed to expound upon and magnify [the doctrine];

the present Emperor does likewise, for he knows that the Western Sage’s learning of purity, stillness, and non-action can assist the great administration. Is this not superior to Han Yu’s imitation of the legacy of Yu?
The Master’s transgression of virtue and ritual is indeed extreme; as for one who speaks falsehoods with eloquence, the Master is such a person.

As for "modeling oneself after Han," when there are those within our school who compose literary works yet instead reject their own fundamental teachings to exalt Confucian arts, they are said to "model themselves after Han."
As for the man Yu: if one takes Māhāyāna as the teacher and considers Māhāyāna’s writings as the model, then one cannot help but denounce Buddhism and must inevitably honor Confucianism;
this is but the natural course of reason. I say that this is not so.
Such a person is not a follower of Han, but rather a transgressor against Han. Allow me to explain why. Now, this man Han Yu wore the scholar’s cap and donned the scholar’s robes.
To orally recite the texts of the Six Classics and mentally savor the Way of the Five Constant Virtues is to be a disciple of Zhongni (Confucius).
Therefore, it was only natural that he should cast aside the doctrines of Śākyamuni, Laozi, and the hundred schools to honor his own teaching and consolidate its foundations.

If the sons of Śākya truly wish to take Han [Yu] as their master, they should expound upon the sutras and vinayas to produce literary works, and cultivate precepts and wisdom as their practice, broadening their compassion.
If one considers governance, when the Way of Benevolence is so lofty as to achieve great merit, he may be called a "Teacher of Han. Alas!
Just as Confucius was to the Minister of Personnel (Li Bu), so too was Nengren to the śramaṇas; he was their sovereign and father.
Since we know that serving one's superior with loyalty and filial piety is what constitutes excellence, it is likewise fitting to lead others by means of loyalty and filial piety in service.

Regarding one's own sovereign as one's own sovereign and one's own father as one's own father, how could one possibly assassinate one's own sovereign or displace one's own father to achieve loyalty for another minister or provide sustenance for another son?
Is this to see the worthy and strive to emulate them, learning from their conduct as men? To take the case of the subject, it would be disloyal;
to apply it by analogy to the son, it would be unfilial; to speak of it in terms of the teacher, it would be a betrayal of righteousness; and to observe it through the lens of human feeling...

Thus, they forget their gratitude in serving [the state] and lose the Way in establishing order; they fail in propriety. Alas! The Ministry of Personnel instructs people in the principles of loyalty, filial piety, propriety, and righteousness;
yet these Buddhist disciples take them as their masters and instead become rebellious ministers and treacherous sons who turn their backs on righteousness and lose propriety.
What greater injury and ruin is there than this? It is said: "They are not followers of Han, but rather the enemies of Han."
On "The Way, Virtue, Benevolence, and the Arts," the Master said: "Set your will upon the Way, rest in Virtue, rely upon Benevolence, and dally in the arts. He Yan said:
"The Way cannot be embodied, therefore one sets one's will upon it; Virtue takes form, therefore it can be rested in; Benevolence extends its benefits to others, therefore it can be relied upon..."
Relying on the Six Arts is insufficient as a basis; therefore, it is said: "The wandering student says: 'As for Dao and De, they are nothing other than what is called the Five Constant Virtues.
Dao means to tread upon; De means to attain. They refer to benevolence (ren), righteousness (yi), propriety (li), wisdom (zhi), and trustworthiness (xin).
To practice these and attain what is appropriate is called De. Han Yu said: "Dao and De serve as its vacant positions; benevolence and righteousness serve as its..."

Because the names are fixed, it is said: "The Way by which man stands consists of benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*). Since the gentleman’s resolve lies in the five constants, it is said: "He sets his mind upon the Way.
Once he has resolved to admire it, he relies upon it to practice it so that things may attain their proper fitness; thus it is said: "He relies upon virtue (*de*).
Ping-shu’s explanation still takes the Laozi’s method of "beating and discarding benevolence and righteousness" and "extinguishing ritual and learning" as its basis.
Is morality not precisely that which the Master inherited from Yao and Shun and took as his model from Wen and Wu?
If one claims that the Way cannot be embodied and therefore speaks of "aspiration" (*zhi*), then consider what Confucius said: "My aspiration lies in the *Chunqiu*.

Furthermore, he exercised the pen to revise and abridge, bestowing praise and inflicting censure so that rebellious ministers and treacherous sons would be struck with fear. Is this not something that can indeed be embodied, yet is called "aspiration"? Observing it from this perspective...
Wang Pi, however, claimed that there exists something else—unrestrained, empty, and grand—which is distinct from the Five Constant Virtues, and which he called the Dao and De.

Alas! His defilement of the Confucian teachings was indeed extreme. Someone asked: "If the Dao and De are identical to the Five Constant Virtues, why do you further say they 'rest upon benevolence' (ren)?
I replied: "This is because those who dabble in the arts may not necessarily possess benevolence; therefore, one must strictly admonish them to rely upon benevolence. Otherwise, it would not be so."

Thus, these are indeed harms. Take for example Hua Yuan of Song: because his charioteer resented not being given a portion of mutton broth, he galloped into the army of Zheng, and Zheng took Hua Yuan prisoner.
Then there was Feng Meng, who studied archery under Yi until he had mastered Yi’s way; fearing that Yi would surpass him, he killed him.
These two men possessed the arts of archery and charioteering, yet they caused great harm. It is like the case of Yu... [text ends]... 庾 (Yu).
That Gongzhi Si could not bear to turn back and harm Zizhuo Ruzi may be called "relying on benevolence while sporting with the arts.

(The people of Zheng sent Zizhuo Ruzi to invade Wei; Wei sent Gongzhi Si to pursue him. Zizhuo Ruzi said, "Today my illness has flared up and I cannot hold a bow; I am a dead man. He asked his charioteer, "Who is it that pursues me?
The charioteer replied, "It is Gongzhi Si. [Zizhuo] said, "Then I shall live. The charioteer asked, "Gongzhi Si is a skilled archer of Wei; why did you say you would live? Gongzhi Si...)
"Yi Gong Zhi Si was learning archery from Yin Gong Zhi Ta, and Yin Gong Zhi Ta was learning archery from me. Yin Gong Zhi Ta is an upright man; he must have chosen upright friends.

When Yi Gong Zhi Si arrived, he said, 'Master, why do you not hold your bow? I replied, 'Today my illness flared up, so I cannot hold the bow. He said, 'I, a humble man, learned archery from Yin Gong Zhi Ta, and Yin Gong Zhi Ta learned archery from you, Master.

I cannot bear to use the Way of the Master to turn back and harm the Master. Nevertheless, regarding today's business, I dare not neglect it. He drew an arrow, struck the rim of the wheel to remove its metal point, took four arrows, and only then returned."
*Collection of Writings from Secluded Dwelling*, Volumes 28 and 29.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
Song Shuji’s Preface:
This summer, I have been recuperating from illness at the foot of Mount Gu. Although I am weary, faltering, emaciated, and gaunt, I maintain my composure by relying on the Way.
My courtyard is silent and secluded, with no trace of the vulgar; occasionally, there is one who casts a glance upon me.
These individuals are all merely what are called great scholars among the clergy. In the eighth month of autumn, according to the monastic regulations, the monks approached me with great solemnity.

Once seated, they withdrew from their mats and spoke, saying they wished to receive from me the books of the ancient sages and study the compositions of those ancient sages, hoping that I would accept them and instruct them.
I greatly admired their ambition, for they were able to transcend the preferences of the common world.
"Since you still admire the Way of antiquity, you are surely one who aspires to follow the Hoofprints of the Steed (the Great Horses).

I then commanded him to sit again and said to him: 'I possess neither profound insight nor far-reaching vision; how could I possibly transmit to you the books of the Sages? I am neither a master calligrapher nor a great writer;
how could I possibly teach you the compositions of the Sages? Nevertheless, outside of my study of Buddhism, I have examined the Zhou [Annals]...'"
If one exhaustively studies the extant writings of Confucius and investigates the words of Yangzi and Mengzi, one may perhaps grasp their subtle purport.

If you do not consider me unworthy and wish to learn from me, what could I have hidden regarding the texts of the ancient sages? As for what is called "ancient prose" (gǔwén), it takes the Way of antiquity as its foundation when formulating speech;
such speech must clarify the Way of antiquity. What is this Way of antiquity? It is the Way of our Sage Teacher Zhongni.
This is the path practiced by nuns. In ancient times, Zhongni (Confucius) followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and established the statutes of Wen and Wu;
though the Six Classics are fully complete, the essence to which they all converge does not exceed benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*), the five constant virtues.

Benevolence, righteousness, and the five constants are called the Way of the Ancients. If one is to be devoted to these writings, it is essential to investigate the principles of the five constant virtues.
Losing oneself in the center and attaining mastery over transformation; transforming and thereby attaining penetration—once penetrated, one endures long; enduring long, one accords with the Dao.

Having thus attained this within the heart, one then gives voice to it as literature and spreads it as edification, so that those who rule may be like Xun and Hua, those who serve may be like Yuan and Kai, and the people of the world may become like the people of Yao and Shun, thereby rescuing the age.
The faults of our corrupt administration and its failure to follow the Way are not few; yet, though my words conflict with the world and are not employed,
I hope to leave behind these empty words for a hundred generations, elucidating the teachings of the four dynasties,

so that those who read them may know that the way of the Son of Heaven and Kings is noble, while the way of hegemonies and war is base, and that benevolence, righteousness, and ritual music should be cultivated.
To ensure that the pure customs do not fall into ruin and that one’s name is celebrated in the annals of history—this is the aspiration of those who compose literature.

The creation of "ancient-style" (guwen) writing truly culminates in this; it is not merely a matter of making the characters obscure or complicating the parsing of phrases that constitutes ancient-style writing.
If one were to consider the obscuration of characters and the complication of phrasing as the essence of ancient-style writing, then [the works of] Laozi, Zhuangzi, and Yangzi...

As for the heterodox writings of Mozi, how could they ever have employed prosody or parallelism? Is it permissible to regard the books of Yang Zhu, Mo Di, Laozi, and Zhuangzi as "ancient prose" (gǔwén)?
It is not. Laozi, Zhuangzi, Yang Zhu, and Mo Di abandoned benevolence and righteousness and discarded ritual and music;
their ways are not the ancient Way of our Confucius, who followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and took the statutes of Wen and Wu as his model. Therefore, when writing enters the realm of Laozi...

Those who follow the Zhuangzi are called "eclectic" (za), while those who follow the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are called "pure" (chun). In the histories of Sima Qian and Ban Gu, Huang-Lao is placed before the Six Classics;
they suppress loyal ministers and gloss over the deficiencies of their sovereigns—this is what the former scholars mean by "eclectic.

In the works of Mencius and Yang Xiong, Yang Zhu and Mo Di are refuted, the hegemonic wars are censured, and the frivolous and the false are rejected in favor of benevolence and righteousness—this is what the former scholars mean by "pure."
I have once attempted to discuss this: if its language is ancient yet it opposes Confucianism, how can it compare to that which is of the present day yet takes Confucianism as its foundation?
That which uses the language of the present and takes Confucianism as its foundation may be called "ancient-style writing" (gǔwén).
However, that which uses ancient language yet opposes Confucianism cannot be called "ancient-style writing. Nevertheless, where both language and meaning are ancient, I [have something to say].

They merely adopt what others have done and imitate their expressions; yet among these literary compositions, none are seen that take benevolence as their root, righteousness as their foundation, or the sages and worthies as their model.
Their writings, spanning many scrolls and pages, do not transcend descriptions of moonlight, dew, wind, and clouds.

Discourse that flatters the times and aligns with power is sufficient only to corrupt social customs; what benefit does it provide for moral transformation? Indeed, such is the nature of their composition.
One who is firm in their resolve and maintains their Way does not allow their learning to change according to the likes and dislikes of worldly custom.
As Han Yu of the Tang dynasty wrote in a letter to Feng Su: "I have long been composing writings; whenever I personally deem something good within my own mind, others consider it bad.
If it is slightly to my liking, people find it somewhat strange; if it is greatly to my liking, people will certainly find it very strange."
When responding to circumstances from time to time, he would produce works that were vulgar and commonplace; yet when he set pen to paper, they caused others to feel ashamed.

When he showed these to people, they considered them excellent. Those who felt slight shame would say they were slightly good, while those who felt great shame would surely consider them greatly good.
Judging by Wen Gong’s words, it is clear that ancient-style writing had long ceased to be esteemed by the times. It was not because [the author] lacked the endowment of refined harmony...
How could one whose temperament delights in the way of pure correctness fail to love it?

If you are still in the prime of your youth, you must apply the whip to this path without ceasing, so that the world does not say you are a "great lover" [of worldly things], nor that your heart feels great shame.
Only then, by sharpening your integrity and conduct so as not to be mixed with the vulgar, shall I expect you to reach the realm of the sages and worthies. If you possess this...

If one speaks of [the Way] while their conduct contradicts it, they are like a phoenix crying out with the wings of a hawk; I do not believe such a person can make the Way prevail. As the saying goes:

"Zi Zhang asked about making a journey. The Master said: 'If your words are loyal and trustworthy, and your conduct is earnest and respectful, you may travel even to the lands of the Man and Mo peoples.

If your words are not loyal and trustworthy, and your conduct is not earnest and respectful, how could you even travel within your own state or district? If his resolve falters even slightly," [he will fail].

He has composed several pieces of writing over the past days for me to peruse; their phrasing possesses considerable intent, and I hope he may cast aside the frivolous and ornate in favor of the profound and reasoned.
Alas! He is one who can be instructed; his capacity as a vessel awaits fulfillment.
From this, I have come to regard him differently than my other peers. In the tenth month of winter, he urgently requested of me: "I have already received your instruction; now I shall..."
When the Master Jia-he was traveling, I was unable to see him early or late to beg for his words as a warning;
I have therefore recorded his instructions on the essentials to present as a gift, so that you may not neglect or forget them. If you practice my words, then the Way can be attained.
Someone said: "You are a follower of the Buddha; why do you speak so extensively of Confucianism? I replied: "Ji follows my teachings."
Since he was a Confucian, I informed him using Confucian teachings and could not intermingle them with Buddhist ones;

when he was nearly about to follow me in studying Buddhism, I then informed him using Buddhist teachings and likewise could not intermingle them with Confucianism. Not to be redundant in one's instruction is the Way of antiquity.
This is the preface of the twenty-ninth day.

Preface to Master Wencong’s Collection of Poetry from Qiantang Someone asked about the Way of poetry, saying, "Is it not to praise the good and condemn the evil? He was asked for further instruction, and replied, "To praise the good means to laud them; to condemn the evil means to satirize them. The questioner asked, "Is it merely that?
Does one satirize so as to cause [the offender] to distance themselves from evil, and praise so as to cause them to reform? Is it not also to delight in benevolence and encourage righteousness?"
If those who are excluded are returned and those with true vision are honored, the Way of the King may be restored.

Therefore, in nothing is the cultivation of human relations and the transformation of customs greater than the teaching of the *Shi* (Odes). Alas! When the Way of the *Feng* and *Ya* ceased, ornate compositions proliferated;

their melodies were altered and their characters were paired, until today they have reached their ultimate limit—all merely depicting mountain scenery and the moods of water, or describing excursions to immortals' realms and the chambers of the bedchamber.
Gradually, this became a prevailing custom of competing in ostentatious embellishment.

Consequently, when a single word touched upon moral instruction or a single phrase fell into the realm of indirect admonition, they would shout with great clamor, baring their arms and glaring with hostility, saying: "This is a word of reproach! It mocks me! It insults me!
This is not what poetry is meant for! Yet, when questioned about the true Way of poetry, they would merely lift their heads and nod in agreement.
The Master looked at him with a smile and replied, "People have a saying: 'That which can be understood by the mind is difficult to describe in words.
Why should I say anything? Alas, how strange! From what source does the Way of Poetry emerge?
Is it from the Buddha? From Laozi? Or from Confucius? If it truly emerges from the Way of Confucius, then I have already seen the Way of Confucius."
One observes that among the works compiled by Zhongni (Confucius), all those praising the good and censuring the evil are merely expressions of eulogy and satire;
how could they compare to the so-called "poetry" of people today, which fills scrolls and covers pages, being all flowery and rootless, unfit for instruction?
Alas, such is the loss of the Way of Poetry! Śākyamuni heard of the Master Chong, whose courtesy name was Yuanshen.
He was a native of Qiantang. His realization of the Way was profound and his conduct was highly cultivated; he lived in leisurely retirement, never mingling with the vulgar.
In the intervals between his Buddhist practice, he composed songs and poetry to harmonize his nature and emotions.
Both pure sages and eminent scholars invariably recorded his name, such that those governing the realm were determined to see him in person. Master Cong and I indeed share a long-standing friendship.
Although he traveled back and forth, resting by night and halting by day, he never once spoke of the Way of Poetry.
At first, I also thought that one who looked up with a haughty air and narrowed his eyes, taking pride in his own poetry, must be someone whose path was different from my own;

thus, even though I had become familiar with his face and our acquaintance had lasted for a long time, I did not dare to question him. Last winter, while visiting me in the forest, he produced a scroll of poetry from his sleeve.

I have examined this work, and finding its language entirely archaic, I have investigated its underlying meaning; it is precisely the path of what was previously called "satire" (*cī*) and "eulogy" (*sòng*).
Through this, I have finally come to understand that the Way of Cóng is not like that of the common, idle folk. Alas!
Had Master Cóng not shown me this, I would have nearly lost the Way of Cóng. Just as I was about to distinguish and arrange it, he suddenly said: "Now..."

In this age, those who can roughly match his couplets and accumulate his chapters—if they are not the compositions of high-ranking ministers of the two systems (the Secretariat and Chancellery)—one would not even deign to seek them out.
How much less could the Way of Cōng’s poetry expect the words of a sick man living in my forest retreat?
Thus, I desisted. This summer, Master Cōng came to visit me again, bringing three volumes of his ancient and modern poems, and said:

I wished for your Honor to provide a preface, so I informed him of my intentions from last winter. He replied, "Since you recognize me as such, I shall seek out a sympathetic soul to compose a preface for it.
Who could stoop their shoulders and lower their brows to curry favor with those in power merely to produce empty words?
I am not one of those people. Although I declined, he would not accept my refusal; thus, I have recorded his words exactly as they were spoken.
At the beginning of this volume, I hope that future generations will know that the Way of Cong and his words were, in this present age,
truly preeminent and stood out from their peers. This preface was written on the sixth day of the fifth month of summer in the second year of the Tianxi era,
the year of Wumu (1018), at DuiCui Pavilion on MaNao Slope.
Preface to the "Poems Illuminating the Lake" Composed in Linked Verses:
In antiquity, the composition of poetry was not constrained by fixed rules; once the meaning was fully expressed, the phrasing would naturally conclude.

Thus, the principle of rectitude was clear and the elegance of refined patterns were manifest. From the Qi and Liang dynasties onward, however, these were restricted by the requirements of parallelism and prosodic meter.

By the time of the Li Tang dynasty, restrictive taboos had become even more severe; thus, there were cases where the phrasing was superfluous while the principle was insufficient, or where the principle was worthy of contemplation while the phrasing lacked merit.
Is it not so that the difficulty of achieving excellence in both lies therein? This allows us to see that poetry was easy in antiquity, but difficult in the present.
In the second month of spring in the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, De Yuan of Xiangchuan [wrote this] at Yujiang.
Xianrun of Xi溪 (Xi-xi), Qingyong of Shanyin, and Zhiren were all men of Chan and exegesis who had attained profound insight.
While discussing the Way at the Yunmen Monastery, they surveyed the vast and remote scenery and observed its sublime wonders, remarking:

"The spiritual Yue region, with its reflecting lake, is a magnificent sight under heaven—a supreme excursion for those beyond the mundane world. Since this pure landscape is now before our eyes, yet there is no poetic inscription for it."

Others shamed it, and I too was ashamed. Thereupon, taking up my brush and dipping my pen, with spirit kindled and thought emboldened, I composed a single chapter of an eight-line regulated verse (lùshī) in the five-character style.
Its tonal register is clear and lofty, while its diction and meaning are plain and unadorned;

that these qualities are combined in such perfection is indeed difficult to achieve. My deep sense of lamentation is thus expressed: "Where is the water-lily flower? For a thousand ages it sinks in azure depths."
To describe its ultimate state of immersion: there is a moist luster as one drifts on a spring excursion, and the clarity of a late afternoon as one passes by birds.
To speak of its vastness: there is cold light penetrating the Cave of Yu, and wintry hues encircling Shanyin. To speak of its function: when forms exist, shadows cannot escape;
where no person is present, hearts are not left unwashed. Such is the way its principles are distributed to move all things. Alas, those four paths!

While all people regard such works as merely the literary output of a single moment produced from the surplus energy remaining after meditation and lecturing, those who can produce such a theme and such lines are truly worthy of admiration.
This year, while I was convalescing in Yuhang and could not attend this assembly, that group of practitioners sent a messenger across the river to show me their composition.
Having read it over and over again with deep appreciation, I found its heights ever more sublime; therefore, I have composed this [preface].
Preface. A Preface for Sending Zhiren Back to Yue.
Regarding the most marvelous and sublime mountains and waters under heaven, the region of Southeastern China ranks first; within Southeastern China, the land of Yue ranks first. Lofty...
From beneath Mount Eyun, one gazes down upon the surging blue sea; its waters reflect the hue of the lake, merging with the vast void.
Since the mountains are so majestic and the waters so clear, those born amidst such an atmosphere must surely be individuals of pure virtue and eminent talent.
Among the monks of the black robes, there were many renowned scholars; figures such as Zhiyong and Lingche were truly produced from this land.

Master Zhiren possesses the spirit of the former sages; his calligraphy rivals that of Wang Yong, its structure and form unerring, and his poetic compositions emulate those of Xie Cheng, capturing their austere essence with perfect fidelity.
I have heard that the Way of Tiantai is sublime and the meaning of the Three Contemplations is vast;
that we should fail to carry this burden would be a source of shame for us. Thus, I crossed the Great River and arrived at Qiantang.
He studied under his teacher until he had thoroughly mastered the essential principles; the teacher once granted him his approval.

Now, the Way has no fixed direction and its nature has no substance—whether one emerges from seclusion or remains within it, whether one speaks or maintains silence, how could these ever deviate from the Way? Consequently, when silent, he equalized love and hate to overcome the self;
when speaking, he distinguished between good and evil to instruct others; when dwelling in seclusion, he discussed the scriptures and edicts to nourish his wisdom and understanding.
When one goes out, one seeks leisurely excursions among mountains and waters to delight the nature and emotions. Is the Way far away? It lies precisely here.
Now, on this journey, you first intended to return to your native land to roam among mountains and waters; I know that you will surely find delight in your nature and emotions there.
On the day you arrive, please describe for me the exquisite forms of the mountains and the clarity of the waters, and compose a poem to send afar so as to convey my feelings.
The will is inherently still and thus serves as the sovereign of the restless; pleasure must not be pursued to excess—the words of our Patriarch are complete on this point.
You, Master Dai, should investigate these subtle principles and practice them with diligence; do not make aimless wandering your primary concern. Exert yourself! Exert yourself!

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
I admonish against evil and exhort toward the good:
alas, the Great Dharma is in decline and the Sages have long since departed. Though those who don the black robes are numerous, those who truly seek the Way are exceedingly rare.

They compete for fame and profit as their sole capability, regarding the circulation of the teachings as a mere child’s play. Consequently, the gates of the Dharma are seldom opened, and the net of the Teachings is on the verge of collapsing.
Truly, it relies upon you, the descendants of later generations, to be able to uphold this Way. You all must empty your minds to request the Dharma and purify yourselves to rely upon your teachers.

In the short term, this aims for establishing one's character and bringing fame; in the long term, it aspires to transform the mundane and achieve sainthood. To manifest the Semblance Dharma, who but you can do so?

Therefore, you must cultivate your person and practice what you preach, being as careful at the end as you were at the beginning. Diligently apply yourselves to study and be prudent regarding both your public conduct and private life, avoiding all that is evil.

Treat friends as one would avoid tigers and wolves; serve good companions as one serves one's parents; honor your teacher with full ritual propriety and sacrifice your body for the sake of the Dharma.
When you encounter goodness, do not boast of it; when you commit a transgression, strive to correct it immediately. Be firm and unshakable in maintaining benevolence and righteousness;

remain joyful amidst poverty and illness so that you may forget your sorrows. In this way, you will naturally distance yourself from calamity and draw near to fortune—needless to say, this does not depend on comparing oneself with others.

To inquire about one’s lifespan, to flatter others in pursuit of honor and advancement, and to select auspicious days and times merely to evade periods of misfortune and stagnation—how could this be the far-reaching insight of a śramaṇa?
It is truly but the deluded sentiment of a worldly person. One ought to see the virtuous and strive for equality with them; when it comes to practicing what is right, one should not yield.
One should emulate the search for the Dharma by those on Mount Himavat and the seeking of teachers by Sudhana; fame and profit are not enough to move the mind.
One harbors no anxiety over birth and death; if one’s concerns are such that merit is achieved and the task accomplished, one will surely ascend from the near to the far.
Without peddling for fame, fame will naturally spread; without summoning the multitude, the multitude will naturally gather.

With wisdom sufficient to illuminate delusion and compassion sufficient to encompass others, one may cultivate one's own person in solitude when in straits, or achieve universal salvation when in prosperity, thereby causing the True Wind to prevail.

To once again raise the torch of wisdom so that what had been extinguished was restored to its brilliance—this may be called the mark of a great man; this may be called being an envoy of the Tathāgata.

How could one merely dwell in lecture halls with one’s traces mingled among ordinary folk, remaining unperturbed by filth and evil while showing no awe toward the practice and realization [of the Dharma], until habits accumulated into character and one’s own person was destroyed? This is how one begins to aspire to the teachings.
Those who were once superior and virtuous ultimately sink into base wickedness; such individuals as these are truly pitiable. As the poem says:
"There is no beginning that does not have an end, yet few are able to maintain it until the end. This is precisely what it refers to. Should those of middling or superior capacity not be cautioned?

Furthermore, although the divisions of wisdom and the schools of the Great and Small Vehicles differ in their doctrines, they all emanate from the Buddha-mind, with their intent residing within the Dharma-realm.
Because they had reached a common goal yet remained unenlightened regarding the Great Design (*mahā-vidhi*), they each relied on their own particular positions:
those who practiced the Sūtras and Śāstras regarded the study of the Vinaya as something to be discarded; those who followed the Vinaya schools regarded the Sūtras and Śāstras as mere empty fictions;

those who practiced the Mahāyāna Dharma subsumed the Hīnayāna, while those who listened to the Hīnayāna disparaged and rejected the Mahāyāna. Seeing only that their respective teachers praised their own partialities, they [fell into sectarianism].
To grasp at these views and engage in mutual contention over right and wrong—how could one know that the Buddha’s intent is eternally harmonious?

If one attains this realization and perceives no distinction between self and other, one should instead support and assist one another to bring all capacities and conditions to maturity. This is like the myriad rivers flowing toward the capital, all of which reach the sea;

it is like the hundred officials attending to their duties, all of whom serve the King. I have never seen anyone who would protect a single stream while intending to block the flow of the many currents.

To seek to abandon the various accomplishments while holding a single office—to examine the origins of how the Dharma Kings disseminated their transformation—each category of being was governed with its own specific jurisdiction.
The minor precepts correspond to the authority of ritual and penal law; the Mahāyāna corresponds to the responsibility of the balance scale.

Cultivating merit is like overseeing the transport of grain, while composing scriptures is like presiding over royal edicts. Thus, among the hundred officials of the state, all duties were fully cultivated according to their respective types.
Within the various schools of my teaching, they compete to expound upon the fruit [of enlightenment] to clarify this principle; how could one who clings to heterodox views be fit for this?

One must measure one's own talent and propagate the teachings according to one’s capacity. If one’s nature is quick-witted, one should study both branches to become proficient; if one’s insight is shallow, it is appropriate to specialize in one field.
If this is done, then though each spreads its own reputation and influence, together they accomplish compassionate salvation, returning as one to the ocean of harmony and sitting together in peace.
This is truly the southern compass for those lost on the path and the wooden gong of the teaching gate;
as one who occupies the seat of a teacher, you are surely free from any lack of virtue. You may proceed toward the fruit of Buddhahood with absolute certainty.

Yet, you harbor no self-congratulation regarding your meager insights and knowledge, nor do you establish the great pride of a "great man" to slight the awakened ones and delude future generations, even though it is said...
Listen as we seek out and rectify any errors or omissions in our words; you all should reflect upon this.
Preface to the Inscription for Master Wú, a Vinaya Master of Qiāntáng, at the Lecture Hall:
Master Wú, a Vinaya Master of Bǎoníng Temple in Qiāntáng, began his studies at Zhōngnán and later made revisions and supplements [to the Vinaya] while residing with Chùyún of the same prefecture.
Having perceived its profound mysteries, the Master closed his door and devoted himself to reciting and expounding the teachings for fifteen years.

Later, at the invitation of the former *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator of Monks) and *Tongjiao Dashi* (Great Master of Penetrating Teaching), Qingyun, he began residing at Zhaokong Temple. From that time on, he took the instruction of sentient beings as his primary task;

this was the fourth year of the Xianping era. Subsequently, his Dharma assembly expanded greatly, and students from afar arrived in droves, whom he disciplined according to the precepts and the Vinaya.

He regulated them through majestic deportment, so that their movements and stillness were all arranged in their proper order. Next, they returned to preserve tranquility; next, they moved toward transformation and enlightenment.
From this state of transformation and enlightenment, they returned once more to preserve tranquility. From preserving tranquility, they shifted toward the fruits of sagehood.

Up to the present day, while he resides in Tuṣita Heaven instructing sentient beings, his disciples such as Zhāoqìng—who possess fame and integrity, cultivate merit and deeds, and have been promoted to the ranks of lecturers—are prominent.
A certain number of disciples and followers requested that their names be inscribed upon the walls of the lecture hall to record their achievements and to encourage those who would come after.
The Master, having formed with me a friendship beyond words and regarding me as one who understands his heart, commanded me to compose this preface, saying:
"In ancient times, when the Sage of Benevolence ruled over the three realms, he took pity on the multitudes who had lost their way and strayed from their true nature."
One may desire to return [to the source], yet not knowing the path of return, one is thereby obstructed;
only by restraining oneself with the precepts, quieting the mind through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and illuminating it with wisdom can delusion be stilled and the true nature restored.

Even when great defenses are established, people still transgress them; if one sets aside these three and speaks of practicing the Buddha-way or heading toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), what is there to say?
"Is this not like setting out for Yue while driving a carriage north? Though it is said that he does not revert to the Classics nor deviate from the Sages, I do not believe it.

His name was Zewu, his courtesy name Yuanyu, and he was a native of Qiantang. By nature upright and square, his speech was correct and pure, and his conduct was exceptionally high such that his reputation was widely renowned.
Although he studied the sutras and treatises and mastered the histories and records, he took the precepts and monastic discipline as his primary responsibility, and furthermore desired—
He showed later students the path for returning [to the Dharma], making it known that the journey must begin with the study of the Vinaya.
Thus, being one who could both speak of and practice the Vinaya, he personally strengthened and re-established the collapsed framework and overturned standards;
consequently, the monks of Wu and Yue who looked north to serve him were beyond counting, and his later disciples became numerous and dignified.
When his movements did not exceed the bounds of propriety, people surely knew they issued from the public gate; thus, many followed him with praise.
Yet, as his perilous words offended the multitude and his conduct did not harmonize with the times, those who followed him with censure became twice as numerous.
Although the clamor of praise and blame was loud, the Way of the Duke remained unchanged.
The world does not advance or retreat, nor rise or fall, based on praise or blame. Critics claim that the Master’s mind was narrow and could not accommodate others;
is there any truth to this? Would such a view be unfit to serve as an instruction for later students? He replied:

"Only those of innate awakening, the Great Sages, are entirely free from the three losses. A virtuous person at the beginning of their practice desires to diminish their faults, yet they cannot achieve it."
Therefore, among the masters of the Li Tang dynasty in Zhedong, there were Qingjiang Xushou and others whose lofty conduct was peerless and renowned throughout the world;
yet Qingjiang suffered from narrowness and impetuosity, while Xushou suffered from abruptness and haste. When it comes to recording the biographies of eminent monks, could one possibly omit them?
Alas! Your own forthright and critical nature is comparable to that of Jiang and Shou; how could it cause any harm to the noble character of these men?
Regarding those who practice after us, students should focus on their strengths while setting aside their weaknesses. Does one who knows others truly obscure great virtue with minor flaws?
Confucius said, "Do not demand perfection from others. I once read the inscription by Li Xiangyang for Xiaoshan Temple, which says:
"From this, one knows that things cannot be complete; it begins by stating that the Sword Pond at Huqiu does not flow toward Heaven."
At Zhushiqiao there is no spring at its base; though human effort may be insufficient to match the wonders of Heaven, the Lingjiu Peak rises before one so loftily that distant gorges cannot be seen.
Since the mountains have little level ground and the springs emerge without forming pools, how much less can one expect to find a friend who fulfills every requirement?
By reading Li’s writings, one can know that they resemble the man himself. Someone asked why you titled your preface as such; it was, in fact, to praise the Master.
"If one follows this path and encourages those who have come to study, would it not be improper to speak of Gong’s errors? He replied:
"Does one who establishes a doctrine do so in vain? Where there is that which must be corrected, one must certainly correct it.

The task of correction lies in offering counsel, admonition, and warning. As for those who are empty, extravagant, boastful, hasty, or sycophantic, using such means merely to please the ears of the times—"
That actor was also able to say: "Your Excellency ought not to seek counsel from me; yet if you cause me to speak, it must be because you desire to hear my admonitions and warnings.
If Your Excellency can follow such admonitions, then toward others you will be free from the fault of harshness and exposure, and will instead enjoy the reputation of being perfectly virtuous.
When people receive such admonitions and warnings, they will no longer hold you to the standard of perfection."
In this act of Gu, there lies the principle of honoring the worthy; herein resides the Way of the Mean. May His Excellency take an interest in this record of names arranged by me.
As for those who have already ascended the hall following the six successive moves of the school, their names are duly inscribed;
let those who come after continue the record. This is intended to extol the spirit of the precepts and serve as a warning to the unworthy.

Preface to the Establishment of the Great Boundary at Zhiguo Monastery on Mount Gushan in Qiandang, from the *Xianju bian* (Collection of Works from Secluded Dwelling),
Volume 31, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Mount Gushan during the Song Dynasty.
When the Great Hero (Mahāvīra) established the dwellings for bhikṣus, he necessarily demarcated their great boundaries (*mahā-sīmā*);

was this not to define the territorial limits of the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*) and to establish the jurisdiction for the assembly of monks? Thus, one avoids the fault of rushing about and thereby damaging the Way, while distinguishing between the cultivation of goodness and the eradication of evil.
Such was his regulation, and such is its arrangement. As for Chigakuen (Jñānaphala-vihāra): [The text continues with the description of the temple complex.]
The West Lake mirrors [the scenery] like a mirror, and Mount Gu leans against it like a screen; the vast waves are limpid and pale with autumn, while the ancient trees are verdant and cool as summer.
This is truly a place where śramaṇas cultivate the Way and rest their minds. The year of its founding was the third year of the Tongguang era of the Later Tang dynasty.
Since then, five generations of masters have served as abbots, including the late Master Ziji, all of whom were diligent in [their practice].
Having completed the repairs, they were negligent regarding the ritual demarcation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*).

Now, the one presiding over this monastery, named Youxiang, fearing that they had not yet complied with the Buddha’s regulations, could not find peace of mind; he therefore requested a master of the *vinaya* to perform the rite and establish the boundary.
This was on the tenth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Tianxi era. Once the boundary had been established, he further requested words from me to serve as a preface for it.
It has been two years since that time; I admire his delight in doing good, and as inspiration arose one day, I have thus recorded these events.
This was on the eighth day of the fifth month of summer in the year of the Wood Dragon, the Xinyou year—the fifth year [of the reign].
Preface to the Re-establishment of the Great Boundary at Tiantai Guoqing Temple.
Tiantai excels among all mountains; Guoqing is preeminent among all monasteries. Its crags and caverns are deep and secluded, the dwelling place of immortals and spirits;
its towers and pavilions are magnificent and grand, the locus where Buddhist affairs converge. Previously, during the Chen and Sui dynasties, there was...
The Sage said: "The Great Master Zhi was expounding the Way on this mountain and left instructions to establish this monastery.
Therefore, the monastery possesses the legacy of the Sage. Its bhikṣus are able to receive the Buddha’s transformation:

when at rest, they partake in the joy of dhyāna; when in motion, they follow the models of the Vinaya. For this reason, the pure assembly throughout the realm all praises it as a 'State Monastery' (Guosi)."
One must purify one’s deportment. Thus, among the great models of the Vinaya, do they not lie in the *posadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and the *anujñā*?
To perform these four requires a place where formal ritual acts (*dharmakarma*) may be conducted.

Viewed in this light, one knows that the matter of establishing boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*) is even greater than the *posadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and the *anujñā*. It is truly the starting point of the *Vinaya* and the precursor to the *ārāma*.
"Your servant observes that our Sovereign has established the Imperial Ultimate and dwells in the Great Treasure, employing the True Doctrine to assist in the administration of great affairs.
Consequently, the barbarians have been harmonized and the common people enjoy peace and prosperity. He has turned his attention to this mountain and renovated this temple;

its halls and corridors have been refurbished, and its altars and courtyards have been renewed. Thus, from the boundaries of the four quarters to the limits of the ordination platform, the standards have all been transformed."

Therefore, the Vinaya Master [Name], courageous in his dedication to the Dharma, assembled the community at their seats to unravel old knots and establish new ones on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month in such-and-such a year.
From then on, the customary statutes of the precepts were applied without interruption, and the regulations for the abbot became elegant and worthy of admiration.
Is it not then false to say that there was the lingering influence of the sages? Thus he was conferred the purple robe.
The śramaṇa Guangjing, who served as the head of the school for the study of the Vinaya, suddenly took up his staff and traveled to the region west of Xi, arriving at the mountain hermitage.
He remarked, "I have studied the Way of Tiantai and thus know this mountain; through the mountain, I come to know this monastery.
Out of reverence for the Dharma and respect for our ancestors, you will surely not begrudge me your words. Thereupon, he requested a preface and introduction, to which I agreed.
It happened that I was afflicted by a deep-seated melancholy and was just then occupied with its treatment, having no leisure for literary composition for three years now.
Recently, a guest informed me of a journey to Mount Tiantai; I have therefore composed these words to entrust to him, fulfilling the request of Master Saijiong.
This was on the thirteenth day of the first month of spring in the fifth year of the Tianxi era, the Xinyou year of the Heavenly Stalwart (the year of the Dragon).
Preface to the Jade-Green Pavilion at Ma-nao-po.
Record of the Establishment of the Great Boundary at Fa-hui Monastery in Hangzhou.
What is the purpose of establishing the great boundary? It is to define its circumscribed domain so that all may conform to the rules of the Vinaya. Regarding these rules of the Vinaya...

What is the reason for this? It is to prevent transgressions and non-virtues, and to bring body and speech into harmony. If the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is not established, the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*) have no means to be implemented.

If the disciplinary rules are not implemented, there is no means to harmonize body and speech. If body and speech are not harmonized, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) cannot arise.
If concentration and wisdom do not arise, the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) cannot be accomplished. Judging by this, one sees that it is through these means that the Noble Path is realized.
Does this not originate from the establishment of the boundary? As for the Fa-hui-yuan (Dharma-Wisdom Monastery), its former name was Da-zhong Xingqing;
it was constructed by the Wukusong King of the Qian clan in the fourth year of the Tianyou era of the Tang dynasty, the Year of the Green Dragon (Yimao).
At that time, as the Kingdom of Wuyue was founded, Wukusong emulated the deeds of Xiao Bai and Chong’er, receiving the calendar of the imperial court to command all his subordinates.
The Marquis was by nature brilliant and spiritual, and he held the teachings of Śākyamuni in high esteem.
Since his birth occurred during the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong, and coinciding with the completion of this monastery, it was named "Dazhong Xingqing" (Great Prosperity of the Dazhong Era).

Now, as the Sage has received a divine mandate from the Supreme Lord, all benevolent shrines and celestial palaces throughout the empire have had their names changed to new ones; thus, there is the present name of the Dharma.
By the grace of wisdom, this monastery has flourished for many years; although it was once formally demarcated by boundary markers (*sīmā*), the inscriptions have long since perished.
Even the senior monks do not know its limits, let alone those who are junior.
Consequently, the *Poṣadha* and *Pravāraṇā* ceremonies, as well as the standard Vinaya regulations, have all been neglected and ceased to be practiced. The Great Master Cihua remarked:
Ren Yong sighed for a long time and then requested that those knowledgeable in the Vinaya assemble the traveling monks; they untied the old cord and tied a new one.

He then inscribed the boundary markers and suspended them in a prominent location so that those who came after would recognize the limits of the domain, thereby allowing the Vinaya precepts to be practiced, body and speech to be brought into harmony, wisdom to manifest, and the Holy Way to flourish.
How magnificent! Is it not here that a single undertaking brings forth numerous virtues?
The Great Master Baoyin, Faming, knocked at my door in the forest retreat to request words from me, saying, "I wish to ensure this shall not perish.
I have therefore recorded these events to satisfy his request. Written on the sixth day of the sixth month in the summer of the fourth year of the Tianxi era of the Great Song (Gengshen).

Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
A Letter on Behalf of Master Yuàn to Mr. Wáng, the Secretariat Drafter of Qiántáng.

I, a śramaṇa, having reverently purified myself through fasting and ritual cleansing, respectfully compose this letter to be presented to you, the Excellency, the Prefectural Magistrate. I, [Name], have formerly...

This means that when great gentlemen apply their minds, they delight in virtue rather than being limited to a single teaching; they seek out worthy individuals rather than being restricted to one region.
Their endeavor lies in encouraging future generations and providing warnings for the present age, establishing the foundation of transformation so that the people may follow the correct path.
How could this concern be confined solely to Confucianism? Why should its definitive application be tied to this particular tradition alone?
How magnificent! The teaching of the Sage of the West is the greatest among those that promote goodness;
the disciples who have received its instruction are likewise numerous in their virtue, talent, integrity, and sincerity. Thus, Li Hanlin was moved by its profound and far-reaching perspective;
Pei Xiangguo looked up to Zongmi for his brilliant enlightenment; and Han Lidu was struck by Da Dian’s realization of the underlying principle.
Wen Chang was a friend of broad learning whom Liu Zhitou praised; these four gentlemen were knowers of men, and these four śramaṇas were those who received their recognition.

For a thousand generations to come, no one will find fault with them. I humbly observe that your esteemed office possesses profound insight surpassing the ancients and a magnificent reputation that startles the age;
you bear the talent of a royal minister and have truly emerged as a sage destined for the world. Thus, critics say: [...the rest of the passage...]

Our Lord intends to employ you in high office to ascend to the rocky corridors of the imperial court; regarding you as a vessel of state (a "ding-nai"), he has sent you forth from this state to follow the ancient rite of successive trials.

Since your arrival on horseback, benevolent transformation has already spread, punishments have been cleared, and administration has been simplified; the people know how to practice ritual and yielding, while officials cannot bear to deceive you.

Furthermore, you have applied yourself to the True Doctrine (the Confucian Way) to augment your vast spirit; thus, even the followers of the Buddha-teacher possess a breadth of knowledge that reaches its limits.

Among those who have polished their reputations and refined their integrity through the various scriptures, I have often had the fortune to encounter their radiant presence and engage in discussions on sagely counsel and profound principles.
Even the Buddhist scholarship of Hui-ling or the devotion to the Śāstra of the Buddha by Pei Guan could not compare to this.

I am a native of Qiantang; from my youth, I understood the principle of suffering and emptiness and thus became a follower of Śākyamuni. Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*...
He spent forty years studying and reciting the treatises on the *Śata-dharma* and *Hetuvidyā*.

Furthermore, he realized that for governing the world and establishing one’s character, nothing excels the Confucian classics; thus, he concurrently studied the Five Classics to supplement his Buddhist learning.

He was singular in his self-reliance and never associated with the mediocre. Even if someone were of noble rank, if they did not accord with the Way or receive him with propriety, he would not accept them.
From the very beginning, I never flattered others to gain favor nor sought to ingratiate myself by aligning with prevailing trends;

yet, upon hearing of your talent and virtue, your diligent humility in receiving subordinates, and how people hold you in high esteem, I came to admire your noble character and sought an audience at your pure presence.

Indeed, I was graced by your not overlooking even a fragment of my meager merits, as you personally took the trouble to guide and polish me. Consequently, the traces of my lifelong conduct have become radiant, surpassing those of my superficial acquaintances and casual friends.
Because of this, my perspective has been transformed. Alas! If it were not for you, who have known me through your service, how could I have reached this point?

Furthermore, your brilliance and nobility far surpass those of the Liang dynasty’s Pei, Han, and Liu; yet I, being so cramped and limited, am like Ran Mi or Dian Chang compared to you—vastly different as the distance between the Tu and Han rivers.
Now, that a person of such cramped nature should receive the recognition of one so brilliant and noble.

Is this not appropriate? It is because you, sir, intend to seek out men of extraordinary integrity and peerless talent from among the thatched huts and mountain caves to assist the enlightened Son of Heaven in surpassing the governance of Yao and Shun;
thus, you look upon even minor virtues and cause them to attain a noble reputation.
This ensures that those more worthy than myself will surely advance upon hearing the wind of your call. Why is this so? Furthermore, as for those of minor virtue—
If I am still favored with your commendation, how much more so should those of extraordinary conduct and talent that transcend the common herd?

If even a śramaṇa is thus honored by your recognition, how much more so a Confucian scholar in his ceremonial robes and wide sash? Therefore it is said: "The mind of a great gentleman delights in goodness;
he does not limit himself to a single teaching, nor does he restrict himself to a single region. I, being lacking in eloquence, have merely set forth this account directly.
My feelings of admiration have been expressed through brush and ink; I have further presented ten volumes of my own compilation, *Verses on Eminent Monks* (*Gāosēngyùn*), at your guest quarters.

Although I lack the talent of a historian, I have paired categories of events and arranged them according to prosodic laws to manifest the magnificent achievements of former sages, thereby providing sufficient edification for future generations.
I humbly hope that, amidst your official duties, you will deign to grant me your favor by reviewing this work.
I, [Name], respectfully submit this letter to the Honorable Official, seeking forgiveness for my offenses. I do not presume to elaborate further.
Preface to the *Tiantai Changji Xu*:
I have long suffered from a deep-seated melancholy; currently undergoing treatment for it, I have consequently wandered aimlessly among the rivers and lakes, engaging in extensive reading.
Seeking self-comfort amidst the scenery, I have always admired the strangeness of summer clouds and the majesty of autumnal tides;
looking left and right, I never grew weary of them. Someone asked: "When you see summer clouds and autumnal tides, you must observe them; what do you mean by this? I replied:
"I love the strangeness of the clouds as if they were broken cliffs and overlapping peaks; it is not for their brilliant colors that they are strange."
The majesty of the surging waves is like that of swans in flight or flying snow; it is not because they are perilous or treacherous that they are considered magnificent.

Since Heaven brings forth human beings, there are those who resemble the clouds of summer and the waves of autumn; likewise, when humans establish their words, there are those who resemble the clouds of summer and the waves of autumn.
Furthermore, the gentleman regards upright conduct and walking the Way as extraordinary, rather than concealing himself in seclusion or practicing strange anomalies.
Furthermore, I consider courage, benevolence, and the cultivation of righteousness to be true strength, rather than glaring with rage while confronting difficulties.

As for speech, I regard gentleness, mildness, and profound sincerity as excellence, rather than brilliant rhetoric or resonant declamation. To use subtle allusions to admonish superiors and humble oneself before inferiors—possessing a hidden purpose—is what I call strength;
it is not the time for wild schemes or seditious slanders. This is how I observe the extraordinary beauty of summer clouds and the majestic power of autumn tides.
I have long thought of finding such a person with whom to associate and of finding such words as I might enjoy.

Recently, when Master Changji arrived from Mount Tiantai and visited me at the foot of Mount Gu, I inquired about him and learned that he had mastered the *Fúshū* and was further skilled in the *Sāo* and *Yǎ* traditions.
His character and his compositions are truly what one might call "summer clouds and autumn tides."
Thereupon, he found the man and befriended him; he mastered his words and delighted in them.
That winter, he again traveled from Lin’an to meet him beneath the forest trees, where they spoke of a certain Du Shen, a scholar of pure integrity whom [the author] had known in the past.
Du was residing in Kuaiji and had sent a letter inviting [the author]; thus, [the author] intended to go there, wandering along the Ruoye River, ascending Mount Yunmen, and visiting Famen Temple.
Flowers serve to delight our innate nature; thus, for this journey, I hoped you would grant me words to record its course, and so I gave my consent.
I have heard that Lord Du is a lover of antiquity, possessed of broad learning and pure integrity, and is truly a rare man of talent within the realm.
Yunmen and Fahua are likewise the most extraordinary wonders in the world. When men of renown travel to famous mountains to seek the Way, they find joy therein.
Xing’er sighed and said, "If Du Hou had not shared my view of waiting for the Superior Man with summer clouds and autumn tides, how could he have reached this state?
As I reclined with my elbows on the armrest, I dictated this preface orally; let this youth record it in writing as a gift for him.
Written at the Cottage by the Grasses on Mount Gu on the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month of winter in the fifth year of Tianxi.
Preface.

I have long heard it said that there was a strange light at Lake Huguang in Qiantang, on West Lake; for a long time I did not believe it, until I witnessed it myself, following the example of Zhi [Daolin].
Huidun purchased a mountain from Daoyou, who had invited him to live in seclusion, and obtained the western slope of Mount Gu known as Ma'nao.
Three full years have passed, and the planet Venus has appeared there eight or nine times; one does not know if this is some divine transformation.

At times, when the great marshes are shrouded in rain and the level lake is bright with moonlight, this light is magnificent and shimmering, stealing away one's eyesight; it shoots into the chamber like a flash of lightning rushing forth.
It appears like a shooting star in the wilds; at times it is as large as a wheel or a canopy, and at other times it is as small as a cup or a jar.
Descending and then ascending again, it vanishes only to return with brilliance. According to Liu Daozhen’s *Qiandang Ji* (Record of Qiandang), this is called the "Light of the Golden Ox.

The *Qiandang Ji* states: "The Mingsheng Lake is south of the county seat. According to the oral tradition of the elders, there was once a golden ox within the lake. In ancient times, people have seen its reflection in the Baoling Spring, its spiritual radiance shining and flowing. Its transformations were unfathomable, and thus it was named 'Ming' (Brilliant)."

Among those dwelling by the water and those inhabiting the mountains who call it a "saint" (a name for a holy being), there are those who call it a portentous anomaly and those who call it a ghost-fire;
I truly do not know its actual nature. Since it has appeared within the lake, it may appropriately be called "lake-splendor" (huguang).
As for its illuminating the pavilion of the secluded monk and shining upon the door of the reclusive scholar, it can serve as a sight for those dwelling in deep seclusion.
Sitting upright, I contemplate this radiance; might it not also augment my own secluded delight? Alas!

Should anyone behold this light upon a famous mountain or a sacred peak, the people of that age would surely call it the light of a divine immortal (*xiānshén*) or the light of a Buddhist monk (*fútú*).

Once it is called the light of a divine immortal or a Buddhist monk, there will inevitably be those who prepare their fasts in advance to seek an audience, prostrating themselves twice and gazing in silent reverence.

Those who pray have already seen [the efficacy]; having prayed, there are many who have transformed from being fierce and stubborn into becoming benevolent and trustworthy, and who have abandoned frivolous contention to delight in purity and stillness—is this not the useful power of the Light? Alas!
Having seen it, they do not find its proper place, but merely judge it by the worldly notions of the "Golden Calf," calamities, monsters, and ghostly fires. Oh, how tragic for humanity!
There is one who resembles the radiance of a lake.
Moved by external things, he composes this verse:
"The famous hawk has its six wings clipped; the stallion in the stable has its four hooves bound. Gazing toward the high heavens..."
Gazing intently at the broad thoroughfare, I let out a long, mournful neigh; the cunning hare is in its prime vigor, yet the road is level and wide.
My sharp claws find no purchase, and what use is my swift pace? King Wen of Chu would not release me, and King Mu of Zhou did not mount me.
Though I possess the power to chase the rushing lightning and the wind, no one knows my worth. Alas! There are scholars who conceal their talents within their own persons.
Alas! I have the will but lack the time; moved by these things, I sigh with emotion.

In this poor dwelling, the wild paths are overgrown with weeds, the low gate is long bolted shut, insects chirp within the ruined walls, and moss grows green upon the secluded steps. There is only thick gruel for sustenance.
I sustain my life by chanting and singing to suit my own disposition; walking, I peruse the works of a hundred schools, and sitting, I embrace the Six Classics.

Though beset by poverty and hardship, I find fulfillment; I linger here abiding in constancy. Alas for those shallow fellows who attach themselves to power and prize reputation! They scurry along the main roads, riding fat horses and wearing light robes.
Settled in ease within magnificent dwellings, they possess the hearts of wolves and the forms of swine. Do they ever consider moderation, or do they know how to guard against complacency?
When one's reputation is full, it perishes along with the body; calamity follows the greed for life.

How could a loyal officer who guards benevolence and righteousness—whose joy remains unchanged even when eating from a single bamboo vessel and drinking from a gourd—fail to leave behind a glorious name for ten thousand generations?
Inscription for a Humble Dwelling (with Preface) The Master of the Doctrine of the Mean resided in a dwelling that was both lowly and dilapidated.

He observed that the world’s ostentation and luxury give rise to a heart of envy and admiration, allowing a mind of greed and violence to enter, whereby benevolence, righteousness, and the Way of virtue may daily perish. Thus he wrote this inscription.
Man must not fail to be cautious; thus he composed the "Inscription on the Humble Dwelling" to admonish himself.
Its text says: The Sage Yao of the Holy Tang dynasty had earthen steps and thatched roofs. The Sage Yu of the Great [Yu] dynasty had a palace of humble proportions.
Their Way was luminous and bright; Their virtue was lofty and majestic. The worthy Yan Yuan lived in a humble alley with a gourd-bowl and a bamboo basket.
The virtuous son Si [Mencius] lived by a jar-window and mulberry-door; his joy remained unchanged and his integrity was never altered.
When decadence and excess arose, the simple and honest nature fell into ruin. Brocade and embroidery, fine timber and brickwork—superiors were deluded and inferiors followed.
High walls and grand palaces were carved and built; the pure source became ever more diluted. Competition for luxury then emerged, and the practice of ritual propriety and yielding collapsed.
To be a remnant is to be a thief; to be scarred is to be wounded. Extravagance and boastfulness are the foundations of calamity—this common vulgarity is pitiable.
As for my dwelling, it has more than enough space for a knee to rest; the clouds and mountains are my companions, and the scriptures are my teachers.
In times of distress, one must discern virtue; the sages and worthies are the model to follow. Do not harbor thoughts of luxury, and do not associate with the hidden multitudes.
