On the twelfth day of the first month of spring in the fourth year of the Tiānxī era of the Sacred Song, the Great Master Yuánjìng, Founder of the White Lotus Society...
Master Chang entered nirvana at the Upper Hall Hermitage of Zhaokong Ben Temple on the West Lake in Qiandang at the age of sixty-two and with forty-four years of ordination seniority.

On the third day of the second month, his disciples wailed and lamented, enshrining his entire body for burial to the right of the grave of Chan Master Niaochao at Lingyin Mountain, constructing a stupa to mark it according to ritual propriety. This was in that year.
The foremost disciple among those from Dongmen, named Xubai, was able to shoulder the Way of his Master.

He personally recounted the events and repeatedly visited my humble abode, requesting my words to transmit the Master’s excellence for engraving upon a grand monument, as he spoke of the final instructions left by his late father.
Unable to decline his request, I have composed this text and preface it. As for the teaching of the Sage of Yuexi, it is pure.
Pure and unconditioned, benevolent and non-violent, he employed profound rhetoric and subtle exegesis; his vast intent and far-reaching indications were fully realized throughout the Middle Kingdom.
Those who received his transformative influence and grasped his minor or proximate teachings would reform their conduct and distance themselves from evil;

those who grasped his major or ultimate teachings would return to the source and restore their original nature. Alas! Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu was one who attained that which is major and far-reaching.

This man dwelt in seclusion like one in the *Kaopan* [poem], maintaining his integrity through constant cultivation; he refined his speech and established his sincerity, possessing insight sufficient to manifest the subtle and conduct sufficient to serve as a model for others.
Consequently, the worthies of the age looked up to his loftiness and aspired toward his brilliance; from this arose the practice of forming literary societies (*jie-she*).

People have praised him to this day, yet none have been able to succeed him. Only Master Gongli was known for the strict gravity of his conduct and the pure simplicity with which he cultivated his mind. Upon hearing of this—
Delighting in the spirit of Mount Lu, he said: "The horse that aspires to follow a steed of the Jiao breed will surely become a steed of the Jiao breed itself;

though I am unworthy, how could I dare forget the admonition to 'emulate those who are superior'? Thereupon, I adorned my person, hollowed out my mind, and pledged my vow for the establishment of the Society.
Indeed, to lead according to the Way one must rely upon the land, and to honor the divine one must depend upon [the sacred site].

In manifesting his transformative influence, he must rely upon words: thus, as West Lake is a place of supreme travel for the world, he sought its secluded tranquility to demonstrate his noble retirement;
as the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is the object of veneration for all living beings, he carved sandalwood to create his likeness;
and as the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the essential pivot for attaining sainthood, he [punctuated it with] needles...
He wrote out the chapters and verses using his own blood; once that place was secured and the image was completed, his teachings spread abroad.
The court nobles held his righteousness in high esteem, and throughout the land, people relied upon his reputation.

Consequently, prime ministers, renowned officials, provincial governors, and regional commanders, having heard of the Master’s character and being moved by it, either sought him out in seclusion to inquire after the Way or beheld his countenance and recognized his true nature.
Some examined the scriptures to grasp their essential meaning; for over thirty years, they formed an unbreakable bond as companions in the White Lotus Society.
Those who joined this fellowship numbered one hundred and twenty-three. Such was the transformation achieved by them.

Through this, it is evident that the community of the West Lake, which succeeded that of Mount Lu, possesses no cause for shame. Let me attempt to discuss this further: in the distant past, there were the sages of the higher realms.
You, sir, are a worthy man of original resolve; though our actual ranks differ and our titles vary, you have come from afar during a period of decline, while I was born in a sagely dynasty.
Those whom you invited were all recluses of hidden virtue, whereas those who have come here are all men of established renown.

By compensating for each other’s strengths and weaknesses, we are equal in both antiquity and the present—can this not be called flourishing and beautiful? Every time you look back upon me, sir, [you treat me as an equal].
The disciples said, "Since the beginning of our dynasty, the gentry and scholars have followed the ancients in composing their writings;

for the most part, they have emulated Han Yu’s character, making it their intent to suppress and exclude the followers of Śākyamuni. Therefore, we made use of Master Yuan’s legacy to entice them with the matter of forming a literary society.
Consequently, many followed our transformation, erecting clusters of steles and piling up panegyrics to praise the Buddha-dharma as their point of devotion."
The wording of this oath is sufficient to obstruct the paths like thorny brambles and to fortify our teaching with walls and moats. The world does not know me;
some may even think I am one who employs artifice to purchase fame, but I am not of such a sort. A gentleman said:

Because of this, anyone who understood the principle could surely laugh at his argument—even a woman or a child would find it ridiculous.
When I read the *Hanzi*, I do not laugh at the people of Song; for what reason? It is because they were engaged in the common labors of carrying, lifting, and peddling goods.
This is indeed the case. I say that those who study for the sake of others, seeking to beautify themselves and praise their own goodness, are all people of Song.

Because they have not yet attained much, they see only a little and say, "My Way is profounder than mere knowledge," or, "Before I have uttered a single word, my Way is more courageous than mere talent.
If someone were to ask them, "Is it appropriate for your knowledge to obscure your talent? they would reply, "You do not understand me."
Thus, resenting Heaven and blaming others, he acted recklessly in his quest for success, wandering across the world to seek an understanding patron. Alas!
His conduct is truly laughable. It is because I do not join in the laughter of the man from Song that I have analyzed this matter.

An Admonition for the Average Person (with Preface) Confucius said, "Those of average intelligence and above can be spoken to regarding the superior; those of average intelligence and below cannot be spoken to regarding the superior.
He further said, "Only the person of supreme wisdom and the person of extreme stupidity do not change. Commentators explain that the person of supreme wisdom cannot be led astray.

The wicked and the most ignorant cannot be compelled to become virtuous; alas, those who establish words to transmit instruction so as to cause others to reform toward the good and distance themselves from evil can only reach those of middling capacity.
Thus, I have composed this "Admonition for the Middling Capacity."
Minimize selfishness and reduce desires; do not indulge in greed or rivalry. Wear benevolence upon your head and embrace righteousness within your breast;
do not lose your integrity or rectitude. To neglect right thought leads to madness; to master right thought leads to sagehood. In learning, one should choose a teacher;

in friendship, one should be close to the virtuous. To practice the Way brings renown; to accumulate evil destroys the person. These words have been proven true; I venture to address them to those of mediocre capacity.

Songjiang Chongyou, a master who excels not only in the study of Buddhism but also in the art of *feng* and *sao*, once took a liking to Li Zhaixian’s "Ten Odes on Guchu" and composed verses in their style as a response.
Monk Zhizhuan of Qiantang, whose courtesy name was Wuwai, wrote this preface: "As for poetry..."

The Way is rooted in the Three Hundred Odes; their purpose is simply to rectify the relationship between ruler and subject, clarify the bond between father and son, distinguish gain from loss, and demonstrate the distinction between the depraved and the upright.
When the traces of the True Kings were extinguished, the Odes were lost; once the Odes were lost, the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed.

Subsequently, there arose the likes of Qu Yuan and Song Yu, Li Yue and Su Wu, the various masters of the Jian’an era, the many lords of the Southern Dynasties, and down to those who wrote during the Great Tang of Li.
In this regard, the expressions are not uniform and the literary colors frequently change; they gallop along diverse tracks.

Those who succeed in this, though they alter their phrasing, do not deviate from the Way of the *Three Hundred Poems*. As for those who fail, they merely strive to compose verses on the wind and moon or depict the forms of mountains and rivers;
bound by prosodic rules and indulging in ornate diction and phrasing, they surely stray far from the Way of the *Three Hundred Poems*.
It is said that Li Baiyao’s discourse on poetry was not answered by Wenzhongzi; it was Li Zhexian of the Tang who attained this [spirit].
His poetry possessed a lofty spirit and plain language, a bitter resolve and a far-reaching sentiment.
While his diction diverged further from antiquity, his Way remained more identical to antiquity than ever; thus, the "Ten Odes of Gushu" stand even more exceptional among his many works. And...
For two hundred years, there has been no one to continue this tradition of harmonizing verses;

now that Master Yu’s compositions match the spirit, sentiment, diction, and tone of the Exiled Immortal (Li Bai) with such fidelity, it is clear that his skill in poetry may be known. Yuan formerly traveled with Master Yu and was requested by him to write this preface;
thus, I have recorded these words directly to serve as the introduction to this work. Written on the ninth day of the month in the year of Jia-yin at Qiantang.
Preface to the Lecture Hall of Chongfu Temple on West Lake.
Preface to the Poems of Master Yuan Residing by the Lake.
In ancient times, Yan Hui received the Odes from Zhongni; he clarified its Way and extended its teaching, and his preface was exceedingly detailed.
In later generations, although poets may value plainness in diction and profundity in meaning, they must not contravene the Way as categorized by Zixia.
Thus, by praising their words, one comes to know the sorrow and joy within their hearts, as well as the beauty or corruption of the state's governance.
Therefore it is said: "Poetry is the direction of the will," and again: "One employs literary elegance to offer indirect admonition."
Those who practice it will be without fault, and those who hear it will have sufficient cause for self-restraint. Alas! How great indeed is the instruction of poetry!
Could it be merely a matter of constraining the four tones, avoiding the eight ailments, describing partings, or depicting the colors of things?

The monk Chongyuan of West Lake in Qiantang is fond of antiquity and possesses broad learning; he understands the Way of Heaven and has lived in retirement among the mountains and waters for many years.

In addition to his service to the Buddha through the offering of incense and lamps, he has devoted considerable attention to the art of verse composition. Although his physical appearance and teeth have already declined with age, his spirit and thoughts remain robust.
One day, he came to visit me and presented me with ten poems written while residing by a lake, requesting a preface for them.
As I read them over and over again, I found that they all describe the beauty of leisure and profound tranquility. Alas! May these be spread throughout the four quarters.

If it were to flow down through a hundred generations so that those who recite its words might come to know the heart of the worthy and the joy of the sovereign’s harmonious transformation, then the poetry produced by superior men would approximate the Way described by Zixia;
how could it be merely a matter of racing through rhymed couplets or being fettered by prosodic constraints? As for those works that attained the highest excellence, their lines included:
Accumulated waters reflect the void’s azure; distant peaks girdled by the moon in autumn. Fragrance wafts from the cold waters;

a candle’s glow illuminates the deep night hall. Solitary birds enter the dense mists; lingering clouds shine upon the evening current. The cries of monkeys echo through the lofty autumn mountains; the moon’s reflection fills the empty night pool.
These several couplets exemplify what is called "elegant diction that prizes simplicity and plainness, and meaning that prizes profound depth. I, your unworthy servant, respectfully [record this].

I have composed this preface to fulfill his request, writing it on the first day of the waxing moon in the intercalary sixth month of the eighth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era of the third reign of the Song dynasty.
Prefaced by Monk [Name] of Qian Mountain Temple.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
Preface to the Boundary Markers for the Qiantang Doushuai Monastery.
The Doushuai Monastery was established by King Zhongyi in the first year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Imperial Dynasty.

Shortly after its completion, the King surrendered his official seals and registers to the Son of Heaven; consequently, the ritual of *sīmā-bandhana* (delineating the sacred boundary) could not be performed.
The Great Vinaya Master, Master Wugu, diligently instructed others and was courageous in upholding the Dharma.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month of the summer in the ninth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, he came from the Shengguo Temple to reside here.

His arrival was requested by those in purple robes—those who had received the *vinaya* transmission and presided over the assembly of śramaṇas—specifically at the request of Cidu. On the very day after his arrival, the multitude...

The eminent guests have arrived and the Dharma assembly has commenced. Those proficient in the Vinaya were appointed to perform the formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*).
With dignified deportment and orderly procedure, the ritual was fully executed, and the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) was thus established.

From this day forward, those who dwell within it shall be able to perform their duties with success and benefit, while those summoned shall be spared the toil of rushing about; all shall be gathered in harmony.
There, robes were provided, food was supplied, the *śīla* were recited, and the *pravāraṇā* was observed; all the time-honored regulations could be implemented and put into practice.
Who would say that this land was weak and incapable? Alas! King Zhongyi laid the foundation in the past, and Master Wugu established the sacred boundary in the present.
Since these two elements are both complete, the Way shines forth because of them. Although the material and the spiritual are distinct, their achievement of the task is one and the same.
I have instructed those who come to study through concentration and wisdom, and I have understood that the Path of the Sages begins with the precepts;
therefore, in accordance with your request, I shall set forth the reasons for this. This is my final testament.

I have often thought that after my death, you should entrust this remaining body to you all to cast away in the wilderness or flow it into a great river to serve as drink for birds, beasts, fish, and shellfish;
yet I am certain you will not be able to follow these instructions.

Therefore, I shall undergo cremation, but since the places where bodies are cut, felled, and burned are close to the pagodas and temples, there would be the fault of foul odors and defilement. Thus, I first intended to bury it in the earth.

Furthermore, I am concerned that the doctrines of the Yin-Yang masters regarding the flow and opposition of forces and the omens of fortune and misfortune might hinder the land for cultivation or waste the wealth of the faithful's offerings—both of which are things my heart does not desire.
Therefore, I have already excavated an earthen cave and stored ceramic vessels within it as provisions for my final rest.
After my death, there is no need for tonsure or ritual bathing; I should simply be enshrouded.

One must not linger with one's bathing robe; immediately using money or the robe to hire a lay attendant (*śucika-puruṣa*) to carry one to the cave, where one enters among the earthenware vessels within.
The cave entrance shall be sealed with two or three layers of bricks and stones. One must not inform worldly relatives, friends, or disciples.
One must not leave a final letter. One must not change one's clothes or wail; if people come to console one, one should not respond with grief.
He merely restrained his tears; this, too, did not violate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). He was not permitted to collect money from the multitude to provide for funeral expenses.
All clothing, alms bowls, and personal effects worth even a single hair’s breadth were to be divided according to the Vinaya.

As for the bedding, mats, bookcases, and internal and external scriptures—excluding those belonging to others—all were to be distributed in accordance with principle. As for the Agate Hall (*musāragalva-maṇḍapa*), it was...
In governing this matter, those of vast talent who have contemplated its alignment—whether they were its initiators or its assistants—I now entrust it equally to my three sons.
Should they travel elsewhere, they shall summon someone to take charge and carry out the work;

alternatively, they may invite a master of the lineage, or reside together with their brothers, or continue the succession of lectures, or transform the site into a Chan monastery, or even renovate it further.
If a monastic institution does no harm to others and is beneficial to the Way, then there is nothing that is not permissible.

As for matters of establishing one's person and practicing the Way, and the principles of calming the mind and realizing the fundamental source, I have already expounded upon them frequently in my writings; there is no need to speak further of these.
Regarding the final instructions you have entrusted to me, if you follow my practice, then you and your kin in the Dharma-gate shall be together for generations to come.
The Master and I have together propagated the wondrous Way; should anyone fail to comply, they are but followers of Māra and not my disciples.
If people of the world should find your conduct strange and reproach you, you should produce this document to show them.
Written by hand on the first day of the final spring month of the Jiwu year of the Tianxi era, and hung to the left of the lecture hall.

The "Sick Man" (Bingfu) was so named because he was weary of his constant illness; he once lived in secluded retirement, eating from a simple bamboo basket and drinking from a gourd ladle, avoiding the ways of the world.
He constantly scrutinized medical texts and prepared medicinal herbs and stones to treat his ailments himself when they were slight.

In my leisure time, I discuss various scriptures for my own amusement; whether deliberating on a single matter or composing a short essay, I invariably take the Way as my ultimate principle and Benevolence as my foundation, censuring evil and encouraging good.
I have often said that the greatness of the Three Teachings must not be neglected.

That there is one who maintains the great substance of human relations—upholding the Five Constant Virtues and rectifying the Three Bonds—is found in Confucianism. To sever the pursuit of sagehood and abandon wisdom, maintaining...
In the Way of the Feminine Preserving the Weak, there is a principle: from cause one attains effect, and by reversing delusion one returns to the True.

Thus, it enables the myriad transformations to revert to the nature of the mind; this is found in Buddhism. Is my mind the disease? Are the Three Teachings the medicine? Moreover, since there are three diseases, can the three medicines be discarded?
Is my Way the tripod? Are the Three Teachings the legs? If one wishes for the tripod not to overturn, [one must rely on all three].
It would be sufficient to refute those who, as Confucian scholars, might accuse him of excessive attachment or attack his heterodoxy as the disease of slander.

For he does not seek to change with the world nor alter his doctrine; sometimes he climbs mountains or gazes upon waters, composing verses and letting his vision roam, appearing carefree and composed.
He does not regard the physical exhaustion of his body as suffering, but finds self-satisfaction in his own solitude.
He feigned illness despite being wealthy, noble, and powerful, refusing to align himself with them; he feigned illness despite great fame and substantial profit, refusing to act with worldly haste;
he feigned illness when refined *qingshang* and *liuzhi* melodies played, refusing to listen;
and he feigned illness when rich foods and delicacies were served, refusing to relish them. Thus, he was not moved by power, nor enslaved by fame, nor deafened by music.
Unperturbed by flavors, unhampered by others, and unmixed with worldly conventions, the utility of preserving life and the Way of manifesting simplicity are fully embodied within illness.
How great indeed is the significance of the occasion of illness! I have once composed a "Rhapsody on Illness" to speak of this Way.
The Rhapsody on Illness (with Preface) I have long suffered from a spleen ailment;
whenever I speak for a long time or eat to satiety, my breath immediately becomes labored, sweat flows, my ears ring, and my vision blurs, such that I cannot endure the suffering.
Now, even those as sagely as Zhongni (Confucius) and as enlightened as Boyang (Laozi), though burdened by their physical forms, were likewise unable [to transcend it].

To escape this affliction, it is something shared by both the ordinary and the sagely, the wise and the foolish; yet whether one attains realization or not, the fluctuations of the inner mind are like the flow of a river.
Thus we know that those who are despondent and unhappy, being constrained by illness, are the lowest of the foolish;

whereas those who remain composed and free from distress, sustaining themselves through the Way, possess the highest wisdom. This is especially true for me, who has received the instructions of the Golden Quarter (the West).
When studying the Dharma of the Truly Real, how can one forget the Way because of being tormented by a minor illness?

Furthermore, I have heard from the Tiantai tradition that there are four ways to treat illness: treatment through medicine, treatment through visualization, treatment through incantations, and treatment through the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*).
Being of dull wit, I aspire to the path of superior intelligence and thus take contemplation according to principle as my primary treatment.
This is what is called the primary truth. Thus, I have composed this rhapsody to guide one’s aspirations:
The four elements contend with one another; The five viscera are not in harmony. Leaning on an armrest, propped by a staff, My feelings are disordered and my mind distressed.
To cultivate one's nature through the Way And to restrain the mind through righteousness— If one hopes to attain this profound principle, From where shall one find its analogies?
In the past, Zhongni likewise suffered from illness; yet his Way remained as bright as the light of day, and he declined prayers for recovery.
In the past, Boyang sighed over the great affliction of existence; yet his Way was found therein, for there is no interval between him and the body.
My Master is silent and still, not departing from that principle; upon his square-foot bed, his demeanor is without error.
Illness arises from the mind; illness is nothing but form, and form is entirely the mind. Why do you thus become your own enemy?
The essence of the mind is fundamentally non-existent; from where could illness be obtained? The medicine is not *zhishi* fungus, and the physician is not Bian Que or Hua Tuo.
When illness is seen as non-illness, who is there to polish and who to grind? Illness! Oh, illness! What can it do to me?
Inscription for the Lecture Hall The Benevolent One has passed away, yet his subtle words remain here. The Four Reliances have not arisen, and their circulation is nearly exhausted.

Therefore, we command a man of wisdom to support what is tottering and sustain what is in peril, To exert his strength in proclaiming the eternal teachings, and to lift up the main pillars and shake loose the frayed cords.
The Dharma drum resounds with a deep boom; the Wheel of the Dharma rolls on smoothly. Be a model for all people; be circumspect in your dignified demeanor.
Have courage in practicing the Way; strike away ignorance without weariness. Do not reject those who come; do not pursue those who depart.
Destroy the heterodox while attending to the root; manifest the orthodox while ensuring its growth. Let your proclamations be free from vulgarity; let your words be free from ramification.

Virtuous in the world, yet not boastful; Extensively learned, yet acknowledging one's doubts; Discerning delusions through wisdom; Gathering all beings with compassion. This inscription is engraved upon the lecture hall, venturing to address the Dharma Master. Inscription on the Insects in the Window: The insects in the window, though small, are numerous; Though they do not know the Way, they are nonetheless diligent.

They toil day and night, seeking their own sustenance; Yet they do not abandon their fellow creatures. If one observes them closely, they are truly worthy of praise; How much more so for those who cultivate the mind! May you all, like these insects, Attain the Way together.
In a sealed chamber there is an insect that longs to roam the great void. The paper of the window has form and blocks it; the empty space has no form and allows passage.
That which has no form is not what the insect sees; that which has form is what it follows.

It strikes its head against the skull as if to shatter it, its chirping and scurrying endless. I drive it into the empty space so that it may cross over, yet it returns to strike the window once more.
Paper as it was before—O worm, O worm! You have merely emerged from your own heart, yet you are ignorant of the way out. To whom shall you attribute this blame?
Chirping and chirping, you lament in sorrow.
*Xianju bian*, Fascicle 34.

*Verses on the Explanation of the Meaning of the Four Truths Being Endowed with Delusion*.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"In the lower realm [the Desire Realm], suffering possesses all [ten afflictions]; origination excludes three; cessation excludes two; and the path excludes two. In the upper realms, hostility does not function.
The commentary explains:

The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully present within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) arises solely by taking the object of suffering as its condition.

Ignorance, karma, and the outflows (*āsrava*) are the causes of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); The essence of cessation (*nirodha*), being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), is the fruit;
None of these are objects of perception for the view of a self-identity, Nor for the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) or the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
These two do not arise even as they follow the body; therefore, the accumulation [of suffering] is extinguished.
The three [aspects of] the Truth of the Path are fundamentally the cause for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not arise.
Since wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) negates the existence of the Noble Path, the observance of precepts and prohibitions must likewise arise from wrong view.
Grasping what is not the path as the true path is therefore the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Among the afflictions regarding the Four Truths, there are those that are distant and those that are proximate; for the Truth of Suffering, there are seven proximate ones and three distant ones.

Grasping at "I" and "mine" constitutes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Following this, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consists of reckoning the self as either annihilated or eternal.
Wrong view denies the existence of cause and effect; The grasping at views clings to the inferior as superior;
The grasping at precepts and observances regards what is not a cause as a cause; Doubt is hesitation and indecision;
Ignorance is confusion and darkness due to lack of understanding. All of these arise based upon the object of suffering.
Therefore, seven afflictions are termed "intimate delusions.
The three afflictions of greed, hatred, and pride do not arise from the objective sphere of the Truth of Suffering; rather, they arise based upon the preceding seven.
For this reason, these three receive the designation of "distant delusions. Among the seven [afflictions] of the Truth of Origination, four are intimate and three are distant.

Wrong view denies [reality], while doubt and hesitation remain; The adherence to inferior views and the darkness of delusion—these three are termed "distant," as their names were previously explained.
Craving and the other [afflictions] arise based solely on these four factors;
In terms of cessation, three are "proximate" and four are "distant. Regarding the distant, the previous three are augmented by the adherence to inferior views.
To regard the inferior Truth of Suffering as superior is the "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa); therefore, it is established as a distinct [defilement].
Now, since the Truth of Cessation is a supreme and sublime dharma, one cannot further claim that the inferior is superior;
rather, it arises from the back of false view, and the act of clinging to the inferior as superior is what is termed "clinging to views."
Therefore, the cessation-truth has four remote [factors]. The aspects of the immediate and remote are all as previously stated for the path:
eight [factors] are immediate, three are remote, and five are of both types. As for the immediate, they are doubt, delusion, and false view;

the remote factors, compared to the previous [path], add the grasping of rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Regarding the suffering-truth, the grasping of rules and rituals serves as its cause.
The fruit of outflows is not the untainted path; because one falsely clings to it as cause and effect, there arises the proximate condition of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Since the Truth of the Path is the true cause and the true path, it cannot serve as a proximate condition for that which is neither cause nor path; it merely gives rise to wrong view through such a condition.
Therefore, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is categorized among the remote [defilements];

both the path and cessation are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, and thus this clinging does not consist of taking what is inferior to be superior. The clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is similar to the former and also belongs to the remote category;
however, its grasping arises from false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The general explanation based on the *Abhidharmakośa* is as stated above.
Based on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the meaning of the sixteenth moment of mind belonging to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is explained as follows:

The verse says: The sixteen moments of mind consist of forbearances (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*). Three and five belong to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); The final one is subsumed under the path of cultivation.

That which was previously unseen by the seeing [path]—namely, the first fifteen moments of mind—is called the "unseen" because from time immemorial one had not yet obtained the Dharma-eye and had never before seen it; therefore, it is named the path of seeing.

Because one has previously seen [the truth]—that is, because the object of the Truth of the Path was already seen at the time of the fifteenth mind, the *mārga-anvaya-jñānakṣānti*—the sixteen minds constitute a "repeated seeing" (*punardarśana*).

Therefore, what was previously seen is subsequently cultivated. It is through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that the principle is finally seen; since both the wisdom of dharma (*dharmajñāna*) and the wisdom of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) take a single truth as their object, they are termed "repeated seeing.
Although the *dharmakṣāntis* and *anvayakṣāntis* occurring in the intermediate stages are also repeated seeings, they are so designated only when they follow the initial vision.
Because the vision is not yet ultimate, it belongs only to the purity of vision.

In the *Jingming jing shi* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), in the chapter explaining "the vision of vision," Jingxi’s *Jingming ji* (Record of the Vimalakīrti) frequently states from the beginning of the section on "reaching the benefit of sound" that there is "the vision of vision. I shall now explain this in three parts: 1. ... [text continues] ... (Note: The provided source text contains a fragmentary list of points regarding the "vision of vision" (*jian-jian*). The translation reflects the structural headings and the opening explanatory statement.)
The first part of the text, concerning the correct understanding and the citation of evidence for the two [vehicles], consists of three sections. Regarding the initial passage:

it means that in the past, having severed conditioned existence and attained assurance in the small fruit, they saw only the Small Vehicle; now, being rebuked by the Great [Vehicle], they give rise to a mind of admiration and again see the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, it is said "seeing seeing.

When they reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the small is opened as the great, and both attachments are entirely forgotten; thus, there is no "seeing seeing. Since this is the case for the two vehicles, so it is for others.

The same applies to the bodhisattvas of dull faculties among the three vehicles. Second, regarding the citation of evidence: Jingxi’s explanation is extremely clear, yet some people may not have seen it;

thus the *Ji* states: "To cling to the Small [Vehicle] is precisely the Small Vehicle. This refers to the word "view" (*jìan*) in the previous passage, which means perceiving the existence of those who produce [the fruit]. It further states:
"Those who admire and look up to the Mahāyāna know that there is the Mahāyāna, and they give rise to views of reverence and submission. This is the explanation.
The next character, "view" (見), refers to the two views of the Two Vehicles.

It is further said that although there are three teachings, the primary intent is to use the Perfect Teaching to critique the Bodhisattvas for being unable to grasp the Great Principle; their "viewing of views" is the same as that of the Small Vehicle.

This refers to the "viewing of views" of the Bodhisattvas, meaning that they formerly gave rise to partial views because they did not realize that the partial is itself the perfect. Furthermore, it is said that this reaches its culmination in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Only upon reaching this point does one see that all [teachings] return to this statement: that the opening of the assembly is the same Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), and there is no longer any "seeing of seeing.

Regarding the threefold analysis, a question is asked: Why did Jingxi suddenly establish the term "seeing of seeing" here? The answer is: This commentary (*shu-wen*) is intended to clarify the meaning.

Since the preceding sutra had not yet clarified the censure [of other teachings], and the commentary had not yet clarified the gathering of conditions (*pratyaya-samudaya*), how could [the term "seeing of seeing"] have been discussed [there]?
The *Shouwen jingshu* (Commentary on the Hand-Inquiry Sutra) does not contain this name or characteristic; why did Jingxi establish it by force? He replied:
The *Dazhilun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) asks, "To which affliction does the 'seeing of seeing' belong? and answers, "It is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*)."
A Praise for Dharma Master Ding, the Commentator on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* of Tiantai, Who Could Speak at Three Months of Age:

The Dharma Master’s name was Guanding (courtesy name Faying); he was a native of Yixing in Changzhou. Because Emperor Wu [of the Liang dynasty] fled to the eastern regions during the turmoil and did not return, he now resides in Zhang’an of Linhai. His father died early, and his mother raised him alone.

When he was only three months old, she wished to give him a name and examined various objects to find one suitable for his character, yet she could not determine what to call him. One night, the mother invoked the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; the infant immediately imitated her voice and recited the syllables with clear articulation, which caused everyone present to be struck with wonder.

When Master Huizheng of Jingsi Temple heard that he had been named after his extraordinary cause, he sighed in admiration, saying, "This child is no ordinary person. He left home at an early age; by the time he was seven years old, he became a disciple of Master Zheng. His talent and learning flourished daily as he pursued both the profound mysteries of Buddhism and Confucianism.

His refined prose and elegant compositions brought him renown in his time. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination and observed the monastic precepts. His virtue was such that the vessel of his morality and the bowl of his alms were objects of deep contemplation. When Master Zheng passed away, he received the Way at Tiantai and inherited the mantle of the patriarchal lineage.

Finding that the threads of the established order were incomplete, in the first year of the Zhizhide era, he followed the Zen Master Zhi-zhe to reside at Guangzhai Temple. There, he investigated and scrutinized the gate of *vipaśyanā* (contemplation), frequently receiving the master’s seal of approval.

"Splitting Stone with a Staff and Banner. (Once, during a break from lecturing at Fulong, while leading his disciples to stack stones for a stupa, they required two additional stones to construct the door. The disciple Guangying first used a cart to transport one stone;

everyone suspected it was too thick and large, and sought another elsewhere, which would have further exhausted human labor. The Master merely raised his staff and gave it a casual flick; the previously transported stone suddenly split apart with a startling crack, becoming two pieces of equal thickness and size. These were then used for the stupa door, fitting perfectly according to their original dimensions.)

It is said that white sand surged forth from the ground at Anzhou on the southern ridge of Le’an—a place of green trees and clear streams where the hidden springs rendered the paths impassable. The Master lingered there, admiring the scenery, and gazing about, he made a vow:

"If this land were to become level and smooth, I would come here to lecture on the sutras. Before even ten days had passed, white sand surged forth everywhere, as level as a jade mirror. The Master did not fail his prior vow; he then lectured on the two sections of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* to repay the spiritual intent of the site.

Incense Flow Cures Illness: (The Master’s transformation flowed through the clamorous world, his divine application being boundless. A villager thirty *li* from Falong Mountain fell ill and was near death;

though treated by many, he did not recover. His son rushed into the mountains to pray for rescue. The Master recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and burned *candana* incense. Although the patient was far away, he smelled the fragrance as it entered his nostrils, and he was immediately healed. Bell Striking Subdues the Evil: (Once, while preaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Shejing Temple in Zhang’an, he encountered pirates plundering the area.

Monastics and laypeople fled in disarray, yet the Master struck the bell and proceeded with the lecture, his countenance showing no sign of fear. The pirates raised their banners and approached the temple, suddenly seeing soldiers’ flags gleaming like the sun, and men holding bows and halberds.)
They were all over ten feet tall, fierce and spirited; the bandits were startled and dispersed. Regarding Zhixi’s vision:

his fellow student, the wise Zhixi, was personally ordained by him and passed away in the first year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. At the time of his death, he said, "I have been born in Tuṣita.

I saw the rows of jeweled thrones of my former teacher, the Wise One (Zhiyi), all occupied except for one, which was empty. He said, 'Six years from now, Dharma Master Guanding shall ascend this throne to preach the Dharma. Verifying this through inference, there was no discrepancy. [The Master died on the eighth month of the sixth year of Zhenguan.]

He passed away at Guoqing Temple on the seventh day, at the age of seventy-two. Initially manifesting a slight illness, he declined medical treatment; however, a wondrous fragrance filled his chamber. As death approached, he instructed his disciples: "The *Maitreya Sūtra* states that when the Buddha enters a city, fragrant smoke rises like clouds.

You must burn much incense, for I am about to depart. His countenance was joyful as he suddenly passed away. His entire body remained supple and soft, and the crown of his head remained warm for days. When his remains were cremated, the examination of the ashes confirmed his intent: this was clearly the descent of Maitreya’s spirit. Calculating the years and considering the timing, it was evident that his words were not false.
The Text for the *Pravāraṇā*:
I, [Name], respectfully state: In examining our Dharma, we behold the sublime wind of the Truth;

twelve years after the Great Master attained enlightenment, the teachings were concise yet the people were sincere, and the *Vinaya* had not yet been codified—until the transgression of Sūdena occurred, whereupon the first section was immediately established.
Next, the remaining *nikāyas* were established according to the offenses committed and the rules formulated, forming a solemn code of discipline.

Since the first chapter already resided within the section on expulsion (*pārājika*), the remaining *nikāyas* opened the way for the methods of confession (*prāyaścitta*). Once these methods of confession were set forth, the sons of the Śākya followed them;

yet, because human minds are often deluded and few are able to confess their own faults, one must rely on the censure and exhortation of others before one may perform confession and purification according to each respective *nikāya*. Thus...
To repair a broken vessel with great care, or to cleanse a soiled garment with purity—how vast is the benefit of the method for repenting transgressions!
Thus, when the summer retreat (varṣā) is completed, the ceremony of self-examination (pravāraṇā) is performed.
Now, while the Western Regions divide the year into three seasons, China opens it into four; since they protect life during the season of heat, we here restrain our feet during the summer months.
Furthermore, while this tradition takes the conjunction of the new moon as the first day of the month, that tradition takes the full moon as the beginning of the month;
thus, they observe the ninety-day summer retreat (*varṣā*) with the first appearance of the dark crescent as its conclusion.

We respectfully consider that your monastery possesses secluded and extraordinary excellence, a serene and refined monastic complex where every person is renowned for their vast learning and everyone embodies noble and lofty conduct. How could there be any concern regarding the loss of the bright pearl?

Why do you doubt this? It is like a fine jade that appears to have many flaws; yet, because he received the Buddha’s command and acted without transgression, he is one who brings great glory to the Sangha.

As for what is called *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence), "self" (*zi*) refers to personally proclaiming one's own offenses, while "indulgence" (*zi*) means allowing the Sangha to raise charges against one's faults.
Thus, one's internal lack of private concealment is revealed, and one's external manifest flaws are made clear; since body and speech are entrusted to others, it is termed "self."
The regulations for this practice were established at the end of summer because the initial assembly began at the start of summer;
if members were to point out each other's faults, it would ruin the Way and hinder one’s practice.

Therefore, as the summer retreat concludes and travel abroad is no longer obstructed, the month-long hall is opened to gather the monastic community, where they follow the texts of their own school to perform the rites themselves.
As for the method of presiding over the assembly, I am like such-and-such a person: my years of ordination are few, my virtue is meager, my learning shallow, and my talent desolate.

Regarding the principles of this permissible practice: since the teachings of the Buddha were transmitted to the East and the Vinaya emerged from the West, although the five schools branched out like stars or stood firm as mountains, competing to transform the land of India, it was the four divisions that rose preeminent like ospreys and soared like hawks, uniquely prevailing in China.

In ceasing evil and preventing transgression, he was as steadfast as a rampart, thereby bringing his Way to prominence. Its greatness is such that it defies praise for its virtue alone. It is my good fortune—

I humbly entreat you to cultivate yourself with compassion and accept my sincere offerings; may you appear in every land to witness this heart of clear faith.

by ordaining them in the Great Precepts, the sacred laws have been made to circulate and shall not fall into ruin. From this day forward, who could say that [the Dharma] is confined to this land?

may the winds of Jishi and the rains of Bishi accord with the seasons, and may the sun of the Buddha and the lamp of wisdom shine forever.

furthermore, I wish for the temple buildings to flourish, the monastic community to remain harmonious, calamities not to arise, and offerings from donors to arrive constantly, so that the true spirits of this land may bestow their hidden virtue.

Four Poems on the Manao Slope Adjacent to the Secluded Spring (With Preface).
The Master Zhongyong was convalescing at the Manao Slope; as his illness subsided, he composed four verses on four objects to express his thoughts according to the four seasons.
The first:
By the agate slope, trees stand; though spring has come, they yet bear no blossoms. When the rain clears and the mist briefly lifts, their dense splendor vies with the morning glow.
Second,
before the Agate Slope, the water is clear and cool, cold even in summer; when the night deepens,
the bright moon rises like a pearl falling onto an ice platter.
Third, on the road ahead of Marṇapō Hill: On an autumn night, I lean alone upon my staff; The grass is deep, hiding ghostly fires;
The moss is ancient, cutting off all traces of human passage.
Those four agate mounds before the cliff— Their solidity and integrity could mend the heavens; Where has Nüwa gone?
She lies cold and desolate amidst the wintry mist.

In years past, I came to Zheyang and met you at Shuixin (the present-day Shuixin Temple); We discussed our aspirations and shared the Way, sitting together until our eyes grew bright with clarity.
