The next day we suddenly parted, drifting apart like water lilies—one north, one south. I sought my dwelling on Mount Gu, while you went to Dongming.
Once we had bid farewell in the human world, seven years of the stars have passed in the heavens.
Since we have looked upon one another from across the rivers and lakes, what need is there to evaluate our mutual kindness? Thus ends the late spring of this year.

In the thatched hall, flowers drift and fall; having just awakened from sleep, I lean upon the railing. Beyond the bamboo, I hear the sound of human voices, suddenly announcing that Master Feng has arrived.
I step out to meet him, my sandals slipping as I go. He asks why I have come, and I tell him the truth of the matter:
The Ministry of Revenue oversees external accounts (at that time, the *zhuan-shu* or transport department was under the Ministry of Revenue).
Evening worship brings me to this city (the Governor is Imperial Censor Wang); both worthies were my old acquaintances, so I was able to renew our covenant.
In summer I came to the west of West Lake to be a neighbor to those who delight in secluded integrity;
in the morning I ascend the Hall of the Recluse (Master Lin Bù), and in the evening I knock at the door of the "Zhōngyōng" (my own self-designation).
Gazing afar at clouds and mountains, The bamboo breeze clears away the summer heat. In discussing poetry, one prizes freedom from depravity;
In embodying the Way, one reaches the formless. In an instant, the seasons have shifted; The autumn wind brushes the eaves and rafters.
Packing our bags, we suddenly bid farewell, Pointing toward the journey home across the Ningjiang River. Since arriving here, there has been nothing to do.
Leaving now, how could it concern my feelings? A solitary sail flies forth at the break of dawn; The oars for returning resound through the night.
Viewing the world’s ways as wind and waves, I realize water and moon reflect transient glory; I further know the nature of the crane on the marsh— It is not entangled by the net of dust.
In this trial of the brush, dwelling in the city is no different from residing in the mountains and forests; there is affinity for both.

My speech is humble yet as sweet as shepherd’s purse, and the Way I follow is noble and straight as a harp string. I sit upright, chanting until the day's end; frail and worn, I have passed another year in sickness.
In stillness, I beckon the cranes by Lake Zhao; Leisurely, I glide upon my boat through the snow. To dispel weariness, wine is indeed unnecessary;
To delight the spirit, I rejoice in Zen. Let the frost settle upon the roots of my hair; Let the fires of worldly traces be extinguished.
With such cold indifference, with whom can I find accord? In carefree ease, I simply cherish myself; When idle, I sit beneath the window.
An Impromptu Piece Written While Experimenting with the Brush:
Reading History, I Admire Bao Xu’s Wailing— With one wail he saved the state of Chu; in serving his sovereign, he exhausted his loyalty.
To leave a name for a thousand generations, I admire the smile of Master Luan;
With one laugh he repelled the Qin army, neutralizing its momentum amidst the wine cups and ritual vessels, His fragrance flows to this day for all to hear. I admire the benevolence of Bo Yi;
He maintained his integrity through yielding and retiring, Starving to death beneath Mount Shouyang, Refusing to serve a ruler of war and strife.
Those who peep and pilfer in later generations are thus not of the same caliber as King Fa of the Ji clan.
Internally harboring plots for usurpation and regicide, they externally tread in the dust of King Wu. Had Bo Yi not departed, how could the teachings of name and virtue have been extended?
If later men were not like these three worthies, their trivialities would be unworthy of mention; one can only weep and lament that their rank and position were so lowly.
The Xiaoxi family feasts on delicacies of fine grain, while those in the mountains and forests suffer from cold and hunger. Their conduct is strange, for they do not seek benevolence;
their minds lack the resolve for universal salvation, plotting only for their own single bodies. As I stroke this book and contemplate the Three Sages, their pure wind vibrates through the ages.
In the West Snow Garden there was no Xi Shi; how then could the state of Wu have been destroyed?

It was because the King of Wu, slighting his own altars of state, was seduced by the beauty that toppled a city. Thus Fu Chai turned strength into weakness, while Gou Jian transformed weakness into strength.
Was it merely the strategy of Tao Zhu? Truly, it relied upon the beauty of Xi Shi. Yet Xi Shi’s words were also sagacious;
how obscure and deluded are the criticisms! They speak only of her crime in toppling Wu, Completely forgetting her merit in establishing the hegemony of Yue.
I long for the song of the Gentleman.
The petty man’s feet are skilled in flattery; the gentleman harbors no suspicion or jealousy.
His open mouth proclaims only sages and worthies; his full belly contains nothing but benevolence and righteousness.
He refines his speech to restore antiquity and revitalize the pure wind; he breaks the railings and strikes the fish-scales to manifest his upright spirit.
He does not boast when living well in the world, nor does he feel distressed when withdrawing from it;
he blends his light with the dust of common customs, refusing to contend with ordinary people over even an inch.
Those who long to behold this man have turned over in their beds and brooded upon him nine times throughout a single night.
Pacing all day long, I meet with nothing; The whistling western wind withers the autumn leaves.
Singing of the Five Mountains upon the sea:
Lofty and towering, they rise from the heart of the ocean; The waves ebb and flow, rising and sinking along with them.
The assembly of immortals went together to petition the Heavenly Emperor; fifteen giant tortoises were subject to celestial decree.
Each giant tortoise bore a mountain, remaining so for thirty-six thousand years at a time.
Suddenly, the Dragon-Ber came to fish for six of the tortoises, and from that point on, two mountains were submerged in the surging waves.
The multitude of immortals have dispersed and become wanderers; The High God relies on clemency, yet the Dragon-Ber has been punished.
Know that joy and pleasure are not eternal; The Three Realms are originally empty—what truly exists therein?
Do not vie for prowess over the tip of a snail’s horn; Even the immortal mountains upon the sea are subject to decay.
A Song Sung in a Humble Lane, Presented to a Friend Alas, Yanzi!
You dwell in a humble lane; though your body is emaciated, your Way is ever more robust.
Shang Zhou received the imperial capital; though his position was exalted, he was but a solitary husband.
In the morning one may indulge in the pleasures of the Jade Terrace, yet in the evening one may meet execution by the yellow battle-axe;
thus we know that unrighteous wealth and honor are like floating clouds, while only the Way and Virtue constitute the essential pivot of life and nature.
By the seashore there was a scholar who admired Yan Hui; his heart valued hearing the Way in the morning and disregarded dying at evening.
Amidst the clamor of those who polish their grain-husks and look down on the heroic and bold, he remained as solemn as ice and frost in his conduct and movements.
In the silence of his thatched door, what petty matters could there be? Holding his scroll, he sat all day long enduring hunger.
Yang Xiong escaped the execution of Zhen Feng, while Zhu Jian ultimately suffered the disaster of Biyang;
when shooting at a high wall, there is always the right moment— regard your lord with neither "yes" nor "no," and sing this song of careful friendship.
Do not say the pine is ever green, for it too is sometimes broken and snapped; Do not say the full moon is ever bright, for it too is sometimes eclipsed and waning.

Do not speak of your pure sincerity with such defiance, Yet those who have pledged their friendship even unto death— Before their years and hair have even reached decline, Their bonds of friendship have already vanished, Suddenly brought about by the struggle for every inch of advantage.
Suddenly they become as distant as Chu and Yue; One loves them and wishes for their life, Another hates them and wishes for their death.
If you wish to know how pines wither and the moon wanes, Please look at Chen Yu and Zhang Er in this ancient poem on the lute.
A skilled craftsman gathered the wood of the *chántóng* tree, Carved it into a "Green Refined" lute. One performance restored the wind of simplicity;
A second performance harmonized the hearts of men. The gentleman did not part from it for a moment, Valuing its ability to restrain extravagance and licentiousness.
Later generations were deluded by the music of Zheng, And this Way consequently sank into oblivion; Now, red strings are being secretly gnawed by rats.
The golden strings are encrusted with dust and dimmed; Cold and neglected, it lies across the empty window.
Abandoned for many years, how might I find Master Xiang to play it, So that I may once again hear the great sounds of antiquity?
*Collection of Leisurely Dwelling*, Volume Thirty-Eight.
*Collected Works from Secluded Dwelling*, Volume 39,
composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
Poem on the Temple of Mount Wú.
The gentleman prizes flexibility and adaptation; flexibility and adaptation value conformity with the Way. Zi Xu recommended Zhuan Zhu to Zi Guang, yet Zhuan was not seeking personal gain.
When father and son share the same sky, they must avenge their mutual enmity. I lament that the request for troops came too late.
Once Zi Guang had attained his ambition, he entered Ying to carry out military expeditions. Having avenged his father, he subsequently performed the ritual of scourging the corpse.
He remonstrated with the king and then sacrificed his life; Only thus were the filial piety of the son and the integrity of the subject fully realized.
The path of the loyal minister was renewed, and his fame spread throughout heaven and earth. How could he be but one of the common, indifferent folk?
The green annals record his magnificent deeds; his blood-offerings honor his lingering dust. His temple hall shines with the first light of dawn; the temple trees blossom in the warmth of spring.
Coming and going, ignorant of the mundane world, I burn incense and pray with diligence. Dare not fail in loyalty and filial piety;
O Spirit, may you surely bestow blessings!
(Reciting a poem by Han Yu.)
Nüwa smelted the five stones, able to mend the breach in the blue heavens; Gonggong struck the Notou mountain, causing the earth’s supporting cords to snap.
Since Yangzi and Mengzi have passed away, the spirit of Confucianism has nearly been destroyed.
Wicked words delude the common ear, and licentious texts corrode the orthodox teachings; in the Southern Dynasties, Xu Ling and Yu Xin were held in high esteem.
When the Tang dynasty flourished, Lu and Luo were esteemed; Their ornate carvings and seal scripts vied with one another for cleverness.
Benevolence and righteousness were entirely cast aside; The Way of Kings and Lords was not clarified. The heart took its refuge in the transient splendor of smoke and flowers.

Literature could not remain in perpetual decline; Heaven gave birth to Minister Han. He rebuked the false and compelled it to return to the true; He lashed the present age and caused it to revert to antiquity.
The heterodoxies have been severed; the gaps in the Confucian tradition are all filled. His sublime compositions, numbering seven hundred pieces, shine as brightly as the sun and moon.
With his strength he upholds the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; with his hand he wields the authority of literature.
Those who come shall know to revere the Confucianists—who would not follow this path? As for me, I am born with a love for ancient ways.
To serve and study, one must first dispel ignorance; why need one necessarily master a single classic? Only when both literature and the Way are honored can one truly be esteemed.
A Poem Written to Invite a Friend to Live in the Mountains:
I have built a dwelling on the shore of a level lake, Where I may give rein to my mind in leisure and ease. From time to time, I climb the peaks to gather medicinal herbs.
Taking medicinal herbs dispels old ailments; Wild amaranth and sorrel suffice for a meal. A thatched hut can accommodate one’s knees;
In this floating life, what is prized is the harmony with one's nature. Why need one envy luxury and ease? The clear scenery is right before my eyes;
How could I find time to worry about the myriad affairs of the world? Heaven and water vie in their chill beauty; Forests and peaks together rise in dense majesty.
Sometimes I drift away in a boat on my way home; At my secluded gate, the setting sun dries its last rays.

The paths are overgrown and human tracks have ceased; The courtyard is so still that spirits emerge. In spring, the purple water-mushrooms ripple in the soup; In winter, the yellow tangerines are arrayed upon the platter.
Even this pit by the well is a source of joy; Who says the inch-worm is ever bent? Let not external conditions delude me.
With a steadfast mind, I have long cherished the One; The Nirvana Sutra is the ultimate scripture. In the empty hall, I discourse upon it constantly, regardless of the rarity of those who understand.
I hope only that I may remain free from error. In "Equanimity Among Things," I despise Zhuang Zhou;
In "Seeing into One's Nature," I take Master Miaojue as my teacher. Tranquil, I blend with both sentient beings and Buddhas; Profoundly still, there is neither void nor reality.
Whether the one who understands comes or not, I sweep my secluded chamber from time to time.
A poem presented to Student Ye:
The pine and cypress differ from other trees; In the cold of winter, they withstand the severe frost. The orchid and mugwort differ from other grasses; [They remain fragrant amidst the withering.]
In the deep forest, a subtle fragrance arises; one must know that this is the Way of the Gentleman. It is not wounded by poverty or distress;
one must know that these are the words of the Gentleman. They serve only to manifest benevolence and righteousness.
Now, as for the true Confucian: how superior and extensive are his words and deeds! His literary tradition combines Mencius and Xunzi; his will detests Mozi and Yangzi.
Rolling up my sleeves, I rebuked the floating and false; a hundred emotions stirred within my resolute heart. Wearing a high cap, I attended to ritual decorum;
the petty crowd feared my dignified bearing. Last year I traveled to Xi溪 (Xixi); meeting there in the cool autumn air, we greeted each other as old friends.
Having pitched our canopies together, we stayed overnight in a room among the woods; opening our hearts, we cast aside the two hegemonies.
We deliberate on the Way, returning to the Three Kings; at the moonlit mats, guests are frequently replaced. In the wind-filled pavilion, frost occasionally drifts.
Our meeting was harmonious, yet our parting brings all the more sorrow. This year I dwell on Gushan, while you, my lord, have come again to Hangzhou.
We frequently seek one another by boat; recounting our old ties, we find ourselves in the setting sun.
You belong to the lineage of the Confucian school; your talent and skill are, moreover, vast and deep. In the end, you shall rectify rites and music;
do not concern yourself with worldly splendor. Soar forth into the blue clouds, and may the spirit of Confucianism be exalted.
This is a poem presented on a slip of paper to Master Shanren.
Ordinary people hide away in forests and springs, yet they are instead entangled by fame and profit.

The man of ambition dwells amidst the bustling markets, yet his heart remains far off in the rivers and lakes. There is a guest devoted to lofty purity; his meditation chamber is closed within the heavy city walls.
In the quiet gate there are no traces of the mundane; in the crumbling walls, the chirping of insects abounds. He lies down as fallen spring flowers cover the stone steps.
Having chanted until the frost-moon was bright, I hope the gentleman will understand my path. Let poverty be as it may, for I am disregarded by the people of this age;
yet I maintain my integrity, vowing never to waver. May I forever preserve the constancy of the solitary pine.
—An Account of the Poetry of Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan.

Tui (Han Yu) rejected the teachings of Śākyamuni, while Zithou (Liu Zongyuan) was largely capable in benevolence. Since the ways of Han and Liu were so similar, how could their likes and dislikes be categorized?
One was exiled, the other offered praise; both served to extend the Way of the Confucians.
Liu Zhou’s inscription for Caoqi speaks of returning to the purity of the Confucian tradition from Buddhism, while the Minister of Personnel (Han Yu) read the *Mozi*.
The Mohists were neighbors to the Confucians; I know that the Mohists practiced universal love.
If one permits this [universal love] in the case of the Mohists, then one must permit it in the case of the Buddhists—this is as clear as looking up at the heavens.

Though their ways of departing and approaching may differ, their underlying principles have always been the same. Yet those of later generations who study Han Yu’s prose bark incessantly against the Buddha.
Unaware of Master Han’s Way, I first studied Master Han’s anger. Forgetting the root to compete for the branches, Ancients and moderns alike have toiled their spirits in vain.
Two Poems on Gushan.
Steep and towering, it rises from the heart of the lake; From its center, one can look out in all four directions.
Its roots coil deep within the vast waters, And its layered emerald peaks dot the cold sky. Its lofty form rivals Mount Penglai, Its perilous tiers vie with Mount Langfeng.
The monks’ pavilions enshroud the thin mist, While the Goose Pagoda obstructs the soaring geese. At dawn, the golden sands glisten in the well.

(The Golden Sand Well is at Guanghua Temple. Sunny slopes of agate-red (the western slope of the mountain is named Agate), Spewing clouds beyond the spring rains, Casting reflections within the evening waves.

Wild vines hang from withered cypresses (the withered cypresses at Guanghua Temple were planted during the Tianjia era of the Chen dynasty), Sparse bells resound throughout the Buddhist temple (there are five such monasteries encircling the mountain).
Secluded springs and crystalline peaks at the summit, A secluded path enters deep thickets. (The secluded springs and secluded path are located at the Agate Garden.
Ancient sites discussed by all are extraordinary; Autumn screens painted cannot fully capture them. Those who enjoy the excursion are no worldly guests; In quiet gazing, they belong to the fisherman.
To purchase it, one knows its price is beyond measure; To dwell within it, how can one’s reflections ever end?
I sigh instead for within the marketplace and the court, where dust and soil are ever hazy and thick.
(II) Its grandeur stands apart from the surrounding peaks; how weary one becomes after ascending its towering heights! The waves are clear, reflecting the inverted image [of the sky].
Clouds cleared away, revealing perilous ridges; The scenery is entirely more excellent than a painting. Forests and springs belong half to the monks;
Who is it that leans upon the prefectural pass? Gazing westward, emerald peaks layer upon layer.
Written in my study during late autumn, expressing my sentiments as I send them to Master Shou-neng.
Shutting my door, I have no worldly associates; let the affairs of the mundane world roll on in their vast expanse.

In this empty chamber, beyond the study of Buddhism, I freely engage in the investigation of the Six Classics. My resolve for benevolence and righteousness remains unshakable; who can trouble me with poverty or illness?
My destiny is my sole joy; I offer no prayers to the hundred deities. Composing my writings, I take Confucius and Mencius as my masters.
In conversation, I reject the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi; Flattery and sycophancy have a harsh sound, while solitude has a fine flavor.
The curtains are drawn aside and my melancholy thoughts vanish; Leaning on the railing, the cold air is already keen.
The shadows of geese sink into the distant sky; Insects chirp through the withered grass. As for me, what am I? I strive to practice the Right Path.
I pray you shall propagate the spirit of the superior man, sweeping away all frivolity and superficiality.
A poem presented to the monk Baoxian:
Celestial patterns hang like the sun and moon; Terrestrial patterns beautify the mountains and rivers; Human patterns shine brightly in the Six Classics.
The four methods of interpreting poetry preceded it; once the Master of Zhongni had performed his selection, the *Feng* and *Ya* were brilliantly arrayed.
Yet their essential meaning remained profound and subtle, transmitted only to Zi Xia.
Through the vast span of a thousand years, there have been those who understood poetry, yet the Teacher Baoxian stands preeminent. He was born in Song, throughout all under heaven.
Within, he clarifies the Way of Confucius; without, he diminishes the price of the *Sao* poets. He taps into that source of pure essence, from which refined expressions flow forth in competition.
His intentions are set upon what is profound and remote; in establishing his words, he avoids the "wild insects" (of frivolous style).
How sublime is this *Tianmu ji*! The four seas vie to copy and transmit it, so as to assist the King’s transformation of the world.
Below, he rectifies human relations; He drives out the depraved so they may return to the right, And urges away the turbid so they may revert to simplicity.
If Heaven has not yet destroyed these sacred texts, His pure wind shall shake for a thousand ages.
Presented to Zhao Pu.
The ways of the world drift aimlessly at will; The upright man seeks no flattery. Ancient cypresses defy the cold frost, and the bright moon shines upon the high autumn;
In heart, he takes Zhou and Kong as his masters, And daily distances himself from the wanderings of Yang and Mo.
The Jing is turbid and the Wei is clear; From the beginning, they have flowed apart.
*Collection of Works from Secluded Dwelling*, Volumes 39 and 40.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
Passing by the old residence of Master Fayao on the small mountain at Wukang:
The Ultimate Way cannot be described; The Ultimate Principle is profound and nameless. The myriad species have lost their source;
how they rush to and fro! Suddenly there arose Fayao, Who refined his thoughts to return to pure essence.

The founder of this school of discourse was Śākyamuni; his glorious reputation has spread for a hundred years. I have come to visit my former dwelling, yet the scenery seems as if it still holds affection for me.
In the quiet courtyard, the colors of the trees grow somber; in the empty mountains, the cries of gibbons are muffled.
This man is now gone; alone in my boat, I seek the path home.
The Section on Xi Shi:

Picking lotuses upon the Yue stream, she was regarded by all as but an ordinary woman. Only when she was formally installed as an official lady in the state of Wu did her beauty spread through the mouths of the multitude.
Once the eyes and ears were satiated with song and dance, even fine silks and brocades were held cheap.
How virtuous is the neighbor! In years past, he knew how to mimic the frown;
yet his indulgence followed licentious and dissolute sounds. Lu received the offerings from Qi (read *gui*); ancient music was harmonious and upright.
On the contrary, it causes Lord Wen to fall asleep; Deceitful words are what the ear delights to hear. The heart, instead, harbors resentment toward the direct path;

Knowing only how to indulge in what it prefers, How could it ever consider the risk of falling into ruin? One should pay heed to the distinction between the music of antiquity and the sounds of Zheng, regarding their orthodoxy and heterodoxy.

A Self-Description While Secluded in the Mountains, Devoting Myself to Writing: Who would say that these mountain streams and hills are insignificant? Reclining in leisure, I prize the nourishment of the Way;
who would say my physical form is emaciated? If these words are to remain without blemish, I shall examine myself within so that I may be free from remorse.
Deep understanding is like the shallow rivers and vast seas; Broad measure encompasses the narrow universe. The neighbor’s girl learned little but mimicked her frown;
The sea-faring husband often pursued what was foul-smelling. When the time comes, sit beneath the pines; A pure breeze fills one’s sleeves— Do not say that the spring days are long.
Do not say that spring days are long; In one sitting, the sun has already set in the west.
The myriad fragrances flourish and then fall; all things newly formed become old. Facing the river, I have long sighed in lamentation;
Who says that a hidden boat is secure? Let these anxieties be swept away in tranquility; Within the empty gate lies the path of return.

In my youth, I studied the teachings of Tai and Heng, refining my understanding of Buddhist principles; in my later years, I read the books of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, whereby the relations between men became clearly illuminated.
Seeking to realize the fundamental and adorn the self, my resolve has been to find like-minded companions.

Though striking away ignorance may seem laborious, Those who come to study find it difficult to achieve success. Yang Xiong esteemed the profound and the white, yet Confucius’ Way could not be put into practice.
In dreams one returns to the green mountains, While gray hairs have grown upon my head these years.
I should only contemplate ultimate emptiness; All worldly affairs are but a frantic bustle.
Exhorting the recluse:
The murmuring waters in the mountain stream do not enter the ears of the greedy man; the vast dust upon the road does not soil the body of the tranquil one.
The tranquil one prizes few desires; the greedy man constantly suffers from poverty.

Hasty advancement leads one into the trap of the sycophant; Purifying oneself alone neglects the great human relations. How much more so in this age of cultural brilliance, when the common people are gathered as men of worth!
In practicing the Way, one should still adhere to the Middle Way; Like a silkworm cocoon, one who has been curled up ought to seek extension—let the mirror reflect this truth.
The fair lady polishes it often, constantly fearing that dust and grime will invade it. Bright is the night moon, clear and deep is the autumn spring;
In vain they distinguish between beautiful and ugly forms, Yet fail to reflect the mind of right and wrong.
Walking in the Mountains.
Drifting slowly are the clouds upon the crags; Gurgling flow the waters in the ravine. The mountain birds, as if calling out to people, Chatter in the deep forest as they see off the monk.
The autumn wind blows upon my traveling robes; I return in leisure to my old mountain home. My alms-bowl cleanses the empty pool;
An ancient chime strikes against the fading light. One must know that this lofty and tranquil mind Is utterly beyond the reach of the mundane world.
—In Reply to a Letter from the Venerable Master Xingjian.
By chance I dwell beside a mountain stream, Three times I have seen the seasons change. Your letter inquires after my whereabouts; Whether walking or sitting, I keep it in my breast.
In studying the Way, I have not improved from before; My indolence remains much as it was of old.
I exhaust myself in bitter verse through the night, And pass the bright days in idle sleep. The ancient house is overgrown with wild moss.
In the secluded courtyard, monkeys and apes frolic; Artifice and hypocrisy are not what I delight in. Uprightness and integrity are naturally bestowed;

At the gates of the nobility, I have severed all requests for audience. I am diligent in the study of the refined classics; The world at large consists only of superficial friends— Who then can discuss with me the matters of withdrawal and engagement?
Written at Xunfeng Pavilion on a Summer Day:
The four fields blaze with the intense heat of summer; Sitting alone in this precarious pavilion, with whom can I share it?
The lake’s light is vast and shimmering, reflecting the fading sun; Bird silhouettes drift irregularly, vanishing into the distant sky.
I rely on ultimate truth to inform myself of this floating life; I depend on the clear breeze to dispel the oppressive heat.
In these enlightened times, I dare not speak of "inviting reclusion"; I simply find joy in the forests and springs, admiring the spirit of Master Yuan Gong.
Composed spontaneously upon ascending Diercui Pavilion on a newly cleared day.
In the vast, distant sky, the rain has just cleared; I leisurely drag my mountain clogs up to the pavilion on the ridge.
The wind is still upon the level lake, revealing the mirror of water lilies; The layered peaks, their clouds withdrawn, stand like a set of painted screens.
I have already realized that all worldly conditions are truly but a dream; How could I allow trivial matters to needlessly weary my form?
Pitiable are those who vie for profit and crave fame, Tumultuously wandering in the human world, their intoxication yet unawakened.
Xiucai Li presented me with a poem on rising early at his mountain studio; I thus respond by matching its rhyme.
In seeking the marvelous and suiting the extraordinary, where does one’s inspiration find its fullness? Your elegant verses clearly rival those of Hui Lian.
The vermilion cassia may be gazed upon by you with equal fortune; In the red dust, I lack the karmic affinity to depart in leisure.
To soothe the spirit, we shall look together at the mountain snows; To dispel drowsiness, we shall brew mountain tea together at night.
Our quiet conversation reveals that both have intentions for the path ahead— Like the "Red Medicine" of Master Xie, and the lotus of Master Huiyuan.
Against the snow’s chill, the level lake freezes, cutting off the passage of oars; Flakes fall profusely, filling the eyes—what can be said of such a scene?
In noble households, songs and dances never suffice to satisfy the gaze; Among the common folk, hunger and cold weary the heart with their abundance.
Wandering through the secluded courtyard, I boast of its jade steps; Leaning heavily against a secluded tree, I vie with its jade-like branches.
Last night, sitting alone beneath my study window, I still relied on its empty clarity to polish myself.
Three Poems on Mount Gu.
The pavilions press against the perilous azure; at the foot of the mountains, one suspects the presence of a giant tortoise.
A thousand ridges are severed by the lake, yet a single peak rises high above the water. The crags are cold with the autumn sky’s moon; the forests are clear with snow and the night monkeys.
As for me, utterly free from all bonds, I am forever able to roam at will.
Its second and fourth peaks cut off the path of dust; the scenery of the solitary mountain is truly solitary.

Its perilous summit reaches into the distant Milky Way, its cold hues soak into the calm lake. The ancient pagoda is named after a Pratyekabuddha (the Pratyekabuddha Pagoda stands at the very peak of the mountain).
The Servant’s Well at Xinquan (located on Ma’nao Slope in Shanxi; excavated by the Master Zhongyong)—where is Wang Wei?
This marvel is even more worthy of depiction than the third.
Beholding West Lake from the Immortal Island, the scenery of the west is truly abundant: In spring, it melts into the welcoming dawn;

in autumn, its azure depths obstruct the void. Bamboo shades the stupas of eminent monks (the stupas of the Tang monk Huilin and the Song monk Wuen remain here), while clouds obscure the dwelling of the recluse (the recluse Lin Bù, whose high integrity led him to refuse office and dwell in seclusion upon this mountain).
If Sima Qian were here today, he would surely store his books here;
The intense heat is like a petty person, Painfully invading everywhere; The pure breeze is like a gentleman.
When it comes, it broadens my heart; Though the scorching heat drives it away, it does not go. The pure breeze cannot retain it;
This feeling is beyond words to tell. Beside the dark, shady trees, I chant;
A traveler stands there.
A guest, a guest, comes knocking at my gate; We meet in silence, from day until dusk.
Propping elbows on the railing, I gaze up and down at heaven and earth. In a hundred years, a mere instant—whose loss or gain shall we discuss?
The distant mountains are green, the vast waters are deep and turbid. Suddenly he departs; in this direct encounter, the Way is preserved.
In response to Master Ren’s poem sent from atop Mount Shan, I follow his rhyme:
Gentle waves reflect a perilous azure; This pure scene differs from the mundane world. After the snow has cleared, the cold penetrates the city walls;
In autumnal clarity, the chill shines upon the void. To sleep amidst the clouds is a pleasure for oneself alone; Who can I invite to join me as I glide my boat upon the water?
Who can recognize these secluded delights? In my search for verses, I am ashamed before Master Yuǎn;
I visited Master Zhòngwēi at Biàncái’s hermitage, but he was not there.
Twenty years have passed since we last met; Seeking him again, the circumstances have changed once more— The gate stands shut against the cold waters.
Birds return toward the setting sun; I fear my chanting will turn my hair white. In leisure, I wonder as I enter the emerald peaks;
Boarding my boat alone, I sail southward— How swift is this flight of inspired spirit!
A verse in the same rhyme to answer Master Ming.
Tending my illness beneath the Solitary Hill, I wander at ease, following the wild heart’s inclination. The quiet gate is submerged in cold waters;
the high balustrade reveals the desolate city. Moonlight on the steps shifts the shadows of the pines; spring from the crags mutes the sound of the chime.
Only you are permitted to come here, to accompany me as we age out our remaining lives.
To My Fellow Practitioner: In this quiet hermitage, no guests arrive; As we miss one another, the day fades into dusk. A few peaks hold snow in their cold embrace;
Upon a single mat, I sleep peacefully amidst the clouds. How often I sigh that the pure wind of antiquity has perished! How can we allow such vulgar ways to swarm about us?
In the end, we shall meet once more; Sitting face to face, we shall discuss new writings.
In mourning for the Venerable Fachong at the Lecture Hall of Dhyānabhadra:
A mournful wind stirs the plain curtains; The swaying pines make it difficult to see our Master again.
Dust gathers on the old couch, so cease unrolling your scrolls; The moon rises over the autumn pavilion, so stop composing your poems.
The True Dharma shall naturally be transmitted to future scholars; Who will carve your pure fame upon a grand monument?
Disciples who have mastered the scriptures cherish your lofty traces; Together they point toward the Dragon Flower Assembly as their future meeting place.
Residing in Seclusion at Gushan, I Respond in Kindred Rhyme to the Poem Sent by My Nephew Ren of Kuaiji:
The mountain towers from the heart of the lake; I dwell there, following my natural lot. I examine the traces of my former life; my thatched cottage is sealed deep within the mist.
The moon is clear over the autumn waters, drawing forth my thoughts for verse; Flowers fill the spring cliffs, their radiance illuminating my weary sleep.
Touching the rocks, faint clouds leisurely bring forth rain; Calling from the marshes, a solitary crane silently hears the heavens.
If you would cast aside these scenes to seek me out, A single sail hangs suspended upon the vast, azure river.
*The Collection of Leisurely Dwelling*, Volume Forty.
*Collection of Writings from Secluded Dwelling*, Volume 41,
composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty,
presented to the Jinshi Ye Shòu.
My traveling traces are as light as drifting feathers, separated from the mundane world; When I move, my high reputation follows my new writings.
I lodge in a monk’s quarters, locked away by the autumn rains; My dreams are drawn toward my home mountains, yet they are severed by sea clouds.
In my studies, I admire Mencius and Confucius as we speak together; As for the Way, I follow Yang Zhu and Mo Di, even if it means leaving the crowd behind.
Famous fields flourish when responding to the actions of men; beneath the drooping sleeves in the Hall of Brightness sits a Sage Ruler.
In summer days, I entrust myself to Vinaya Master Liang;
the vast, clear river reflects a thousand peaks. Sitting out the summer retreat within a mountain cell, all is visible at a single glance.
By day, the lecture hall’s sparse bells pass by with clear resonance; At night, the lingering moon chills as it hangs low in the void.
I sweep the courtyard to find stillness, avoiding the sharp edges of the steps and the moss; To dispel the summer heat, I rest idly amidst the wind through the bamboo slits.
Gazing at you with mutual longing, I cannot yet depart; By the water’s edge, the slanting sun shines upon the wutong trees.
The sound of the carriage passing through the distance rolls daily over the red dust; for what reason has my noble husband not yet returned?
Moss locks the inner chambers and letters have long been cut off; under the bright moon in the deep night, only the wild geese come empty-handed.
The cold penetrates the bamboo leaves, making it hard to become drunk; Dust obscures the rhombus-shaped mirror, and I am too weary to open it again.
The distant clouds and mountains have no known location; As the evening sun repeatedly climbs the highest terrace, I send this to Master Wenzhao.
Correspondence with the two systems of government has come and gone many times; Dwelling in seclusion within the city, one stays far from the dust and grime.
In the stillness of the night, the moonlight opens upon the recitation hall; On the lecturing stone, deep in autumn, the green moss is swept away.
An old inscription from a worldly life remains at Xueyuan; With a secluded longing for the clouds, one dreams of Tiantai.
Amidst the forest trees, he embraces his ailment while cherishing lofty aspirations; He laughs at Tang and Xiu for their vain display of talent.
To Master Biancai:
Having twice received imperial grace, all worldly anxieties have ceased; Reclining in high repose in Zheyang, he declines the summons of the feudal lords.
In meditation, the moss on the secluded chamber grows old; Having finished the lectures, the shadows of trees linger in the empty courtyard.
Clouds and springs of India often hang in my dreams; I am too weary to revisit the scenery of Liangyuan.
The sound of the stream and the scent of cypress seeds—whom shall I speak to? Silently leaning against the Zen seat, I nod my head to myself. (Master’s Exegesis)
Deeply versed in the study of Chan, he dwelt in seclusion on Mount Gu. On this occasion, he wrote of his circumstances while sending them to his former teacher:
"Past the age of forty, my temples have turned to silver threads; Having arrived by chance among the woods, I have settled here."
Studying the Way, I have not yet forgotten my passion for mountains and waters; Loving leisure, I have always remained aloof from profit and fame.
The cool night brings the bright moon to the precarious pavilion; In the still wind, the vast lake reflects the azure void.
Turning my head, I find no acquaintance among the powerful and haughty; Only wild clouds and solitary cranes roam together with me.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the Venerable Wencōng’s verse on his springtime reflections sent to me:
The scenery is harmonious and radiant as ten thousand plants renew themselves; I know in secret that the Azure Emperor has once again traveled to the East.
On the shaded cliffs, bamboos and trees still lean beneath the lingering snow; Yet upon the warm steps, the orioles and flowers already sense the arrival of spring.
Sighing in sorrow, my white hair gradually grows disheveled; In leisure, I ultimately dread the company of worldly folk.
To whom can I speak of this profound sentiment? Turning my head, I find an old friend within the gates of Chan.
On a Spring Day, dwelling in leisure, I record these matters and send them to the Venerable Master Yuanmin.
The gate is closed against the plain lake to avoid the clamor of the world; In quiet contemplation of the scenery, I recognize the morning of spring.
The courtyard plum faces the sun with its blossoms fully opened; The mountain trees reach the clouds, yet the snow has not yet melted.
It is startling that youth diminishes unnoticed with the passing years; Yet in this secluded dwelling, one finds that sleep is all the more abundant.
I rely on the son of Caoqi as my true companion; Beyond Zen, he comes at times to comfort my solitude.
Ascending the tower and moved by the passing of events, I send this to my friend in Tiantai:
Leaning idly against the precarious railing, my thoughts grow dark; In this floating life, who can share my sighs over the fleeting years?
Grief hastens the growth of white hairs without end; The heart is pledged to the green mountains, for there is a karmic affinity to depart.
In the desolate, empty river, the evening colors are clear; Scattered wild geese vanish into the cold mist.
After finishing my verse, I further envy the guests in the woods, Who lie high in deep clouds, listening to the waterfall’s spring.
Master Shutong’s Zen Chamber in the City:
Secluded and elegant, with heavy gates closed fast; The Patriarchal intent made clear, all affairs are at ease.
Sometimes reclining high, he passes the white days; In silent verse, free from thought, he recalls the green mountains.
Sweeping the flowers from the late-autumn steps, I leave behind the green moss; Shaving my hair by the autumn pond, my sickly face is reflected in the water.
How laughable are those who hide deeply in forests and springs, Unaware that such secluded delights exist within the human world.
*Written on the Occasion of My Lake Dwelling, Sent to My Nephew Ren*
Having finished my lecture, I approach the stream and lean alone upon my staff; There is no place for the traces of my idle life amidst the dust.
The heart that longs to return to the green mountains remains ever-present, Yet with the growth of white hair, worldly affairs grow ever more weary.
The path is deep with grass as the plum-rain ceases, And the lamp in the image-shrine dims as the mist thickens over the water.
The only one who understands me is the visitor who shakes the pines; I am often honored by your letters, which comfort my sickened countenance.
Recalling my old dwelling at Shi-bi, I briefly address the Venerable Shao:
Where precipitous cliffs and crags reflect the clear, cold spring, How many times have I contemplated these secluded scenes while sighing over the passing of years?
Returning to rest, we naturally unite with the traces of the immortals; In such profound seclusion, who would say there is no "Heavenly Cavern"?
The cold sound of tall bamboos stirs at the first movement of the wind; Upon the ancient pool, the autumn reflection of the moon is full.
I, too, intend to follow the example of Zhi Dun, Reclining on stone and sleeping amidst the clouds before the green peaks.
To the Retired Scholar Lin Bu:
Deep in his dwelling, monkeys and birds share his forgetfulness of artifice; with the talent of Xunzi and Mengzi, he wears a crane-feather robe.
As spring illness lifts him from the fallen blossoms on the steps, he returns as a fisherman under the bright moon over the lake at night.

On the road, Mount Zhongfeng’s peaks wind and coil; Dust and traces are difficult to reach their end.
The shadows of autumn cypresses cast upon the sutra window are cold; The sound of night waves shakes the sleeping couch chill.
Clouds pass over the quiet pavilion as the incense seals grow moist; The sun shifts across the secluded steps where moss marks have dried.
After finishing my recitation, I stood quietly by the railing for a long time; my gaze reached out to the vast expanse of the Yangtze River.
(2) The Buddhist temple is pure and serene, far removed from worldly clamor; ascending it at this moment brings a refreshing inspiration to the soul of the poet.
The high snow brightens the curtains above Mount Ji; Autumnal surges rise from the sea-gate atop the tower.
The cold shadows of myriad trees stretch to the ancient pagoda; The chill resonance of sparse bells reaches the riverside villages.
The springs and rocks within the city are scenes from a poem; In leisure, I discourse with Master Wen all day long.
Zhao Wanzong entered the Way after sending a lamb and a goose as a gift;
it was already heard that he would not rise to respond to the imperial summons. Instead, he sought the tonsure to dwell in purity at Yuetai;
with his pillow leaning against the moonlit hall, he dreams of the Three Purities, while ten thousand scrolls of books gather dust upon his autumnal couch.
Cold traces circle the altar; spring moss is emerald green. A crane perches on a cold silhouette; snowed pines stand sparse.
In recent years, I have not been able to seek out these secluded traces. On a quiet night, who else would listen to the *bǔxū* chant?
Written on Spring Day while dwelling by the lake, sent to Master Zixuan.
Living in seclusion, I compose rhapsodies in imitation of Anren; My lofty ambitions have vanished, while white hairs grow anew.
Amidst calm mists and waves, the dreams of coming and going are drawn forth; Deep within the blossoms and songbirds, my solitary self finds solace.
The wild ponds turn green with grass as the lake village fades at dusk; In the mountain temple of spring, the fragrance of incense rises from the stone cauldron.
In the end, I shall follow Master Zhi Gong’s example of buying a mountain to dwell; deep within the white clouds, I await you as my neighbor.
Your solitary cry like a wild goose passing through the old forest, Master Zhengyan—where can we meet to discuss our shared hearts?
Sleeping amidst the clouds, I have not betrayed my vows of years past; Gazing at the snow, I find it hard to forget my all-day chanting.
News from the river is scarce as the cold waves stretch wide; Beside the bamboo, the cottage door is closed as the evening sun sinks low.
In solitary stillness, I sit idly beneath the western window, Vainly entrusting my lingering emotions to the jade zither.
To Master Qingyi:
You have mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka, a rarity in this world; Your lofty, detached disposition has long since forgotten artifice.
In your quiet meditation chamber, blue-green moss spreads everywhere; When you rise from your meal, a solitary bird returns to the empty window.
The night bell of Mt. Seorak passes clearly over my pillow; The autumn moon at the waterside pavilion chills my robes.
With no other affairs remaining after chanting and lecturing, I occasionally knock on the bamboo gate to visit those beyond the mundane world.
Visiting Kaehwa Temple.
The earth is severed from even the finest dust, and the ten thousand sounds are pure; the secluded charm before the gate is difficult for a painter to capture.
The peaks and ridges cast high and low shadows as if with dark makeup; the waves roll like unrolled silk, their sound echoing from dawn to dusk.
Ancient corridors are invaded by bamboo and autumn moss has grown thick; in the cloud-reclining meditation pavilion, the night lamp shines bright.
High above lies a secluded retreat, where trees and rocks stand in jagged array, suiting my rustic sentiments.
In response to Master Ziwen’s verse, I offer this in the same rhyme:
The gate is silent; solitary clouds depart and return. After the lecture, all other thoughts are severed from connection.
Leaving fame behind, you idly dwell in a city temple; Summoning the reclusive, you once lived on a mountain by the sea.
Lying ill in a snow-chamber, the moss grows old; Practicing dhyāna in an autumn path, the tree-shadows are still.
Together we have realized the profound mystery; the mind is free from affairs. Meeting thus, how could one worry that the hair at the temples is gradually turning gray?
At the highest peak above Nantasi Temple, dwelling in deep seclusion, ten thousand anxieties are stilled; The path winds around perilous rocks where moss turns green in the rain;
The river reflects the distant heavens, providing leisurely views; Snow illuminates the secluded window as I unroll my old scriptures.
The *qing* stone strikes through the morning frost as meditation briefly awakens; The pillow shifts upon autumn waves as dreams first stir.
Among our neighbors, there is one who has naturally forgotten artifice; Under the moon, he occasionally knocks upon the bamboo gate.
Sent as a gift to Vinaya Master Zizheng.
His dignified bearing is so serene and detached, whom could he possibly share it with? The mossy path remains as it was, utterly devoid of footprints.
At the frost-covered well, filtered spring water seeps through the hue of dawn; In the snow-clad chamber, leaning on a pillow, he dreams of the myriad peaks.
A chill arises upon his quiet couch from the moonlight within his verse; The cold echoes back from the lake to the bell tolling during the lecture.
Throughout the day, with a tranquil mind, I recall your lofty pursuits; In three lifetimes of practice, you have cultivated the Way amidst the pines.
Recalling Master Qingzhao at the Upper Hall of Nantag, I send these words:
Pine and bamboo stand dense as one path leads through; For six years, you have dwelt in seclusion within this lofty cloister.
Cool breezes shift across steep cliffs as autumn deepens, the moon; Cold light reflects off the Long River peaks after the snow.
While chanting, summer clouds thin out under the clear sky; When the lecture ends, the spring trees cast a dense green shade.
The exquisite scenery of the four seasons is truly worthy of love; I have often leaned on my staff alongside Master Zhi.
The pine in the courtyard has branches like those of the Immortals, its canopy spreading as if to surpass the clouds; planted alone in this secluded garden, it has passed through many springs.
Its flowering and falling have never been the same as those of common trees; in its solitary integrity, it has long accompanied me, the idle man.
The wind arises in the still night with a robust, cold sound; After the snow has cleared, the distant peaks reveal fresh, verdant hues.
This serene atmosphere is most suited for rising from meditative concentration; Sitting in contemplation or walking in circumambulation, one remains far removed from the dust of the world.
—Sent to Master Xizhao.
Beyond the dust, the meditation hall is secluded and vast; Your lofty spirit forever diverges from the common stream.
Through many bouts of bitter chanting, your hair has turned white; Sitting in silence through the night, you remember the green mountain mists.
The wind carries the fragrance of lotuses to the quiet couch; The rain nourishes the moss, staining the idle gate.
How many times have I been obstructed by the heavens while seeking you? In vain I lean against this perilous tower, facing the setting sun.
