Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
Self-Admonition:
Words for the Mind, Beyond the External World. Listen to my instruction: Do not practice deceit and hypocrisy; Do not turn your back on benevolence and righteousness.
If you act with deceit and falsehood, you will ultimately face disaster; if you practice benevolence and righteousness, you will ultimately meet with fortune.
Do not peddle your reputation, nor indulge in eccentricity according to your whims; do not align yourself with power, nor resort to flattery to control others.
Do not boast of your own abilities, nor conceal the virtues of others; do not rejoice when praised, nor be angry when disparaged.
Do not hesitate to correct your errors; devote yourself solely to the Way. Do not fear death, nor crave life.
Delight in goodness and cultivate the mind. When the time comes, act. O body, O body!
I make this covenant with you. The Seven Admonitions (with Preface)
Zhongyongzi, harboring a deep sense of gratitude and inspiration, composed these Seven Admonitions so that one’s speech,
conduct, thoughts, steps, grasp, vision, and hearing shall never lose their rectitude.
Although they are called self-reproaches, can they be anything other than intended as instruction for the world?
Admonition for the Mouth: Let not the mouth speak; let not the mouth remain silent. If speech may be beneficial, ten thousand people will take it as a model;
if speech may be harmful, one brings slander upon oneself and harms oneself. When it is for the sake of benefit, do not speak; when it is for the sake of benefit, do not remain silent.
Be free from delusion in speech;
as a self-admonition for the body, maintain your outward demeanor and be circumspect in your conduct.
Do not envy the warmth of fox-fur robes; do not feel shame for the poverty of worn-out hempen cloth.
Do not flatter or fawn to be compliant; do not be so arrogant as to pretend to virtue like the "Elephant of Respect.
One may sacrifice life to achieve benevolence, but never follow what is contrary to righteousness.
O body, O body! The Way resides within your heart;
your nature is good, having been received from the mandate of Heaven. Yet when the seven emotions become entangled and disordered, you consequently lose that correctness.
If one brings their emotions back to their true nature, the Way of the Sages will become clear;

there will be no changing in response to external objects, nor any tilting according to shifting circumstances. I have composed this admonition so that the mind may take it as its standard—this is sufficient for self-exhortation.
Do not tread upon spring ice; do not step through the gates of power. Spring ice is easily broken through; the gates of power are easily where one loses one’s footing.
Be cautious! Do not lose this body of mine. This is the Hand Admonition.
Do not follow the impropriety of Cao Mo, who seized a blade to hold King Huan captive;
rather, learn from Zhu Yun’s righteous remonstrance, which broke the palace railings to manifest heroism.
Embrace righteousness and do not fear failure; drive out the depraved with urgency and diligence; guard yourself with constant vigilance day by day.
An admonition for the eyes: Do not gaze at even the finest hair, lest you damage your pupils; do not look upon the five colors, lest you lose your clarity.
You should observe whether the Way is deviant or correct; you should examine whether affairs are empty or full.
O Eyes, guard this: do not betray my covenant.
O Ears, when hearing the Right Path, you should be keen of hearing; when hearing perverse doctrines, you should be deaf.
"Already clear-sighted, already deaf—this is the time for achievement. O ears, strive!
Leaving this and approaching that, I inscribe this upon the two temples of Fantian and Shengguo, while simultaneously addressing the two venerable monks, Zhao and Wu.
(With Preface) The two monasteries of Fantian and Shengguo face one another; their lofty carriages and empty pavilions fully capture the finest views of the rivers and mountains.
Because I recited the lines of Xie Xuancheng, "I recognize the returning boat at the edge of heaven, and distinguish the river trees amidst the clouds," which closely resembled that scene,
I have composed ten stanzas using those phrases as rhymes to send to the two Bodhisattvas, Master Zhao of Fantian and Master Wugu of Shengguo.
Although they are insufficient to fully develop the spirit of the *Sao* or the elegance of refined poetry, they may perhaps express my feelings of mutual longing.
The color of the Yangtze stretches into the infinite distance, Vastly merging with the far-off heavens. Returning sails depart with the setting sun; Flying birds sink into the cold mist.
These secluded vistas are unlike any other to behold; From these reflections, this composition was formed.
Towers and pavilions rise loftily, Staggering toward the very limits of the clouds. Through the high windows, the colors of dawn appear first.

The lingering evening glow is beautiful; In the vast silence, all movement has ceased. With a mind merged in darkness, far removed from the dusty world, I am cold and solitary, difficult to find a companion.
This profound delight I alone recognize; My lofty sentiments thin the clouds and mists, And my pure discourse polishes metal and stone.
I do not study like those worldly men Who rush for fame and compete in ornate embellishment.
Nature is tranquil as a hundred anxieties are forgotten; In the leisurely carriage, the myriad phenomena return.
The empty river answers the night bell; Upon the high ridge, the lingering glow remains. On the secluded steps, the traces of dust are severed.
The solitary cloud lingers of its own accord. One regards evil as if touching boiling water; Encountering things, one is like an empty boat. Others may not know me.
This path was originally what I sought; Sitting alone, I often cherished it in my heart. The slanting sun shines upon the perilous tower beside the towering high mountain;
A single cloud arises from touching the rocks, Anticipating wind and rain, it does not join the ranks of dust and soil.
Vastly it wanders through the Great Void; Facing this, how many times have I thought of you?
With lofty traces, whom will you seek as kin? You dwell in seclusion amidst the white clouds. On the quiet steps, azure moss sprouts; From the ancient trees, a pure breeze arises.
At times, you take up the scriptures of Western India To expound their meaning and instruct the ignorant.
The tranquil and the restless each have their own preferences; How could one distinguish right from wrong? Fame and profit are like my enemies.
If Yun and Quan would but encourage one another, In the profound silence of the deep forest, The fragrant orchids may be plucked at will.
A multitude of peaks rise in perilous azure; Their reflections sink into the empty river. Pure scenery arises in the evening clarity;
Cold colors are contained within the vacant window. Leisurely strolling, I indulge in recitation and appreciation, Which can cause my mind to find its peace.
The sun shines upon my study by the sea, The river wind stirs the trees in the courtyard. Such scenes delight the leisurely mind;
who can recognize this lofty interest? Ascending the tower, I gaze alone toward the south, Where the distant mists and fogs hang over the lake.
*Poems on Miscellaneous Feelings West of the Lake* (with preface)
The *Poems on Miscellaneous Feelings from the West of the Lake* were composed by Zhongyongzi while dwelling in the seclusion of Gushan to the west of West Lake;

they were written out of sorrow over the superficiality and insincerity of contemporary customs. Although these are mountain songs and rustic chants, their praise of the good and censure of the evil accord with the intent of the "men of the wind" (the poets of the *Shi jing*).
Because their themes and sentiments vary, they are called "Miscellaneous Feelings," comprising twenty chapters in total.
The lake waves are cool and serene, utterly free from even a speck of dust; Cloud-capped mountains fill the eyes as neighbors on every side.
A single path deep with grass where no person reaches— On a bamboo bed with a rush fan, I nurture my true nature.
I gaze at the clouds in stillness, releasing Zhi Gong’s crane; Beside the water, I watch idly as Huizi’s fish leap.
In the silence beneath the window, what else is there? Scrolls of the Indian scriptures and the books of Confucius;
In the quiet courtyard, a wutong tree stands by the side. Upon it, fresh cicadas chirp through the evening breeze;
Their clear, lingering tones are truly worth listening to, Until they are needlessly startled and broken by a child.
Having moved several bamboos from the misty creek, I planted them in my quiet courtyard; their cool green shade is cold.
Their hollow hearts and lofty nodes are truly worthy of love, for they do not permit ordinary people to enter and gaze upon them even for a moment.
The phoenix is a rare omen of the age, its fame passed down through generations; when it appears in the villages and hamlets, all the people are filled with wonder.
Calling it a strange bird, one should shoot it dead; Only then does one know that vulgar customs value empty fame.
The straight tree is broken by the wind, the autumn orchid withers; Observing idly at the edge of the courtyard, one cannot help but sigh deeply.
Qu Yuan drowned in the waters, Wu Yuan died; Solitary purity has always made independence difficult.
The Great Master (Confucius) established his words to honor ritual and music; the Benevolent One (the Buddha) bestowed his teachings to encourage compassion.
Alas for those who busily toil upon the worldly path—cunning, sycophantic, greedy, and cruel—they know nothing and reflect on nothing.
The great affliction of this transient life is that they spend their days seeking through flattery, rushing about in the red dust.
One morning death arrives and one’s name perishes with it; The gold filling the house belongs to others.
A fierce tiger gnashes its teeth, crouching in the shade of the forest; Deep and dark, the single path is shrouded in evening smoke.
Travelling gentleman, do not harbor doubt or fear; This creature has always had the heart of a beast.
Heedfulness, frugality, and yielding are the Way of the Ages of Tang and Yu; Willful greed and seeking are the lot of Jie and Zhi.
Sitting idly, I contemplate beneath my thatched cottage: Deep at night, the autumn moon shines upon the calm lake.
The orchid in the deep forest still possesses its own fragrance; How could it be hindered by wind and rain, or cease its song at cockcrow?
From of old, the gentleman must plan for the Way, Not weighing his actions by the whims of the times.
This white dog, roaming at night as if possessed of feeling, Watches for bandits until the break of dawn.
Lately, its defense has been of no avail; It does not bark at human forms, but only at the sound of voices.
The Way and Virtue of Boyang and the Mind of Śākyamuni, The writings of Confucius—all may be sought therein.
Yet they care not for full bellies or warm clothes, Pitifully letting the light of their years pass away in ease.
When the snow melts, the mountain courtyard is a fit place to climb; The king’s trees and jade towers reflect upon the azure stream.
At twilight, one is suddenly startled to see all consumed by the flames; The affairs of a hundred years of wealth and status end in the same way.
The moon shines upon the empty pavilion, waning and waxing; The trends of fortune and misfortune incline toward one another.
One must know that human affairs follow the Way of Heaven; Honor and disgrace have always been causes for alarm.
Sitting idly in my thatched hall, I contemplate the common people: Most prize the empty and the vain, while few honor the true.
When ritual and courtesy are not cultivated, it is difficult to attain blessings; They know only to burn paper to sacrifice to licentious spirits.
The doctrines of the Yin-Yang masters delude the common folk, And thus the Way of Filial Piety loses its proper order.
Who would be willing to dwell in a hut by a grave for three years? They compete in discussing the geomantic power of mountain ridges to increase human fortune;
The saying that "the virtuous prosper and the wicked suffer" is credible, And the words that "good and ill fortune depend on oneself" can be cited.
Those who violate benevolence and betray righteousness have no shame; They care only to record the auspicious dates and hours when departing this life.
Silently reflecting on the vast and boundless affairs of the mundane world, I take up my staff and wander forth from the thatched hall to chant in leisure.
If one wishes to understand the nature of this floating life, why seek it far away? The *bājiǎo* plant has already been struck by frost last night.
A new spring has been hewn at the head of the ancient stone steps; The flavor of the brewed tea flows with an extraordinary excellence.
Last night, in leisure, I gazed upon the clear and luminous nature; In the heavens, there are no clouds, and the moon is at its peak in autumn.
*The Collection of Leisurely Dwelling*, Volume 42 *The Collection of Leisurely Dwelling*, Volume 43
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty, sent to Master Xūjǐ of Huátíng:
I am too lazy to respond to the letters of high officials; My lofty slumber and rustic interests are deep. In the empty hall, the night moon opens its light.
Passing autumn chimes on a solitary pillow, I compose this new work by the water. Gazing at the clouds, I recall the old peaks;
Still harboring illness within the woods, When shall we finally meet?
Expressing my thoughts in a traveler’s inn.
In this inn, acquaintances are few; I chant alone, separated from worldly ways. The traveler’s heart stirs at the night rain; my dreams of home enter the autumn clouds.
On the cold steps, fireflies pass by frequently; in the secluded window, wild geese are suddenly heard.
The springs and rocks of the western peaks remain there; I shall surely depart to bid farewell to the multitude.
Appointed as Governor of Qiantang by Imperial Decree, you have traveled far to the commandery of Jiang;
Your noble rank stands among the Seven Elders, while your ancient style preserves the pure customs of old.
In these tranquil times, your pen for remonstrance rests at ease; The tower is high where the evening bugles resound, and the hall is cool, locked away from the autumn mountains.
In this sagely age, there is hope for the adjustment of the sacrificial cauldron; The imperial carriage shall soon return by imperial decree.

I present these words to the Master of Ability, who dwells in high repose upon the lakes and mountains; Let the workings of the mundane world take their myriad turns— The pavilion for chanting amidst the clouds remains serene.
The water-crossing bell tolls coldly as I lecture; The secluded door remains closed during the flowering season.

New books are carved in the snow at night (the Master once composed one hundred scrolls of the *Dianlei*). Yet those who pursue worldly competition Must surely laugh at me for hiding among the forests and peaks.
The rākṣasa rises from the heart of the river; its tides at dawn and dusk never err. Its cold sounds clamor at the distant marshes;
its autumnal force sweeps across the level sands. Standing and gazing, one’s heart is filled with peril;
startled birds fly off in slanting shadows. How can one ask about the source? All the more so, the vast blue sea has no shore.
Seeing off Master Yin as he returns to Daochang Mountain:
Step by step he carries his staff, parting from me; As we reach the secluded scenery, the mountain divides.
Remnants of snow remain through the spring; Sparse bells are heard crossing the water. The pines are deep, giving rise to evening breezes; The pool is still, reflecting idle clouds.
The lecture hall atop the cliff opens once more; Incense smoke drifts in as night falls.
Having stayed one night in this mountain monastery, a realm free from dust, We remain together for a long while in quiet conversation, As the sounds of autumn return to the ancient trees.
The moonlight fills the empty corridors; Mist and mists invade my robes with dampness. The mountain stream rinses my teeth with coolness;
I vow that one day I shall gather my jar and staff To come here and close myself within this quiet chamber.
—Presented to Master Jian.
Tranquil, beyond the ways of men, I have no further pursuit of the myriad affairs of the world. In the flower garden, the spring deepens for discourse;

Upon the clouded mountains, the summer fills for wandering. Drawing water from the mossy well at dawn, Striking the sounding-block by the bamboo window in autumn— There lies another profound commitment:
With incense and lamps, I grow old on Mount Wozhou.
Moss and secluded crags abound in division; The deep azure is called "Quiet Recitation. On the empty steps, rain has spread everywhere;
Across the steep cliffs, autumn deepens. Cold colors divide the tracks of birds; Subtle traces enter the shade of trees.
The simple gate remains closed throughout the year, And chariots and horses never intrude upon it.
I recall parting by the river in years past with the teacher from the south of Chu; His lofty traces are now remote and difficult to find, For those who drift in this world rarely behold him.
The green mountains hide deeper still; I exhaust my poetic craft to capture the realm of forms. In embodying the Way, I have reached the ultimate state of no-mind;
I feel ashamed that I have failed the promise to sleep amidst the clouds. On the western peak, the evening sun casts its shadow;
From the riverside pavilion, I gaze at the twilight.
Gazing idly from the riverside pavilion, the autumnal scenery is truly boundless: Birds vanish beyond the cold clouds; sails return amidst the evening gloom.
Pale mist rises at the distant shore; withered leaves fall in the cool breeze.
Along the winding path, the sound of fishermen’s songs is heard; The dwellings of men lie hidden behind a thicket of reeds.
Ascending the thousand-fathom peaks of Wulin, cold emeralds are piled high;
At the summit, all traces of the mundane are severed. When the rain clears, one hears the pure whistling of the wind;
As the clouds part, other peaks come into view. Falling water sprays against the strange rocks; Startled birds fly into the deep pines.
Having finished my verse, I lean upon the railing for a long while; from the distant heavens, the evening bell arises.
I miss Master Ziren;
his traces in the world are vast and far. Beyond meditation, idle thoughts stir; after the people of the water-town have returned home, silence reigns.
When the moon is white in the autumn window, Crickets chirp within the ruined walls; A solitary bird perches on a cold branch.
Sitting alone, who can ask of me? I hum a faint chant while plucking out my ailing beard—thus I record my thoughts.
With a single staff, I wander west and east; Who can share this solitary heart? As I chant, my beard secretly turns white;
Human affairs quickly turn to emptiness. I gaze idly at the moon from the autumn pavilion; Lying by the cold window, I listen for the wild geese.
Taking this sense of stillness and solitude, I entrust it to the strings of the zither in the deep night.
Taking refuge with Master Bai deep within the secluded, empty forest, Pure and serene, he is utterly free from external entanglements. Rain seals the mountain peaks upon his window;
moss filters the autumn spring at his well. The gate is still as sandbirds arrive; the courtyard is quiet as evening cicadas chirp.
Leaning on the railing, I recall you alone; The setting sun sinks low beneath the distant sky.
Presented to the Recluse Hao:
Your homeland lies far from the Yi River; You dwell deep before the emerald peaks. In your poetic recitations, you have only cranes for company.
In the lofty pursuit there are no other immortals; On Mount Yue, I truly respond to idleness and sloth. The cinnabar scriptures are kept secret and not transmitted;
With a staff of aged wood, you visit me from time to time. All day long we discourse on Southern Chan while wandering through Lingyin Mountain.
Steep cliffs reach to the ends of night; Sacred traces one never tires of seeking. In quiet reflection, I recall my dreams of returning to seclusion—how could I have had no heart for it?
The azure peaks and mists are magnificent; The secluded crags and caverns are deep. How can I bear to think of Huìlǐ?
As the setting sun fades, the white monkeys cry out.
Lawyer Xie Zewu kindly bestowed upon me this bamboo staff, harvested from the side of a secluded crag.
A high monk suddenly saw it and left it behind; I gaze at the clouds leaning against it all day long, and grasp the snow-white cane for many hours.
Its joints are cold where tiny insects have subtly eaten away; Its roots are idle, where dark moss grows in secret.
The old mountain springs and rocks remain; returning home, I rely on their support.
Written while dwelling in leisure at Fantian Temple:
Pine and cypress surround my quiet chamber; My traces are far removed from the throngs of men. Bereft by illness, my hair has turned white.
Gazing at the mountains, I envy the white clouds; The traces of moss grow longer after the rain. The sound of cicadas is heard carried on the wind;
Sitting alone with no guests arriving, The sun has already faded in the western chamber.
The well for refining elixirs— The well for refining elixirs.
The traces of the departed immortal remain, Cool and clear beside the verdant peaks. Cool radiance reflects in the azure tiles, While hidden veins release the cold spring.
The moon shines upon the shallow crystal pitcher; Autumn clarifies the ancient mirror’s full orb.
The abode of the feathered immortals is near; In leisure, one draws water to irrigate the fields of *lingzhi* fungi.
The Cold Spring Pavilion stands solitary and secluded, devoid of any vulgar air; its pure scenery washes away all vexation.

The steps press upon the shallow, cold stream, while the eaves divide the deep accumulation of emerald green. Late-blooming flowers idly reflect their shadows, and ancient trees hang down their cool shade.
Leaning on the railing, I cannot depart; In this limpid clarity, I give rise to a quiet chant.
Presented to the monks who have searched everywhere for the patriarchs: Wandering at ease, my hair is not yet white, Yet my old chamber remains locked away beyond the seas.

A solitary figure dwelling at the ends of the earth, Chiseling verses by the autumn window moon; Observing emptiness amidst the evening flowers on the steps— At such times, one speaks of lofty interests.
In the end, I shall depart to hide among the mists and clouds.
*Lake Dwelling: Rising from Illness on an Autumn Day (Six Rhymes)*
Old acquaintances rarely visit; The desolate, ruined room lies in silence. The cauldron is deep with the remains of medicinal herbs;
The jaw is gaunt and the white beard grows long. Dust specks cling to the book-cases; Moss stains the stone bench.
In the eaves, silent insects weave their webs; On the cold steps, chrysanthemums hold their fragrance. In stillness, I reflect with pity upon this deep night.
Pure and emaciated, fearing the evening chill, I have not yet returned to the cloud peaks. Sitting idly, I chant the "Canglang" verses;
This is a gift to Master Yizhong.
Serene and aloof, you turn your back on worldly trends; Your spirit is carefree, beyond the dust of the world. In silent verse, you wait for the frost-moon to end.
In my dreams of returning home, the sea clouds are deep; The chamber is cold, and moss grows upon the couch. The window is still, birds watch from afar;
In this secluded dwelling, we share a common delight. Moved by inspiration, I have come to seek you out several times.
—Sent to Elder Yuan.
In tranquil contemplation, I dwell in a secluded realm; Leisurely, I take water and stone as my neighbors. The robe of faith transmits the legacy of past patriarchs;
Zen words are shown to those who come after. In the evening cottage, the tea smoke is fine; In the sunny pavilion, the mountain greens are uniform.
With mutual longing, I gaze alone toward the south; The forest trees have already passed through spring once more.
Staying overnight at a mountain temple with a friend, we both relied upon this pure environment for our lodging; we conversed on the Way and further discussed the treatises.

The moon in the deep autumn pool is clearly seen, and the mountain bell is heard after midnight. The chirping of insects lingers upon the ancient stone steps, and the glow of fireflies vanishes into the lingering clouds.
Having gathered, we agreed to dwell here long; Incense is burned beneath the trees at dawn.
The Master’s Way is supreme and worldly mechanisms have ceased; After the lecture, the forest leaves wither. His pure fame remains high as he reclines in seclusion.
With black hair, I toil in bitter verse; the courtyard is still and autumn clouds are pale. The window is quiet, the night moon solitary;
occasionally hearing sounds that suit my secluded interest, I ascend the pavilion to gaze upon the level lake, sending this in remembrance to Master Decong.
In the ancient monastery beneath Mount Xi, I dwell in seclusion, weary of visitors seeking me out. Worldly thoughts have vanished beyond meditation;
poetic inspiration grows deeper with the onset of illness. The water in my jar freezes into ice-cold slush; the pine wind carries the evening bell’s fading resonance.
If you should ever wish to summon me from these recluses’ lives, let the incense and lamps continue the tradition of Donglin.
The Zen gate of Shangfang Monastery opens at the mountain’s summit; The color of the sea reflects the tiered peaks. The shadow of the temple spire sinks into the vast void;
The sound of the bell drifts across the boundless expanse. Wild moss makes the secluded path slippery; Winter snow brings cold to the evening window.
Having finished my verse, I am too weary to turn my head; Slowly and alone, I lean against the balustrade.
Ascending the tower, I long for Zunyì;
The leisurely scenery stretches on infinitely. Leaning against the balustrade, what do I contemplate? Birds fly away toward the distant mountains.
Autumn colors fill the vast blue waves; Letters have been cut off for years. New sorrows multiply as evening falls;
I gaze longingly while chanting alone. I have neglected our old pact by the misty vines.
*The Collection of Writings from My Leisure Dwelling*, Volume Forty-Three.
*Xiánjū biān* (Collection from Secluded Dwelling), Volume 44.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
A Poetic Gift to the Monk Bǎoxiān.
At the railing for chanting, cold waters ripple; On the level lake, the misty scenery is tranquil.
No one recognizes this lofty interest as he faces the empty mountains all day long. In the evening trees, birds warble as they peck at grain; Through the bright window, the night moon returns.
All these new compositions are elegant and correct, Requiring no editing by Confucius himself.

A Poem Sent to the Elder Xingguang at Shicheng: Secluded in retreat, worldly thoughts have ceased; The mountain pavilion leans against cypress and pine. In meditation, the flow of poetic inspiration is exhausted;
After his illness, the frost-white beard has grown thick. The stream is tranquil, reflecting the clear night moon; The mountains are still, answering the autumn bell.
In solitude, I cherish lofty aspirations; As the setting sun fades, I lean alone on my staff.
Dear nephew Ren, the western wind stirs the trees in the courtyard; In the quiet pavilion, fallen leaves thicken; I awaken from a dream as the frosty moon rises at dawn.
Faith cuts through the autumnal sea and mountains; the nature of the Way returns to thoughtlessness. Alone I chant, my sorrows already severed, as I make an appointment beneath the sparse woods.
On the misty waters and winding paths, the mountain journey stretches on and on.
Cane in hand, I take advantage of my leisure; The mountains are deep and human tracks are rare. A broken bridge bears the weight of last night’s rain;
Tall trees catch the fading glow of the sun. In the stillness of the crags, clouds rise alone; In the emptiness of the pool, birds fly solitary.
Upon the front peak lies a hermitage; In poetic appreciation, I forget to return home.
Feeling moved by events on an autumn day, everything before my eyes is familiar; yet when we discuss the mind, our perspectives naturally differ.
The quiet gate is locked against the evening light, withered leaves fall in the western wind. All past affairs have become entirely a dream; this floating life gradually reveals its emptiness.
Resting my chin, I alone remained speechless; The four walls echoed with the sound of autumn insects.
Gazing at the lake at dusk, I sent this to a friend from whom I have received no news from afar;
Longing grows intense as I face the scene before me; A chilling wind blows down the fallen leaves.
The setting sun rests on distant peaks, Illuminating the fishing villages’ fires upon the water; Fading incense smoke rises from the wild temple’s bell.
To whom can these secluded thoughts be told? Standing still, leaning my staff, I send this to Master Wencong.
Tranquil and aloof, worldly cares are severed; Beyond meditation, one finds the bitterness of poetic rhapsody. In nature, awakening, he dwells secluded amidst the clouds;
For his fame, he turns his back on the mundane world. Mist and smoke steam the paper curtains; Frosty hair makes the bronze blade stiff.
Having stayed several nights in an autumn river temple, He chants idly while listening to the night tides.
Seeing off a Monk Returning to Ráoyáng:
Holding hands at parting as the evening falls at the pavilion, The thoughts of returning home are beyond restraint. One’s native land lies a thousand li away;
For ten years, one has harbored the heart of a traveler. The sail’s shadow rests upon the cold, silent river; The cries of monkeys echo through the deep, snowy peaks.
The springs and rocks of Raoyang remain; when I withdraw from my lectures, I can but sigh.
Master Guangjun, a monk from the North, has passed away; his lofty traces are now difficult to find. Only the rooms of his former country remain empty.
The grass by the new grave is already deep; Clouds and springs have broken our old appointment. Wind and moon, the discourse on the mind has ceased;
In silent sitting, I gaze at the remaining verses as the moon sinks behind the western window.
*In the same rhyme, I respond to my neighbor-monk, Master Zhòu.*
Dwelling in seclusion, we are close to one another; Facing the stream, the wild colors are divided. In the deep autumn, the mountains are seen together;
At the clear night, the sounding of the *ghaṇṭā* is heard in unison. The still couch shifts with the bright moon; The sparse curtain rolls back the evening clouds.
There is a distinct interest in our mutual companionship; In this state of quietude, we share the same company.
Parting from Zhao Pu during my travels, I mount my horse as I am about to set out upon the road; The Milky Way and the light of dawn divide the sky. A dying lamp illuminates our seats of parting;
arriving geese moan through the cold clouds. The hometown is far away and letters are hard to reach; My poetic frenzy grows wild and wine easily intoxicates me.
How lamentable are the arts of statecraft, Failing to bring a wise sovereign to power!
On a matter at hand while traveling, I send this to my friends:
Leaning on my pillow, sleep eludes me; Cold insects chirp against the dark walls, And the tall wutong trees are drenched by the night rain.
The heart of a traveler far from home is divided; It turns its back upon fleeting fame.
As years advance and white hair creeps in, I must finally follow the example of Zongbing To form a society at Donglin Temple.
Written in an autumn evening guesthouse, sent to a friend-monk on my native mountain.
Leaning on my elbow-rest, I cannot sleep; who can console this desolate stillness? On the empty steps, crickets chirp; cold rain drips onto the banana leaves.
In silence, the lamp by the window grows dim; the heart’s longing for the sea temple is far away.
Only Master Huiyuan of the Śākya clan could invite me to join his Lotus Society.
Entrusted to the Great Master Zhengjue, who translates scriptures in the capital, my dreams of returning to the watery land have faded;
The imperial grace has deepened over these years. Sanskrit texts are rendered into the Song language, and the discourse on the Way is transformed into the Wu dialect.
In the quiet chamber, pure incense lingers; In the secluded courtyard, the ancient trees cast their shadows.
The former affairs of Yuhua remain; to whom may one entrust the search for such lofty traces?

Entrusting my feelings to the Dharma Master Ruṇ, the trees in the courtyard gather the colors of autumn. Lingering, I cease my bitter chanting in this desolate place; the letters from Jiang have been cut off.
Deep in a dream of solitude amidst the rain, Water birds idly peep into the inkstone; The window lamp casts a cold light upon the zither— Who knows this inspiration of the moment?
Gray hairs have already crept in unnoticed.
Presented to Master Yuanjing, Patriarch of the White Lotus Society.
The guests at the shrine are all high ministers and officials, Yet my thatched hall lies amidst clouds and trees. The scenery shares the splendor of Mount Lu;
the people here possess the leisure of Master Huiyuan. At night, meditation opens the bright moon; in autumn, chanting faces the evening mountains.
Only Xie Kangle could have occasionally knocked upon the pine gate.

Expressing My Feelings at Late Spring, Sent to the Venerable Master Cóng In the evening trees, returning birds flutter in confusion; The ancient cloister is desolate and serene. Pure discourse is for the distant gentleman;
My secluded interest is set upon the strings and bamboo. My short hair has become entirely white as snow; Fading flowers fall halfway with the wind.
In the end, I hope to join true companions And retire among the drifting clouds.
An Inscription on Stone-Nan Flowers at Yinsiyuan:
The warm harmony nourishes all trees, Yet these alone differ from the common flowers; They reflect upon the grass, startling the remnants of the scorched earth.
Gazing out the window, I recognize the dawn’s rosy clouds; Though their color has faded due to the rain, Their form does not lean with the wind.
Fortunate indeed is the power of cultivation, As lush branches vie with the sun’s brilliance.
—Sent to Master Jingwu.
The waves of the level lake stretch far and wide, Its traces are distant and difficult to find. Within the city one never arrives; Deep behind closed doors at the edge of the clouds.
A cold lamp illuminates the ancient image; An evening chime emerges from the sparse forest.
In solitude, I cherish this lofty interest; On the western veranda, the sun sinks quickly.
An Inscription for Mr. Wen’s Forest Pavilion:
Before the eaves of the small mountain, the forms are strange and perilous; Within a few paces, one perceives pure seclusion. When birds descend, one suspects Mount Lingjiu;
When monks pass by, one mistakes them for those of Wozhou. The moonlight on the precarious, open balustrade wards off the cold; It steals the autumn from the distant peaks.
Only now do I believe that within the dust of the mundane world, the noble families possess such superior excursions.
Staying overnight in the room of the Venerable Zhongxi:
I happened to follow the appointment with Zhi Dun to stay the night in a quiet chamber deep in the evening; the windows are still, and the lamp leaves behind its embers.
The courtyard is cold, the trees are covered in frost; The Zen mind is discussed with clarity, While worldly affairs are realized as vast and boundless.
Speaking again of departing for Tiantai, He sweeps the stone bed within the forest grove.
—Inscribed at the Forest Pavilion of Master Cong.
On all four sides, far from the traces of the dust; Passing by in song, one’s rustic sentiments are praised. The steps are quiet as autumn fruits fall; the pool is cold as the moonlight arises.
Leaning against the bamboo, the sound of cicadas ceases; Opening the zither, the crane’s dream is startled.
Yet there is still an appointment for when you return; Do not yet grow weary of our meeting.
The secluded study of the Venerable Shu Jiu within the city is surrounded by cypress and bamboo along its poetic paths;
The windows and balconies are utterly free from dust. A pure breeze arises in the late night, and the profound scenery pervades all neighboring quarters.
The chime of the *ghaṇṭā* cuts short the dreams of nesting birds, And the lingering incense remains upon the body as he emerges from meditative absorption.
Within the city there is lofty aspiration; Why envy those who linger by the river?
Past events upon the waters cannot be broached; The long river stretches empty and vast, And the solitary city is sealed by the setting sun.
Wild mounds accumulate cold mist; Sands rise high, making the central islets broad. The tide erodes the ancient path, leaving it crooked.
Do not doubt the shifting of hills and valleys— what you see before your eyes is already transformed into mulberry fields.
—Composed by Master Huaibao Xian.
Where has your lofty trace gone? My longing for you—when will it cease? I sigh in bitter verse as I face the moon alone;
closing my door, I further forbid the autumn from entering. The cold insects on the cracks of the steps are piercing;
the fallen leaves beneath the branches are thick. News and letters are faint and hard to send; the heavens are vast and the waters flow on endlessly.
Presented to Great Master Xuānmì on His Refusal to Leave the Monastery and Cease Receiving Visits:
Incense and lamps attend to true cultivation; The ancient monastery is sealed with verdant moss.
Other mountains are empty of former excursions; The moon rises over the meditation hall at dawn, And the bamboo window opens to the autumn air.
Having already found repose in secluded delights, why need one purchase Mount Wozhou?
Since my nephew departed for the forest from within my breast, A year has suddenly passed; the old appointment remains, though the mountain is empty.
As we think of one another, months have passed since the moon was full; The bell of the prefectural temple cuts short my dreams at night. The trees along the river sink into evening smoke;
to whom can I entrust a letter? Moreover, the waves and tides stretch out boundlessly, as I lodge here at Daochang Mountain Temple.
At the summit, the autumn air is clear; leaning against the perilous railing at the treetops, I look up and see the Milky Way near, while gazing down, the myriad peaks appear small.
In the empty pond, the night moon rises; the wind-whipped branches call out to the nesting birds.
Sitting in contemplation, I cannot fall asleep; the sparse temple bells begin to toll as dawn approaches.
Seeing off Master Yuzhen as he returns to Mount Siming;
After lingering by the river, we part. A single staff rests upon a small boat; It sails far across the fading light, pointing toward the old haunts among a thousand peaks.
Sparse bells sink into the misty gloom; The myriad trees shed their leaves in the high autumn.
Do not fail the promise made when we met; the mind of meditation is fundamentally free.
In autumn evening, I send this to a fellow monk:
you who lie high amidst the white clouds, I am detained by lingering illness and cannot go to seek you out; the letter has been cut off as the blue waters stretch wide.
The chamber door is shut amidst the depths of the emerald peaks; Cold insects hide within the ruined walls. Dewdrops fall from the courtyard trees after the lingering rain;
Morning and evening, we share idle conversation, As a solitary lamp illuminates this bitter verse.

Palace of Chén.
The dragon coiled and the tiger crouched—its traces are still worth seeking; The royal aura has vanished, truly a calamity for those who indulge in excess.
Where now are the Jieqi and Linchun towers? Amidst the deepening evening mists, a few birds cry out.
On this spring day, I part from my companions.
Roads diverge to the south and north, to the east and west; I stand long and linger, grieving our parting.
How can I bear to pluck willows by the farewell pavilion? Evening flowers fall, and the cuckoo cries.
Sent on a summer day from the lake to the Elder Taibai.
The wind shakes the lotus, its fragrance entering the seat; Sitting idly by the water pavilion, how long is this delight!
This scene of longing is not of the human world; On the opposite bank, returning birds clamor in the evening cool—West Lake.
The clear moonlight carries its radiance, contained within the bamboo door; The cold, translucent autumn colors shine upon the monk’s robe.
How much does this surging flow benefit all things? Gazing to the horizon at the vast, cold waves, I bid farewell to the departing meditator as the sun sets.
The Patriarch’s intent was once clear: all things are at ease. Who says that beyond the world is different from the human realm?
Rolling up my robes by the river, we part as autumn arrives; Everywhere is the mind of meditation, mountain after mountain—this is the ancient spirit.
Climbing the mountain to gather firewood, the branch suddenly snapped; drawing water from the well, the rope was severed.
With no news arriving, there is nowhere to speak of it; the north wind blows steadily as snow fills the heavens.

Cold light shines upon the emerald pool, its stillness boundless; Tranquil against the azure sky, its reflection divides even more clearly. In its unfolding and rolling up, it shall ultimately become rain for the fields; It does not seek to delude the Lord of Chu at the Terrace of Yang. Three Poems on Moss Coins: [Poem 1] The moss coins lie scattered upon the ancient stones, A silent witness to the passage of time. Though they have seen countless autumns and springs, They remain unmoved by the shifting tides of fortune.

[Poem 2] Round like ancient currency, their form is unchanging; Amidst the weeds, they bear the marks of antiquity. To seek wealth from these humble things is folly; Better to let them rest in the shade of the cliff. [Poem 3] I pluck the moss coins from the mossy ground, Their surfaces worn smooth by the passing years. Yet they possess no power to buy fame or status; They are but remnants of a world long gone.
Yifú’s silence does not place him among your kind; Lǔ Bāo composed his treatise by mere coincidence of name.
Autumn has come, filling the empty and leisurely space to its full; It requires no skilled artisan to forge it into being.
Seeking much does not necessarily increase greed and rivalry; hoarding wealth serves only to invite solitude.
Beside the old dwellings of Yanzi and Qianlou, scattered across the level ground, we wander in carefree ease. (2)
The furnace and forge should rely only on humble lanes; Prosperity and abundance do not belong to the wealthy houses.
When the evening rain has ceased outside the thatched hall, They scatter across the quiet courtyard, purchasing fallen blossoms.
(Verse Three)
Three Poems Written for Myself In this old house, the moss grows wild as my recent illness has finally abated; The woods of the village ahead seem to have felt autumn arrive first.
At dusk by the wild pond, I stand leaning on my staff; The clouds have no fixed resting place, and the waters flow on of their own accord.
When the lectures conclude, he often practices his art of bitter verse; Already his heart has no desire for worldly fame or profit.
By the waterside he enjoys a scene of pure leisure: The rain has cleared, the distant peaks loom, and the night moon is deep.
In his second decade, he was still four years short of reaching the age of non-delusion; with lofty sentiments for the Way, he felt ashamed of those who came before him.
How much of the pure wind and bright moon does he know? He merely studies the art of planting white lotuses on Mount Lu.
Third:
Seeing off a Monk My free body is difficult for myriad conditions to bind; How could my monastic nature hinder me from learning from worldly people?
Drafting a Parting Gift for the East Gate: On the long embankment, the willows have not yet seen spring;
The bamboo from the courtyard has been moved away to plant here among the flowers. The entire garden is filled with cool green, free from any dust.
In the heat of summer, wandering at leisure, my weary mind is entirely relieved; Yet there remains the pure breeze borrowed from the four neighbors.
The rooster perches before the eaves beside the thorn bushes; In heralding the dawn through wind and rain, you have performed your service.
The parrot has no power to rely on its flattering tongue; In the nobleman’s gate, it is instead raised within a golden cage.
Sending a Monk to Jinling:
Carrying his solitary golden staff, he inquires of the journey ahead; The wild grasses grow lush, as the evening smoke settles over the plains.
Beside the Qinhuai River lie the ancient traces of the Six Dynasties; Listening to the sound of the water, one should feel the resonance of rise and fall.
Composed on the Road to Daochangshan:
Descending alone through the layered peaks, the scenery is autumnal; The clouds and trees linger as if wishing to detain me.
A solitary boat glides at dawn across the smooth waves, Turning once more its head toward the green mountains.
I take this to Xi River to bid farewell to Master Zeyu:
In the depths of the white clouds, your thatched cottage is tranquil; There you once accompanied Master Zhi as he returned at the close of day.
Alone I board a solitary boat, intending to sail west; leaning against the mast, I look back, seeing only green mountains.
I send this to Master Wuzhen at Jingci Temple, recalling how we spent a cool night lodging in the upper hall; In quiet verse and leisurely conversation, what long-lasting was our delight!
Since we parted, there has been no way to send word; my gaze is fixed on the distant heavens where a flight of wild geese passes.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the Venerable Master Fantian:
A few peaks of lingering snow face my secluded gate; the ways of the world are so vast and weary that they cannot be discussed.
In my quiet chamber, after a session of meditation, I suddenly remembered you; I scraped away the ashes and sat alone until dusk.
An Account of My Circumstances While Dwelling by the Stream, Sent to Dharma Master Fantian:
Pines and bamboos stand dense as I close my door all alone; In this world of dust, who else loves to forget artifice?
Moss covers the steps; no one comes to visit, Yet I am moved by the solitary birds returning night after night.
Four Poems on Occasion Sent to Master Baoyin from My Dwelling by the Wukang Brook:
I have come by chance to the brook to indulge in leisurely verse; The springs and rocks, hidden in their depths, stir my heart.
Do not hope to visit these secluded traces in years to come; White clouds and green peaks will be even harder to find.
In the first month, by the mountain beside the waters where monkeys cry, Lying down to listen, gazing while chanting, one should simply remain at ease.
The thatched gate remains unbarred, for no guests arrive; Yet spirits occasionally pass to and fro.
(2) Driven along the worldly path until one’s hair turns white— How can this compare to lying idle and renouncing all seeking?
Before the gate, the desolate mounds remain; the stele is broken and the pines withered, marking the graves of former marquises.
Beyond the three stages of dhyāna, I long for you as the snow clears; when will your letter finally reach this rustic door?
Leaning alone upon a precarious tower as the setting sun fades, I gaze to the horizon where the mountain light appears as but a few specks of green.
(IV) Three Poems Written Playfully While Residing at Maṇi Monastery.
Reclining idly by the water’s edge, all worldly ties are stilled; In speech one seeks flawlessness, and in conduct one cultivates virtue.
Letting one's thatched hut and humble gate endure poverty and hardship— To slay the dragon is ultimately far superior to slaying the ox.
The lake’s light, faint and subtle, reflects within the secluded chambers; Mossy hues, lingering and pervasive, fill the broken corridors.
In its solitude, it is like the Temple of Confucius— No vulgarities enter here as one burns incense. (II)
I petitioned for a site on the emerald slope west of Chuanhu Lake; The windows and eaves are elegant and refined, overlooking vast waves of mist and smoke.
After my lectures, I sit burning incense all day long; What can praise or blame, prosperity or decline, do to me? (3)
Recently, I selected a dwelling beneath Mount Gushan; my friend Yuan Min has sent me four quatrains in jest, to which I have responded by matching his rhyme.
Dwelling in poverty, I have already trodden the path of Qianlou; this solitary island is but a mere "Marnao Slope."
With parched grain and millet soup, he dwells in leisure and joy; No carriage or horse ever passes by his abode.
The secluded charm of this retreat differs from the human world; A wild boat returns to the green waves in autumn.
The setting sun and thin mists linger where I gaze; from amidst the staggered pavilions and towers, I recognize Mount Gu.
(II) Mist-wrapped waves and cloud-shrouded trees reflect upon the quiet gate; for one nursing illness in deep seclusion, this is most fitting.
He intended to ascend and seek the inner courtyard, yet remained for a long time among the springs and rocks.
In the Hall of Emptiness, he entered summer to lecture on the remaining scriptures; instead of the sound of the bell, the sound of the drum resounded.
In the forest depths, only you may inquire into the subtle wonders; Ji Yang’s ritual for ascending the hall was only recently perfected.
(Dong Chun, styled Ji Yang of the Later Han, would strike the drum three times whenever he ascended the lecture hall; I have recently emulated this practice. IV.
Zhi Dun released you from the courtyard—truly he had noble intent; Duke Wei’s pity for you was far too excessive.
Unfit for crowing at dawn or guarding against intruders, With frost-white feathers atop your head, you are simply meant to be admired.
Entrusted to the Venerable Shou Neng of Tiantai:
The forests and springs of the Terrace Peak surpass the Ten Islands; Forgetting artifice, you have gone away forever, free from sorrow.
Who can recognize your lofty inclination for the "Kao-pan" song? Where have your new compositions on "Summoning the Recluse" been left?
Deep in the night, I shall surely return under the moon atop Huading; For years, letters have been cut off during the autumn at Haimen.
Who knows that I am nursing illness here on West Lake? Gazing south toward the clouds and mountains, I long for a sublime excursion—sent to those I know.
Honor and disgrace do not concern his thoughts; his fame grows ever new each day. He pities only that the Way remains within him;
who would mind frequent demotions? His native land is cast beyond the heavens; his entire family dwells by the water's edge.
The hall is empty with few birds in their nests; the gate is cold with no visitors. Yet his upright spirit ultimately reaches the Dipper and the Northern Star.
A firm will would have wept for the Qilin; XIAOYAO held the succession lightly.

He mocked ANREN’s empty pursuit of favor and ever longed for the imperial court; Seeking the profound, he nurtured his spirit. Accompanying idleness, he first planted bamboo; as a former envoy, he buried his wheel.
The tongues of flatterers shall finally be severed; The grievances of the people shall surely be redressed.
In years to come, when the histories are compiled, who will be able to follow in this pure dust?
Upon the Stone Wall Mountain, the Venerable Shao gazes from the Pavilion of Observing the Wind;
Ten thousand mountains border the river, yet the Stone Wall alone is serene and secluded. Within it dwells one who has forgotten all artifice.
Transcending the world, I find joy in these rocky hills; I have built a pavilion named "Beholding the Breeze. Magnificent scenery is naturally gathered here:
The myriad peaks display their late-afternoon azure, And the long river pours forth its cold currents.
Sight and sound are sufficient to delight the spirit; How could one seek for anything else? I once remarked that on a day of departing summer, Upon entering, it seemed like the clear autumn.
The appearance of the clouds is already somber and cold; the resonance of the pines is once more whistling.
Amidst the bustling dust of the nine thoroughfares, who knows of this lofty and tranquil wandering? *Xianju bian*, fascicle 45.

composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān during the Song Dynasty.
"Verses on Wáng Cháojiān (Zhāojuń)"
Zhaojun halted her carriage and her tears briefly ceased, As she presented her merits for office to the Son of Heaven.
That the Hu dust was stilled rests solely upon her person; The civil and military officials of the Han dynasty ought to die of shame before this aged general.
Ascending and descending in the painted hall, supported by grandchildren; With hair as white as drifting fluff, his courage remains coarse.
Unaware that times are peaceful while his own body has already grown old, He still speaks of "slaying the Shanyu" whenever he meets someone.
Two Poems on a Frontier General.
How could any renowned general surpass him? His commands rouse the heroic army as his sword is first sharpened.
The snow stirs the vast sky and horses stand frozen stiff; tonight he shall raid the camp and cross the Jiao River. (1)
Having won a hundred battles as before, his valor remains intact; Advancing deep into the remote frontiers, he brings his elite troops to glory.
The felt tents are burned to ashes and the Dragon Court is shattered; He ascends Mount Yanran once more to engrave his inscription. (II)
When Zhi Yin drank from the Spring of Greed, he refused to do wrong; From ancient times to the present, its depths have reflected the azure heights.
It is simply that the greedy man’s nature craves bribes, So he takes this spring water as his own reliance.
I have heard that Bo Yi and Shu Qi once struck their horses and rebuked the sovereign’s countenance; The pure wind of ten thousand ages fills the world.
If one could replace the clash of arms with the ritual of bowing, Bo Yi and Shu Qi would never have died in the empty mountains.
While the world was in turmoil and men vied for merit through the sweat of war, Yan Guang remained aloof on his terrace; who among the worthy would be willing to dwell in poverty and emptiness?
Yan Guang was of the same class as Yi Yin and Shu Qi, casting his line in the azure stream to honor the spirit of yielding.
The fields lay fallow as the people of Yu and Rui felt shame upon witnessing the rites of courtesy; from that time forth, weeds grew long in these vacant lands.
Although this is now the transformation brought by King Wen, it remains difficult to dispel the greed of men so that both sides might cease their strife.
Reading the *Zhongshuo* of Wang Tong, [I find that] Mencius, Xun Kuang, and Yang Xiong—though separated by different eras and distinct expressions—their Way is one and the same.
The Master’s literary brilliance was not lost to Heaven; thus, in the Sui dynasty, Wang Tong was born.
Reading the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry, the three hundred chapters selected by the Master; their admonitions and regulations are clear, aiding the Kings of the Age.
Lately, however, poetic compositions have concerned only wind and moon; the "Poetry Official" at the Tree of Censure has long since ceased its function.
Reading the Collected Works of Sun He:
the Tang dynasty was about to perish and the royal bounty had withered; returning to seclusion in Siming, he wept upon the desolate road.
Were one now to compile a record of talent and fame, what other idle monk could have found entry therein?
(Compiled by He; Shi Zongliang was among those involved.
Reading the *Chan Yue Ji*, one finds that the inspiration it evokes is difficult to forget—of waters and mountains, and how within them lie admonitions for saving the age.
Having finished reading, I feel regret that my birth was so late; I cannot obtain a single exchange with such a person.

Beholding the painting of the swordsmen, their flying blades darting hither and thither, one might be momentarily startled; Yet I suspect it is merely the sound of their fame spread through popular custom.
Now, where does this ultimate truth reside? It is none other than whether one’s poetry is balanced or unbalanced.
When the Zen mind is disturbed by the demon of poetry, what can be done when the moon is cold and the wind is clear?
One night I sought to bring down [the rain], but could not; The followers came in ever-increasing numbers.
I thank the monk for the gift of a rush fan;
How marvelous that it was fashioned from rushes! May it assist my pure influence, A thing rarely known in this world.
In the seclusion of the forest, the gentle rustling of leaves brings smiles to visiting guests; a bamboo bed and thatched cottage are perfectly suited to this setting.
Inviting Master Yuanyu, who visited my humble abode last year, we stayed overnight; as dewdrops fell upon the verdant moss, our night conversation lingered on.
The lake waters have never been so clear as they are now; once again this autumn, the moon is full.
In my humble mountain dwelling, moss stains the hearth and stove, and the begging bowl gathers dust, for there is not a grain of food within.
Pitiable are the sparrows and mice, unaware of poverty, Perforating the roof and walls without a moment's rest.
In response to the poem sent by the Venerable Shangren:
Lying ill amidst the forest, I am too weary to receive visitors; Of all those I know, who is most pleasing to my heart?
Only Lord Jian was leisurely and refined; In his solitude, he was instead slighted by the worldly crowd.
Seeing off a monk returning to Gusu:
Beside the Gusu Terrace, the trees hold autumn; Cicadas chirp in the west wind as the rain has just ceased.
Laughing idly and chanting leisurely, he suddenly departs; beneath the bright moon, where does his solitary boat find lodging?
In the remote chamber, as autumn evening deepens, I think of you more; my jeweled lute lies neglected as the day fades into dusk.
Geese pass through the vast sky, yet letters do not arrive; Yellow leaves fall thickly and profusely across the courtyard.
The Venerable Master Xie Ren has kindly sent me tea, Named "Before the Rain" from Mount Shancha; After my midday meal, I leisurely taste it with water from Pufu Spring.
(These were written by me while dwelling in the mountains.
Though I have cast off the demon of sleep, it still beckons; Instead, the demon of poetry draws me back before my eyes.
Two poems on reading the Biography of Xiang Yu.
Having enjoyed victory in battle year after year, he relied upon his own might; yet the destiny of the mandate clearly rests with Heaven above.
It is laughable that Fan Zhongyan lacked discernment, failing to recognize that it was not he who could lead his lord to serve the Great Emperor.
He sighed aloud as he lamented that the fortunes of Lady Yu were already exhausted; this evening at Wu Jiang, a hero was lost.
Had he known the mandate of Heaven at that time, he would have assisted Han and surely achieved the foremost merit.
(Part Two)
The autumn night rain at the thatched hall extinguishes the summer heat and transforms it into autumnal colors; A sudden coolness settles within the thatched hall.
The recluse sits through the entire night without sleep; The moon shines upon the empty steps as dew sprinkles the void.
Two Poems Written after the Biography of Chan Master Jingxi The True Teaching of the Wisdom Sage discusses the single nature; It was transmitted through six generations to Jingxi.
With his lofty brush he revealed the profound meaning, And those who came to study were endless, all their delusions shattered.
First: His pure wind-like verses remain throughout the world; after his passing, the traces at Tiantai are even more desolate.
Steles broken and stupas crumbled, no one takes heed; one cannot bear to close one's eyes and contemplate these empty mountains.
The second is an inscription dedicated to the stupa of Chan Master Zhang’an.
The tombs and stupas of the patriarchs are located on Mount Tiantai; that they have been ruined by rain and ravaged by wind is truly lamentable.
The incense burner is deserted, its traces alone remaining; Deep in the night, the bright moon shines upon the verdant moss.
Sent to Master Neng of Tiantai.
In the profound seclusion of Tiantai, who can share this company? In this bustling floating world, all things are empty.
At last, I vowed to take my flask and visit the Master; by the waterside beneath the pines, I sighed with the pure breeze.

Reading the "Basic Annals of the First Emperor of Qin," I saw that his pursuit of desire and exhaustion of the people had not yet ceased, And that the Arpang Palace and the Wangyi Palace arose one after another.
Later generations lost sight of its origins, Frivolously claiming that the First Emperor of Qin could command ghosts.
Reading Yangzi’s *Fayan*, one sees that the Qin burned the books while the Han mixed them;
how solitary was the Way! How vast and majestic is the imperial wind—how easy is it to fathom?
Though his words on emptiness and existence served as a model for the world, No one knew that he would come to act upon them.
Thirty years have passed since the compassionate light of this stupa’s sacred remains were not interred; I have now come to collect them and bury them on Mount Gu.
In this place, the building of a stupa is not required; its great fame already extends throughout the world.
The bitter heat of the lake is like boiling water scorched by the sun; the trees in the courtyard have withered, and the birds die of thirst.
Someone drives his carriage across ten thousand li; Red dust fills the sky as he enters the market.
An ancient mirror, eroded by earth and its rhombus-pattern obscured, Has a tiny hole; suspended in the autumn hall, its light shines forth.
He painted the beautiful and the ugly of every person; Only then did Xi Shi escape the laughter of Mo Mu.
Inscribed upon the Stupa of Vinaya Master Daoxuan at Zhongnan:
Cold, azure Zhongnan pierces the vast void; The ramie-robed hermitage was his former quiet dwelling.
After Upāli’s passing, no one succeeded him; desolate in the autumn wind, fallen leaves fill the channels.
Mocking the writing of a portrait, my own body is originally but a bubble and an illusion; How could your painted image possibly be real?
My body and your shadow are both devoid of reality; together we dwell as two people in a thatched hall.
In winter, we suffer from the cold as we rake the soil of the quiet courtyard until it cracks; the wind howls at the gate, and no visitors come.
How pitiful that myriad affairs do not concern one's own person; Leaning on the railing, let us gaze upon the snow upon a thousand peaks.
I admonish my junior disciples:
when facing food, you must reflect upon the toil of plowing and harvesting. What use is it for a monk to pursue worldly prowess?
The original intent of shaving one's head was to seek Buddhahood; it was not for a high seat at a banquet.
Even a tiny firefly, though a mere insect, possesses a clear light by nature; its traces cannot be hidden within a dark chamber.
Since Che Yin passed away, people have fallen into neglect of their studies; Throughout the autumn courtyard, they fly and soar at will all night long.
Singing of geese as he returns by boat, the wild geese fill the chilly pond; Sitting idly in his returning vessel, he bears the setting sun.
Each one appears as if able to follow ritual and instruction; Suddenly startled awake, they set out in a boat to return home.
The vast, boundless lake reflects the clear, cold waters; A solitary boat floats serenely within the pure light.
I am ashamed that I am not yet one who is intimate with seagulls; Everywhere the ducks and gulls are startled up.
A captive monkey and exotic fruits provided for his meals, Though noble at the gates of lords, his nature finds no ease therein.
Crying at night, I only remember the banks of the Ba River; A thousand frost-covered trees lean coldly against the heavens.
I release the monkey, I release you, solitary monkey, let him be free; On ten thousand mountains, clouds and trees are steeped in autumn.
Unaware that tonight they cry before the bright moon, Who else will cause their tears to flow in secret?
Gazing at the Moon over the Lake—Two Poems:
The autumn waters are limpid and the trees are windless; The icy wheel of the moon slowly ascends the distant void.
Reflecting idly on the scene for tonight’s verse: In cold hues and clear light, where else can such a sight be found?
(1) The cold radiance shines brightly, reflecting upon the calm lake; The color of the water and the form of the sky are indistinguishable from one another. (2)
Studying the Way, I have not yet attained the state of the *wangxiang*; Yet, in the depths, I beheld a perfect pearl.
(II) A Poem on Chan Master Wangyou’s Mountain Cottage and His Rearing of Macaques.
In the secluded courtyard, tree after tree bears fruit hanging like frost; Listening to the Dharma, I still cherish entering the thatched hall.
How could beings of different species understand the rules of propriety? Yet they come time and again to sit together upon the meditation platform.
Presented to the Venerable Guang.
The interests of the imperial palace gates and the forest springs are fundamentally the same; As one comes and goes according to conditions, how can one’s joy ever be exhausted?
On a quiet night, you visited me to stay overnight at my thatched hall; The lake water is rippleless as the moon shines upon the void.
Composed on the final day of the first month.
On a spring day, the lingering sun shines upon the level plains; Old and young walk hand-in-hand along the ancient bank.
Who would believe that wealth and honor reside in Heaven? By the flowing stream, they vie to set free a boat bound for its end.
—Reading the Collected Poems of Luo Yin.
Not non-being, yet not being, this is the true way of human relations; How many times have moonlit nights and flowery mornings impaired the spirit?
The vulgar world knows not the intent of admonition and encouragement; On the contrary, they resent Luo Yin for his lifelong resentment toward falling flowers.
The blossoms opening and falling are entirely at the mercy of the wind; in a few days, the cycle of flourishing and decay differs.
Yet in the evening beneath the courtyard, they remain worth admiring, where green moss and fragrant grasses are interspersed with lingering petals of red.
— *The Weaver Woman* (Zhi Fu)
In the ninth month, the wind is high and clothes have not yet been distributed; before the lamp, the shuttle whirs through the night as the loom sounds.
When weary, one does not notice the head resting on the arm while falling asleep, as mice gnaw at the threads and scatter them in all directions.
Mellow spring colors accompany the flourishing flowers; Dense greenery appears in irregular layers as the rain has just cleared.
Low-hanging over the cold mist at Yuan Liang’s dwelling, Tranquilly enshrouding the bright moon at the camp of Ya Fu.
Leaves float upon the evening waters like delicate brows of sorrow; Fluff falls onto spring garments like light flakes of snow.
Do not ascend the Sui Embankment to brood over the past; ten thousand withered trees murmur beside the river.
Who has leisure to inquire about the cultivation of peonies? Red and white blooms, fresh and radiant, reflect in the painted hall.
Tears moisten thick makeup like morning dew; A fire consumes cold jade as it reflects the slanting sun.
Gold is spent on more purchases yet the heart knows no satiety; At idle banquets, one’s excitement grows wilder.
Who would realize, before the wind, that all things fall away? A hundred years of glory and prosperity are not long-lasting.
Year after year the wild geese follow the sun, arranging their wings and feathers; Soaring aloft, they pass once more beyond the clouds.
Their mournful cries break on and off as the frosty wind grows fierce; Their clustered shadows appear scattered as the night moon wanes.
The hawks and eagles have already fled the perilous passes of the Yu barrier; The misty waves have just descended upon the vast expanse of Lake Dongting.
The traveler’s longing for home grows keen across ten thousand li; Gazing into the distant void, it is difficult to send a message.
Evening View from the West River.
The scenery lingers before my eyes; leaning on my staff, I gaze idly, my thoughts filled with melancholy.
Beyond the clouds, a clear chime rings from a temple by the mountain; A solitary lamp reflects on the water at a ferry crossing.
The vast expanse of the ebbing tide levels the shore; Scattered wild geese vanish into the distant sky.
Where now lies the imperial enterprise of the Money King? In desolation, the ruined city accumulates wild smoke.

Sent to the Elder of Xuědòu:
For long you have remained hidden on the mountain peak; Your mind is at ease, and your Way is even more true. Deep within the mountains, beneath the forest snow.

The hall is tranquil and empty of people by day; clouds embrace the stone where one sits reading the sutras. Birds enter my body as I enter meditative absorption. How could I dare speak of otherworldly covenants?
I vow to be close to you in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. (The Master sought rebirth in the Pure Land, and my aspirations were largely the same;

hence these words. You, Master Qu, dwell as a retired scholar; we have long had a pact to enjoy the moon and sail upon the lake together. I— (Note: The final line is incomplete in the source text, ending with "I—").
Lying ill, I have failed to meet my previous appointment; for this reason, I compose this chapter to briefly express my thoughts.
A cool breeze blows through the myriad trees, My debility grows even more severe than before. Prostrate upon my pillow, who will inquire after me?
The Mid-Autumn moon is once again full. Its clear radiance floats over distant peaks, Its cold hue blends with the level plains.
I may not stay with those of my own branch; I board this boat to enjoy the vast and free.
Entrusted to the Chan master Zhidao of West Mountain, His cultivation of pure karma has long endured.
