Sent to Master Huiyun.
The splendor of the imperial carriage has been left behind, And I cherish the solitude of mountain forests. My aspirations have grown indifferent to floating fame;
The chamber door is closed within the depths of an ancient temple. Through the poetry-window comes the bright moon; From the meditation-bell descend the secluded birds.
I shall finally meet you amidst the fresh snow, To pass our leisure time in conversation on a tranquil mind.
Entrusted to Great Master Haihui at Yunmen Busheenyin— Who else shall follow this lofty track? The old temple has abandoned its twin gates;
new verses are inscribed upon the ten peaks. (There is a "Ten Peaks Ode" by the Great Master. Zen opens the moonlight path through the cypress groves.
I wait for the lecture as the bell sounds from Xuelou; do not wonder why I seek you so late. Ji Kang’s nature was inherently indolent.
In Dongxiao Palace, all is elegant and free from worldly traces; painted immortals line the empty corridors, while the spiritual caverns penetrate secretly to the sea.
The mountains rise steeply as if rushing toward heaven; Ancient pines host cranes in their lofty nests. In the quiet courtyard, strange springs well up;
If there were a way to attain longevity, Who would sigh over the long passage of years and enduring illness?
In the fifth month I lay in the thatched hall; through the depths of autumn my ailment has not yet been cured.
The leaves have fallen from the lofty trees, and old acquaintances have all grown distant. Spiderwebs entangle the lecture chamber; the books on my desk harbor long-lived woodworms.
The King of Physicians possesses wondrous medicine; having drunk it, the ten thousand conditions are seen as empty.
The Mountain Hall is completed; I invite Master Lin to visit.
A pavilion is constructed upon a lofty ridge, Where ascending and descending one is called a reclusive immortal.
Clear waves chill as they soak the town, Layered emerald peaks coldly support the heavens. Wild boats drift amidst the fading light, And monastic towers are set against the pale mist.
In this place there are no mundane things; one may naturally commune with the pure and worthy.
On the night of the full moon in the ninth month, I invited Lin Jun of Shu to sail upon the lake and enjoy the moon;
yet, being ill, I failed to keep my promise for the Mid-Autumn festival. The autumn moon remains bright and new, while the cold waves submerge the white orb.
The azure void turns its ice-wheel; the wind stilled, the sound of the mortar ceases. Smoke vanishes and the mountain shadows merge as one.
Why should it hinder our enjoyment this evening? All the more so for one such as I, a man of no fixed station, rising from illness.
The autumn ends and the accumulated rains cease; my melancholy illness gradually subsides. My eyes ache at the small characters, and as my body grows thin, I find my clothes loose.
Leaning on my staff, I guard against the moss-slippery ground; opening the stove, I fear the chill of night.
How many days can this floating life last? I shall forever regard it as a water bubble.
On Assignment: Seeing Someone Return from the Imperial Capital to Wu The broth of water-mallow and the minced carp are exquisite;
Zhang Han suddenly yearned for home. The misty waters stretch wide toward the southeast;
The wind-swept sails fly on this evening. In quiet verse, the new moon is just right; Gazing idly, the old mountains appear faint.
I alone envy those upon the Changjiang, Whose enduring fame conceals their bamboo door.
Presented to Luo Yan:
Your talent is lofty, yet you remain in a low station; In this sagely age, worthy men are still overlooked. Jia Yi would surely shed tears for you now.
Yang Xiong was composing the *Xuan* in his own hand; Opening the zither, I encountered the bright moon. I tested the tea, selecting clear spring water;
In my chest, there remain the volumes of my writings, Which at times allow later students to transmit.
In the rain-soaked night while ill, I long for my like-minded companions.
Pine and bamboo compete in their constant drizzling; the season of Heaven is one of deep, accumulated gloom. Facing the window, the autumn candle grows dim;
leaning on my pillow, the night hall is profound. The moon is shrouded by heavy clouds; fireflies sink away in the damp air.
Lacking any solace, I cannot find sleep—how much more so when I long for one who understands me?
Visiting Fengshui Cave Monastery: The wind and water divide the twin caves;
Its secluded wonders resemble Wozhou. The gibbons' cries ring clear through the night;
The mountain hues are cool, suited for autumn. Clouds gather before the stones at the steps; The bell's echoes linger by the bamboo pavilion.
How virtuous is Prefect Bai! Once, as a governor with his five horses, he traveled here.
Now, his white hair and silvered locks are like spring blossoms; though they grow thick and fill his head, it is entirely due to the care of old age.
Irrigating [the fields] depends half on sorrow; who can avoid the ways of the world? Do not seek in vain for the elixir of the immortals;
looking back at those who met an early death, there is no further way to see them.
At night, I harbor these thoughts for the man of transcendent ease, Zhang.
Sitting in silence, I cherish secluded pleasures; who knows that my heart is stirred with deep melancholy?
The window is empty as the waning moon hangs in the sky, and in stillness the minor star shines high. My words in this letter cannot fully express my thoughts; even in sleep, my dreams remain weary.
In the end, I shall venture through wind and snow, following my inspiration to drift upon a light boat.
In praise of the dhūta-monk Shangxing: Contentment alone is his sole aim; how could he be easily matched by those of this age? His single body rests beneath a tree;
myriad anxieties are stilled within dhyāna. Begging for food in the village amidst drifting snow; Descending to sleep as the moon falls into the void.
One should feel compassion for those adrift upon this world, For the affairs of affliction are endless.
Amidst the hidden emerald-green depths of the Brahma-palace Within the stone-walled mountain temple, I wandered frequently in years past; The moon rises over the cold stream in stillness.
Clouds gather at the steep cliffs; the secluded steps are covered with medicinal herbs. Ancient trees harbor monkeys and langurs.
I wait until the end to take up my flask and staff, To dwell in leisure and dispel my melancholy.
—A Night Conversation with a Friend.
Sitting together through the clear night, In a thatched hall west of the wild waters, Broken windows with autumn candles cold, Tall trees where old monkeys cry.
My traces are like solitary clouds; My person is equal to a single dream.
My profound thoughts have not yet ended, When the bright moon sinks into the stream before me.

Cruel was Qin Shi Huang, who extinguished the state; reckless was Han Wudi, who returned to the wilds. The General was enfeoffed for his Five Li, while divine elixirs were sought on the Three Mountains.
He prized beauty by building the Golden House, and exhausted his military might beyond the Jade Pass.
How could one know that the Way of Yao and Shun remains within humanity for a thousand ages?
Wan Zhigu, having passed the Jinshi examination,
though his mastery of the Classics and cultivation of conduct were but in vain, He was repeatedly selected as a candidate in the Imperial Academy’s spring examinations.
The current timing is unfavorable; this is not the fault of war. I shall retire to the mountains and don the clothes of Lao Lai.
In these clear times, poverty and low station are truly a source of shame; Zhu Rong was overfed while Shuofang starved.
A man must eventually receive his share of ancestral emolument; How could he continue to lower his brow for long among springs and rocks?
My bundle of books remains as before as I enter the capital from the west; my noble ambition secretly aligns with the azure clouds.
The autumn wind whistles and my solitary soul is severed; the ancient road stretches far and the departing horse moves slowly.
A steed is praised for its virtue, not its strength; only Bo Le can truly know its divine excellence.
To a Recluse:
With hair unbound beneath the empty forest, He knows nothing of the affairs of the world. The wind is high and the orchid-curtains grow cold;
The heavens are distant and the imperial summons slow. The jar is empty on the day of flowers; The door remains closed through the cold night chess-game.
Having no means to visit these secluded realms, my tracks are blocked by the river's edge.
I present this to the monk who recites the sutras:
serene and pure, free from all other thoughts, He chants the Buddha’s words with a clear, resonant voice, As a fragrant incense drifts through the still night.
The bright moon shines coolly upon the quiet pavilion; From the secluded ravine, spirits and monsters emerge.
In the frost-covered woods, the cries of separated monkeys fall silent— How lamentable is this floating world, where worldly affairs compete in clamor!
I entrust myself to the upper reaches of the Brahma Heaven, my nephew Zheng.
Once lectured, there is nothing more to do; Tranquil and aloof, naturally beyond the crowd. A leisurely heart with the moon over the river, A solitary trace with clouds before the railing.
The path is cold as autumn moss grows thick, The pines are chill as roosting birds part ways.
The sound of the tides draws near at evening; One must surely hear it upon emerging from meditation.
Moved by my long illness, I offer these reflections for the sake of future students:
My frail, sickly body has not yet died, Yet those who were once light and at ease have repeatedly perished. The high heavens cannot be questioned;
This floating world only adds to my sorrow. At thirty, we all lament our brevity; At a hundred, we would equally wish for longevity.
Unable to unify my dreams, how can I serve the King of Emptiness?
In the mountains I hear of those who know me; meeting those with whom my hearts accord, we are in perfect harmony.
Whether we remain in seclusion or emerge into the world, let our paths diverge as they will; Only beneath the moon shall I pluck the cassia flowers of success.
Gathering bracken by myself in the mountains, I hope for a method to serve the sovereign;
Retreating from the world is valued for its lack of artifice—graying hair is a matter for another time, And one may return to the clouds and springs.
Entrusted to a monk on the riverbank.
I look forward to spending my final years at this river temple, Where fragrant incense burns during the lecture sessions.
The moon is cherished when seen after autumn, And the tide is loved when heard deep into the night. Ancient trees merge in a lush canopy of green, And scattered clouds part in stillness.
Though I long for you, I cannot yet depart; The returning geese have already formed their flocks.
Seeing off a man returning to his old retreat:
At this important place, I am too weary to offer my card; My firm resolve shames the bending of the waist.

The longing to return to the old mountains is keen, As the setting sun marks the distant journey ahead. The vast fields are bright with lingering embers, And the empty river resounds with the falling tide.
Arriving at that time beneath the clouds and trees, I listen in silence, weary of my suspended gourd.
Beside the steps, the old plum tree’s roots are fully exposed; The bamboo, veiled by gathering mist, is half-concealed. Deep in the twelfth month, it vainly braves the snow.
Blooming only when spring has grown old, its power to quench thirst must be slight; yet its flavor for soups is also excellent.
Travelers pity its strange form as it ascends the Milky Way to become a floating raft—sent to you, Xiucai.
Last autumn you once visited me; A year has passed since our parting. The setting sun brings no news;
From the west wind, only the sound of cicadas fills my ears. Your head must have grown white with age; Your poems surely have new compositions.
Do not disdain the vermilion cassia tree; Wasted time grows old by the seashore.
The Sūtras and the Wisdom-Monks have recorded his deeds;
he passed serenely into the realm of truth. His transformation in the human world was already complete;
the two courts revered his supreme achievements, and the four seas looked up to his lofty fame. Ancient traces remain at the Flower Society; his surviving writings fill the imperial capital.
Pacing back and forth, I recall past events; In the courtyard trees, crows crouch and cry.
Living in deep seclusion, desolate and forlorn—who knows its true flavor? In deep seclusion, wild joys abound; Firm in poverty, I await the presence of the Way.
Few with whom I find affinity; the vulgar times are turbid. The path is still and the moss grows green; the mountains are cold and the snow has not yet melted.
With a light staff in hand, I gaze idly toward the village bridge in the fading sunlight.
A Record of Affairs.
Past forty, my years have already brought decline; The ebb and flow of this floating life leaves all affairs at rest.
I am filled with gratitude that before my eyes there are no worldly things; Lifting my head all day long, I behold only clouds and mountains.
*Written upon entering Shibakusan.*
Huiyuan’s refined elegance was hidden on Mount Lu; Zhi Gong’s noble aloofness rested at Wozhou.
In quiet contemplation, I think the Stone Wall is fit for a long departure; I intend to tread upon the floating clouds to ascend the stone ladder.
*On the Māṇikya Slope: A Matter of the Moment*
Dwelling before the Agate Slope, Pure and secluded, severed from worldly ties; The lake is clear with the autumn night moon, The mountains are verdant under the evening clear sky.
Only by realizing one's nature does one become a Buddha; To refine elixirs is but to vainly seek immortality.
If one meets Wenbo Xue, A single glance and the Way is fully realized.
I mock myself that my path is left to the wildness of moss; For many years I have slept upon a single bed. In sickness I pass the white days;
in poetry I unleash my refined madness. The window is dark as clouds hide the moon; The forest is bright as leaves fall with frost.
How many days can there be in a hundred years? My two temples are already graying white.
I compose this verse of my thoughts at the thatched hall:
long since have vain and flowery ambitions ceased; I love reclining in leisure within this cottage of rushes, where beyond the door the azure marshes stretch wide.
In leisure, the white days are long; The courtyard is cold, and fruits fall frequently. The hearth is warm, and suddenly the fragrance drifts forth.
In this profound stillness, there are no other concerns; Who knows the bustle of the world’s paths?
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, I await the moon, yet it meets with rain.
The year is now at its end; tonight, from the heights, rain suddenly falls. Pale shadows sink into the empty window;
sparse bamboo stirs with the sound of autumn. Already enclosed by the darkening clouds, I harbor in vain thoughts of the long night’s light.
Pacing back and forth, leaning against the mountain pavilion—who can see the feelings of this moment?
The young man’s servants have repeatedly broken their oaths, bringing shame upon our Son of Heaven of Han. With eyes blazing in anger, he speaks with difficulty:
“You youths of the Five Tombs, lift up your hands and take up your three-foot blades; repaying the state lies in a single death.”
A single horse established a marvelous merit; how magnificent was the legacy of Jiezi!
Yet worldly conditions revolve like a wheel; in this weary life, when can one find certainty? When misfortune reaches its end, prosperity shall surely follow.
When joy reaches its peak, sorrow arises; The Shang dynasty honored Yi Yin, Yet the court of Qin executed Li Si.
If one cannot understand the nature of illusion and transformation, How can one realize non-action and avoid losing the crane?
A solitary crane suddenly flew away, Its clear cry can no longer be heard. Far off it must seek its phoenix companion;
In seclusion, it fears avoiding the flocks of common chickens. The banks are still, so cease your descent upon the water; The courtyard is empty, so stop your dance amidst the clouds.
Only its ancient traces remain, Seal-like characters imprinted on the patterns of the moss.
Seeing off my nephew Zhong at Siming, his former retreat: Secluded and still, this abode harbors immortals; Cold pines mingle with purple mists, and flying springs cascade from deep crags.
Moved by autumn, my heart yearns to return; I take up my staff and board the river boat.
Clear waves ripple with the fading glow; A multitude of peaks pierce the clear sky.
Beneath the deep, silent woods, upon a single stone, I await the stillness of meditation— Written on the wall of a mountain hermitage.
Strolling beneath the pines, he knocks at the door; They invite him to stay all day long, discussing the true mechanism.
Smoke hides the Flower Island as the Blue Ox lies down; When guests disperse, the solitary crane returns to the immortal’s chamber.
The spring in the cinnabar well is clear, its reflection of heaven small; On the jade altar, the wind is cold and the sound of the chime is faint.
Seizing this leisure, I intend to learn the arts of soaring to the clouds; The nine realms are vast and boundless, those who attain them are rare.
Living in the mountains, I have by chance formed worldly friendships, yet their clamor is unheard; Deep within the misty vines, I am utterly removed from the throngs of men.
Unchanged through the cold of winter, I cherish the lofty cypress; Without artifice in its unfolding and rolling, I love the white clouds.
I gather medicinal herbs at leisure to treat my chronic ailments, And quickly weave crimson leaves to write new verses.
Should someone come to ask about my intent in dwelling in the mountains, The thatched hall is silent as the sun sinks toward dusk.
*The Collection of Writings from Secluded Dwelling*, Volumes 47 and 48.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
An Ancient Poem:
Autumn Day on the Lake, with the Southern Mountains Just Cleared of Rain The setting sun shines bright upon the eastern shore; I lean my staff and stand by the winding pond.
Suddenly my ears and eyes feel clear; The cranes on the marsh know the autumn’s intent, Calling out three or four times in the wind.
Red smartweeds play with the autumn colors, Fluttering everywhere across the front marsh. Willow paths have solitary smoke-white haze;
Fish villages and wild waters are level. My兴致 (xìng) spent, I return alone; In solitude, I close the wooden gate.
The new moon is my superior; The cicadas in the courtyard are my song. My life is originally free from affairs;
Facing this, one may find delight.
This is an analogy for the seller of pines.
Do not begrudge that people do not buy it; people also love its verdant green. Yet its roots endure the cold of winter and cannot be planted in dusty soil;
return for now to plant it at the bottom of a mountain stream. Reflected in the water, it creates a sublime scene.
If in years to come it should grow large enough to embrace one’s arms, they will gather it and never cast me aside, for the Son of Heaven shall erect the Hall of Enlightenment.
This is for the rafters and beams;
prepared for autumn’s ailments, the medicine bag lacks gold. Prostrate upon the pillow, hoarfrost gathers on my head; Deep into the night, I cannot sleep.
A crescent moon shoots its light upon the autumn bed;
I happen to compose this as the sun hastens westward to set. Vast and vast, the waves flow eastward; The sun sets, yet the waves do not cease.
How long can this fleeting life last? The azure heights have not yet been ascended, yet white hairs already abound upon the head.

The golden seal has not yet adorned the waist; one's path has become a wasteland of missed opportunities. In a single morning, if one suddenly achieves their ambition, they instantly forget the affairs of poverty and low station.
Eight delicacies fill the square tables, and magnificent chariots with heavenly steeds draw the ornate wheels.
The people’s ailments have no means to heal; the greedy and rapacious indulge their hearts at will.
Without fail they provoke the heavenly net; the punishment of the licentious is surely unfailing. Residual calamities reach their descendants; how could it be that only their bodies depart?
I entrust these words to those seeking fame on earth: when you attain your ambitions, do not act like this. One should know beforehand what is unwholesome.
Walk the Path with care and do not stop; Extend benevolence and forgiveness to all living beings. Serve the Son of Heaven with loyalty and integrity, And noble rank will naturally entwine you.
Your great achievements shall endure for a thousand ages; Let the setting sun and the eastward-flowing stream, And the relentless cycles of cold and heat, take their course.
You must know that for a man of noble character, Though the body dies, the name does not die.
Pine winds, green;
several pines Spread their branches within the empty courtyard. A gentle breeze comes from the south, And pure sounds arise in all four directions.
The worldly, upon hearing this, must surely grieve; I, however, rejoice when I hear it.
Lifting my head, I leave the stone pillow; leaning on my frail frame, I rest against the rattan desk.
Listening intently and gazing afar, I cannot stop for even a moment. Delicate leaves dance amidst the light mist; dense shadows sway over the cold water.
What need is there for the music of the Heavenly Court? Why should I envy the dancers in the rainbow robes? Of all things, I seek nothing more.
The deep mountains are truly beautiful; Solitude is indeed a source of joy. Robes of honor and high office are truly shameful.
Who would say that it is only Master Tao Who finds delight in the mountain retreats?
Ancient Sword.
The Diamond Sutra, tempered a hundred times, Can be broken but never softened; Three feet of living green serpent, one casket of autumnal still water.
It can sever the body of a dragon, And cut off the head of a sycophantic minister.
Below, it removes harm from the common people; Above, it eliminates enmity against the Son of Heaven. In the past, it was buried in Feng City.
Its brilliant light shoots toward the Dipper and Ox; Those such as Lei Huan and Zhang Hua Obtained it, yet their fame has long since faded.
Now that these two worthies have passed away, They have transformed into twin dragons at the bottom of the pool.
People may cherish the sword for its sharpness, But the Daoist does not seek it. How can one speak of the Way of the Sword? Only Zhuang Zhou truly understands it.
Exhorting oneself:

The man of realization prizes the absence of thought; Even the marketplace and the court are like mountain forests. The narrow-minded scholar dwelling in mountain forests finds it difficult to still the heart that craves the marketplace and the court;
While sitting, his mind races through a single room, As myriad objects of perception invade him in confusion.
Nülan Xian wears jade pendants; sitting upon a rock, he longs for gold. A sheep’s nature with a tiger’s skin; a falcon’s wings with a phoenix’s cry.
His will is set on seeking worldly profit, yet his mouth chants verses on non-arising. I am not one of such men;
vast and open, I look toward the restoration of antiquity. Leaving or staying, I simply follow the conditions of the moment.
Noise and quietude follow one’s circumstances; Be content and free from seeking. What is there to discuss regarding mutual invitations?
A human life lasts a hundred years, Yet few reach seventy before death.
I am now forty-five, And my vigor gradually fades. Last year my hair turned gray; This year a tooth has fallen out.
Even if one should live to seventy, how much time could there possibly be? In studying the Way, one should be tireless;
in advancing toward goodness, one should never cease. As for all other miscellaneous affairs, subdue yourself and eliminate them entirely.
Strain yourself to support this illusory body, adding medicine and tonics morning and evening; for this body is but an external object.
How much more so for that which is external to this? Both internal and external are alike a dream. Exert yourselves! You should contemplate this:
The drum is hollow within; its essence is the Way. It awaits a strike to raise its sound; Entering a dream to proclaim a verse, The setting sun casts its likeness.
Speaking by day without indolence, there are signs of the Western Return. Wielding my brush to compose this inscription, I venture to address all sentient beings:
illness arises from within oneself;
Zaozhi died beneath his window, and Bo Niu suffered from a malignant disease—seemingly, the retribution of karma lacks visible proof.
The vast and azure meaning is difficult to fully comprehend; yet upon examining the teachings of India (Zhugan), their purport is clearer than the sun.
They argue that karma spans three lifetimes, and thus affairs do not conclude within a single existence.
Originally, I was fond of the Way and held fast to virtue with long-term concern, yet without cause my six viscera fell ill, and I constantly suffered from my physical form.
The hundred limbs lose their harmony; there is little ease throughout the four seasons. Now that summer has reached its full extent, the autumn heat is like a furnace.
A spleen ailment has arisen because of this; suddenly I feel my sleep and food diminished.
Having mistakenly taken medicine, the resulting diarrhea is manifold and bitter. My guests are filled with anxiety and alarm.
The children trembled with fear, yet my heart was secretly glad. "From this point on, the ephemeral life shall end," he spoke, entrusting his disciples:
"In this matter, you need have no concern. At forty-five years of age, I depart; it is neither premature nor deficient.
In the ultimate truth, there is no coming or going; it is only through deluded thoughts that one distinguishes between misfortune and fortune."
I have previously excavated a mountain cave; you should hide there in secrecy. There is no need to inform relatives and friends, nor should those beyond training (aśaikṣa) weep in this world.
Perform the funeral rites during the four seasons, providing an abundance of offerings.
The three hundred scrolls of literary dispatches may be studied as empty words; but when seeing evil, one should recoil as if from scalding water.
Beholding the good as if it were beyond reach, In profound stillness, there is no source of arising. One should draw from the depths for oneself;
just as these words of instruction ended, I suddenly felt my illness slightly abate. Supported by a table, I rose and sat for a moment;
gradually my four limbs grew light. After another three or five days had passed, Leaning on my staff, I ascended a precarious pavilion.
Bending my head, I gaze upon the multitude of things; Lifting my face, I contemplate the Great Clarity.
The autumn mountains are layered with emerald green; The night moon is full and bright. Who would have thought that on this very day, I still possess this fragile and precarious form?
Leaning on the railing, I cannot bear to return; I simply let my mind find its ease amidst these illusory three realms.
My sojourn is not for long;
I travel alone through the city, yet it is not that I have no kin. I have not seen them for years already deep; on the rivers and lakes, it is not that I have no friends.
For years there has been no word from you; I thus know my own nature is coarse and clumsy. I am out of step with the hearts of men;
with whom shall I share these pure scenes? Carrying my staff, I seek only myself;
I ascend the towering peaks and let loose my melancholy chants. Only the wild deer are intimate with me; only the secluded birds harmonize with me.
I see only clouds arising and vanishing, Knowing not who ascends or sinks.
Tarrying beneath the crimson trees, Autumn dew wets my breast.
—A Statement of Intent.
In the past, I studied the art of prose, Aiming to exhaustively realize the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius;
My mind was weary, yet the Way was not reached, And in my prime, I grew old and decrepit. In the past, I studied the art of poetry, Taking the *Feng* and *Ya* as my models;
I composed many words of satirical allegory, Yet I was instead ridiculed by the people of the age. I wrote both poetry and prose, But to no avail.
Alas! The ancient ways are not restored; my instruction of the world yields no slight benefit. Why do I toil for myself?
Since I no longer frequent the gates of power, how could I betray the green mountains? Having come once to dwell beneath the forest trees, I have stayed within my door for four years.
Retiring to reflect, I became a follower of the Buddha, expounding the sutras to supplement my own practice.
Multitudes of students come from afar, often entering deep valleys; The Wise One is my own lineage, Nāgārjuna is my ancestor.
At the cold window at night, I wield the brush; In the empty hall by day, I wave the fly-whisk.
To support the minds of these two sages, I wish to let all beings behold them; Yet, frail and worn, I long have been ill.
At forty-five years of age, I dwell in a thatched cottage of three or four bays. Lonely and desolate, the Cloud-Linked Cave has seen no guests arrive for a long time;
the low gate is cut off from all coming and going. Upon my couch lies a zither without strings, which I occasionally play once as the wind blows;
by the window are arranged the scriptures of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, whose essential words I chant and recite constantly.
Truth and falsehood are both unattainable; Transcending all, with whom can one share this? Ordinary beings and sages are but eye-diseases;
Birth and death are but dreams in a spring night. When the illness is cured and the dream has ended, The myriad creatures toil in vain— Like gazing at the moon while still within a sickness.
Year after year on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, we would enjoy the moon while drifting upon the broad lake.
Now, overcome by illness, I lie prostrate upon my pillow and have failed this appointment. Turning over and over upon my mat and bedding, my four limbs are as withered as a pine tree;
bitter flavors increase my distress, and my leisurely moods pass away as the night deepens and the moon rises higher.
Brilliantly it illuminates the corridors and eaves; Its cool radiance strikes the windows and porches. A refreshing air invades the weeds of the courtyard;
By the marsh, a solitary crane cries out, Each call as if calling to another. At this moment, I rise and cast off my robe, Suddenly feeling my weary soul restored.
Leaning on my staff, I come to the front porch And bid someone spread a bamboo mat.
Sitting face-to-face with the moon, we enjoy its company as if among old friends; Our glances extend to all things, their radiance how extraordinary!
Distant mountains stand like rows of silver screens; The empty pond reveals a jade pitcher.
Towers and pavilions are adorned with jasper and agate; The steps and courtyards appear as if covered in ice. I send these words to those who seek immortality:
Why must you go to the Mysterious Capital? As the moon sets in the west, I linger and hesitate; Standing still once more, I am filled with lingering regret.
One parting and another year passes; Who knows if we shall meet again next year?
—A Poem by Qianfu.
There was an old man who concealed his name, calling himself Qianfu (The Hidden Man).
He lived in seclusion among clouds and springs, and immersed his mind in the void. With both body and mind hidden away, he was upright and simple;
the wise called him wise, while the foolish called him foolish—yet the distinction between the foolish and the wise belonged only to them.
The Hidden Man has never been exceptional; he joyfully delights in the harmony of Heaven. Following his nature, how could he ever be constrained?
He studied Mencius as a Confucian, yet loved the Way and commented on the *Yinfu Jing*.
Sitting upon a high terrace in an empty hall, he often spoke of the Buddha. Though his teachings have no fixed school, the Great Dharma values having no corners.
Worldly people always cast sidelong glances at me, labeling me a madman. I have long practiced reclusion and acted with eccentricity;
the authorities ought to execute me first. But Heaven has preserved me, and by good fortune my humble person remains.
I climb high mountains through the falling snow, and sail upon calm lakes under the moon. My spirit rivals the leisure of the drifting clouds.
This physical frame is like a withered pine; how can one avoid hunger and cold? If you recognize the jewel within your robes, you shall naturally dispel [suffering] beneath the pine.
This body is formed by the gathering of vital energies; it is a temporary lodging based on false conditions in this world. How pitiable is this nature of self-mastery!
Originally free from the fetters of affliction, I wander beside waters and climb mountains.
Tranquil and profound in my realization, By day I roam beneath the trees; At evening, I lodge beneath the trees. For drink, I use the springs by the crags;
For my kitchen, I gather chrysanthemums before the railing. Every half-month I shave my hair; Every half-year I bathe.
I shall simply indulge my own indolence; When have I ever known honor or disgrace? The fresh autumn rain has just cleared, And the full moon shines upon my cottage.
Rising from my illness to gaze at the moon, I sit for a long while until this verse spontaneously forms:
"Human life within heaven and earth— Each person’s nature and lot are complete in themselves. Why must one rejoice so much upon receiving an official summons?"
When the path is exhausted, why must one weep? Longevity is not what makes one "long," nor is brevity what makes one "short.
These four things are all like dreams; why then do you bind yourself? He laughs at me for being too wild, and I laugh at him for being too conventional.
We laugh at one another, yet there is no record of truth in our judgments.
It is better to remain long in silence, Passing through dawn and dusk with tranquil detachment. The fish in the deep waters and the birds in the forest each obtain what they desire;
Lifting my head, who is my companion? Only the wind, the moon, the pines, and the bamboos— They shed their leaves and grant me company.
Hearing this spring that you had failed the examinations, my heart was filled with sorrow for you. Binding my books, I returned alone to the south;
resentment fills the space within my breast. My traces are now beside the Zhe River, while your family remains by the Southern Sea.
Having fallen ill and become critically frail, your single life has been cast away; there is no gold remaining in your satchel.
A collection of scattered empty texts; turtles and cranes are but minor creatures, yet they enjoy a lifespan of a thousand years.
How is it that you, a gentleman scholar, have returned to the deep springs at thirty? The heavens are high and cannot be questioned;
for your sake, I shall press the heavens on your behalf.

Reading the collected works of Bai Juyi, one sees that Li Bo and Du Fu modeled their poetic lines upon mountains and waters; the poetry of Qian Luan, however, takes as its theme the depiction of gods and ghosts.
While his satirical intent is not clear, he has not yet abandoned the spirit of the *Feng* and *Ya*.
Magnificent indeed was Bai Juyi, Rising preeminent among the worthies of the Tang. Looking down upon the Nineteen Old Poems, He followed in the footsteps of the Three Hundred Odes.
Every line returned to exhortation and admonition; Each piece became a model of counsel and reproof.
His "Poem on Rejoicing at Rain" was forthright and sincere, His "Ainzhong Yin" was impassioned and piercing— Fifty chapters of *yuefu* songs.
How profound and subtle is this indirect admonition! How magnificent is the work of the poet!
How expansive is the heart of the noble gentleman—how could he heed those who slander him as "melting gold"? His resolve is to suppress disorder and restore the refined sounds of the Odes.
The narrow-minded and ignorant merely despise it as the style of Yuan and Bai; a fine jade is mistaken for a mere pebble, and ginseng is called by the name of *qinai* (plantain).
One must know that even a hundred generations hence, there will naturally be those who understand; thus,
the *Changqing ji* fills the courts and fields today,
while peach blossoms bloom on the solitary mountain.
Leading my children in leisure, I carry a hoe To bury seeds among the various trees. Others look at me and laugh;
do they truly examine the depths of my heart? I desire a thousand peach trees, Lush and flourishing throughout the valleys.
Upon the mountain peaks they would be as brilliant as brocade, In the mountain hamlets like clusters of rosy clouds, Shining down upon the waters of the level lake.
Circling above the cottage of the reclusive man, A fragrant scent fills the neighboring villages. Its lush splendor obscures the forest slopes, seizing the springtime of Wuling;
It comes to delight the eyes of wandering travelers. Flowers bloom and then fall again—know that glory must inevitably be followed by disgrace.
If one can remain equanimous amidst honor and dishonor, Then every person’s heart shall find its own sufficiency.
You should know that I plant peach trees, Which may transform the local customs.
At the recluse Lin Bū’s dwelling, the lake and mountains reflect each other in serene clarity; How could the dust of the world ever invade this realm? It is but the color of distant mist and waves.
Vast and azure are the clouds and the shadows of the trees; Moss overgrown, the stone path is perilous. A dog barks deep within the Peach Blossom Spring;
Therein dwells a man of the High Sovereign era, Sleeping soundly, his mind at ease in leisure. When flowers bloom, he drinks alone; when they fall, he chants alone.
In the empty courtyard grow long strands of jade grass; In the secluded trees, immortal birds sing.

It has been three years since I last saw you; base and parsimonious thoughts fill my empty breast. I look forward to the clarity of the autumn moon and shall seek you out at leisure when the occasion arises.
—Early Autumn.

The rain has ceased and the climate has changed; In the empty courtyard, leaves fall one by one. Listening idly to the wind on a single branch, one knows that autumn has come from a thousand miles away.
A hundred insects chirp against the four walls; A new moon rises over the high tower.
Ascending the tower to gaze at the bright moon, its purity first fills the forests and hills. Human life lies between a single inhalation and exhalation.
What cause is there for sorrow or grief? Once the hair has turned white, it will not turn black again. Like a hare fleeing, life cannot be paused even for a moment.
Wandering and reflecting upon the ancients, they urged me to take up the candle and roam;
their hearts were as pure as fine jade.
A heart-friend is like a fine jade; Though passed through fire, it never grows hot. A face-to-face acquaintance is like drifting clouds, Vanishing and changing in an instant.
Sitting together, they become as distant as the stars Shen and Shang; Within a few feet, they are as far apart as Hu and Yue.
I have had those with whom my hearts were joined, Yet I have not seen them for many years and months; Mountains are layered, waters are vast and boundless.
With feelings held within, to whom can one speak?
The ancients and those of today—how different are their service for emolument! The ancients valued the practice of the Way.
The people of today value high office; the ancients valued reaching their kin. The people of today value what pleases the mind;

the ancients were like the white sun, whose radiance overflowed heaven and earth. The people of today are like those treading a perilous path, where a single movement of the foot easily leads to a fall.
If the Way of the ancients could still be practiced, these words would not be cast far aside.
Written on behalf of another, sent to the Venerable Chan:
You reside on Mount Wukang. In years past, I once traveled there; The pine paths were steep and rugged, and the bamboo huts were cold and desolate in autumn.
Once we clasped hands, we laughed with joy; I brushed the mats for us and asked you to stay.
Staying for over ten weeks, morning and evening I delighted in the pure seclusion. Speaking of the matters of Vimalakīrti, I washed my inkstone to encourage my practice.
(I have thus composed the *Record of Vimalakīrti’s Bequeathed Teachings* in ten volumes and the *Six-Section Index to the Sūtra Commentary*.
Barbarian incense burns with ancient seals; mountain tea is shared from Yue bowls. We gaze at the snow together, huddled around the brazier.
Riding the moon, we drift together upon the boat; The metaphor of the mind points toward the vast void. Beholding the world as akin to floating bubbles, I shall return to spring;
I will hide away among the forested hills by the lake. Having shut my gate for five years, my spleen ailment has gradually improved;
On a quiet night, sitting beneath the moon, Past events come crowding back to my heart.
I write this letter to entrust it to you; the road is far and the waters flow on endlessly.
(48) *Idleness in Dwelling*, Volume 49.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
Lamenting While Dwelling by the Lake (Fifty-four Verses) Lost to truth, the beginning is vast and without start;
Drifting karma produced me in Qiandang. My maternal kin hail from Nanjun;
my family tradition traces back to King Yan. A subtle affinity was sown in a prior kalpa; Latent habits manifested in my tender youth.
My parents grieved for my many illnesses; my relatives marveled at my unusual nature. I patterned flowers upon cloth to expound the Way and chiseled characters into stone to practice calligraphy.
The seal of precepts was worn at the age of ten; the mind-monkey’s will was wild in its pursuit of learning.
Empty fame was vainly anticipated, and the official robes were recklessly imagined. Yet in ritual and music, I took the Duke of Zhou and Confucius as my masters.
Embracing the void of the Unlearned, Laozi, and Zhuangzi, I am restless, for I lament that my capacity was realized too late. My mind vies with every passing moment in its diligent toil;
I cultivate the noble rank of Heaven with tireless effort, And am ashamed to stand like one facing a wall in ignorance. Within, I harbor the spirit and ambition of a Confucian;
Without, I borrow the robes of a Buddhist. I constantly loathe the mouth that wastes gold on idle talk, And often weary the bowels that harbor malice toward others.
In hand, one anticipates grasping the cassia branch; with an arrow, one awaits the piercing of the willow leaves.
The foolish deer follows the flames, yet the solid ice suddenly encounters the sun. Knowing the bound pearl resides within the body, one is honored to taste the ambrosial dew personally.
The essential Way transmits the three contemplations; the true mechanism attains wondrous constancy. Otherwise, the fire of mind and traces shall burn on.
Let the roots of one's hair be bound with frost; Harness the twin wheels upon the path of awakening. Soar with both wings through the void of true emptiness.
When hunger comes, one encounters a meal; When thirst departs, one has already found a draught.
In stillness, dwell in the Tathāgata’s chamber; On high, sleep upon the bed of liberation. The Principle is like a mountain, steep and towering; The Way is like the great ocean, vast and wide.

Bravely battling, the demon armies were dispersed; His merit aided the flourishing of the Buddha’s transformation. In the empty mountains, he pities the profound stillness; Along the dusty paths, he laughs at the vast confusion.
Upon encountering objects, he knows they are without attachment; In his leisurely dwelling, he prizes the state of "sitting and forgetting.
He wanders freely, hoping for self-realization; What hindrance could even words and explanations pose? As he composes his work, the sparse windows grow cold.
Waving the pine branches in the ancient hall, it is cool; I have come to receive transformation according to my capacity. The True Edict responds to the occasion, exalting the Way;
though the principles may seem brief, seeking through the texts, they may prove extensive. To perfect the self and bring about awakening, let the attachment to dharmas perish;
let nature freely harmonize the mundane and the sacred; in practice, one should demonstrate what is right and what is wrong.
With a mind hidden in stillness, a dream appeared as a response; I take this omen as proof that blessings may descend. Serving the Buddha, my body is burdened with many constraints;
as a teacher, my Way is truly desolate. My humble gate is joined by bamboo and stone; my thatched cottage borders the forest and the pond.
In winter, I wear fine and coarse silk together; for midday meals, I lack rice and grain. By the water’s edge, the clouds are my companions.
Cypress trees beneath the crags serve as incense; The sights and scenes one beholds never weary the eye.
In this secluded dwelling, inspiration knows no end: On the evening fence, the *fei-cui* birds cry out; In the spring pond, mandarin ducks bathe. The *han-dan* lotuses are like paintings;
The precipitous peaks are as if adorned with makeup. The pine tones drifting through the window are faint; The chrysanthemums turning over the steps are yellow.
Releasing cranes, I often ascend the ridges; Watching fish, I sometimes linger by the beams. How could I worry about physical ailments?
I always rejoice in the world’s peace and security. Nowhere can afflictions be found; I follow the times within the tranquil radiance.
The sun of wisdom hangs over the dark paths; The ship of compassion floats upon the sea of suffering. I vow to sit beneath the Bodhi tree.
He ascends loftily to the field of nirvana, Mystically uniting with reality throughout the Dharma-realm. His responsive manifestations pervade all directions;
The gates of sudden and gradual teachings are all profound. The medicines of both partial and perfect teachings are all excellent;

The thunderous roar of his eloquence awakens the deluded, And the power of his Dharma wheel crushes ignorance. First, he convened the assembly on Vulture Peak; Finally, he sealed the treasury by the Golden River.
His physical form remains as a legacy of later virtue, And his bequeathed Dharma benefits beings boundlessly.

The four immeasurable minds are ever more expansive, And the threefold compassion transforms all with great detail. In the Way, he is equal to all the Sublime Awakened Ones; In his deeds, he resembles the Sovereign Śākyamuni.
Birth and extinction are not his true land; Perfect clarity is his native home. In the single emptiness, there is eternal stillness.
The myriad species are fundamentally filled with dread; How could they possibly understand the essence of non-arising?
That non-arising is even more tragic.
Reading the *Qingsai ji*, I conceive the intent to create the plain and simple; Through silent searching, I transcend common sentiments. Who knows what has been attained?
In later ages, its name is but a vain legend; Clouded trees and hungry monkeys sever the branches.
When the moon’s fragment sinks into the icy pool, If there were no Ziqi to listen, For whom would the green lute still resound?
Sent to Zhao Pu.
Leaving my hometown, the state of Goujian, I unfasten my seal and hoist my sails to return home.

My verse is bitter and my countenance is lean, yet through pure office my path is naturally nourished. The hall is secluded and my mountain clogs remain; the kitchen is cold and dust flies from the steamer.
Do not go beneath Yunmen; sing aloud and gather the *wei* roots.
Night Conversation with a Friend in the Mountains Sitting idly in a thatched cottage on a quiet evening, We leisurely discuss matters of concern. Clarifying the mind guards against attachment;
In deep seclusion, one prizes anonymity. The moonlight upon the steps shifts the shadows of the pines; The wind in the stream blends with the sound of the chime.
Together we pledge that our Way shall endure; Let the myriad affairs of the world bustle on as they may.
Dwelling in leisure, I record these matters, Indifferently forgetting external concerns; Beneath the forest trees, my heart finds its own delight, As the room grows cold with the hue of autumn moss.
The moon shines brightly in the empty pavilion at night; Sleeping amidst the clouds, I am ashamed of my meager realization of the Way. Taking medicinal herbs, I feel my body grow light;
I intend to emulate Zi Yi, changing my name from time to time, And visit the Temple of Yu.
The floods brought no harm; the common people received many blessings. The Way was honored through ritual courtesy, and great merit was achieved without the use of arms.
The superior ruler relied on the tributes of the feudal lords; the legacy of counsel remains in the "Song of the Five Sons.
Mount Xi endures for a thousand ages; its palaces and towers lean against the towering peaks.
Traveling early with my staff, I have no companion; I journey alone through the frost. The broken bridge holds the waning moon;
at the solitary inn, the cock crows at dawn. In the dense thickets, the birds scatter from their perches; Upon the desolate plains, the lingering mist clears away.
Turning my gaze back, I behold the colors of the distant mountains; already I perceive the great sun’s brilliance.
Upon the river, I hear the flute;
as the night grows deep, I listen to the transverse pipe. The vastness of the scene extends even further; the countenance of heaven hangs over the extreme shore.
The moonlight is cold upon the level sands; In stillness, it draws the longing for home ever further away. Idly startled, I see my traveler’s hair turning white;
The mournful sounds have not yet ceased— Where, then, do the plum blossoms fall?
I sing of the swallows.
Coming and going, they know the seasons; pitiable, they differ from other birds.
Flying as a pair in the fine rain of spring, they converse deep within the painted hall. They nest securely upon the carved beams; carrying mud, they settle in the shade of the willow banks.
Having their own place to dwell, let not the gathering hawks encroach upon them.

Reading the Collected Works of Du Mu: The slanderous and sycophantic spit upon one’s face; To slight life is not to be permitted by the staff. To remove the depraved, though the will remains, is in vain;
To loathe the wicked, alas, there is no companion. In later generations, fame shall hang far-reaching; In his own time, his Way was likewise solitary.
In my desolate study, I alone harbor these feelings; The setting sun illuminates the withered weeds of the courtyard.
An Inscription for the Room of Venerable Cong:
Bamboo takes root by the quiet steps, Its elegant grace reflecting the meditation hall; Its lofty nodes surpass all other trees.
Green shadows pass over the low wall; The night sounds clamor upon my dreaming pillow. Autumn dew drips onto the zither stand;
I imagine it adding to my poetic reflections. I gaze idly until the setting sun at the Temple of Emperor Wu.

After the virtue of Earth declined, the way of loyalty and sincerity was no longer prevalent. He vowed his merit upon the covenant of the girdle and clasp, and his hegemonic enterprise rivaled that of Huan and Wen.
His subtle strategies struck terror into treacherous heroes, and his illustrious fame was heard throughout the four seas.
Beside the mountain stands a neglected shrine, desolate and closed off by deep clouds.
Sent to the Daoist Wang of Shuchuan:
How long have you delayed your departure? The waters and rocks of Min and E are secluded and profound. Riding the wind like Liezi, you dream of butterflies as Zhuang Zhou did;
Lying drunk beneath the moon in the empty forest, you sing wildly in the autumn at the ancient shrine.
When shall we return to the Garden of Lang? In leisure, may we roam with the Aged Immortal.
To a Daoist:
I have long heard you wear the crane-feather robe; Though you frequent the city with constant coming and going, The man who has attained the Way is difficult to fathom.
His harmonious light makes his traces easy to follow; In the quiet hall, one pounds medicinal herbs in autumn. The altar is cold as he pays court to the Perfected at night;
How often does he recall the peaks of Penglai and Fuzhou, Where the peach trees flourish in spring?
—Sent to County Magistrate Xu of Dinghai.
I have heard it said that in the district of the Plum Immortal, The waves and tides merge with the profound darkness. In the court of litigation, autumn moss grows thick;
In the pavilion for poetry, sea clouds awaken the soul. Loving the moon, you keep guests overnight; Seeking monks, you close the gates by day.
When your public duties end, your refined interests remain; At times, you dream of the green peaks of your old mountain home.
Entrusting this to the Venerable Ruon by the riverbank, we spoke of our parting; In a flash, more than ten years have passed. Moved by old memories, I vainly await dreams;
idly reclining, I am too weary to send a letter. The cool steps resound with crickets; the cold pond reflects the moon.
Gazing north, the blue waves stretch wide; there is no way to visit where he dwells.
Seeking the feathered guests among the mountains, I do not meet them;
leaning on my staff, I trace their hidden traces. Passing through layered forests and springs, the flowers are warm and the secluded birds sing.
In the empty hall, auspicious beasts slumber; The pines by the mountain stream have a cold, resonant air. The tea hearth is cold and smokeless—where on which peak-top do you dwell?
In high discourse, you gather with the ranked immortals as I see you off on your southern journey.
Difficulties have hindered my ambition to travel south; Inebriated by song, I emerge from the old forest. The road divides before the vast blue sea;
Mountains layer upon layer as the miasmic clouds deepen. Does the stele of Ma Yuan still stand? Can the temple of Chonghua be sought out?
In years to come, when I return here again, I shall idly converse while learning the local dialect.
Holding fast to our shared ideals, we have grown old in solitary chanting; For ten years we have been parted from those of like voice. In this coastal realm, letters are hard to reach;
in the empty hall, dreams arise too easily. We find joy together in hearts that cherish pure customs; Yet the world holds little regard for those who walk the straight path.
Not yet knowing when we shall meet again, The waves stretch for ten thousand li.
Hearing the crickets chirp as autumn deepens, Their plaintive sounds continue one after another, Amidst the stillness of night in the depths of the thatched hall.
An empty bed reflects a solitary candle;
sitting idly by the lake all day at the lakeside pavilion— Vast and lingering, ten thousand anxieties are stilled; what is there before one’s eyes?
In the cold water and autumn mountain pond,
bubbles arise and then vanish; the moisture of the water remains fundamentally unchanged as one leans against the railing to watch all day long.
No one knows this intention;
at my thatched hall, I pass the year with nothing to do.
Leisurely I nourish my rustic simplicity, My heart’s aspiration is for leisure beyond the mundane world.
The conditions toward the bubble have ceased; Entering the room, it accommodates the clear breeze. Ascending the hall, the bright moon is permitted;
In the empty courtyard, what is there? Only the withered pine and snow—reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* upon the desk— I look at it now, washing away my grief over illness. In the quiet courtyard, short shadows shift;
At the window, I encounter the chill of the high autumn. With eye-disease, flowers bear no fruit; With a wild mind, reflections lose their heads.
Vainly hoping to recognize the moon through its reflection, I mistake the finger for the moon, drifting further and further astray.
While Ill, Recalling Master Shao’s “Strolling at Stone Cliff” Stone Cliff, spring has already departed;
Gushan, autumn has not yet arrived. Deep in the night, I sit up in my illness, As the bright moon shines upon the azure moss.
The Venerable Xie Kezi has graciously bestowed upon me the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, along with a prescription for treating the spleen.
These scriptures wonderfully dispel afflictions and delusions; these medicines are spiritual healers for the body. The Way reveals clarity without coming or dwelling;

the formula proves effective through its sovereign and ministerial components. In quiet contemplation, I realize the stillness of the mind; in occasional partaking, I perceive the harmony of the vital breath.
Wandering about, I perceive myself; In my own lot, I feel increasingly intimate.
