Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
I recall traveling south with my dharma friends;
I have heard that your flying staff entered the region of Mǐn. Like the posture of a crane and the tracks of clouds, you are beyond human reach.
In the still night, I chant alone facing the empty moon; Of those who once gathered for conversation, none remain.
The waves block the road and letters are hard to deliver; My spring-fed stone chamber is quiet, yet dreams come often.
I have not yet discerned the day we shall meet again, As the autumn winds wither along the banks of the Zhe River.
I planted flowers and transplanted blossoms to grow before my thatched cottage; amidst the profusion of reds and purples, they are veiled by thin mist.
Do not sigh for their opening in the morning and falling by evening—for the affairs of human life, from honor to disgrace, are all just like this.
Two Poems on Rising from Illness My humble gate lies desolate as rain stains the moss; Rising from illness in late autumn, the atmosphere is tranquil.
Gazing at the water, I cannot help but sigh over my white hair; Leaning against the railing, I once again behold the green mountains.
The wind rises high and the cicadas still chirp upon the wooden steps; The community festival approaches and the swallows have already returned to the thatched hall.
Sitting alone and chanting alone all day long, who comes here to inquire after this withered face?
The lake sky is vast and serene, wild geese fly in scattered lines; For my pleasure stroll, I lean on my staff as I circle my dwelling.
On ancient walls, moss overgrows as crickets chirp; In the water pavilion, the wind is cold and the lotuses have withered.
Gazing at the clouds, I silently recite the verses of the Empty King; Sweeping the mat, I leisurely open the books of the Sage of Kong.
The door closed and empty, there is no one to comfort this desolation; In the deep night, the thatched hall reflects the light of the moon.
An Inscription Dedicated to Tiger Hill:
A solitary peak rises up, named Tiger Hill; Its wondrous traces can never be matched by other mountains.
The moon reflects the coldness of Qin Shi’s Sword Pool; Moss-stained, the lecture stone of Master Sengsheng lies in seclusion.
Though I long to summon the reclusive to dwell upon the highest peak, I lie amidst the clouds, vainly wishing to emulate the former sages.
Gazing at the painting all day, my body cannot reach that place; In the distance, the misty waves of the Maoyuan gardens shroud the autumn.
An old fisherman with white hair leisurely combs his locks while gently rowing a small skiff; Deep within the reeds, he finds his greatest delight.
He cherishes that beyond this body there is only mist and moonlight; Who would believe that in this world there is profit or fame?
Leisurely unfastening my raincoat as the spring showers clear; I sleep drunk by the deep cove while the evening sun shines bright.
Reveling thus until the end of the year, no one knows me; They must surely laugh at the words of the Three-Liu man who spoke of solitude and purity.
Its nature is clear and bright, the same for all eternity; Flowing on, it nourishes all things, truly without end.
The hundred rivers rush toward the blue sea, And the five regions dwell in peace through the merit of Yu.
In motion, it carries the evening wind as it surges past the islands; At rest, it contains the autumn colors, merging with the void.
Floating a boat to bury bones—what purpose does this serve? Fan Li knew the opportune moment; Wu Xiang was loyal.
Years have passed since white lotuses were planted in the empty pool; When they bloom in the heat of summer, they differ from all other flowers.
Clear waves reflect her form, like autumn egrets; In the still night she holds incense, blending with the moon’s radiance.
Her snowy beauty is naturally pitiable, surpassing the emerald-green feathers; Her jade-like buds would ultimately feel ashamed to approach the reeds.
Coming idly to lean against the railing, one never tires of gazing; For she resembles the meditative mind, fundamentally free from flaw.
In the deep autumn, the wild geese cry out as they follow the sun; The hare runs and the crow flies, both equally busy.
The dew grows cold and the lotuses in the small pond lose their green; The wind rises high and the chrysanthemums on the secluded steps turn yellow.
Perfectly luminous, naturally joyful, my heart is like the moon; Who would grieve that my hair is white as frost?
Lying idly, I cannot bear to reflect on past events; The Milky Way shines brightly, and the night is especially long.
Nurturing my illness.
The deep courtyard is deserted and my illness gradually lightens; The western wind fills the empty garden with yellow leaves.
Walking, I unfold the five thousand words of the *Laozi*; Sitting, I read the ten fascicles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Beneath the hedge, fragrant chrysanthemums endure the cold; At the window, faint shadows remain where no fireflies appear at night.
Who would have known that the pearl remains through the night? How lamentable, drifting on and on, still not awakened from the wine!
You did not come;
last year I saw you off upon the empty river, Setting sail just as the western wind began to rise.
Today the west wind blows but you have not returned; Vast and boundless, I see only the empty river waters.
For fanning frost and for lining silk, one relies on the golden blade; In its cool simplicity, it is well-suited for painting ocean waves.
In the height of summer, its efficacy brings cool breezes from afar; In the cool autumn, its utility lies in its lofty structure.
At banquets, it repeatedly dispels the heat of vexation; On long journeys, it constantly relieves the burden of melancholy.
Yet I have not yet attained the mastery held in Yuan Hong’s hands; Where can the exertion of spreading benevolence be applied?
A newly planted small pine, a solitary tree barely a foot in height, Is already well-suited to the thin mist and sparse bamboo.
In leisure, I shall enjoy its appearance as it withstands the frost; Who will witness the time when it grows large enough to encircle one's arms?
How could cool jade be stained by dust? How could a steadfast heart wither along with the grass?
When a pure breeze rises in the courtyard at night, its subtle melody is difficult for vulgar ears to perceive.
Thus I chant in leisure.
In the creation of all things, there is no remainder; how could there be partiality? Why then do the myriad creatures differ so from one another?
The flock of crows is naturally black without being dyed; the pair of egrets have no cause for sorrow, yet their crests are white as silk.
The rock-olives are lush and verdant even in the depths of snowy nights; the well-trees turn yellow and fall in the twilight of late autumn.
The void and the worlds are all like illusions, Do not let the idle mind pursue objects with thought. (The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Due to delusive error there is space;
depending on space, worlds are established. It also says: "If one does not grasp at one's own mind, then what is not illusion?
Since even non-illusion does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established?")
Newly planted bamboo beside the steps—sparse canes I have planted with my own hands; A few stalks of verdant green surpass the blooming of flowers.
Tonight, as I sleep deeper beneath the window, The sound of the cold wind must surely come drifting upon my pillow.
Reading the Writings of Yuan Jie:
Returning to Antiquity and Restoring Simplicity. By Yuan Jie. Pitifully, Yang Jun alone knew you;

at that time, he styled himself the "Old Man of Sound" (the phonetic transcription *shēng-sǒu* is pronounced with the second tone on *sǒu*, corresponding to the character for "sound"; this was the Daoist-style title of Master Cishan).
Establishing deeds and leaving behind words, one’s faith does not indulge in common play;
The night-blooming tree opens by day and closes by night, as if it knew the proper time. In its use and abandonment, its movement and concealment, the warning lies herein.
Green leaves and red blossoms by the ancient wall; The spring scenery puts the *shinan* branches to shame.
Moved by illness, I am touched that Master Tiyuan has come to visit me;
The dog barks at the gate of my humble dwelling as the lingering mist clears away. In the study hall, the wind is cold and the bamboo whistles.
Were it not for an old friend pitying my failing health, who would be willing to visit this desolate place at dawn?
You have sent me the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* and the *Notes on the Yin Fu Jing* from Master Tiyuan;
I have read them both thoroughly. As I prepare to return these sealed volumes, my thoughts linger with lingering intent.
I am ashamed that my talent and insight are neither comprehensive nor quick; Unable to follow the same path, I have instead fallen ill with heterodoxy.
Sick in spirit, I mock myself:
beneath the forest trees, this emaciated frame; For forty days I have leaned upon my pillow, my flesh and skin diminished.
In my leisure time, I have tried to gaze upon the autumnal spring to observe my reflection; its features are gilded like gold and its whiskers are dyed white as snow.
I have playfully composed these four quatrains (with preface).
The dwelling of this "Submerged Man" borders a lake and leans against mountains, where wild cranes and wild deer dwell for me to enjoy as sights for my ears and eyes.
There were domestic chickens and dogs for the purpose of providing security and defense.

Qianfu (the "Hidden Man") would often characterize his crane as being "in the shade," his deer as "eating the *ping* grass," his dog as "barking at the moon," and his chicken as "presiding over the dawn.

Once, when the rain had cleared and the autumn air was crisp, the crane cried out in the great marsh while "in the shade," the deer bellowed in the secluded valley while "eating the *ping* grass," and the dog barked at the moon.

The *fèi* bird cries in the quiet pavilion, and the rooster crows at the lofty trees; their sounds alternate and resonate like those of the "hidden man" (the recluse), each formerly boasting of its own skill.
The records tell us that Jie Gelu distinguished the bellowing of oxen, and the world says Gong Yechang could understand the speech of birds—truly so!
Among the ancients, there were those who possessed the ability to communicate with the language of birds and beasts, yet I lack the capacity of those ancients.
I have conjectured that he must have attained some realization, and thus composed four quatrains to express his intent; this is perhaps sufficient to provoke laughter at myself.
In the past, when Bai Juyi composed eight quatrains—concerning the crane, the rooster, the crow, the vulture, and the goose—he expressed the spirit of poetic exchange through these responses;
therefore, I was able to imitate his frown. Alas, there is also something here to serve as a warning; it is not merely for the sake of literary composition.
I jest that these four verses, which respond to the aforementioned poem—“We laugh at one another;
right and wrong have no factual record”—are close to capturing the truth.
The crane prides itself on its own [elegance].
Roaming freely through the Purple Abode and Green Fields, a single clear cry fills the autumn of ten thousand mountains.
Since this immortal talent possesses a lifespan of a thousand years, how could it be matched by common deer, dogs, or chickens?
The deer yields to the crane.
Your body bears white spots and your markings are complete; upon your head you tower with twin horns and your martial prowess remains intact.
I am both civil and martial, a rare omen for these times; you, however, are merely a white dog whose years pass in vain as you vie for merit with other dogs.
Its snowy down and patterned fur are but a hollow facade; it serves no purpose in warding off villains or repelling bandits.
Who can understand why it barks so incessantly in the dead of night? The courtyard is bright with the autumn moon, and the trees sway in the breeze as the rooster laments its grievances.
Why do these three each insist on their own strength, vying to boast of their own virtues while concealing the excellence of others?
Amidst the dark, silent wind and rain, the thatched hall remains shut; in the end, who will first herald the light of dawn?
*The Record of Secluded Dwelling*, Fascicle 51.
Written by the Śramaṇa Zhìyuán of Gūshān, Song Dynasty.
Formerly deep in seclusion at Fǔlǐ, the old residence of Lù Guīméng by the Sōngjiāng River:
The Way of the Master could not be realized; His pure fame remains after his passing.
The bright moon rises at night; once, I cast my line into the cold waters.
For long the spring fields have been abandoned to the plow, yet the legacy of the reclusive man remains. Through the ages his lofty spirit is seen;
the lake reflects the traces of Fang Gan’s former dwelling.
The fisherman who dangled his line at Panxi Ultimately was able to display his talent. Why does the Master hide away, not meeting a wise sovereign?
The sound of the spring ceases with the autumn rains; The moonlight appears as the night clouds part.
Facing this, I am filled with empty sorrow; When will my soul in verse return?
I have gazed upon the moon for a long time since last autumn; The bright orb has now fallen to the ends of the earth.
At first I lamented our year-long separation, But now I rejoice in this night’s reunion. Crickets chirp in silence upon the ancient steps, While startled magpies circle the cold branches.
Do not weary of leaning long upon the railing; the icy wheel [of the moon] is felt to be gradually shifting.
Recalling the Lóngshān Monastery and briefly addressing the Venerable Chán:
the secluded scenery lies far from the clamor of the mundane world; my enthusiasm for returning remains inexhaustible— the sound of the bell drifts from within the emerald mists.
The reflection of the temple lands in the azure stream; The ground is cold and the courtyard pines are withered. The gate stands empty as a wild path leads through;
Several times we have conversed deep into the night. As thick snow falls from the cold void, I show this to my friend while dwelling in seclusion.
Who knows the flavor of this detachment? In a quiet room, my pillow rests by the water’s edge. The autumn window opens to the evening scene;
on a solitary pillow, I dream of distant horizons. The Way is straight, yet the currents of the age mock it; The mind is pure, known only to the night moon.
When shall we be able to follow Zhi Dun, Making a pact together to purchase a mountain retreat?
Retiring to Live in Solitude at Gushan:
A Verse in the Same Rhyme as Master Biàn Cái’s The place is remote and few people arrive; With illness come, there is no end to my talklessness.

I have not yet been able to roam the distant mountains; All day long I lie here, gazing from within. The medicinal casket has grown damp with plum-season moisture; The pine-window grows cold after the passing rain.
Only my teacher knows my destination; worldly affairs have no concern for me.
In the mountains, I am moved by the visit of a friend;
after our discourse, I remain mostly afflicted by lingering illness. With the heavy doors closed beneath the forest trees, few people come to see me as I pass my days.
The setting sun sees but a solitary bird return; The mountain light approaches with momentum. Upon what does the shadow of the clouds rely as it departs?
How can one bear to speak of the ways of the world? Only you, O Lord, contemplate the cessation of worldly machinations.
While traveling by boat, I visited Qianyuan Temple.
Ancient trees hang down their pure shade; I moor my boat and ascend for a while. In leisurely verse, worldly thoughts cease;
Sitting long, the celestial music falls silent. The shadows of banners flutter in the clear sky; The light of the stream clarifies the evening hues.
Hanging my sails, I seek the path ahead; Mist and water stretch on, infinitely remote.
The wind’s transformations are unfathomable, yet clearly it has something upon which it relies:
It cools and stirs the autumn leaves, escorting travelers as evening sails return; It sweeps away mist from distant peaks and wafts fragrance out from the quiet gates.
Sitting alone in the western chamber, I chant; A cool breeze fills my monastic robes.
The rain nourishes all things with profound efficacy, Drizzling down through half the sky; Its cold sound clearly penetrates the bamboo.
Slanting currents rush with the wind; Mossy fragments deepen the autumn green. The flower branches lose their late-day red;
The mountain man alone leans upon his pillow, Silently listening for the sound of grass within the thatched hall.
Pale azure and deep green, Lushly growing by the ancient bank. Traveler’s sorrows arise with the evening hues;
The impulse to chant awakens in the clear light. Passing rain invades the secluded path; One climbs upon the ruined wall through the mist.
Even more unbearable is the thought of past events: The old ruins of Jin-gu in years gone by.
Having resided at Ci-chuan Temple for several years, you now wear your robes while dwelling among the forested clouds. Your longing to return to the capital has utterly ceased;
your dreams travel deep into the thousand peaks. You read the remaining sutras as the snow falls, and listen to the autumn chanting for its fine verses.
Once I sought out lofty traces, In a meditation hall beneath the shade of ancient trees.
On an autumn evening by the vast river, as the season’s colors deepened at dusk, Melancholy thoughts arose within me in my secluded dwelling; The wind-blown leaves, cold, invaded my dreams.
The window lamp casts a cold light upon the books; Deep in the courtyard, the chirping of insects is hushed. The sky is pale and the geese fly thin;
At last, bidding farewell to the crowds of men, I await the building of a hut upon the solitary peak.
—Inscribed at a Monastery on Lake.
Deeply secluded and far from city walls, The scenery of the level lake is tranquil. Painstakingly chanting through the night moon, Pure dreams penetrate the Cold Mountain.
The path is cold where autumn moss has closed over; In the secluded courtyard, mountain birds return.
Among those who hasten and compete in the red dust, Who can knock upon the pine gate?
Seeing Master Yue Return to Xiyuan:

A Parting Poem Written Lightly on the Nature of the Way In this desolate city, the evening sun casts its shadows; The waves carry him on his distant homeward path, while the clouds and trees shroud his old mountain deep.
At night he shall settle into meditation upon the frosty isle; At midday he will take his meal in the company of wild birds.
The serene scenery of the meditation hall remains; A flying waterfall reflects the sparse forest.
Listening to the zither, one spontaneously grasps the essence of the "Southern Wind"; This evening, in the empty hall, it is not easy to transmit this true sound.
Ordinary ears find it difficult to hear at last; On the precipitous cliff, the chirping of insects has ceased. Upon the lofty branches, the crane’s dream of sleep is broken.
Sitting here, ten thousand anxieties are dissolved. The slanting moon rises over the perilous railing.
—Sent to the Venerable Xianrun.
The common world knows not his dwelling; Deeply settled, his realm grows ever more secluded. His quiet chamber is shut within emerald peaks;
Distant news is cut off from the azure isles. When meditation ends, flowers wither upon the steps; When a poem is finished, snow fills the tower.
Longing for one another, we cannot depart; North and south, the roads stretch on and on.
Entrusted to Master Shangren at Ge Stream:
Having pared away all thoughts of vanity, you dwell in leisure; the Way is already perfected. In dreams, the water and rocks of the secluded pass remain;
the gate is coldly closed by cypress and tamarisk. The hundred-seamed robe grows worn within meditation; gray beard grows after the onset of illness.
Someone asks about the True Principle; With a smile, he points to the sound of the Ge Brook.
Below the Meditation Hall, one gazes down upon the peaks; Clouds and springs cut off all neighbors. This brief visit is not for a worldly guest.
Deep and secluded, it belongs only to those who dwell in leisure; The stone steps are slippery with autumn moss, And the moonlight in the vine-covered grotto is ever fresh.
I vow at last to join fellow seekers of the profound, To come here and bid farewell to the red dust of the world.
—By the Mountain Man of Wuqian.
Beyond the birds he has long since departed; How many years have passed in the world of men? His wild chanting treats time and seasons as light;
his lofty spirit is intimate with the immortals. He sleeps drunk upon a couch steaming with clouds; when the fisherman returns, the boat is filled with snow.
Though we yearn for one another yet do not know each other, throughout the night I dream of forests and springs.

I miss my friend, remembering our parting on the desolate plain; The lingering sun shines as the snow first clears. Several nights have turned into dreams of departure, and through the intercalary month, no letter has come.
My indolence toward the ways of the world cannot be diminished, And my addiction to sleeping amidst the clouds remains uncured.
To whom shall I speak my secluded thoughts? Last night, facing the moon, I heard cicadas;
the river and sky are cool as the rain clears. *Hui hui*, they emerge from the sparse forest within the purity of the setting sun.
Sorrow arises in the heart of a traveler far from home; At the parting pavilion, the autumn grasses are verdant green. In the desolate moat, the evening smoke is deep;
Unable to bear listening for much longer, I inscribe these lines upon the wall of my friend’s study— The beard of one who chants poetry is overtaken by snow-white age.
I ask not of worldly affairs, Dwelling beyond the birds for years on end. Amidst white clouds I chant, and upon green cliffs I write while drunk;
Sweeping the stones, the autumn moss is variegated; Opening the window, the night moon is vast.
At such a time, all thoughts have ceased; My livelihood consists only of wood-gathering and fishing.
Lamenting for the Late Monk Bianduan:
In his lifelong devotion to poetry, he refined his craft with diligent search and ceaseless scrutiny. Now that the ruined room lies empty beyond the birds, his pure verses fill the world.
His slender silhouette hangs upon the neighbor’s wall; his solitary tomb adjoins the ancient mountains.
Returning from my visit, I paused beneath a lofty tree; the cold water murmured on its own.
I traveled to Shibi Temple, a secluded place renowned as a supreme realm; taking up my staff, I ascended it alone, where the verdant peaks and thousands of crags were steep and perilous.
A single path shaded by cold pines, The fragrant incense makes the autumn palace chill. Sparse chimes echo through the ancient corridors;
Standing still in silence, I forget the desire to return. As the setting sun fades, a bird suddenly sings;
I inscribe these lines upon the walls of the Hermit of Shulin.
The lofty traces lie far from the city; the scenery of lake and mountain is wondrous. The sound of water clamors at the sleeping couch;
the misty air presses upon the curtains of my study. Birdsong reaches the bamboo by the eaves; fish are startled in the moon-drenched pond.
Though the day may come for the imperial carriage to arrive, I shall forever fail to fulfill my promise to the white clouds.
Dwelling in seclusion, the traces of dust cannot reach; Moss colors invade the low-set gate. The ancient cypress sighs with a cold autumn melody;
On the secluded path, the moonlight is deep. In the still window, a monkey peers at the inkstone; In the quiet pavilion, a crane listens to the lute.
To the east lives a true recluse; I took up my staff and sought him out at night.
I sent this to the Recluse of West Lake:
The gate is closed amidst layered emerald peaks; He sleeps idly, his arm bent beneath his head. Broken fences pierce the evening waves.
In an old house, autumn lamps leak light; the moon rises and beckons my neighbor for a moment. A poem is finished, sent to a monk on Mount Yue.
Among the courtiers with their many hairpins, who recognizes one so intoxicated and carefree?
Presented to Master Bang.
Deeply dwelling, I abound in rustic delights; The gate is cold, entered by cypress and pine. Beyond the birds, I wander idly and frequently; Human affairs are rarely encountered.
At the water-side pavilion, I chant beneath a sliver of moon; Upon the autumn bed, I dream of a thousand peaks.
Remembering the sight of fresh snow, I invite you to join me for a quiet conversation once more.
Seeing Xi Zhong off on his journey to Xia: at evening the cicadas cry urgently. Facing the flowing waters, I sing a verse of parting: A single sail cuts through the late sunlight;
returning birds enter the distant forest. The moonlight makes the cold stream still; the bell sound lingers deep within the mountain temple.
Meeting an old acquaintance on Pingzhou, we must surely speak of the mindless state.
The herons and egrets amidst the misty rain and dense reeds—how easily can their flight be sought? The tracks they leave upon the sand are naturally shallow.
Beside the water, his intent grows deeper; Shaking his head, the thread of his life is hard to sever. His feathers drift like snow that has not yet settled;
In the end, he should be a mate for the mandarin duck— How could he ever deign to mingle with common birds?
Far-off mountains...
A few points of azure mist, Fading away over thousands of leagues. Leaves first fall upon secluded railings; The high heavens have just cleared from rain.
Lofty peaks take on faint outlines; Their depths remain unnamed. Who would go forth forever to invite the recluses?
Sleeping amidst the clouds, my feelings stir of their own accord. Wen Jun’s eyebrows are easily likened to these.
Māṭhara’s painting is difficult to complete; where has the bird ever truly gone? The flow of the spring—how could its sound be perceived?
Through autumn it grows increasingly cool and clear, becoming even more distinct as evening falls. You, O Benevolent One, have always delighted in quiet contemplation, your mind never frivolous.

From the nineteenth day of the second month in the first year of the Qiánxìng era,
the Great Dharma Master— whose name was Zhìyuán, his courtesy name Wúwài, and his sobriquet Zhōngyōngzǐ— passed away at the Mǎnào Monastery on Gūshān Island in the West Lake of Qiántáng.
The *Xiánjū biān* (Collection of Leisurely Dwelling), which he had previously composed, has remained extant until the Jiāyòu era without falling into ruin.
The "Dì" (Earth) volume is but a single thread [of the whole].
In the *Biography of the Dharma Master* composed by Wu Daizhi (Zunlu), it states:

"Although the sixty fascicles of the *Xiánjū biān* (Collected Works from Seclusion) have been cataloged, one can ultimately not see his complete collection. Now, in opening this edition, I have consulted various scholars and searched for it everywhere.
I have obtained forty-eight fascicles of the *Bingke ji* (Collection of Medical Prescriptions), which were previously not included in the compilation;

fearing they might be lost or omitted, I have now added them, bringing the total to fifty-one fascicles. Should there be those whose search remains incomplete, I await future scholars to continue the work.
(Hao Gung) Being solitary, limited, and of little learning, I am unable to examine and correct errors; rather, my priority is that the writings of the broad and erudite ancients be preserved.
It is merely that, by adhering to the fundamental source, one may avoid falling into error;

furthermore, having heard of the Dharma Master’s pure reputation, the faithful layman Yao Jundao, whose innate disposition is refined and noble, joyfully wished to provide the funds and lead his compatriots to carve woodblocks for printing, so as to propagate this literature. At that time—

Recorded by Dharma Master Liaokong (Haoqiong), courtesy name Zhongfu, at the Shifang Lecture Hall of Fantian Temple in Qiandang on the full moon of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Jiayou era of the Sagely Song dynasty, the cyclical year being Gengzi. Yuanjing:
It is my duty to occupy this ancestral seat and restore what has fallen into ruin. When I first arrived at this mountain, it was desolate and overgrown.
He was particularly distinguished for being the first to establish a pagoda pavilion and to restore the ancestral images.

Furthermore, reflecting that the master’s writings had fallen into obscurity, he solicited donations to reprint them. Through the contributions of patrons, he accumulated two thousand and one hundred vouchers; over two years of offerings, he amassed one thousand nine hundred vouchers, finally completing the project.
It commenced in the Wushen year of Chunyou (1248) and was finished in the Guiyou year of Baoyu (1253).
Alas! My strength is meager, making this difficult to accomplish; it has proceeded so slowly.

The circulation of this compilation is intended to manifest the Way of our ancestors and spread their lingering fragrance, to provide a slight moisture for the roots and continue the remaining embers.

Beyond the costs of paper, ink, and labor, whatever is obtained shall be used to assist with the oil for lamps at temples, pagodas, pavilions, and monastic halls. Those who redeem [the texts] may also rely upon this.
This can awaken one’s own spiritual radiance; truly, it is a case of gaining two benefits with a single effort.

Those who dwell on this mountain in the future should embody this intent and not neglect it. Written by Master Jie’an (Yuanjing) of Maṇi while residing in the mountains, this is a preface to the *Xianju bian* (Collection of Writings on Leisurely Dwelling), a miscellaneous work concerning Gushan.
The woodblocks were lost over time. Reprinted by Layman Zhang Leshan of Yiqi.
Delighting in charity, he esteemed the legacy of Hanshan and the writings of Hanshan;

moved by this sentiment, he composed a verse and donated two thousand strings of cash to commission artisans to re-carve [the blocks] at Ma'nao Rock on West Lake. This collection is merely the residual fruit of Hanshan’s teachings;
as for his support of the religious tradition and his exegesis of the various scriptures, there are ten commentaries that circulate separately in the world.
Written by Manzhuo Zhushan (Yuanjing) in the autumn of the Wushen year of the Chunyou era.
